“Be exact, my friend. What do you mean by ‘disappear’? To which
class of disappearance are you referring?”

“Are disappearances classified and labelled, then?” I laughed.

Japp smiled also. Poirot frowned at us both.

“I should say that for a man of Mr. Davenheim’s position, it is well-nigh impossible,” I replied. “He is a well-known figure, his features are familiar to the public, and he could not travel far without being recognized.” Japp chuckled, leaning back in his chair as he accepted a cup of tea from Poirot. “That’s what we all thought, Captain Hastings. But the facts are these: on Saturday afternoon, Mr. Davenheim left his country house, The Cedars, at Chertsey, to walk down to the village to post some letters. He promised his wife he would be back in time for tea. He was seen by several people on the road, yet he never reached the post office, and he certainly never returned home. It’s as if the earth had swallowed him up right in the middle of a sunny afternoon.”

“Well, in this particular instance,” said Japp, leaning forward as he accepted a cup of tea from Poirot, “it’s a bit of a teaser. Mr. Davenheim left his house, The Cedars, at Twickenham, on Saturday afternoon to walk down to the village to post some letters. He never reached the post office, and he never returned home. His clothes, his money, his watch—everything he had on him—have vanished into thin air. There’s no trace of a struggle, no apparent motive for a voluntary disappearance—the man was a millionaire, after all—and as for loss of memory, well, it’s been three days now and not a whisper of him from one end of the country to the other. Miller is fair dithered, I can tell you.”

“I should say the first is the easiest, and the third the most difficult,” I replied, settling back in my chair. Japp shook his head and helped himself to a piece of hot buttered toast before continuing. “In the case of Mr. Davenheim, we are not yet sure which category we are dealing with. On Saturday afternoon, he left his house, ‘The Cedars,’ at Chertsey, ostensibly to post some letters in the village. He never arrived at the post office, he never returned home, and from that moment to this, not a trace of him has been found. It is as though he stepped into another dimension entirely, leaving a vacuum where a wealthy and influential banker used to be.”

“Not impossible, perhaps,” I admitted, “but in these days of a prying press and the ubiquitous camera, it is surely a feat of some difficulty for a man of Mr. Davenheim’s prominence to vanish into thin air. He is not a nonentity, after all.” Japp leaned forward, his face growing serious. “That’s the devil of it, Captain Hastings. The man is as well known as the Bank of England. Five foot ten, thick-set, with a distinctive bushy beard and a mane of dark hair—hardly a figure to pass unnoticed in a crowd. Yet, from the moment he stepped out of his front door at The Cedars, Chertsey, last Saturday at 5:30 P.M., he might have been swallowed by the earth for all the trace he’s left.”

“I should say the first is the most difficult,” I ventured. Poirot shook his head. “On the contrary, my friend, to the man of intelligence, it is the easiest. But let us hear what the good Japp has to say. Which ‘pigeon-hole’ does he assign to our disappearing banker?” Japp chuckled, reaching for a piece of bread and butter. “Well, that’s just it. Miller is leaning towards the third—foul play. You see, the circumstances are peculiar. Davenheim left his house, ‘The Cedars,’ at Twickenham, on Saturday afternoon at approximately four o'clock. He intended to walk to the village to post some letters, promising his wife to be back by five. He was seen passing through the gate by his gardener, and again a few hundred yards down the road by a Mr. Lowen—a gentleman with whom Davenheim had some rather strained business relations. Since that moment, not a soul has set eyes on him. He never arrived at the post office, and he never came home.”

“Very nearly so, I should think. You might lose your own memory,
but some one would be sure to recognize you—especially in the case
of a well-known man like Davenheim. Then ‘bodies’ can’t be made to
vanish into thin air. Sooner or later they turn up, concealed in
lonely places, or in trunks. Murder will out. In the same way, the
absconding clerk, or the domestic defaulter, is bound to be run
down in these days of wireless telegraphy. He can be headed off
from foreign countries; ports and railway stations are watched;
and, as for concealment in this country, his features and appearance
will be known to every one who reads a daily newspaper. He’s up
against civilization.”

Poirot settled himself back in his chair and meticulously squared a plate of biscuits. “The intelligence, my friend, is all. One does not need to run to and fro, to measure footprints with a little rule, or to examine the cigarette ash with a magnifying glass. One needs only to sit in one's armchair and think. I would even go so far as to say that without moving from this room, I could solve the mystery of your Mr. Davenheim, provided that you place the facts before me with absolute accuracy. I would bet you five pounds that I could do so within a week, simply by using the little grey cells.”

Poirot stirred his chocolate with a tiny spoon, his eyes twinkling with a sudden green light. “That is a very interesting question, Japp. You think that because a man has vanished, the police must run about like chickens with their heads cut off, looking for footprints and cigarette ends. I tell you, to find a man, one does not need to move. One needs only to sit back in one’s chair and use the little grey cells of the brain. If you will give me the facts of the case, I will bet you five pounds that I can tell you the exact whereabouts of Mr. Davenheim within a week, without so much as leaving this room.”

“I am not the egotist,” said Poirot, his eyes twinkling with a sudden green light. “But I have a certain confidence in the little grey cells. It is a matter of the psychology, is it not? You have the facts—I have the brain. I will make you a wager, Japp. Without leaving this chair, without so much as putting on my boots, I will tell you within a week exactly what has happened to Mr. Davenheim, provided you give me all the facts known to the police.”

Poirot settled himself comfortably in his chair. “I would not go so far as to say that,” he murmured, “for modesty, it is my middle name. But I will say this: to solve a case, one does not need to run to and fro, to measure footprints with a magnifying glass, or to examine the dust of the road. No, it is sufficient to sit back in one’s armchair and use the little grey cells. If I were to bet you, my friend, I would wager that without leaving this room, I could tell you within a week exactly what has happened to your missing banker.”

“That,” said Poirot, “is a question of a very different order. To deceive the heavy boots of the police is child's play; to deceive the little grey cells of Hercule Poirot—ah, that is a different matter entirely! But tell me the facts, Japp. I have read the newspapers, but they are full of many things that do not matter, and they omit the things that do. Let us have the official version.”

Poirot endeavoured, with a marked lack of success, to look modest.
“Me, also! Why not? It is true that I approach such problems with
an exact science, a mathematical precision, which seems, alas, only
too rare in the new generation of detectives!”

Japp grinned more widely.

“I don’t know,” he said. “Miller, the man who’s on this case, is
a smart chap. You may be very sure he won’t overlook a footprint,
or a cigar-ash, or a crumb even. He’s got eyes that see everything.”

“So, _mon ami_,” said Poirot, “has the London sparrow. But all the
same, I should not ask the little brown bird to solve the problem
of Mr. Davenheim.”

“Come now, monsieur, you’re not going to run down the value of
details as clues?”

Japp gave a short, incredulous laugh. “Well, if you are so sure of yourself, let us have a little flutter. I’ll lay you five pounds that you can’t tell us what has happened to Mr. Davenheim within a week, without so much as putting your hat on! I will give you the facts as we know them, and you can exercise your little grey cells to your heart’s content.” Poirot’s eyes twinkled as he accepted the challenge with a slight, formal bow. “I accept, my friend. It will be a recreation for the mind. Proceed with the facts, I pray you. Tell us of this disappearance from the house you call ‘The Cedars.’”

Japp gave a hearty roar of laughter. “A wager, then! I’ll bet you five pounds, Monsieur Poirot, that you can’t solve the mystery of Mr. Davenheim’s disappearance within a week, without so much as leaving this room. It’s a fair offer, for I’ll give you every fact we’ve got hold of, and I’ll keep you posted as to any new ones that turn up.” Poirot’s eyes twinkled with a green light as he leaned back in his chair. “I accept,” he said softly. “It will be an exercise for the little grey cells. Proceed, I pray you, with the facts.”

“Japp laughed heartily. ‘A wager, then? I’ll tell you what, Monsieur Poirot; I’ll bet you five pounds that you cannot solve this mystery without leaving this room. It is a fair offer, for Miller has been over the ground with a fine-tooth comb, and even he is at his wits’ end. If you can sit there and tell us what has become of Mr. Davenheim, the money is yours.’ Poirot’s eyes twinkled with a sudden green light. ‘I accept, my friend. It will be a pleasure to demonstrate the superiority of the little grey cells over the mere collection of cigarette ends. Proceed with the facts. Let us have the history of the disappearance of Mr. Davenheim.’”

Japp roared with laughter. “A wager!” he cried. “I’ll bet you five pounds, Monsieur Poirot, that you can’t solve the mystery of Mr. Davenheim’s disappearance without leaving this room. It’s a case that’s got the whole department scratching their heads, and even Miller is beginning to look a bit blue. What do you say?” Poirot’s eyes twinkled with a green light. “I accept,” he replied. “Five pounds is a sum not to be despised. It will buy many bottles of the excellent syrup for my cough. Proceed then, Japp. Give me the facts. Describe to me the house, the inhabitants, and the exact manner of the disappearance.”

Japp's laugh rang out across the room. “A wager, then!” he cried. “I’ll bet you five pounds that you can’t solve this Davenheim mystery within a week—and without so much as stepping outside your front door!” Poirot’s eyes twinkled with a sudden green light. “I accept,” he replied with alacrity. “It is a challenge that appeals to me. But I must have the facts, Japp—all the facts—and you must answer any questions I may care to put to you. Tell me, then, what happened on that Saturday at ‘The Cedars.’ I understand that is the name of Mr. Davenheim’s country residence at Twickenham?”

Japp slapped his knee. “Hanged if I don’t take you at your word.
Bet you a fiver that you can’t lay your hand—or rather tell me
where to lay my hand—on Mr. Davenheim, dead or alive, before a week
is out.”

Poirot considered. “_Eh bien, mon ami_, I accept. _Le sport_, it
is the passion of you English. Now—the facts.”

“About a quarter to six,” Japp continued, “this Mr. Lowen arrived at the house. He was shown into the study according to instructions. At seven o’clock, Mr. Davenheim had not yet returned, and Lowen left, seemingly much annoyed. It wasn’t until the following morning that the household became seriously alarmed. A search was instituted, but without result. By Monday, the news of the disappearance was public property. But here’s the interesting part. On Sunday morning, it was discovered that the safe in the study had been opened—not forced, mind you, but opened with a key—and a vast amount of jewelry and securities had been removed. This wasn't known when Lowen was there—at least, so the servants say.”

“At six o’clock, Mr. Lowen duly arrived. He was shown into the study, as directed. At a quarter to seven, Mrs. Davenheim began to feel uneasy. Her husband was usually very punctual for his meals, and seven o’clock was the dinner hour. She went to the study, but found only Mr. Lowen. He stated that he had been waiting there for three-quarters of an hour, and had seen and heard nothing of Mr. Davenheim. They waited together until seven o’clock, and then, getting really alarmed, Mrs. Davenheim telephoned to the village. But Mr. Davenheim had not been seen there, nor had he posted any letters in the local pillar-box. From that moment, the search began in earnest, but not a trace of the man has been found from that hour to this.”

“At six o’clock,” continued Japp, “a gentleman arrived at the front door and asked for Mr. Davenheim. This was the Mr. Lowen whom the banker had mentioned. He was shown into the study, as directed. Mrs. Davenheim, who was still in her boudoir, heard him arrive. At seven o’clock, since her husband had not yet returned, she went to the study. To her surprise, it was empty. Mr. Lowen was gone, and there was no sign of Mr. Davenheim. She rang for the servants, and it was then discovered that the safe, which was hidden behind a picture, had been broken open and its contents—a large sum in bearer bonds and a quantity of very valuable jewelry—had been stolen.”

“About six o’clock,” Japp continued, “a gentleman called at the house, and asked for Mr. Davenheim. This was Mr. Lowen. He was shown into the study, according to the instructions given. At a quarter past seven, Mr. Davenheim had not returned, and Mr. Lowen, after speaking to Mrs. Davenheim, left. About eight o’clock, the household became seriously alarmed. A search was instituted, and the police were notified. On Sunday morning, a discovery of some importance was made. The big safe in Mr. Davenheim’s study had been broken into, and a large sum in notes, as well as a quantity of bearer bonds and some very valuable jewelry, had been abstracted.”

“About a quarter of an hour later,” Japp continued, “a gentleman duly arrived at the front door and asked for Mr. Davenheim. This was Mr. Lowen. He was shown into the study, as he had been expected. At five o’clock, Mrs. Davenheim began to wonder what had become of her husband. She went to the study, but found only Mr. Lowen there. He informed her that he had been waiting for some twenty minutes, and was beginning to wonder if Mr. Davenheim had forgotten the appointment. They waited together for another hour, but as the master of the house did not appear, Mr. Lowen eventually took his leave. It was not until later that evening, when the dinner hour passed without any sign of Mr. Davenheim, that the household became seriously alarmed. On Sunday, the police were notified, and on Monday morning, a most significant discovery was made. The large safe in the study had been forced open and its contents—consisting of a vast quantity of bearer bonds, a large sum in notes, and several pieces of valuable jewelry—had been stolen.”

“About a quarter of an hour later a tall, dark man with a thick
black moustache rang the front-door bell, and explained that he
had an appointment with Mr. Davenheim. He gave the name of Lowen,
and in accordance with the banker’s instructions was shown into
the study. Nearly an hour passed. Mr. Davenheim did not return.
Finally Mr. Lowen rang the bell, and explained that he was unable
to wait any longer, as he must catch his train back to town. Mrs.
Davenheim apologized for her husband’s absence, which seemed
unaccountable, as she knew him to have been expecting the visitor.
Mr. Lowen reiterated his regrets and took his departure.

“Now for the next point. On Monday morning, a further discovery was made. The safe in Mr. Davenheim’s study was found to have been broken open and rifled. Its contents—consisting of a large amount of bearer bonds and some very valuable jewelry belonging to Mrs. Davenheim—had vanished. Naturally, the suspicion falls upon the man Lowen. He is known to be a man of somewhat shady reputation, and it has since transpired that he and Davenheim had been involved in some rather acrimonious business dealings of late. He was, as I told you, alone in the study for nearly an hour.”

“And now we come to the serious part of the business,” Japp continued. “On Monday morning, the safe in Mr. Davenheim’s study was found to have been opened. A large sum in bearer bonds, which Mr. Davenheim had brought home from the office the previous day, was missing, as well as a quantity of jewelry belonging to Mrs. Davenheim. Naturally, our suspicions turned at once to Mr. Lowen. He was alone in that room for nearly an hour, with the safe right there behind the desk. It seems a bit too much of a coincidence, doesn't it?”

“Now we come to the interesting part,” continued Japp. “On Monday morning, the safe in Mr. Davenheim’s study was discovered to have been broken into. The contents—a large sum in bearer bonds, a considerable amount of cash, and some very valuable jewelry belonging to Mrs. Davenheim—had vanished. The safe had been opened with a key or by someone who knew the combination. It was no bungling burglar’s job. And that, of course, brings us to Mr. Lowen. He was alone in that study for nearly an hour, and the safe is concealed behind a picture in that very room.”

“Now for the search,” continued Japp. “Miller went down there on Sunday, and he made a discovery. The safe in the study had been opened. It hadn’t been forced; it had been opened with a key, or by someone who knew the combination. And it was empty! Gone were a large amount of bearer bonds and some very valuable jewellery belonging to Mrs. Davenheim, which her husband had been keeping there for safety while the local police were busy with the crowds for the race-meeting. The value of the missing property is estimated at something like fifty thousand pounds. And remember, Lowen was in that study alone for nearly an hour!”

“That is the situation regarding the man himself,” continued Japp. “But there is a further complication which brings the matter into the sphere of active crime. On Sunday morning, it was discovered that the safe in the study had been broken into and rifled. A large quantity of bearer bonds, together with a considerable amount of jewelry, had been stolen. Naturally, our suspicions turned at once to this Mr. Lowen. He was the last person known to have been in the study, and he was left alone there for nearly an hour. We’ve had him under observation, of course, and we’ve discovered that he and Davenheim had some rather shady dealings together in the past. But there’s no direct evidence against him, and he stoutly denies having touched the safe.”

“On Monday morning a further sensational discovery came to light.
Behind a portière in Mr. Davenheim’s study stands a safe, and that
safe had been broken into and rifled. The windows were fastened
securely on the inside, which seems to put an ordinary burglary
out of court, unless, of course, an accomplice within the house
fastened them again afterwards. On the other hand, Sunday having
intervened, and the household being in a state of chaos, it is
likely that the burglary was committed on the Saturday, and remained
undetected until Monday.”

“_Précisément_,” said Poirot dryly. “Well, is he arrested, _ce
pauvre M. Lowen_?”

Japp grinned. “Not yet. But he’s under pretty close supervision.”

Poirot nodded. “What was taken from the safe? Have you any idea?”

“Lowen is a bit of a dark horse,” Japp replied. “He’s a financier too, but on a smaller scale. It seems there was some old grudge between them—some deal where Davenheim had bested him years ago. He claims he came by appointment to discuss a merger or a truce of sorts, but the servants' evidence is a bit damning. One of the maids swears she heard the sound of a heavy metal door clanging in the study while Lowen was alone there, though he maintains he never moved from his chair. To make matters worse, Lowen was seen by the gardener walking near the lake on the edge of the estate just before he reached the front door, looking, as the man put it, 'mighty suspicious and hurried.'”

“They were business rivals, it seems,” Japp replied. “Lowen is a bit of a dark horse—speculates a lot. He and Davenheim had been at daggers drawn over some South American oil concessions. Miller’s found out that Lowen was seen near the lake on the grounds that evening—long after he supposedly left the house. One of the gardeners saw him. That looks bad, doesn’t it?”

“Lowen claims that his visit was of a private nature, connected with some speculation in South American copper. He and Davenheim have had several business dealings of late, and not all of them, it is whispered, have been of the most amicable description. Lowen, of course, denies having seen Davenheim at all that evening. He says he waited in the study for the best part of an hour, and then, as the banker did not appear, he left. One rather significant point has come to light, however. A maid, who happened to be passing the study door, declares that she heard the sound of high words between the two men. If that is so, it proves that Davenheim *did* return to the house, and that Lowen saw him.”

“Lowen is a bit of a mystery man,” replied Japp. “He’s a financier, but on a smaller scale than Davenheim. There’s been no love lost between them for years. It’s said they were rivals in several big deals, and that Lowen has a bit of a grudge against the older man. According to his own account, he came down to discuss a merger, waited as I told you, and then left. He was seen by the lodge-keeper going out, and by several people on the way to the station. But there’s a curious fact—a small one, but Miller’s made much of it. Between the house and the station, the road runs alongside a deep, disused quarry. It’s just possible, you see, that there might have been a meeting there—a meeting that ended in a struggle.”

“He is a financier of sorts,” Japp explained, “and it appears there had been some rather sharp friction between his firm and Davenheim’s lately. Lowen claims that Davenheim had sent for him to discuss a compromise regarding a certain South American mining venture that had gone sour for both of them. He says they had not spoken for months, and he was quite surprised to receive the summons. Naturally, Miller is suspicious. It is a trifle too convenient, is it not? A man is shown into a room, left alone for nearly an hour, and subsequently a safe in that very room is found to have been rifled of a fortune.”

“Well, the two men were apparently not on very good terms. Lowen
is a speculator in quite a small way. Nevertheless, he has been
able once or twice to score a _coup_ off Davenheim in the market,
though it seems they seldom or never actually met. It was a matter
concerning some South American shares which led the banker to make
his appointment.”

“Had Davenheim interests in South America, then?”

“I believe so. Mrs. Davenheim happened to mention that he spent
all last autumn in Buenos Ayres.”

“Any trouble in his home life? Were the husband and wife on good
terms?”

“I should say his domestic life was quite peaceful and uneventful.
Mrs. Davenheim is a pleasant, rather unintelligent woman. Quite a
nonentity, I think.”

“Then we must not look for the solution of the mystery there. Had
he any enemies?”

“We’ve made one arrest already,” continued Japp, with a note of satisfaction. “A fellow by the name of Billy Kellett. He’s a local character—half-tramp, half-thief, and a known pickpocket. He was seen loitering near the gates of The Cedars on Saturday evening. But the clincher is this: this morning he attempted to pawn a very distinctive diamond ring in the village. Mrs. Davenheim has positively identified it as one that her husband always wore on his little finger.”

“But we haven’t been idle,” Japp continued. “Miller had the lake dragged yesterday—there’s a big ornamental sheet of water in the grounds, you know. And he found something. A suit of clothes, identified as those Mr. Davenheim was wearing when he left the house, and in the pocket was his silver cigarette case. But that wasn’t all. Protruding from the mud at the bottom was a heavy iron safe-breaker’s jemmy.”

“There is one development you might find interesting,” said Japp. “A man was arrested this morning at Entfield—a petty thief and tramp by the name of Billy Kellett. He was attempting to pawn a diamond ring which has been positively identified by Mrs. Davenheim as her husband’s. Furthermore, when he was searched, he was found to be wearing a very expensive silk shirt, also marked with the banker’s initials. Kellett’s story is that he found the clothes and the ring in a ditch near the boundary of ‘The Cedars’ on Saturday evening. He claims he saw a man—whom he describes as tall and dark—hurriedly throwing a bundle into the lake, but that the bundle struck a branch and some items fell out into the long grass, where he later retrieved them.”

“That brings me to the next point,” said Japp. “We’ve had a bit of luck in the shape of a common tramp—a fellow named Billy Kellett. He was picked up on Saturday night, blind drunk and singing at the top of his lungs in the village. When the police searched him at the station, they found a very valuable diamond ring in his pocket. Mrs. Davenheim has since identified it as one her husband was wearing when he left the house. Kellett claims he found it in the road, but we have our own ideas about that.”

“Miller’s been over the grounds with a fine-tooth comb,” Japp continued, “and this morning they dragged the lake—the ornamental one, you know. No body, as I said, but they did fish up Mr. Davenheim’s walking-stick. It was weighted with lead, and it’s a bit of a mystery how it got there if he just ‘walked away.’ And there’s another thing. A local fellow, a bit of a bad character named Billy Kellett, was picked up by the village constable last night. He was caught trying to pawn a very distinctive diamond ring in the next town. Mrs. Davenheim has identified it as one of those that was in the safe on Saturday.”

“By the way, one of the gardeners says he saw a figure going round
to the side of the house toward the rose-garden. The long French
window of the study opens on to the rose-garden, and Mr. Davenheim
frequently entered and left the house that way. But the man was a
good way off, at work on some cucumber frames, and cannot even say
whether it was the figure of his master or not. Also, he cannot
fix the time with any accuracy. It must have been before six, as
the gardeners cease work at that time.”

“And Mr. Davenheim left the house?”

“About half-past five or thereabouts.”

“What lies beyond the rose-garden?”

“A lake.”

“With a boathouse?”

Poirot was leaning back in his chair, his eyes closed, his fingertips joined. “Tell me, Hastings,” he said suddenly, “does it not strike you as remarkable that a man of Mr. Davenheim’s wealth and position should choose to walk to the village to post his own letters when he has a staff of servants at his disposal? And then there is the matter of the hair. Did Japp not say it was long and wavy? A man who is meticulous about his appearance, as a banker usually is, does not usually affect a Leonine mane unless there is a reason for it. It is a detail, perhaps, but in these details lies the clue to the character, and in the character lies the clue to the crime.”

“You find it amusing, Hastings?” Poirot’s eyes twinkled. He was busy rearranging the salt-cellars on the table with his usual meticulous care. “To you, it is a joke. To Japp, it is a joke. But to me, it is a problem of the most interesting. Tell me, Hastings, did you notice anything peculiar in the description of the missing man? The long hair, the bushy eyebrows—it is almost too complete a picture, is it not?”

Poirot was sitting with his eyes closed, his fingertips joined. He did not move as I approached. “You think it is a joke, Hastings?” he murmured without opening his eyes. “To you and to Japp, it is a matter of searching for a body or a man in hiding. For me, it is a matter of the psychology. Let us consider the facts. A man of wealth, a man of habit. He walks out of his house and vanishes. The safe is robbed. Is it a coincidence? Or is it the design?” He opened one eye and looked at me. “Tell me, Hastings, if you were to disappear, would you first shave off your moustache?”

Poirot was sitting with his eyes closed, the tips of his fingers pressed together. He did not move as I approached. “Well, Poirot,” I said, “you have a difficult task before you. To find a man who has vanished into thin air without even leaving your chair!” Poirot opened one eye. “On the contrary, Hastings, the task is of a simplicity most refreshing. I have already several ideas. Tell me, did Japp mention if any of the stolen jewelry was particularly recognizable? A ring, perhaps? It is often the small, personal objects that provide the most interesting history. And another thing—did Mr. Davenheim wear his hair long because of a whim, or was it a permanent characteristic? These are the questions the ‘eyes that see everything’ might overlook, but which the little grey cells find most suggestive.”

Poirot was sitting with his eyes closed, the newspaper containing the portrait of Mr. Davenheim lying across his knees. He did not move as I entered, but his voice reached me, precise and clear. “You find it amusing, Hastings? That I, Hercule Poirot, should stake a five-pound note upon the strength of my little grey cells, without so much as leaving my _fauteuil_? To you, it is the madness, the arrogance of the ego, is it not?” I confessed that the odds seemed somewhat against him, given the lack of physical inspection. Poirot shook his head slowly. “The physical inspection, it is for the Inspector Miller. He will find the footprints, the cigar-ash, the broken twig. But the brain, Hastings, must look for the pattern. For instance, why does a man of wealth, expecting an important business visitor, choose that exact moment to walk to the village to post letters? Does he not have a servant for such tasks? Does he not have a post-box at his gate? The action, it is not—how you say—harmonious.”

“_Eh bien!_” said Poirot immediately. “You make fun of Papa Poirot,
is it not so?” He shook his finger at me. “You do not trust his
grey cells? Ah, do not be confused! Let us discuss this little
problem—incomplete as yet, I admit, but already showing one or two
points of interest.”

“The lake!” I said significantly.

“And even more than the lake, the boathouse!”

I looked sidewise at Poirot. He was smiling in his most inscrutable
fashion. I felt that, for the moment, it would be quite useless to
question him further.

We heard nothing of Japp until the following evening, when he
walked in about nine o’clock. I saw at once by his expression that
he was bursting with news of some kind.

“_Eh bien_, my friend,” remarked Poirot. “All goes well? But do
not tell me that you have discovered the body of Mr. Davenheim in
your lake, because I shall not believe you.”

“We haven’t found the body, but we did find his _clothes_—the
identical clothes he was wearing that day. What do you say to
that?”

“Any other clothes missing from the house?”

“He denies it, of course. Says he never left the study from the moment he was shown into it until the moment he rang the bell to say he couldn’t wait any longer. But there is another development. We’ve picked up a fellow named Billy Kellett—a common tramp, well known to the local police as a petty thief and a drunkard. He was arrested on Saturday night at Entfield, five miles away, for being drunk and disorderly. When he was searched at the station, they found a very valuable diamond ring in his pocket. Mrs. Davenheim has identified it as a ring which her husband was wearing when he left the house that afternoon. Kellett’s story is that he found it on the grass by the side of the road near the lake.”

“He denies it, of course,” said Japp. “Says he never left the study until he rang for the servant to show him out. But Miller doesn't believe a word of it, and neither do I. It looks black for him, especially with those clothes turning up. And there’s another thing. We’ve got a lead on a fellow named Billy Kellett, a bit of a bad character known in the district. He was seen hanging about the grounds that evening. We’re picking him up for questioning to see if he saw anything—or if he was an accomplice.”

“Denies it, of course. Says he never left the study from the moment he was shown into it until the moment he rang the bell to leave. But it’s his word against the girl’s, and she’s a steady sort of young woman. Then there’s another point. We found a diamond ring—identified as one of Mrs. Davenheim’s—dropped in the grass near the lake. It looks as though he were making for the water to dispose of the body, and dropped the ring in his haste. What do you say to that, Monsieur Poirot?”

“He denies it, of course. Says he never left the study from the
moment he was shown into it until he rang the bell to go. But
Miller’s not satisfied. He’s been doing a bit of scouting on his
own, and he’s come across a very interesting character—a fellow
called Billy Kellett. A bit of a bad lot, known to the police. He
was seen hanging about the Chingside district on Saturday afternoon.
And what do you think? Yesterday he tried to pawn a ring—a very
valuable emerald ring—and the description tallies exactly with
one of those missing from the safe.”

“Denies it, of course,” Japp replied, leaning back and looking thoroughly satisfied with himself. “Claims he never moved from his chair in the study. But his word won't go far against the girl's. And there is further evidence. A local fellow, a common tramp by the name of Billy Kellett, was taken into custody on Saturday night for being drunk and making a nuisance of himself in the village. When the police searched him, they found a small silver ring—a signet ring—in his pocket. Mrs. Davenheim has identified it as one her husband always wore on his little finger. Kellett says he ‘found’ it near the lake, but Miller isn't swallowing that story for a moment.”

“Denied first of all that he had ever left the study. But the maid
was positive, and he pretended afterwards that he had forgotten
just stepping out of the window to examine an unusual species of
rose. Rather a weak story! And there’s fresh evidence against him
come to light. Mr. Davenheim always wore a thick gold ring set with
a solitaire diamond on the little finger of his right hand. Well,
that ring was pawned in London on Saturday night by a man called
Billy Kellett! He’s already known to the police—did three months
last autumn for lifting an old gentleman’s watch. It seems he tried
to pawn the ring at no less than five different places, succeeded
at the last one, got gloriously drunk on the proceeds, assaulted
a policeman, and was run in in consequence. I went to Bow Street
with Miller and saw him. He’s sober enough now, and I don’t mind
admitting we pretty well frightened the life out of him, hinting
he might be charged with murder. This is his yarn, and a very queer
one it is.

“This person, according to Kellett, was looking about him as if he
was afraid of being followed. He stopped when he came to a little
clump of bushes, and after a good deal of looking about, he took
something from his pocket and threw it into the bushes. Kellett,
sensing that there was something up, waited until the man had
passed on, and then searched the bushes. He found a small leather
bag, which contained a gold ring set with a diamond. He also found
some papers, which he says he threw away as being no use to him.
Then he hurried back to London to pawn the ring. His description
of the man tallies with Lowen to a T. The only thing is that the
time he gives—well, he’s a bit vague about that, as is only natural
after a day’s drinking. He says it must have been between six and
seven, probably nearer seven than six. Now, that would just fit
Lowen’s return journey to town.”

“The case against Lowen is becoming very strong,” I remarked.

“Yes,” said Japp. “Wait until you see the result of to-day’s work.
The lake has been dragged, and although we haven’t found the body,
we’ve found something almost as good.”

He produced a small, sodden object. “A wig!” he exclaimed
triumphantly. “A wig that exactly reproduces the hair of the
missing man!”

“And the clothes?” Poirot asked. “How were they found?”

“Under a heap of stones at the edge of the lake—drenched, of
course.”

Poirot’s eyes twinkled. “It is a truly remarkable case. And what
about Billy Kellett?”

“Still in the cells, awaiting his trial on the charge of assaulting
the police. He’s been identified as a well-known pickpocket.”

“And the papers he says he found?”

“Miller’s going to have a good hunt for them to-morrow. If they’re
part of the contents of the safe, it’ll be a pretty clear case.”

“And what do you think yourself, Japp?”

“Well, I’m not sure. It looks as though Lowen might have done for
Davenheim, and then, finding him a bit of a handful, decided to
frame the disappearance. But why the wig and the clothes? That’s
what beats me.”

Poirot smiled. “One thing more, my friend. Was Mr. Davenheim’s hair
his own, or did he wear a wig?”

Japp laughed. “Oh, it was his own, right enough. His wife says so,
and she ought to know!”

“True,” said Poirot. “And one other thing. Did Mr. Davenheim
habitually use much money—I mean, in his private capacity?”

“He was known to be very wealthy, and he lived on a scale to match
his income. But as for his personal pocket-money, I really couldn’t
say.”

“One last question. Has he any hobby?”

“Boating. He was very fond of it, hence the lake and the boathouse.”

“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes lit up. “The boathouse again! A most important
point, that.”

“I don’t see that it’s of any importance at all,” said Japp. “But
there, we’ve each our own methods. I’ll let you know how Miller
gets on to-morrow.”

He went off, evidently well-pleased with the progress of the case.
Poirot sat for a long time after he had gone, his eyes closed, his
head on one side.

“Hastings,” he said at last, “I should like you to go down to
Chingside to-morrow. There are one or two points I should like
cleared up.”

“With pleasure, Poirot. What are they?”

“First, find out if Mr. Davenheim was in the habit of frequenting
any particular spot in the grounds of The Cedars. Secondly, try
to get a look at the boathouse—it might be instructive. And
thirdly, see if you can find out anything about Mr. Davenheim’s
personal habits. Did he, for instance, use much perfume? Did he
smoke? If so, what?”

“I’ll do my best,” I promised.

I spent the following day at Chingside. It was a pleasant little
place, and I had no difficulty in finding The Cedars. I spent a
good deal of time wandering about the grounds, which were extensive
and well-kept. I saw the lake, a large sheet of water with a small
island in the middle. The boathouse was a substantial stone
building, with a landing-stage in front of it. I could not get
inside, as the door was locked, but I looked through the windows.
There was nothing very remarkable to be seen—just a couple of
punts and some oars.

I had better luck with my other inquiries. I found a gardener who
had been in Mr. Davenheim’s service for some years. He told me
that his master was a very quiet, studious man, who spent a great
deal of his time in his library. He was not much of a smoker, though
he occasionally enjoyed a cigar. As for perfume, the gardener had
never noticed that he used any.

I returned to London well-satisfied with my day’s work. Poirot
listened attentively to my report.

“Good, Hastings, very good. And the boathouse—you say it was built
of stone?”

“Yes, a very solid-looking building.”

“And there was no sign of anything unusual about it?”

“None whatever.”

“H’m! And the island in the lake—did you visit that?”

“No, I couldn’t get a boat. But it didn’t look as if there was
anything on it but trees and bushes.”

“I see. Well, we shall see what Japp has to tell us to-morrow.”

But Japp had very little to tell. Miller had found the papers
Kellett spoke of, but they were of no importance—just some old
circulars and a few receipted bills. There was nothing to connect
them with the robbery at The Cedars. As for Lowen, he still
maintained his innocence, though the evidence against him was
certainly strong.

“It’s a queer case,” said Japp. “I’m beginning to think that Lowen’s
not our man after all. But if he didn’t do it, who did?”

Poirot smiled. “Patience, my friend, patience. All will be revealed
in good time. In the meantime, I have a little experiment I should
like you to help me with.”

“An experiment? What kind of an experiment?”

“I want you to bring Billy Kellett here to-morrow morning. I should
like to have a little talk with him.”

Japp looked surprised, but he agreed to Poirot’s request.

The following morning, Japp arrived with Billy Kellett in tow. He
was a miserable-looking object, with a face that suggested a
misspent life. Poirot greeted him with his usual politeness.

“Now, Monsieur Kellett,” he said, “I want you to tell me exactly
what happened on Saturday evening. Do not be afraid—I am not a
policeman.”

Kellett told his story again, much as Japp had related it to us.
Poirot listened with close attention, occasionally interrupting with
a question.

“And this man you saw—you are sure it was Mr. Lowen?”

“Well, it looked like ’im, sir. ‘E ‘ad the same kind of moustache
and the same kind of clothes.”

“I see. And the bag—what did you do with that?”

“I threw it away, sir, after I’d taken the ring out. It wasn’t no
use to me.”

“And where did you throw it?”

“Over a hedge, sir, just outside the village.”

“I see. Well, that will be all for the present, Monsieur Kellett.
Thank you for your help.”

When Kellett had been led away, Poirot turned to Japp.

“Well, what do you think of him?”

“A poor specimen,” said Japp. “But I don’t see what you expect to
get out of him.”

“Perhaps nothing—and perhaps a great deal. We shall see. And now,
my friend, I have another request to make. I should like to visit
The Cedars this afternoon. Would it be possible for you to arrange
it?”

“Of course. I’ll come with you myself.”

We arrived at The Cedars about three o’clock. Mrs. Davenheim
received us with a kind of fluttering anxiety. She was, as Japp
had said, a pleasant-looking woman, but she seemed completely
overwhelmed by the tragedy that had befallen her.

Poirot was at his most charming. He expressed his deepest sympathy,
and then asked if he might see the study where the robbery had
taken place.

Mrs. Davenheim led the way to a large, comfortable room at the back
of the house. The safe was pointed out to us—a modern,
substantial-looking affair, which had been neatly forced open.

Poirot examined it with interest. “A very professional piece of
work,” he remarked. “Our friend the burglar knew his business.”

He then turned his attention to the rest of the room. He peered
into the waste-paper basket, examined the books on the shelves,
and even went so far as to sniff at the curtains.

“And the window?” he asked. “It was from here that Mr. Lowen was
seen to emerge?”

“Yes,” said Mrs. Davenheim. “The maid saw him from the bedroom
above.”

Poirot stepped out onto the terrace. “A very pleasant view,” he
remarked. “And the rose-garden—it is indeed beautiful.”

He wandered off among the rose-bushes, sniffing at the flowers and
occasionally pausing to examine a leaf. Japp and I followed him,
feeling rather mystified.

Suddenly Poirot stopped. He was standing in front of a large stone
urn, which was filled with geraniums.

“Ah!” he exclaimed. “What have we here?”

He reached into the urn and drew out a small, dark object. It was
a man’s glove—a heavy, leather glove, such as a motorist might
wear.

“Now, that is very interesting,” said Poirot. “A glove—and only
one glove. What do you make of that, Japp?”

“It might belong to anyone,” said Japp. “Lowen, for instance.”

“True. But why only one glove? And why leave it in a flower-pot?”

He continued his search, but nothing more was found. We returned to
the house, and Poirot spent some time talking to the servants. He
seemed particularly interested in the maid who had seen Lowen in
the rose-garden.

“Tell me, mademoiselle,” he said, “when you saw this gentleman,
was he wearing a hat?”

“Yes, sir, a dark felt hat.”

“And did you notice anything else about him? His walk, for
instance? Did he walk like a gentleman?”

“Well, sir, I didn’t notice anything particular about his walk.
He just seemed to be strolling along, as if he was looking at the
flowers.”

“I see. Thank you, mademoiselle.”

As we were leaving, Poirot turned to Mrs. Davenheim.

“One last question, madame. Your husband—did he have any particular
fondness for the lake?”

“Oh, yes, he loved being on the water. He spent hours in his punt,
just drifting about.”

“I see. Well, thank you, madame, for your kindness.”

On the way back to London, Poirot was very silent. He sat with his
eyes closed, his brow furrowed in thought.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” said Japp at last, “have you solved the
mystery?”

Poirot opened his eyes and smiled. “Not yet, my friend, not yet.
But I am beginning to see the light. There are one or two more
points I must clear up, and then—we shall see.”

The next morning, Poirot received a letter. He read it with great
interest, and then handed it to me. It was from a well-known firm
of private investigators, and it contained a brief report on the
movements of Mr. Lowen during the past few months.

“It seems,” said Poirot, “that Mr. Lowen has been in some financial
difficulty of late. He has been seen in the company of several
well-known moneylenders, and it is rumoured that he is on the verge
of bankruptcy.”

“That would certainly give him a motive for the robbery,” I
remarked.

“Yes, but does it give him a motive for the murder—if indeed there
was a murder? That is the question.”

Poirot spent the rest of the morning in deep thought. At lunchtime,
he announced that he was going out for a few hours.

“I have a little business to attend to,” he said. “I shall be back
in time for tea.”

He returned about four o’clock, looking very pleased with himself.

“Well, Hastings,” he said, “I have made a most interesting
discovery. I have found the other glove!”

“The other glove? Where?”

“In a most unlikely place, my friend. In the pocket of a coat
belonging to—Billy Kellett!”

“Billy Kellett! But how—?”

“Patience, Hastings, patience. All will be explained in good time.
In the meantime, I have another little task for you. I want you to
find out if Mr. Davenheim had any connection with a man named
Jabez Salmon.”

“Jabez Salmon? The junior partner in the firm?”

“The same. I have a suspicion that there may be more to their
relationship than meets the eye.”

I spent the next few hours in research. I found that Jabez Salmon
was a man of very different character from his partner. While
Davenheim was quiet and studious, Salmon was known as a bit of a
man-about-town, with a fondness for horse-racing and high living.
It was also rumoured that he had been involved in some rather
shady financial dealings.

I reported my findings to Poirot. He nodded thoughtfully.

“I thought as much. And now, my friend, the time has come to reveal
the truth. Japp should be here any moment.”

Indeed, a few minutes later, Japp arrived, looking very excited.

“I’ve got news for you, Monsieur Poirot! We’ve found the body!”

“The body? Where?”

“In the lake—near the island. It’s Mr. Davenheim, right enough.
He’s been strangled.”

Poirot did not seem surprised. “I see. And have you arrested
anyone?”

“Not yet. We’re still looking for Lowen. He seems to have
disappeared.”

“I don’t think you’ll have much trouble finding him,” said Poirot.
“But first, I have a little story to tell you.”

We all sat down, and Poirot began his explanation.

“The case of Mr. Davenheim,” he began, “is a very clever piece of
work—but not quite clever enough. It was a carefully planned
disappearance, designed to look like a murder.”

“A disappearance? But the body—?”

“The body, my friend, is not the body of Mr. Davenheim. It is the
body of—Billy Kellett!”

“Billy Kellett? But we saw him only yesterday!”

“You saw a man who called himself Billy Kellett. But he was not the
real Billy Kellett. The real Billy Kellett was a poor, half-witted
tramp who was murdered by Mr. Davenheim.”

“Murdered by Mr. Davenheim? But why?”

“Because Mr. Davenheim needed a body—a body that could be mistaken
for his own. He knew that his financial affairs were in a desperate
state, and that his only hope was to disappear and start a new
life elsewhere. But he knew that a simple disappearance would not
be enough. He had to make it look as though he had been murdered,
so that the search for him would eventually be called off.”

“But the clothes—and the wig?”

“All part of the plan. He wanted the police to find them, so that
they would be convinced of his death. He even went so far as to
plant the ring on the man he had murdered, so that it would be
found and identified.”

“And Lowen? Where does he come into it?”

“Lowen was the perfect scapegoat. Mr. Davenheim knew that Lowen had
a motive for wanting him out of the way, and he took care to make
it look as though Lowen had been at The Cedars on the night of the
disappearance. He even went so far as to dress up as Lowen and
allow himself to be seen by one of the maids.”

“But the glove?” I asked. “How do you explain the glove?”

“Ah, the glove! That was the one mistake he made. He had intended
to plant both gloves on the body of Billy Kellett, but in his
haste, he dropped one of them in the rose-garden. When he realised
his mistake, he tried to recover it, but it was too late. He had to
leave it where it was, hoping that it would not be found.”

“And where is Mr. Davenheim now?” asked Japp.

“He is, I believe, at this very moment, attempting to leave the
country. But I have taken the liberty of informing the authorities,
and I have no doubt that he will be apprehended before he can
make his escape.”

And indeed, a few hours later, news came that Mr. Davenheim had
been arrested at Southampton, as he was about to board a ship for
South America.

The case was over. Poirot had once again proved the power of his
little grey cells. As for Japp, he had to admit that he had been
soundly beaten.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, as he prepared to leave, “I have
to hand it to you. You’re a marvel, and no mistake.”

Poirot smiled. “It was a simple matter, my friend. A matter of
method and logic. And, of course, the little grey cells.”

And with that, he returned to his tea, and his carefully
straightened cups and saucers.

“The man was walking quickly, and looked rather agitated. He
wasn’t looking where he was going, and he tripped over a stone in
the road, which sent him sprawling into the ditch. Billy, thinking
he saw his chance, was on him in a moment, and—well, he relieved
him of his watch and chain, his tie-pin and this ring. The man
didn’t seem to have any money on him. He says that the gentleman
was so scared that he made no resistance, but just took to his
heels and bolted. Billy, not caring to stay too long in the
neighbourhood of his crime, made tracks for the station and got
a train to London. He’s quite positive about the identity of the
man he robbed—it was Lowen.”

“And what about the clothes in the lake, my friend?” Poirot asked.

Japp’s face fell a little. “We haven’t quite cleared that up yet,”
he admitted. “The gardener says they are the ones Mr. Davenheim
was wearing that day. We found them in a bundle, together with
a heavy stone, at the bottom of the lake. Miller’s theory is that
Lowen murdered Davenheim, put on his clothes to deceive anyone who
saw him, and then, after the robbery, changed back into his own
clothes, and threw Davenheim’s into the lake.”

“Wait a minute,” I said. “Lowen was seen coming _towards_ the study
at a quarter past six. Davenheim had then been gone three-quarters
of an hour. If Lowen was in his (Davenheim’s) clothes, why didn’t the
maid recognize him? And why should he change? It seems a most
unnecessary proceeding.”

“Miller says it was to make people think Davenheim was still
somewhere about the place,” Japp explained. “But I agree with you,
it’s a bit thin. Still, we’ve got Lowen, and we’ve got the ring.
That’s something.”

“And you think you have solved the mystery?” Poirot inquired.

“Not quite. There are several points to be cleared up yet. But
I think we’re on the right track. Don’t you?”

“I? Not in the least.”

Japp’s face fell. “You don’t believe it’s Lowen?”

“_Non, mon ami_.”

“But the ring?”

“The ring, yes. That is very important. That is a _point lumineaux_!”

“Well, if it wasn’t Lowen, who was it?”

Poirot shook his head. “I have not yet made up my mind.”

Japp sighed. “Well, I must be going. I’ll keep you posted.”

He went out, and Poirot returned to his chair. For a long time
he sat in silence. Then he looked up at me.

“Hastings,” he said, “I have a little commission for you. Will
you go down to Chingside to-morrow? I want you to find out one
or two things for me.”

“Certainly, Poirot. What are they?”

“I want to know if Mr. and Mrs. Davenheim occupied the same bedroom.
I want to know how often Mr. Davenheim has been to the barber lately.
I want to know if he has any particular hobby—and what it is. And,
lastly, I want you to find out if there are any unusual guests
staying at The Cedars.”

I was somewhat surprised at these requests, but I promised to do
my best.

“Kellett was about to ask for a copper, when he saw the man stoop
and pick something up out of the road. It was a small morocco-leather
case. To his surprise, the ‘toff’ didn’t even open it, but just
tossed it over a hedge into a field of tall grass. Kellett waited
till the man had disappeared round a bend in the road, then he
climbed through the hedge and started to hunt. It took him some
time, as the grass was long, but at last he found the case. Inside
was a beautiful ring. He didn’t know it was a diamond at the time,
thinking it was just a piece of glass, but he thought it would
be worth something, so he brought it to town and pawned it.”

“What’s your theory, Japp?” I asked.

“Well, it’s pretty clear what’s happened. Davenheim must have
lost his ring, or had it stolen, and Lowen’s the man who threw it
away. Why? That’s what we’ve got to find out.”

Poirot looked thoughtful. “A leather case—a ring—a man in a
ditch—it is all very interesting. And the clothes, Japp? Where
were they found?”

“Under the boathouse. They were tied up in a bundle and weighted
with a large stone. The valet has identified them beyond a doubt.”

“Was the lake dragged?”

“Yes, but nothing was found. We are going to have it pumped out
to-morrow. It’s only a small piece of water, and it won’t take
long. If Davenheim’s body is there, we’ll find it.”

“I do not think so,” said Poirot.

“Why? What do you think has become of him?”

“_Eh bien!_” said Poirot. “He may be in the lake, but I do not
think so. I think it is more likely he is in London.”

Japp laughed. “In London! With all the police of England looking
for him? Not likely!”

“All the same,” said Poirot, “I have a little idea. I should like
to see the gardener’s cucumber frames, and the study window, and—yes,
the boathouse.”

“Well, you can’t,” said Japp shortly. “Miller would never allow
it. He’s as jealous as a cat.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Well, I must rely on my imagination.”

He sat for a long time in silence after Japp had gone. Then he
suddenly turned to me.

“Hastings, have you ever noticed that I am a very good-looking
man?”

I was so taken aback that for a moment I could not answer.

“_Enfin!_” said Poirot. “You do not agree? Well, perhaps you are
right. But at least you will admit that I have a very fine
moustache?”

“It is certainly a very remarkable one,” I said, trying to be
polite.

“_C’est vrai_,” said Poirot. “It is the pride of my life. But if
I were to shave it off, do you think people would recognize me?”

“I should think it very unlikely,” I said. “The character of your
face would be entirely changed.”

“_Précisément!_” said Poirot. “That is what I thought.”

He relapsed into silence again.

The next day Japp brought us the news that the lake had been
emptied, but that no trace of a body had been found.

“I told you so,” said Poirot.

“Well, where is he, then?”

“I have told you—in London.”

“But how did he get there?”

“That is what I am going to find out,” said Poirot.

He spent the rest of the morning in deep thought. In the afternoon
he announced his intention of going out.

“I have a little business to attend to,” he said. “I shall not be
long.”

He returned in about two hours’ time, looking very pleased with
himself.

“I have made a discovery, Hastings,” he said. “A very interesting
discovery.”

“What is it?” I asked eagerly.

“I have found out where Mr. Davenheim is.”

“Where?”

“In a very safe place,” said Poirot. “In a place where no one
would dream of looking for him.”

“But where? Tell me!”

“Patience, my friend. All will be revealed in good time. In the
meantime, I have a little commission for you. I want you to go
down to Chingside and see Mrs. Davenheim. Tell her I am a friend
of Inspector Japp’s, and that I should like to ask her a few
questions.”

“But what am I to ask her?”

“I want you to find out two things. First, did Mr. Davenheim’s
hair and beard grow very fast? And second, did he and his wife
occupy the same bedroom?”

I looked at Poirot in amazement. “What on earth have those things
got to do with it?”

“A great deal, my friend. A great deal. Now, go, and do not fail
me.”

I went, though I must say I felt very foolish. Mrs. Davenheim
received me very kindly, though she seemed a good deal surprised
at my questions. However, she answered them quite readily.

“Yes,” she said, “my husband’s hair and beard did grow very fast.
He had to have them trimmed at least once a week. And as for the
other matter, no, we have had separate bedrooms for some years.”

I thanked her and took my leave. When I got back to town, I found
Poirot and Japp together.

“Well, Hastings?” said Poirot.

I gave him the information I had obtained.

“_Bien!_” said Poirot. “Everything is as I thought. Now, Japp, I
can tell you where to find your man.”

“Where?” said Japp.

“He is in prison,” said Poirot.

“In prison! Which prison?”

“In the one where Billy Kellett is,” said Poirot. “For he _is_
Billy Kellett!”

Japp and I stared at him in speechless amazement.

“It is quite simple,” said Poirot. “Mr. Davenheim knew that his
affairs were in a very bad way. He knew that sooner or later he
would have to disappear. So he prepared his way. Last autumn,
instead of going to Buenos Ayres, he went to a small town in the
north of England. There he created the character of Billy Kellett.
He was careful to be arrested for a small theft, and spent three
months in prison. In that way, the character of Billy Kellett
became a real person to the police. When he returned home, he grew
his hair and beard again. On the Saturday of his disappearance,
he went out of his house, changed into some old clothes he had
hidden in the boathouse, and threw his own clothes into the lake.
Then he went to the village, where he was seen as Billy Kellett.
He had already arranged to be arrested again that night. He pawned
his own ring, knowing it would be traced, and then got himself
arrested for being drunk and disorderly. In prison, with his hair
cropped and his beard shaved, no one would recognize him as the
great financier, Mr. Davenheim. It was a very clever plan, but he
forgot one thing.”

“What was 그게?” said Japp.

“He forgot that the character of Billy Kellett was already known
to the police. When I heard that Billy Kellett had been in prison
last autumn, at the very time Mr. Davenheim was supposed to be in
Buenos Ayres, I began to suspect the truth. And when Hastings
told me that Mr. Davenheim’s hair and beard grew very fast, I was
sure of it. For in prison, his hair and beard would be kept short,
and no one would know how fast they grew. It was a very pretty
little problem, was it not?”

“Well, I’m damned!” said Japp. “I must get off at once and see
about this.”

He hurried out of the room. Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“You see, Hastings? The little grey cells! They never fail!”

“While he was watching him, a small, dark man—apparently a
gentleman’s servant—walked up to the first-named, and spoke to
him. The ‘city toff’ seemed very angry, and said, ‘Tell him he’s
only got another five minutes, then I’m coming for my money!’
Kellett then saw the ‘toff’ draw something from his pocket, and
fling it from him. ‘Here, take that,’ he said. ‘You know what to
do with it!’ and then walked off in the opposite direction.

“Kellett scrambled out of the ditch, and searched about for what
the man had thrown away. It was a small, round object, which rolled
down the bank into the road. He picked it up and found it was a
diamond ring! He couldn’t believe his luck! He walked straight
on into the village, and got on a motor-bus to Entfield, and thence
to town, where he tried to pawn the ring at several places, as I
told you.”

“A very interesting story,” said Poirot, who had listened with
the closest attention. “_Très intéressant_! Do you believe it?”

“I don’t know. It’s a very unlikely story, but then, if he’d stolen
it from the house, why didn’t he take everything else as well?”

“That is a very good point. Now, what does the valet say about
the clothes that were found in the lake?”

“He says they’re the clothes his master was wearing on Saturday.
He’s quite positive.”

“No possibility of a mistake?”

“Not likely. There was a handkerchief in one of the pockets with
Mr. Davenheim’s name on it.”

“H’m! And what was in the other pockets?”

“A small bunch of keys, a silver match-box, and a penknife.”

“Anything else?”

“No.”

“Then,” said Poirot, “I am afraid that Billy Kellett is telling
the truth.”

“But look here, Poirot, the description of the man who gave him
the ring—‘a dark-complexioned gent with a big moustache’—tallies
exactly with Lowen’s appearance. And if Lowen had just broken into
the safe, he would naturally want to get rid of anything that could
be identified as belonging to Davenheim.”

“Exactly. But if he had just broken into the safe, he would have
several thousand pounds in his pocket. Is it likely that he would
part with a valuable ring to a total stranger? No; Lowen is a man
of business, and men of business do not do such things.”

“But Lowen is under arrest, isn’t he?” I asked.

“Yes, but only on suspicion. He’s been remanded for a week.”

“I’m going down to Chingside to-morrow,” went on Japp. “If you
like to come with me, I’m sure Miller would have no objection.”

“I thank you, my friend, but I do not go.”

“Not even to see the lake?”

“Not even to see the lake. I have all the facts I require. But
I should like to ask you one or two questions.”

“Fire away.”

“How long did Mr. Davenheim wear his hair?”

“Rather long for these days, I should say.”

“And his moustache and beard?”

“Both very full. The beard was pointed.”

“And he was in the habit of using a good deal of hair-wash?”

Japp stared. “I really couldn’t say. But his valet would know.”

“Ask him, my friend. Also ask him if Mr. Davenheim has had a large
amount of money in the house lately.”

“We know he had. We’ve already gone into that with the junior
partner.”

“I do not mean in the safe. I mean in his own pockets.”

“The valet says he had very little—only a few pounds.”

“One more thing. Did Mr. and Mrs. Davenheim share the same
bedroom?”

Japp’s stare became even more pronounced. “No. They had separate
rooms, with a door between.”

“I see. Well, that is all I want to know at present.”

“You’re a queer fish, Poirot!” said Japp as he took his leave.
“But I suppose you know what you’re after.”

“I think so,” said Poirot, with a little smile.

“What on earth did you want to know about his hair-wash for?” I
asked, as soon as we were alone.

“I have a fancy to see if his hair was as luxuriant as his
photograph represents it to be. If it was, he must have used a
good deal of hair-tonic.”

I looked at Poirot. He was perfectly serious.

“And the other thing?” I said. “About their having separate
bedrooms?”

“That, my friend, is a very important point.”

“I don’t see why.”

“Don’t you? Well, I will tell you this much. If they had shared
the same room, I should have been very much inclined to believe
that Mr. Davenheim was dead. As they did not, I am inclined to
believe he is alive.”

“I don’t see the connection.”

“Don’t you? Well, think it over.”

I did think it over, but I was no nearer to a solution when Japp
called again on the following Saturday. He looked a little
crestfallen.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, “I’m afraid the week’s up, and
we haven’t found our man.”

“Then the fiver is mine?”

“I suppose so. But I can’t help feeling that it’s a bit of a
swindle. You haven’t really done anything.”

“On the contrary, I have done everything. I have used my ‘little
grey cells.’”

“Well, where is he?”

“I will tell you. But first I should like to ask you one or two
questions. Did you ask the valet about the hair-wash?”

“I did. He said Mr. Davenheim never used anything of the kind.”

“_A la bonne heure!_ And did you find out if he had any large
sum of money in his possession?”

“His valet says he is almost certain he had none. He had only some
loose change in his pockets on the Saturday morning.”

“Exactly. Now, there is one more thing. I should like to see Mrs.
Davenheim.”

“That’s easily managed. She’s in town at the present moment, staying
at the Ritz.”

“Then we will go there at once.”

We found Mrs. Davenheim in her private sitting-room. She was a
faded, rather anxious-looking woman, with a somewhat nervous
manner.

“I am very glad to see you, Mrs. Davenheim,” said Poirot. “I
believe I can give you some news of your husband.”

The poor woman turned very pale. “Is he—is he—alive?” she gasped.

“He is alive, madame. But I am afraid I have some rather
disagreeable news for you. He is—at the present moment—in prison.”

“In prison!” she cried. “What for?”

“For—let me see—for an assault on the police, I think it was.”

“An assault on the police!” Mrs. Davenheim looked as though she
thought Poirot was mad. “But what name is he under?”

“He is known,” said Poirot, “as Billy Kellett.”

“Billy Kellett!”

Japp and I both uttered an exclamation of surprise.

“But Billy Kellett is a well-known thief!” cried Japp.

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “That is why it was such an excellent
disguise.”

“But his appearance!” I cried. “The photograph showed a man with
long hair and a beard. Billy Kellett is clean-shaven, with his
hair cropped close.”

“Exactly,” said Poirot again. “Don’t you see? It was the beard and
the long hair that were the disguise! Mr. Davenheim knew that his
affairs were in a desperate state. He knew that if he ‘disappeared’
in the ordinary way, he would be hunted down and caught. So he
determined on a much more original plan. He went to Buenos Ayres,
not on business, but to prepare his ‘double.’ He spent his time
there in a low-class thief’s den, learning the slang and the ways
of the criminal classes. Then he came back, but he didn’t come
back as Mr. Davenheim. He came back as Billy Kellett. For several
months he lived a double life. As Mr. Davenheim he wore a clever
wig and a false beard and moustache. At other times, he was Billy
Kellett.

“On that Saturday afternoon, he didn’t go to post letters. He went
to the boathouse, changed his clothes, and threw the Davenheim
suit into the lake. Then, as Billy Kellett, he made his way to
London, having first carefully ‘found’ his own diamond ring and
offered it for pawn. He knew that he would be arrested, and he
knew that as a common thief he would be perfectly safe from any
connection with the missing banker. The only person who might have
found him out was his wife—which is why I was so anxious to know
if they shared the same bedroom. As they did not, he was able to
remove his wig and beard every night without any fear of
discovery.”

“But the man who spoke to him on the road?” I asked. “The ‘dark-complexioned
gent’?”

“That,” said Poirot, “was Lowen. He had probably discovered
something of Davenheim’s double life, and was trying to blackmail
him. That is why Davenheim was so anxious to get rid of him. He
wanted to be safely in prison before Lowen could do any mischief.”

“Well,” said Japp, “it’s the most extraordinary story I ever
heard! I suppose we’d better go and identify him.”

“You will find it quite easy,” said Poirot. “If you look closely,
you will see that Billy Kellett has a small mole behind his left
ear—just like Mr. Davenheim.”

“And the safe?” I asked. “Who broke into the safe?”

“Mr. Davenheim, of course—before he left the house. He wanted to
make sure of having plenty of money when he came out of prison.”

“Well,” said Japp, “I suppose I owe you a fiver, Monsieur Poirot.
But I must say you’ve earned it!”

“_Au contraire_,” said Poirot, “it was very simple. It only required
the exercise of the little grey cells!”

“You’re a queer one, Monsieur Poirot,” said the Inspector, and

I looked at Poirot. He was leaning back in his chair, with a
curious little smile on his face.

“Well?” I said. “Have you solved it?”

“I have several ideas, Hastings. Several very interesting ideas.
But as yet—no, I cannot say that the case is solved. There are
one or two points—the silver pencil-case, for instance—which I
do not yet quite understand.”

“But surely the case against Lowen is very strong?”

“It is almost too strong, my friend. That is what I do not like

“And Billy Kellett?”

“Ah, Billy Kellett! He is the most interesting person in the whole

“Well, you can’t. He’s in gaol.”

“_C’est dommage_,” sighed Poirot. “But no matter. I can at least

The next day Japp did not appear, but we had a visit from a very
agitated lady. It was Mrs. Davenheim. She was a small, fair woman,
with a rather vacant expression, and she was evidently in a state
of great nervous excitement.

“Oh, Monsieur Poirot!” she exclaimed, as she sank into a chair.
“I have come to you because I am so terribly worried. The police—they
seem to think that Mr. Lowen—but I’m sure he had nothing to do
with it! He was always so kind and—and——”

“Calm yourself, madame,” said Poirot soothingly. “I am sure that
everything will be cleared up in time. Now, tell me, why do you
think Mr. Lowen is innocent?”

“Because—because he was such a friend of my husband’s! They were
always together.”

“But I thought they were business rivals?”

“Oh, that was only on the surface! In reality they were the best
of friends. My husband had the greatest respect for Mr. Lowen’s
ability.”

“I see. And was there anyone else who might have had a reason for
wishing your husband harm?”

“No—no one! He was the kindest, most generous of men.”

“And you have no idea where he can be?”

“None—none at all! It’s all so—so mysterious!”

“Tell me, madame, was your husband’s health good?”

“Yes, fairly good. He suffered a little from his heart, but nothing
serious.”

“And his memory? Was that good?”

“Excellent. He had a wonderful memory for faces and names.”

“I see. Now, madame, I want you to tell me something. On the
Saturday evening, after your husband had left the house, did you
hear anything unusual? Any sound of a struggle, for instance?”

“No—nothing. I was in my boudoir, and I didn’t hear a sound until
Mr. Lowen was shown into the study.”

“And you didn’t see your husband again?”

“No—not after he looked into my room at half-past five.”

“I see. And you have no idea what was in the safe?”

“Only what the police have told me. My husband always kept the key
on his watch-chain.”

“I see. Well, madame, I will do my best for you. In the meantime,

When she had gone, Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of Mrs. Davenheim?”

“A very pleasant woman,” I said. “But, as Japp said, not very
intelligent.”

“_Précisément_. But she has given me one or two things to think
about. For instance, she says that her husband and Lowen were the
best of friends. Now, Japp told us they were rivals.”

“Perhaps she didn’t know the truth about their business relations?”

“Perhaps. And then there is the question of the safe. She says
her husband always kept the key on his watch-chain. Now, if Lowen
robbed the safe, how did he get the key? He couldn’t have taken
it from Mr. Davenheim unless he had already murdered him—and in
that case, why should he have gone back to the study and waited
there for three-quarters of an hour?”

“It certainly seems very strange,” I admitted.

“And then there is the matter of the clothes. Why should Lowen—if

“But in that case, why was the safe robbed? No, Hastings, there

missing link in the chain—and I have a suspicion that Billy
Kellett is that link!”

The next few days passed without any further developments. Japp
dropped in once or twice, but he had nothing new to report. Miller
was still searching for the body, and for the keys of the safe,
but so far without success. Lowen was still in custody, but the
police were beginning to realize that the case against him was not
as strong as they had at first thought.

Poirot, meanwhile, remained in his chair, thinking. He hardly
spoke to me, and seemed to be entirely absorbed in his own
reflections. From time to time he would murmur something about
the silver pencil-case, or Billy Kellett, but for the most part
he was silent.

On the sixth day of our week, Japp arrived looking very crestfallen.

“Well,” he said, as he sat down. “I’m afraid you’ve won your bet,
Monsieur Poirot. We’re no nearer finding Mr. Davenheim than we
were a week ago. Miller’s searched every inch of the grounds, and
dragged the lake from end to end, but there’s no sign of a body.”

“And the keys?”

“Not a trace of them.”

“And Billy Kellett?”

“He’s still in gaol. He’s to be brought up before the magistrates
to-morrow on the charge of pawning the ring.”

Poirot stood up. “_Eh bien!_” he said. “The time has come.
Hastings, my hat and stick! Japp, we will go to Bow Street.”

“To see Billy Kellett?”

“Precisely.”

“But what for? He’s told us all he knows.”

“Perhaps. But there is one question I should like to ask him.”

When we arrived at Bow Street, we were taken to the cell where
Billy Kellett was confined. He was a miserable-looking object,
with a low forehead and a shifty eye. He seemed terrified at the
sight of us.

“Now then, Kellett,” said Japp. “This is Monsieur Poirot, the
great detective. He wants to ask you a question.”

Kellett looked at Poirot with a mixture of fear and curiosity.

“I ain’t done nothing!” he whined. “I told you all I knowed! I
found the ring, I did, just like I told you!”

“I do not doubt it,” said Poirot gently. “But there is one little
thing I want to know. When you saw the gentleman in the lane—the
gentleman who threw away the ring—did he have anything in his
hand?”

Kellett thought for a moment. “Yes,” he said. “He did. He ‘ad a
little silver thing—a pencil-case, I think it was. He was biting
the end of it, like as if he was worried about something.”

Poirot’s eyes flashed. “_Aha!_” he cried. “I thought so! And tell
me, my friend, when he threw away the ring, did he also throw away
the pencil-case?”

“No, he put it back in his pocket.”

“I see. And was there anything else? Anything at all?”

“Only his hat. He was wearing a soft felt hat, pulled down over
his eyes.”

“I see. Thank you, Kellett. You have been very helpful.”

As we left the cell, Poirot turned to Japp.

“Well, my friend, what do you think of that?”

“I don’t see that it helps much. We knew about the pencil-case
before.”

“But we did not know that he was biting the end of it! That is a
very important detail!”

“I don’t see why.”

“Because, my dear Japp, it shows that he was nervous! And why
should a man like Lowen—a man of method and calculation—be
nervous at such a moment? No, it does not fit! It does not fit
at all!”

“Then who was the man Kellett saw?”

“That is what we are going to find out. Japp, I want you to do
something for me. I want you to find out if anyone else was seen
in the neighbourhood of Chingside that Saturday evening—anyone
who might have been mistaken for Mr. Davenheim or Mr. Lowen.”

“I’ll do my best,” said Japp. “But I don’t think there was anyone.”

The next morning, Poirot was in a state of great excitement. He
paced up and down the room, his eyes shining with a strange light.

“Hastings!” he cried. “I have it! The silver pencil-case! Of course!
Why did I not see it before? It is so simple—so incredibly simple!”

“What is simple?” I asked, bewildered.

“The whole thing! The disappearance, the robbery, everything! It
is all as clear as daylight!”

“Then who is the culprit?”

“Wait, my friend, wait! We must have one more piece of evidence.
Japp should be here any moment.”

As he spoke, the door opened and Japp entered. He looked more
puzzled than ever.

“Well,” he said. “I’ve found out one thing. There _was_ another
man seen near Chingside that evening. A man who looked very like
Mr. Davenheim—long hair, beard and all. He was seen getting into
a car about two miles from the village.”

“_Aha!_” cried Poirot. “And the car—did anyone see the number?”

“Yes. A passing cyclist noticed it. It was a London number.”

“And have you traced it?”

“Yes. It belongs to a garage in South Audley Street. It was hired
for the day by a gentleman who gave the name of—Lowen!”

“_Mon Dieu!_” I exclaimed. “Then it _was_ Lowen after all!”

“Not so fast, Hastings, not so fast!” said Poirot. “Japp, tell me
one thing. The man who hired the car—what was he like?”

“The man at the garage says he was a tall, dark man with a thick
black moustache. Just like Lowen’s description.”

“I see. And the man who was seen getting into the car near
Chingside—what was _he_ like?”

“The witness says he was an older man, with greyish hair and a
beard. Just like Davenheim’s description.”

“I see. I see very well! Japp, my friend, the case is solved! We
have only to go to Chingside and collect the culprit!”

“But who is it?” I cried.

“It is very simple, Hastings. The culprit is—Mr. Davenheim!”

“Mr. Davenheim!” Japp and I exclaimed in one breath.

“But he’s the man who disappeared!” said Japp. “And besides, how
could he have robbed his own safe? And why should he have hired
a car in Lowen’s name?”

“Because, my dear Japp, he wanted to frame Lowen for his own
murder! He knew that Lowen was his rival, and he wanted to get
him out of the way. So he planned the whole thing—the disappearance,
the robbery, the clothes in the lake—everything! He even hired
a car in Lowen’s name, and made sure he was seen getting into it
while wearing a disguise that made him look like himself!”

“But the ring?” I asked. “Why did he throw away the ring?”

“Because he wanted Billy Kellett to find it! He knew that Kellett
was a well-known thief, and he knew that if he were found with
the ring, he would be arrested. And he knew that Kellett would
describe the man he saw—and that description would fit Lowen
perfectly!”

“But the pencil-case?” said Japp. “What about the pencil-case?”

“Ah, the pencil-case! That was his one mistake. He was so nervous
that he started biting the end of it—a habit, no doubt, of many
years. And Billy Kellett noticed it! And when I heard that, I
knew the truth. For who would be more likely to bite his pencil-case
in a moment of stress than the man whose pencil-case it was—Mr.
Davenheim himself!”

“But where is he now?” asked Japp.

“He is where he has been all the time,” said Poirot. “In gaol!”

“In gaol!”
