“Yes! Don’t you see? Billy Kellett was not the only man who was
arrested that Saturday night! There was another man—a man who
had ‘assaulted a policeman’ and was ‘run in in consequence.’
A man who gave a false name, no doubt, and who has been sitting
in a cell at Bow Street ever since, waiting for the week to pass
so that he could disappear for ever!”

“But you said he looked like Davenheim!” said Japp. “The man in
gaol is Billy Kellett!”

“No, no, Japp! There are _two_ men in gaol! Billy Kellett, and the
man who called himself—whatever he called himself! The man who
had shaved off his beard and moustache, and cut his hair, and who
looked so different that nobody recognized him as the great banker!”

Japp stared at him for a moment, and then a look of understanding
dawned on his face.

“By Jove!” he whispered. “I believe you’re right! We’ll go to Bow
Street at once!”

And so it proved. The man who had been arrested for assaulting
a policeman was indeed Mr. Davenheim. He had planned to spend
a week in gaol, where no one would think of looking for him,
and then, when the hue and cry had died down, to disappear to
South America with the proceeds of the robbery.

“It was a clever plan,” said Poirot, as we sat once more in our
rooms. “But he forgot one thing—the little grey cells of Hercule
Poirot!”

“And the fiver?” asked Japp with a grin.

Poirot smiled. “I think, my friend, that I have earned it!”

“Kellett was half concealed from the road by a heap of stones. Just
before he got abreast of him, the man looked quickly up and down
the road, and seeing it apparently deserted he took a small object
from his pocket and threw it over the hedge. Then he went on
towards the station. Now, the object he had thrown over the hedge
had fallen with a slight ‘chink’ which aroused the curiosity of
the human derelict in the ditch. He investigated and, after a short
search, discovered the ring! That is Kellett’s story. It’s only
fair to say that Lowen denies it utterly, and of course the word
of a man like Kellett can’t be relied upon in the slightest. It’s
within the bounds of possibility that he met Davenheim in the lane
and robbed and murdered him.”

Poirot shook his head.

“No, that would not account for the clothes. Besides, if Kellett
killed him and took the ring, why throw the ring away, only to
go and pick it up again? No, no, _mon ami_, that will not do. What
about the safe? Has that been examined? Has anything been missed
besides the bonds and the money?”

“Wait a bit. I’m coming to that. Some of the jewellery has been
recovered. A small diamond brooch, and a ring set with a single
large pearl. They were found in a little wood on the further side
of the lake—the side where the boathouse is. They’d evidently been
flung away.”

“What about the clothes? Were they in the lake?”

“No, they were found in the boathouse. All rolled up in a bundle
and hidden in a corner.”

“Is there any other news, Japp?”

“Yes, and this is the most important of all. Miller’s had a
telegram from a man in Buenos Ayres. It seems Davenheim’s been
speculating heavily in South American shares, and has lost every
penny he had. The firm of Davenheim and Salmon is on the verge of
bankruptcy.”

“So the motive for a voluntary disappearance is not far to seek,”
I cried. “He has cleared out, after first robbing his own safe.”

“He might have done that,” said Japp, “but if he’s cleared out,
why has he left his clothes behind him? He can’t very well have
gone off in his skin!”

“That is true,” Poirot murmured. “That is very true. It is a
difficulty, is it not?”

“Now, Monsieur Poirot, what do you say to it all? The clothes,
the jewellery, the safe, and the bankruptcy? It’s a pretty little
collection of facts, isn’t it?”

“Most interesting—most interesting.”

“I’m beginning to think you’ll lose your fiver, monsieur.”

“It is possible,” Poirot admitted. “I have never claimed to be
infallible. But I should like to ask you one or two questions, if
I may.”

“Fire away.”

“This Billy Kellett—what is he like?”

“A very ordinary-looking fellow. Medium height, reddish hair,
clean-shaven. A typical specimen of the ‘waif and stray’ class.”

“Has he any distinctive features? Any deformity?”

“None that I noticed.”

“Good. Now for my second question. Did Mr. and Mrs. Davenheim
occupy the same bedroom?”

Japp stared. “No. They had separate rooms, with a door between.”

“_Très bien_. And my third question—did Mr. Davenheim have much
correspondence?”

“He had a good deal, I believe. All of it went to his office in
the City.”

“And he had no study at The Cedars except the one where the safe
was?”

“No. He used that as his private sitting-room.”

“I see. Now, just one more. It is about the hair. Does Mr.
Davenheim wear his hair long?”

“Yes. It’s quite a feature of his appearance.”

“And he has a large moustache and a pointed beard?”

“Yes.”

“And bushy eyebrows?”

“Yes.”

“And he is a man of—about what height?”

“Five foot ten, I should say.”

“Exactly. Now, about this man Billy Kellett. Is he the same
height?”

“No, he’s a good bit shorter. Not more than five foot seven, I
should think.”

“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes twinkled. “That is very interesting. Very
interesting indeed.”

“Is it?” Japp looked puzzled. “Well, I must be getting along.
I’ll let you know if anything fresh turns up.”

“_Au revoir_, my friend.”

When Japp had gone, Poirot sat for a long time in silence. At last
he looked up at me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it all?”

“It seems to me that Lowen is the man,” I said. “The fact that he
was seen near the study window just before he left the house—and
the finding of the ring which he had thrown away—it all points to
him.”

“And the clothes in the boathouse?”

“That is certainly a difficulty,” I admitted. “But perhaps he
intended to make it look like suicide.”

“By leaving the clothes _in the boathouse_? That would be a
singularly ineffective way of doing it!”

“Well, perhaps he intended to burn them, and was interrupted.”

“And the jewellery found in the wood?”

“Again, he may have been afraid of being searched, and have
thrown them away.”

“It is possible,” Poirot said meditatively. “It is possible. But
I confess I am not satisfied. There is something—something that
I do not understand.”

“What is that?”

“The hair, Hastings. The hair!”

“The hair?” I stared at him. “What on earth has the hair to do
with it?”

“I do not know. But it is a point that interests me. A man who
wears his hair long—and has a large moustache and a pointed
beard—and bushy eyebrows! It is a very striking appearance, is
it not?”

“I suppose so. But I don’t see what that has to do with the
case.”

“Perhaps nothing. And yet—I wonder!”

He sank into a brown study. I did not disturb him. At last he
roused himself.

“Hastings, I should like you to go down to Chingside to-morrow.
I want you to see Mrs. Davenheim.”

“Mrs. Davenheim? But Japp said she was a nonentity.”

“Precisely. That is why I want you to see her. A nonentity often
sees more than a more intelligent person. She may be able to tell
us something—some little thing—that will give us the clue we
seek.”

“But what am I to ask her?”

“Anything you like. Your own intelligence will guide you. But
try and find out if there was anything unusual in her husband’s
manner lately—anything, however small.”

“Very well,” I said. “I’ll go.”

The next morning I duly started for Chingside. It was a pleasant
little village, and The Cedars was a large and imposing house. I
was shown into a small morning-room, and a few minutes later Mrs.
Davenheim joined me. She was a pleasant, motherly-looking woman,
but I saw at once what Japp meant when he called her a nonentity.
She seemed completely overwhelmed by the tragedy that had befallen
her.

“It is so terrible,” she said, her eyes filling with tears. “I
cannot believe it even now. To think that he should have
disappeared like that—in broad daylight!”

I expressed my sympathy, and then proceeded to put one or two
questions to her. But I soon found that Japp was right. Mrs.
Davenheim could tell me nothing. Her husband’s manner had been
absolutely as usual; he had had no worries that she knew of; and
he had said nothing to her except that he was going to post some
letters and was expecting Mr. Lowen.

“He was always so kind and thoughtful,” she said. “Only the day
before he had given me a beautiful diamond brooch—the one the
police found in the wood. It seems so heartless of them to have
thrown it away like that!”

“Did he often give you presents of jewellery?” I asked.

“Oh, yes! Scarcely a month passed without his giving me something.
He said he liked to see me well dressed.”

I asked her a few more questions, but with no result. As I was
leaving, I happened to notice a photograph of Mr. Davenheim on the
piano. It was a large, well-executed portrait, and it bore out
Poirot’s description in every detail. The long, wavy hair, the
large moustache, and the pointed beard were all there. But what
struck me most were the eyes. They were dark and piercing, with a
singularly direct gaze.

I returned to London and gave Poirot a full account of my interview.
He listened with great attention.

“So she could tell you nothing?” he said. “That is a pity. And
yet—one never knows. The brooch—he gave her the brooch only the
day before? That is interesting.”

“Why?”

“I do not know. But it is a point. And the photograph—you say his
eyes were very dark and piercing?”

“Yes, they were.”

“H’m! Well, we must wait and see. Japp may have some more news
for us soon.”

Two days later Japp appeared again. He looked more jubilant than
ever.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, “I think the case is as good as
over. We’ve found the rest of the jewellery.”

“Where?”

“In Lowen’s house! Hidden behind a loose brick in the cellar.
What do you say to that?”

“It is very damaging,” Poirot admitted. “Very damaging indeed.”

“Damaging? It’s conclusive! The man’s as good as hanged already.”

“And what does Mr. Lowen say to this new discovery?”

“Oh, the usual thing! Knows nothing about it—someone must have
put it there to frame him. But that won’t hold water for a minute.
The evidence is too strong.”

“And Mr. Davenheim? Have you found any trace of him?”

“Not yet. But we’re still searching. We’ll find him sooner or
later—dead or alive.”

“I wonder,” Poirot murmured. “I wonder.”

“You’re still skeptical, I see. Well, a week’s nearly up. You’ll
have to pay up that fiver soon!”

“It is possible,” Poirot said. “It is possible. But I should like
to ask you one more question, Japp.”

“Go ahead.”

“This man Billy Kellett—is he still in custody?”

“Yes. He’s doing his time for the assault on the policeman.”

“I see. And has he been visited by anyone?”

“Only his lawyer. Why?”

“Oh, nothing. I just wondered. And Mr. Lowen—has he been allowed
to see anyone?”

“Only his solicitor, of course.”

“I see. Well, Japp, I will not detain you any longer. You have
much to do, no doubt.”

“I have that! Well, good-bye, Monsieur Poirot. See you in a day
or two.”

When Japp had gone, Poirot turned to me.

“Hastings, I have a little commission for you. I want you to go
down to the police-station where Billy Kellett is confined. I want
you to find out—quietly, you understand—if he has had any other
visitors besides his lawyer.”

“But Japp said he hadn’t.”

“Japp may be mistaken. Or he may have been misinformed. I want
you to make sure. And find out if he has received any letters or
parcels.”

I went down to the police-station as Poirot had requested. After
a little difficulty, and the judicious use of a few half-crowns,
I managed to get the information I wanted. Billy Kellett had indeed
had no visitors except his lawyer. But he had received one parcel—a
small box of cigars.

“Cigars!” Poirot cried, when I told him. “That is very interesting!
What kind of cigars?”

“I don’t know. The gaoler said they were very good ones.”

“H’m! And who sent them?”

“There was no name. Only a note saying they were from a ‘well-wisher’.”

“A well-wisher! How touching! And did Billy Kellett smoke them?”

“The gaoler said he’d smoked nearly all of them already.”

“He has a good appetite, our friend Billy! Well, Hastings, I think
we are near the end. To-morrow is the last day of our week. We
shall see what it brings forth.”

The next morning, to my surprise, Poirot suggested that we should
go down to Chingside ourselves.

“But I thought you were going to solve the case from your
armchair?” I said.

“I have solved it, Hastings! But I wish to see the final scene.
It is a little whim of mine.”

“You’ve solved it? Then who is the murderer?”

“Wait, my friend, wait! All will be revealed in good time.”

We reached Chingside about eleven o’clock. Poirot led the way
straight to The Cedars. As we were walking up the drive, we met
Inspector Japp coming towards us. He looked surprised to see us.

“Hullo, Monsieur Poirot! What brings you here? Come to see the
end of the play?”

“Precisely, my friend. Is there any news?”

“Well, we’ve found something else. In the lake this time.”

“The body?” I cried.

“No, not the body. A heavy iron weight—the kind they use for
tethering horses. It was tied to a piece of rope.”

“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes flashed. “That is the last link! I have all
the pieces of the puzzle now.”

“You mean you know who did it?” Japp stared at him.

“I do. If you will come with me to the house, I will show you.”

We followed Poirot into the house. He led the way to the study,
where Mrs. Davenheim was sitting. She looked up in surprise as we
entered.

“Monsieur Poirot! Inspector Japp! Is there any news? Have you
found my husband?”

“Not yet, madame,” Poirot said gently. “But I believe I can tell
you what has happened to him.”

He turned to Japp. “Will you be so good as to send for Billy Kellett?”

“Billy Kellett? But he’s in gaol!”

“He is here, my friend. Or rather, he will be here in a few
minutes. I took the liberty of telephoning to the governor of the
gaol this morning. He is sending him over under escort.”

Japp looked completely bewildered, but he gave the necessary orders.
A few minutes later a taxi drove up to the door, and Billy Kellett,
looking very sheepish and uncomfortable, was brought into the room.

Poirot looked at him for a moment in silence. Then he turned to
Mrs. Davenheim.

“Madame, I have a question to ask you. When your husband returned
from Buenos Ayres last autumn, did you notice any change in him?”

Mrs. Davenheim looked puzzled. “Change? No, I don’t think so. He
seemed just the same as ever.”

“Think again, madame. Was there nothing? No little habit that he
had dropped—or a new one that he had acquired?”

Mrs. Davenheim thought for a moment. “Well, now you mention it,
there was one thing. He used to be very fond of gardening—especially
roses. But since he came back, he didn’t seem to care for it at
all. He never went near the rose-garden if he could help it.”

“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes twinkled. “And was there anything else? His
appetite, for instance?”

“He did seem to have a better appetite than he used to. He was
always asking for more.”

“I see. And his hair—did it grow very fast?”

“It did seem to. He had to have it cut much more often than he
used to.”

“Precisely! Now, Japp, I will show you how the trick was done.”

He turned to Billy Kellett. “My friend, will you be so good as to
remove your wig?”

Billy Kellett stared at him. “My wig? What are you talking about?
I ain’t got no wig!”

“No? Then perhaps you will allow me to remove it for you?”

Before anyone could move, Poirot had stepped forward and snatched
at the man’s hair. To my intense surprise, it came away in his
hand, revealing a head of short, reddish hair!

“And now,” Poirot said, “the moustache and the beard!”

He gave another tug, and the moustache and beard also came away.
We stared in amazement. For there, standing before us, was not
Billy Kellett, but Mr. Davenheim himself!

Mrs. Davenheim gave a scream and fell back in her chair. Japp stood
as if rooted to the spot. I was equally thunderstruck.

“Mr. Davenheim!” Japp gasped at last. “But—but Billy Kellett?”

“There is no Billy Kellett,” Poirot said calmly. “Or rather, Billy
Kellett is Mr. Davenheim. It was a very clever plan, was it not?
Mr. Davenheim knew that his firm was on the verge of bankruptcy.
He knew that he would soon be a ruined man. So he decided to
disappear—but in such a way that he could take a large sum of
money and jewellery with him.

“He created the character of Billy Kellett. He went to London,
disguised as a vagrant, and committed a small theft. He was caught
and sentenced to three months’ imprisonment. This gave him a
perfect alibi for the time of his disappearance.

“On the Saturday afternoon, he went out of the house, changed his
clothes in the boathouse, and threw them into the lake—or rather,
he intended to, but the iron weight wasn’t heavy enough, and they
floated. Then he went to the lane, where he had hidden his Billy
Kellett clothes, and changed into them. He threw his ring over the
hedge, where he could find it later, and then went to London and
gave himself up to the police for his old offence.

“He had already hidden the jewellery and the money in Lowen’s
house, knowing that Lowen would be the first person to be
suspected. He had even managed to let himself be seen by one of
the maids, so as to draw suspicion onto Lowen.

“It was a very clever plan, as I said. But he made one or two
mistakes. He forgot that a man’s hair does not grow quite so fast
as he pretended. And he forgot that a man who has been in prison
for three months would not have such a good appetite as he showed
when he came back!”

Poirot turned to Mr. Davenheim, who was standing white and
shaking. “A very clever plan, monsieur. But you did not account
for the little grey cells of Hercule Poirot!”

Japp stepped forward and laid a hand on Davenheim’s shoulder.
“I arrest you, Mr. Davenheim, for—well, I’ll have to think what the
charge is. But you’re coming with me anyway!”

As they led him away, Poirot turned to me with a smile. “Well,
Hastings, what do you think of my ‘armchair’ solution?”

“It was wonderful, Poirot!” I said. “Absolutely wonderful!”

“It was simple, my friend. Quite simple. When you have excluded
the impossible, whatever remains, however improbable, must be the
truth. And it was impossible for Mr. Davenheim to have disappeared
into thin air. Therefore, he must still be here—in some form or
other. And Billy Kellett was the only possible form.”

“But the fiver, Poirot?” I said. “You’ve won it!”

“So I have!” Poirot’s eyes twinkled. “I must remind Japp of that.
_Le sport_, Hastings, _le sport_! It is a great thing, is it not?”

“Is there any other evidence against Lowen?”

“Yes, and very damaging too. Mrs. Davenheim’s maid, who was coming
along the road towards Chingside about five-and-twenty past six,
saw a gentleman whom she described as ‘dark-complexioned, with a
big moustache’—which is Lowen’s description to a T—leaving the
lodge gates of The Cedars and walking towards the station.”

“Does Lowen admit to having left the grounds at that time?”

“He says he left exactly at half-past six, by the front door, and
was at the station for the 6.42. The servants at The Cedars,
however, are positive that he left the study at twenty minutes
past six, and was shown out by the footman.”

“Then there is a discrepancy of ten minutes?”

“Exactly. Ten minutes during which he might have been doing
anything—murdering Mr. Davenheim, for instance, and disposing of
his body.”

“In the lake?”

“Well, we haven’t found it yet.”

“No,” said Poirot, “I don’t think you will.”

Japp looked at him. “You think Lowen’s innocent?”

“I am not at all sure that he is.”

“What about Billy Kellett, then? Is he telling the truth?”

“He is probably a very fine liar,” said Poirot. “But I should like
to see him.”

“Miller’s got him at Chingside,” Japp told him. “He was only taken
before the magistrate this morning and remanded for a week.”

“I will go to Chingside to-morrow,” Poirot announced. “Will you
come with me, Hastings? I have a desire to see this Billy Kellett
and his famous ring.”

I was delighted at the prospect. The next morning saw us at the
little country town of Chingside. We were shown into a small cell
at the police station, and Billy Kellett was brought in to us. He
was a miserable-looking specimen, with a weak, shiftless face.

Poirot studied him for a few minutes in silence. Then he said
quietly:

“My friend, I am here to help you. If you will tell me the truth,
it may be possible to get you out of this trouble.”

Kellett began a long, rambling story, to which Poirot listened
with the greatest patience. When he had finished, Poirot said:

“Thank you. Now let me see the ring.”

The ring was produced from the inspector’s office. It was a very
fine stone, and Poirot examined it with interest.

“You say you found it in the ditch?”

“Yes, sir.”

“You did not meet Mr. Davenheim on the road?”

“No, sir.”

“And you did not see any one else?”

“Not a soul, sir.”

“You are quite sure of that?”

“Positive, sir.”

Poirot handed back the ring and we left the cell. In the passage we
met Inspector Miller. He was a tall, fair-haired man, with a
keen-looking face.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he said with a grin. “Have you solved our
little problem yet?”

“Not yet, Inspector,” said Poirot with a smile. “But I am
progressing—I am progressing.”

“I’m glad to hear it,” said the inspector. “For my part, I think
the case is pretty clear. Lowen is our man.”

“You may be right,” said Poirot. “But there are one or two things
that puzzle me. For instance, why should Lowen, after murdering
Mr. Davenheim, throw away a valuable diamond ring?”

“Perhaps he was afraid it might be found on him,” suggested the
inspector.

“But why throw it where it was almost certain to be found? Why not
bury it, or throw it into the lake?”

The inspector shrugged his shoulders. “Criminals are often very
foolish,” he said.

“True,” said Poirot. “But Lowen is not a fool. He is a very clever
man.”

“Well, we shall see,” said the inspector. “In the meantime, we are
doing our best to find the body.”

“I wish you luck,” said Poirot.

As we were walking back to the station, I said to Poirot:

“What do you think of Billy Kellett’s story? Do you think he’s
telling the truth?”

“I think he is a very fine liar, as I said before,” said Poirot.
“But I also think there is a grain of truth in what he says.”

“And what about Lowen?”

“Lowen is a very interesting character,” said Poirot. “I should
like to know more about him.”

“Do you think he murdered Mr. Davenheim?”

“I do not know, Hastings. But I am beginning to have an idea.”

“An idea? What is it?”

“I will tell you later, my friend. In the meantime, let us go and
see Mrs. Davenheim.”

The Cedars was a large, modern house, surrounded by extensive
grounds. We were shown into a small, elegantly furnished morning-room.
Mrs. Davenheim was a middle-aged woman, with a pleasant, but
rather weak face. She seemed very much distressed by her husband’s
disappearance.

“It is so terrible, Monsieur Poirot,” she said. “I cannot imagine
what can have happened to him. He was always so kind and
considerate.”

“I am sure he was, madame,” said Poirot sympathetically. “Can you
tell me anything about his business affairs?”

“I am afraid I know very little about them,” said Mrs. Davenheim.
“My husband never discussed his business with me.”

“Did he seem worried about anything lately?”

“No, not at all. He seemed quite his usual self.”

“And you have no idea who might have wished him harm?”

“None at all. He had no enemies that I know of.”

“What about Mr. Lowen?”

Mrs. Davenheim’s face clouded. “I never liked Mr. Lowen,” she
said. “He and my husband were always having disagreements.”

“I see. And was your husband expecting Mr. Lowen on the evening
he disappeared?”

“Yes. He told me he was going to post some letters and that if Mr.
Lowen should arrive before he returned, he was to be shown into
the study.”

“And that is all you can tell me?”

“I am afraid so.”

Poirot thanked her and we took our leave. On our way back to town,
Poirot was very silent. He sat with his eyes closed, his brow
puckered in thought. I did not disturb him. I knew that he was
busy with his “little grey cells.”

When we reached our rooms in Revel Street, Poirot went straight to
his desk and began to write. After a few minutes he looked up and
said:

“Hastings, I want you to do something for me.”

“Certainly, Poirot. What is it?”

“I want you to find out everything you can about Mr. Lowen’s past
history. I want to know where he was born, where he was educated,
what his business career has been—everything.”

“I’ll do my best,” I said.

“Good. And I also want you to find out if there have been any
unusual occurrences at The Cedars lately—any strange visitors,
any unusual telephone calls—anything out of the ordinary.”

“I’ll see what I can do.”

For the next few days I was busy with my investigations. I found
out that Lowen was born in London and had started his career as a
clerk in a stockbroker’s office. He had gradually worked his way
up and was now a successful speculator. He had never been married
and lived in a small flat in Mayfair.

As for The Cedars, I could find nothing unusual. The servants all
spoke highly of Mr. Davenheim and seemed genuinely distressed by
his disappearance.

When I reported my findings to Poirot, he seemed pleased.

“Thank you, Hastings,” he said. “You have done well. Now I think
it is time we had another talk with Inspector Japp.”

Japp came to see us the following evening. He looked rather
dejected.

“No luck so far, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “We’ve dragged the
lake, but we haven’t found the body. And we haven’t been able to
find any more evidence against Lowen.”

“I am not surprised,” said Poirot.

“What do you mean?”

“I mean that I do not think you will find the body in the lake.”

“Then where do you think it is?”

“I do not think there is a body,” said Poirot quietly.

Japp stared at him. “No body? But what about the clothes?”

“The clothes were a very clever touch,” said Poirot. “But they
were only a touch.”

“I don’t understand.”

“Wait a little, my friend. All will be clear in good time. In the
meantime, I have a request to make.”

“What is it?”

“I want you to bring Billy Kellett here to-morrow morning.”

“Billy Kellett? Why?”

“Because I have a few more questions to ask him.”

Japp looked skeptical, but he agreed to Poirot’s request.

The next morning Billy Kellett was brought to our rooms. He looked
more miserable than ever.

“Now, Billy,” said Poirot kindly. “I want you to tell me the truth
this time. Did you really find that ring in a ditch?”

Kellett hesitated. “Yes, sir.”

“Are you quite sure?”

“Yes, sir.”

Poirot looked at him for a moment in silence. Then he said:

“Billy, do you know what happens to people who tell lies to the
police?”

Kellett turned pale. “I’m telling the truth, sir. I swear I am.”

“Very well,” said Poirot. “Then perhaps you can explain how it is
that the ring was found in the ditch _before_ it was thrown there?”

Kellett stared at him in amazement. “What do you mean, sir?”

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that the ring was pawned in London on
Saturday night. But it was not thrown into the ditch until
Sunday morning.”

Kellett gasped. “How did you know that, sir?”

“Because I am Hercule Poirot,” said Poirot simply. “Now, Billy,
tell me the truth. Where did you get that ring?”

Kellett broke down and began to sob. “I didn’t mean no harm, sir.
I really didn’t. I found it in the road, near the gate of The
Cedars.”

“When?”

“On Saturday afternoon, sir. Just after five o’clock.”

“And did you see anyone?”

“Yes, sir. I saw a man coming out of the gate. He was a tall, dark
man with a big moustache.”

“And did he see you?”

“No, sir. He was in a hurry. He dropped the ring and didn’t seem
to notice.”

“And what did you do?”

“I picked it up and went to the station. I was going to give it to
the police, but then I thought of all the money I could get for it.
I’m sorry, sir. I really am.”

“I believe you, Billy,” said Poirot. “Now, Japp, I think you can
take him away.”

When Japp and Kellett had left, I turned to Poirot.

“Poirot, how did you know that the ring was found on Saturday
afternoon?”

“I didn’t, Hastings. It was a little bluff. But it worked, did it
not?”

“It certainly did. But what does it mean?”

“It means, my friend, that Lowen is not the murderer of Mr.
Davenheim.”

“But he was seen coming out of the gate at the time the ring was
dropped.”

“Exactly. And that is why he cannot be the murderer.”

“I don’t understand.”

“Think, Hastings. If Lowen had murdered Mr. Davenheim and stolen
the ring, would he have dropped it at the gate for anyone to find?
No, he would have been much more careful than that.”

“Then who did murder Mr. Davenheim?”

“I told you before, Hastings. I do not think anyone murdered him.”

“Then where is he?”

“He is much nearer than you think, my friend. Much nearer than you
think.”

The following day Poirot asked me to accompany him to Chingside
once more. We went straight to The Cedars.

“I want to see the study,” said Poirot.

We were shown into the study by the footman. It was a large,
comfortable room, with a large desk and a safe in one corner.

Poirot began to examine the room with the greatest care. He looked
at the desk, the safe, the windows, the carpet. He even looked
behind the pictures on the walls.

After a few minutes he stopped and looked at the safe.

“A very fine safe,” he murmured. “But not a very difficult one to
open.”

“Do you think Lowen opened it?” I asked.

“No, Hastings. I do not think Lowen opened it.”

“Then who did?”

“The person who had the key, of course.”

“But Mr. Davenheim had the key.”

“Exactly. And that is why I think Mr. Davenheim opened the safe
himself.”

“But why would he do that?”

“To make it look like a burglary, of course.”

“But why would he want to do that?”

“Because he was in financial difficulties, Hastings. Very serious
financial difficulties.”

“But I thought he was a wealthy man.”

“He was—until he began to speculate in South American shares. He
lost a great deal of money, and he was on the verge of bankruptcy.
He needed a way out, and he came up with a very clever plan.”

“What plan?”

“He decided to ‘disappear’ and take as much money and jewellery
with him as possible. He would then start a new life in another
country, under a new name.”

“But what about the body?”

“There was no body, Hastings. I told you that before.”

“But what about the clothes?”

“They were a plant, my friend. He left them in the lake to make it
look as if he had been murdered.”

“But where is he now?”

“He is here, Hastings. In this very house.”

“In this house? But where?”

“Wait a little, my friend. All will be revealed in good time.”

Poirot went to the door and called the footman.

“Will you please ask Mrs. Davenheim to come here?” he said.

A few minutes later Mrs. Davenheim entered the room. She looked
very pale and nervous.

“You wished to see me, Monsieur Poirot?” she asked.

“Yes, madame,” said Poirot. “I have some very important news for
you.”

“News? What news?”

“I have found your husband.”

Mrs. Davenheim gasped. “Where? Where is he?”

“He is in this room, madame,” said Poirot quietly.

Mrs. Davenheim looked around the room in bewilderment. “In this
room? But I don’t see him.”

Poirot walked over to the safe and pointed to it.

“He is in there, madame.”

Mrs. Davenheim stared at him in horror. “In the safe? But that’s
impossible!”

“Is it, madame? Let us see.”

Poirot took a small key from his pocket and inserted it into the
lock of the safe. He turned the key and the door of the safe swung
open.

Inside the safe, crouched in a small space, was a man. He was thin
and pale, with a long, grey beard and bushy eyebrows.

“Mr. Davenheim!” I cried.

The man looked up at us with a terrified expression.

“It’s no use,” he said in a weak voice. “You’ve found me.”

Mrs. Davenheim burst into tears. “Oh, Arthur! How could you do such
a thing?”

Mr. Davenheim came out of the safe and sat down in a chair. He
looked like a broken man.

“I had to do it,” he said. “I was ruined. I thought I could start
again in another country.”

“But why did you hide in the safe?” I asked.

“I didn’t hide in the safe,” he said. “I was locked in.”

“Locked in? By whom?”

“By Lowen.”

“Lowen?”

“Yes. He came to see me that evening. He knew about my financial
difficulties and he offered to help me. But he wanted a price. He
wanted me to give him the bearer bonds and the jewellery from the
safe. I refused, and we had a fight. He knocked me unconscious and
locked me in the safe. He then took the bonds and the jewellery and
left.”

“But how did he get the key?”

“I had it in my pocket. He must have taken it when I was unconscious.”

“And how did he know how to open the safe?”

“He’s a clever man, as Monsieur Poirot said. He must have figured it out.”

“But why did he leave the clothes in the lake?”

“He didn’t. I did. I had already planned my disappearance, and I
had left the clothes in the lake before Lowen arrived. I was going
to leave the house that night and never come back.”

“But what about the ring?”

“I must have dropped it when I was struggling with Lowen.”

Poirot looked at Mr. Davenheim with a grave expression.

“It is a very sad story, monsieur,” he said. “But I am afraid you
will have to come with us to the police station.”

Mr. Davenheim nodded. “I know. I’m ready.”

As we were leaving The Cedars, I turned to Poirot.

“Poirot, how did you know that Mr. Davenheim was in the safe?”

“I didn’t, Hastings. It was another little bluff. But it worked,
did it not?”

“It certainly did. But how did you know that Lowen had locked him
in the safe?”

“I didn’t, Hastings. I only suspected it. But when I saw the safe,
I realized that it was the only place where he could be hiding.”

“But why didn’t he call for help?”

“The safe is soundproof, Hastings. No one would have heard him.”

“But how did he survive for so long?”

“There were some biscuits and a bottle of wine in the safe. He must
have lived on those.”

“And what about Lowen? What will happen to him?”

“He will be arrested for robbery and attempted murder. I think he
will be spending a long time in prison.”

“And Mr. Davenheim?”

“He will also be going to prison, I’m afraid. But at least he is
alive.”

As we walked back to the station, I couldn’t help but marvel at
Poirot’s brilliance. He had solved the mystery of the disappearance
of Mr. Davenheim without moving from his chair.

“You are a truly remarkable man, Poirot,” I said.

Poirot smiled. “It is the little grey cells, my friend. The little
grey cells.”

“_Du tout, du tout_, my friend. Not for a moment! It’s far more
probable that Lowen threw the ring away, as the tramp says. If it
hadn’t been for that, we shouldn’t have had a scrap of evidence
against him. He’d probably have made off with his booty by now,
if it hadn’t been for that. However, that’s all I’ve got to tell
you for the present.”

“One question,” said Poirot. “Were there any other rings on the
body? I mean on the man’s hands?”

“Why, no, he only wore one ring.”

“Thank you,” said Poirot. “I think that is all I want to know at
present.”

Japp turned to me as he was going out. “The little man is getting
more and more ‘off it’ every day, isn’t he? Asking about other
rings! Why, a child could see the importance of that ring!”

“And its being pawned by Billy Kellett?” I added.

“Just so. Well, I must be going. I hope I shall have more news for
you by to-morrow evening.”

“I have no doubt of it,” Poirot called after him. “The little grey
cells, they work without ceasing.”

When the door had closed behind Japp, Poirot turned to me with a
smile. “You see, Hastings, the case is becoming more and more
interesting. What did I tell you? Obscure! Very obscure! And yet
the solution is simple—so simple that it is positively absurd.”

“Then you have solved it?” I asked, in some surprise.

“Not yet—not yet. There is still one point that is not quite clear.
I must reflect. One must use the little grey cells. But I have
already a very good idea of the truth. It is all a matter of
method.”

I was about to ask another question, but Poirot checked me.

“No, no, my friend. I must be alone. I must think.”

He sat down in his large armchair, and closed his eyes. I knew from
experience that it was useless to disturb him, so I took up a book
and began to read. Half an hour later he rouse himself, and there
was a look of satisfaction on his face.

“It is finished!” he exclaimed. “The mystery is solved! I know now
the truth about Mr. Davenheim.”

“You do?” I cried. “Then tell me!”

“Not yet, my friend. Not yet. I must have one or two more facts to
confirm my theory. Japp will provide them to-morrow. In the
meantime, let us go to bed. I have a feeling that we shall have an
eventful day to-morrow.”

I could get nothing more out of him, so I was forced to be content
with that.

The next morning, Poirot was in high spirits. He was humming a
little French song to himself as he ate his breakfast.

“You seem very cheerful this morning,” I remarked.

“And why not, my friend? The sun shines, the birds sing—and I have
solved a very pretty little problem. What more could a man desire?”

“I wish you’d tell me about it,” I said.

“Patience, Hastings, patience! All in good time. Japp will be here
presently, and then you shall hear all.”

“I suppose you’re quite sure you’re right?”

“_Mais oui_, my friend. There can be no doubt about it. The facts
all point to one conclusion.”

“And what is that?”

“Ah! That you shall hear in due course.”

I saw it was useless to pursue the subject, so I turned to the
morning paper.

About eleven o’clock, Japp was announced. He looked even more
excited than he had on the previous evening.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, as he came into the room. “I’ve
got some news for you. We’ve found the body!”

“The body?” I cried. “Where?”

“In the lake?” asked Poirot quietly.

“No, it wasn’t in the lake. It was in the boathouse!”

“The boathouse?” I repeated.

“Yes. It seems that Miller, with his usual thoroughness, decided
to search the boathouse again this morning. And there, hidden
under a pile of old sails and lumber, he found the body of a man.”

“Was it Mr. Davenheim?” I asked.

“Well, that’s just the point,” said Japp. “The face is so badly
battered that it’s quite unrecognizable. But the clothes are
undoubtedly those of Mr. Davenheim.”

“And what does Mrs. Davenheim say?” asked Poirot.

“She’s naturally very much upset. She’s seen the body, but as I
said, the face is so disfigured that she can’t be sure. However,
she recognizes the clothes, and she’s identified a small pocket-knife
which was found in one of the pockets.”

“Anything else?”

“Yes. There’s a wound on the back of the head which might have
been caused by a blow from some heavy instrument. It looks like
murder, right enough.”

“And Lowen?”

“We’ve got him, safe and sound. He’s been formally charged with
the murder of Mr. Davenheim.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And what about Billy Kellett?”

“Oh, we’ve still got him, too. He’s being held as a material
witness.”

“I see,” said Poirot again. “Well, Japp, I must congratulate you.
You and Miller have done a very good piece of work.”

“Thank you, Monsieur Poirot. I must say, I didn’t think we’d find
the body so soon.”

“Neither did I,” said Poirot. “But then, as I said, the case was
obscure. Very obscure.”

“Well, it’s clear enough now,” said Japp. “Lowen murdered him,
and hid the body in the boathouse. Then he tried to get rid of
the ring by throwing it away, but unfortunately for him, Billy
Kellett was there to see him do it.”

“It certainly seems very clear,” I said.

“Does it not?” said Poirot. “And yet, there are one or two things
that still puzzle me.”

“What are they?” asked Japp.

“Well, for one thing, why should Lowen have hidden the body in
the boathouse? It seems a very risky thing to do.”

“Oh, I don’t know,” said Japp. “It was a good place to hide it
for the time being. He probably intended to move it later on.”

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “And then there’s the question of the
ring. Why should he have thrown it away? It was a very valuable
ring. Surely he would have tried to sell it?”

“Well, he probably realized that it was too dangerous to keep,”
said Japp. “He might have been afraid that it would be identified.”

“True,” said Poirot. “But then, why throw it away in such a
public place? He might have been seen—as indeed he was.”

“Well, people do foolish things when they’re in a panic,” said
Japp.

“That is true,” said Poirot. “But Lowen does not strike me as a
man who would be easily panicked.”

“You never can tell,” said Japp. “Anyway, the evidence against
him is very strong.”

“It is,” said Poirot. “Very strong indeed. And yet, I cannot help
feeling that there is something—something missing.”

“Missing? What could be missing?”

“I do not know,” said Poirot. “That is what I must find out.”

He fell into a brown study, and for some time no one spoke. At
last he looked up.

“Japp,” he said, “I want you to do me a favour.”

“What is it?”

“I want you to take me down to Chingside. I should like to see
The Cedars for myself.”

“Certainly, if you like. But I don’t see what you expect to find
there that we haven’t found already.”

“Perhaps nothing,” said Poirot. “But I should like to see it,
all the same.”

“Very well. We’ll go down this afternoon.”

And so it was arranged. After lunch, we all three set off for
Chingside.

The Cedars was a large and imposing house, set in extensive
grounds. We were met at the door by Mrs. Davenheim, a pale,
anxious-looking woman who seemed to be on the verge of a
nervous breakdown.

“It’s all so terrible,” she moaned. “I can’t believe it’s true.
To think that my poor husband should have been murdered in
his own grounds!”

Poirot spoke a few words of comfort to her, and then asked if
we might see the study.

“Of course,” she said. “This way.”

She led us into a large, comfortably furnished room. Poirot
walked over to the window and looked out.

“The rose-garden,” he murmured. “And the lake beyond.”

He turned back into the room and began to examine the safe.

“A very professional piece of work,” he remarked.

“Yes,” said Japp. “Miller says it’s one of the neatest jobs
he’s ever seen.”

Poirot nodded. He then began to wander round the room, looking
at the pictures and ornaments. Suddenly he stopped in front of
a large photograph in a silver frame.

“Mr. Davenheim?” he asked.

“Yes,” said Mrs. Davenheim. “That was taken just before he went
to South America last year.”

Poirot studied the photograph for some time. Then he turned to
Mrs. Davenheim.

“Madam,” he said, “I understand that your husband had a great
many jewels?”

“Yes, he was very fond of them. He used to buy them for me,
but he really bought them for himself, I think. He loved to
look at them and handle them.”

“And they were all in the safe?”

“Yes, all of them.”

“I see. And was there anything else in the safe? Any papers?
Any documents?”

“Yes, there were some bearer bonds, and a large sum in notes.”

“I see. And were they all taken?”

“Yes, everything.”

Poirot nodded. He then turned to Japp.

“Japp,” he said, “I should like to see the boathouse.”

“Certainly. It’s just down by the lake.”

We all walked down to the lake. The boathouse was a small,
wooden building, standing at the edge of the water. Inside,
everything was in a state of confusion. Old sails, oars, and
other lumber were scattered about.

“This is where we found the body,” said Japp, pointing to a
corner of the room.

Poirot walked over to the spot and looked down. Then he began
to look around the room, poking into corners and examining
the various objects. Suddenly he stooped and picked something
up from the floor.

“What have you found?” I asked.

Poirot held up a small, dark object. It was a piece of black
silk.

“A piece of a man’s tie,” he said.

“A tie?” said Japp. “What of it?”

“It is a very unusual tie,” said Poirot. “It is made of a
very fine quality of silk, and it has a very peculiar pattern.”

He handed it to Japp, who examined it closely.

“You’re right,” he said. “It is an unusual pattern. I don’t
think I’ve ever seen anything quite like it before.”

“Neither have I,” said Poirot. “And yet, it seems strangely
familiar.”

He stood for a moment, lost in thought. Then he turned to Japp.

“Japp,” he said, “I want you to do something for me.”

“What is it?”

“I want you to find out where Mr. Davenheim bought his ties.”

“His ties? What on earth for?”

“Never mind what for. Just find out, if you can.”

“Well, I suppose I can ask his valet.”

“Do so, my friend. Do so at once.”

Japp went off to find the valet, and Poirot and I were left
alone in the boathouse.

“What’s the idea, Poirot?” I asked. “What’s the tie got to do
with it?”

“Everything, my friend. Everything. But I must be sure. I must
be absolutely sure.”

He walked over to the window and looked out across the lake.

“A very beautiful spot,” he murmured. “A very beautiful spot
indeed. It seems a pity that it should have been the scene of
such a terrible crime.”

A few minutes later, Japp returned.

“Well,” he said, “I’ve seen the valet. He says that Mr.
Davenheim always bought his ties at a shop in Bond Street
called ‘The Golden Fleece’.”

“‘The Golden Fleece’?” repeated Poirot. “I know it. A very
exclusive shop. And did he buy this particular tie there?”

“The valet doesn’t know. He says he’s never seen it before.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “That is very interesting. Very
interesting indeed.”

He turned and walked out of the boathouse.

“Well, Poirot,” said Japp, as we walked back to the house.
“What do you make of it all?”

“I make a great deal of it, my friend. A great deal indeed.
But I must have one more piece of evidence before I can be
sure.”

“And what is that?”

“I must see Billy Kellett.”

“Billy Kellett? But why? We’ve already got his story.”

“I know. But I want to ask him one or two questions myself.”

“Well, I suppose it can be arranged. We can go to Bow Street
on our way back.”

“Excellent,” said Poirot. “Excellent.”

And so, after saying goodbye to Mrs. Davenheim, we drove back
to London. At Bow Street, we were shown into a small room where
Billy Kellett was waiting for us. He was a miserable-looking
object, with a red nose and watery eyes.

“Now then, Kellett,” said Japp. “This is Monsieur Poirot. He
wants to ask you a few questions.”

Kellett looked at Poirot with suspicion.

“I’ve told you all I know,” he said surlily.

“I am sure you have, my friend,” said Poirot pleasantly. “But
there are just one or two small points I should like to clear up.
For instance, you say that the man you saw threw something over
the hedge?”

“That’s right. A small object it was. Fell with a chink.”

“I see. And was it a ring?”

“Yes, it was a ring. A big gold ring with a diamond in it.”

“I see. And what did the man look like?”

“I’ve told you. A dark-complexioned gent, with a big moustache.
One of them city toffs.”

“I see. And was he wearing a tie?”

Kellett looked surprised.

“A tie? I suppose so. Most gents do.”

“And do you remember what kind of a tie it was?”

Kellett thought for a moment.

“Well, now you mention it, it was a dark-coloured tie. Black,
I think.”

“I see. And did it have a pattern on it?”

“I didn’t notice no pattern.”

“I see. Now, think carefully, Kellett. Was there anything else
about the man that you noticed? Anything unusual?”

Kellett shook his head.

“No, I can’t say as there was. He just looked like any other
city gent.”

“I see. Well, thank you, Kellett. That will be all.”

As we left the room, Japp turned to Poirot.

“Well,” he said, “did you get what you wanted?”

“I did, my friend. I did indeed.”

“And what was that?”

“The final link in the chain. The mystery is now completely
solved.”

“It is? Then for heaven’s sake, tell us! Who murdered Mr.
Davenheim?”

Poirot smiled.

“All in good time, my friend. All in good time. First, we must
go back to my rooms. I have a little surprise for you.”

We drove back to Poirot’s rooms in silence. I was burning with
curiosity, but I knew it was no use trying to get anything out
of Poirot until he was ready to tell us.

When we arrived, Poirot led us into his sitting-room. On the
table was a small parcel.

“What’s this?” asked Japp.

“A little something I picked up at ‘The Golden Fleece’ this
morning,” said Poirot.

He unwrapped the parcel. Inside was a tie—the exact double of
the piece of silk Poirot had found in the boathouse.

“You see?” said Poirot. “It is the same tie.”

“But what does it mean?” I asked.

“It means, my friend, that the man who was in the boathouse
was not Mr. Davenheim.”

“Not Mr. Davenheim?” I cried. “Then who was it?”

“It was the man who murdered him,” said Poirot.

“But who was that?” asked Japp.

“Think, my friend. Who was the man who was seen coming towards
the study through the rose-garden? Who was the man who was
seen throwing the ring over the hedge? Who was the man who
had an appointment with Mr. Davenheim that evening?”

“Lowen!” I cried.

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “Lowen.”

“But why should he have been wearing Mr. Davenheim’s tie?”
asked Japp.

“He wasn’t,” said Poirot. “He was wearing his own tie. But it
was a tie that he had bought at ‘The Golden Fleece’—just as
Mr. Davenheim did.”

“I don’t understand,” said Japp.

“It is quite simple, my friend. Lowen and Davenheim were both
customers of ‘The Golden Fleece’. They both liked the same
kind of ties. And on that Saturday, they both happened to be
wearing the same kind of tie.”

“But how does that help us?” I asked.

“It helps us a great deal, my friend. Because, you see, the
piece of silk I found in the boathouse was not from Mr.
Davenheim’s tie. It was from Lowen’s tie.”

“How do you know?”

“Because Mr. Davenheim’s valet had never seen it before. If
it had been Mr. Davenheim’s tie, he would have recognized it.”

“I see,” said Japp. “But if Lowen murdered Davenheim, why
did he leave a piece of his tie behind?”

“He didn’t,” said Poirot. “It was left there by the man who
really murdered Mr. Davenheim.”

“The man who really murdered him? But you just said it was
Lowen!”

“No, no, my friend. I said that the evidence pointed to Lowen.
But the evidence was too good. It was too clear. And as I
told you, when a thing is clear as daylight, I mistrust it.”

“Then who was it?” I asked.

“Think, my friend. Who had the most to gain from Mr.
Davenheim’s death? Who had access to the safe? Who could have
hidden the body in the boathouse without being seen?”

“Not—not Mrs. Davenheim?” I gasped.

“No, not Mrs. Davenheim,” said Poirot. “But someone very close
to her. Someone who knew all about Mr. Davenheim’s affairs.
Someone who knew where the jewels were kept. Someone who knew
about the appointment with Lowen.”

“The junior partner?” suggested Japp.

“No, not the junior partner,” said Poirot. “The man who
murdered Mr. Davenheim was Mr. Davenheim himself!”

“Mr. Davenheim?” we both cried in unison.

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “Mr. Davenheim murdered himself—in
a figurative sense, of course.”

“But the body?” I cried. “Whose body was it in the boathouse?”

“The body,” said Poirot, “was that of a man who had been
murdered by Mr. Davenheim. A man who had been lured to The
Cedars for that very purpose.”

“But who was he?” asked Japp.

“He was a man who bore a certain resemblance to Mr. Davenheim.
A man who could be made to look like him—especially after his
face had been battered beyond recognition.”

“But where did he find such a man?”

“He didn’t have to find him,” said Poirot. “He was already
there. He was a man who had been in Mr. Davenheim’s employ for
some time. A man who had been seen around the grounds of
The Cedars.”

“Not—not one of the gardeners?” I asked.

“No,” said Poirot. “It was Billy Kellett!”

“Billy Kellett?” I cried. “But Billy Kellett is alive! We saw
him this morning!”

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “And that is the beauty of the whole
plan. Billy Kellett is alive—but the man who was murdered
was also Billy Kellett!”

“I don’t understand,” said Japp.

“It is quite simple, my friend. There were two Billy Kelletts.
Or rather, there was one Billy Kellett, and another man who
called himself Billy Kellett. The man you saw this morning
was the real Billy Kellett. The man whose body was found in
the boathouse was the other Billy Kellett—the man who had
been murdered by Mr. Davenheim.”

“But who was this other Billy Kellett?”

“He was a man whom Mr. Davenheim had met in South America. A
man who bore a striking resemblance to himself. He brought
him back to England, and kept him in hiding at The Cedars.
Then, on that Saturday, he murdered him, dressed him in his
own clothes, and hid the body in the boathouse. He then broke
into his own safe, took the jewels and the money, and
disappeared—taking on the identity of Billy Kellett!”

“But what about the ring?” I asked. “And Lowen?”

“That was the most brilliant part of the whole plan,” said
Poirot. “Mr. Davenheim—as Billy Kellett—purposely allowed
himself to be seen by Lowen. He then threw the ring away,
knowing that Lowen would be blamed for the murder. He then
went to London, pawned the ring, and got himself arrested for
a minor offence, knowing that he would be safe in prison
while the police were looking for Mr. Davenheim!”

“It’s incredible!” I gasped.

“It is more than incredible,” said Poirot. “It is
_magnifique_! But unfortunately for Mr. Davenheim, he made
one small mistake.”

“What was that?” asked Japp.

“He forgot that I, Hercule Poirot, would be on the case. And
he forgot about the tie!”

“The tie?”

“Yes. He had forgotten to change his tie. He was still
wearing the tie he had bought at ‘The Golden Fleece’. And
it was a piece of that tie that I found in the boathouse—a
piece that had been torn off in the struggle with his victim!”

“But how did you know it was his tie?”

“Because, as I told you, it was a very unusual tie. And when
I saw the photograph of Mr. Davenheim, I noticed that he was
wearing a tie of the same pattern. I then went to ‘The Golden
Fleece’ and found that only two such ties had been sold—one
to Mr. Davenheim, and one to Mr. Lowen!”

“But you said it was Lowen’s tie!”

“No, I said it was a tie like Lowen’s. But it was actually
Mr. Davenheim’s tie. And since the man who was murdered was
wearing Mr. Davenheim’s clothes, he should also have been
wearing Mr. Davenheim’s tie. But he wasn’t! He was wearing
a different tie altogether. And that tie was the one I found
the piece of in the boathouse!”

“I see,” said Japp. “So the man who was murdered was not
wearing the tie that Mr. Davenheim was wearing when he left
the house?”

“Exactly! And that could only mean one thing—that the man
who was murdered was not Mr. Davenheim!”

“And the man who murdered him was?”

“Mr. Davenheim himself! Who is now safely in prison under
the name of Billy Kellett!”

Japp slapped his knee.

“By Jove, Poirot! You’ve done it again! I’ll go and get him
at once!”

He rushed out of the room, and Poirot and I were left alone.

“Well, Hastings,” said Poirot, with a smile. “What do you
think of my little grey cells now?”

“I think they’re amazing, Poirot. Simply amazing.”

“_Merci, mon ami. Merci._ And now, I think we have earned
our tea. Let us see if we can find some of those little cakes
that you like so much.”

And as we sat down to tea, I couldn’t help thinking that
Hercule Poirot was indeed the greatest detective in the
world.

“You forget that he has not been found. If he were murdered, the
body would be there for all to see. To dispose of it would have
been impossible for a man like Kellett. As for the ring—what did
he say about it?”

“Said he didn’t know it was a diamond! Thought it was a bit of
glass.”

“That is quite a likely thing for a man of his class to say.”

“Exactly,” said Japp. “Well, that’s how the matter stands. We
arrested Lowen this afternoon.”

Poirot looked at him thoughtfully. “And what about the safe?”

“Oh, that’s all right. We’ve found out that the contents were
intact until Saturday afternoon. Davenheim had been seen at the
safe by the head gardener. He was putting some papers inside it.
Then, about half-past five, a housemaid who was dusting in the
hall heard him go into the study and lock the door after him.
The window was already fastened. No doubt the theft took place
immediately after he had left the house.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “By the way, did any one see him leave the
grounds?”

“Not a soul.”

“Is there any other way out?”

“There’s a small door at the bottom of the rose-garden which leads
out on to a footpath across the fields to the station. It is
ordinarily kept locked, but the gardener says he saw it open on
Saturday afternoon.”

“Was it open when he came back?”

“No, it was locked again.”

“Wait a moment,” said Poirot. “This is most interesting. The
gardener saw it open, and then he saw it locked. When did he see
it locked?”

“Just before he left off work—at six o’clock.”

“Then it must have been opened and locked again between half-past
five and six?”

“Exactly.”

“You are sure of that?”

“Yes. The gardener is quite positive.”

“One other point. What was the weather like on Saturday afternoon?”

“Fine. A beautiful day.”

“And on Sunday?”

“Rained hard all day.”

“H’m!” Poirot sank into a brown study.

Japp rose. “Well, I must be off. I’ve a lot to do. You’ll be seeing
Miller to-morrow, I expect. He’s going down to Chingside again.
Any message for him?”

“Only one,” said Poirot. “Ask him if Mr. Davenheim’s hair was
long or short?”

Japp stared. “Short, I should think. In fact, I know it was. Why?”

“Nothing. I merely wondered.”

Japp laughed and went out.

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, turning to me, “I am going to ask you
to do me a little service. Will you go down to Chingside to-morrow,
and see if you can get a glimpse of Mrs. Davenheim?”

“Certainly, if you wish it. But what for?”

“I want to know if she has any jewels—or if she has had any lately.”

“Japp said her husband was always giving her some.”

“Exactly. I want to know if she has them still.”

“I see.”

“And there is one other thing. Find out if she has any brothers.”

“Brothers? What on earth——”

“Never mind, my friend. Just find out. It is a little idea of
mine.”

I did as Poirot requested. I went down to Chingside the following
morning, and by a little judicious questioning of the local
tradespeople I soon found out all I wanted to know. Mrs. Davenheim
had several very fine pieces of jewellery, and had been seen
wearing them quite recently. As for brothers, she had one, a man
called David Salmon, who was a partner in her husband’s firm. He
had been in South America for some years, but had recently returned
to England.

I duly reported these facts to Poirot. He seemed interested, but
made no comment.

The next few days passed without any further developments. Japp
dropped in once or twice, but had nothing of importance to
communicate. The lake had been dragged, but without result. No
trace of the missing man had been found.

On Thursday morning, however, Japp arrived in a state of great
excitement.

“We’ve got him!” he cried. “We’ve got him!”

“Whom have you got?” asked Poirot.

“Davenheim! We found him this morning.”

“Where?”

“In a small hotel in London. He’d been staying there under an
assumed name since Saturday night.”

“Was he alone?”

“Quite alone. He seems to be in a state of great nervous
exhaustion. He says he can’t remember anything that has happened
since he left his house on Saturday afternoon.”

“Aha!” said Poirot. “The second category—the loss of memory!”

“Exactly. But Miller doesn’t believe a word of it. He thinks the
whole thing was a plant to get away with the money and the jewels.
You see, the firm of Davenheim and Salmon is on the verge of
bankruptcy. This disappearance was a last desperate effort to
save something from the wreck.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And the safe?”

“Oh, he had the key of that with him. He’d evidently helped
himself before he left.”

“And the clothes?”

“He must have had a spare suit with him in a bag. He probably
changed in the boathouse.”

“I see,” said Poirot again. “And what about Lowen?”

“We’ve had to let him go, of course. There’s no evidence against
him now. It’s a bit of a blow for Miller, but it can’t be helped.”

Japp laughed. “Well, Monsieur Poirot, I’m afraid you’ve lost your
fiver. We’ve found Mr. Davenheim, and it wasn’t through any of
your ‘little grey cells’!”

Poirot smiled. “Are you so sure of that, my friend?”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean that if you will have the goodness to wait a few minutes,
I will show you that I have not lost my fiver after all.”

He went to the telephone and spoke a few words in a low voice.
Then he returned to his chair.

“In a few minutes,” he said, “a gentleman will be here who will,
I think, throw a new light on this little problem.”

We waited in silence. Ten minutes later the door opened and a
man was shown in. He was a tall, dark man with a thick black
moustache. I recognized him at once from Japp’s description. It
was Mr. Lowen.

He looked from one to the other of us in some surprise.

“I was told that Monsieur Poirot wished to see me on a matter of
importance,” he said.

“That is so,” said Poirot. “Will you be seated, Mr. Lowen?”

Lowen sat down. “I must confess,” he said, “that I am at a loss
to understand why you should wish to see me. I have already told
the police all I know about this unfortunate business.”

“_Précisément_,” said Poirot. “But there are one or two points
which I should like to clear up. For instance, why did you go to
the rose-garden on Saturday afternoon?”

Lowen hesitated. “I have already explained that. I went to look
at a rose.”

“A very natural proceeding,” said Poirot. “But why did you go
at that particular moment? Why did you not wait until Mr.
Davenheim returned?”

“I—I really don’t know. I suppose I was restless.”

“I see. And did you see anyone in the rose-garden?”

“No one.”

“Not even Mr. Davenheim?”

“Certainly not.”

“That is strange,” said Poirot. “Because the gardener saw a
figure in the rose-garden at that time. He could not say for
certain who it was, but he thought it was his master.”

“He was mistaken,” said Lowen shortly.

“Perhaps. Now, Mr. Lowen, I am going to ask you a very direct
question. Did you, or did you not, see Mr. Davenheim on Saturday
afternoon?”

Lowen’s face turned a curious grey colour. “I—I have already
told you,” he stammered.

“I know what you have told the police,” said Poirot. “But I am
asking you now. Did you see him?”

Lowen did not answer. He sat staring at Poirot as though
fascinated.

“I will tell you what I think happened,” said Poirot. “I think
you did see Mr. Davenheim. I think you met him in the
rose-garden, and that you had a very heated interview with him.
I think that, in the course of that interview, he told you
something which—shall we say—surprised you?”

Lowen still did not speak.

“Shall I go on?” asked Poirot.

Lowen made a gesture of assent.

“I think,” said Poirot, “that Mr. Davenheim told you he was
going to disappear. I think he told you that he was going to
rob his own safe, and that he was going to leave his clothes
by the lake to make it appear that he had committed suicide.
And I think he asked for your help.”

“My help!” cried Lowen. “Why should he ask for my help?”

“Because,” said Poirot, “you were in his power. You had been
engaged in certain transactions which—shall we say—would not
bear the light of day. Mr. Davenheim knew of these
transactions, and he used his knowledge to force you to assist
him.”

Lowen sank back in his chair. “It’s true,” he whispered. “He
forced me to do it. He said if I didn’t help him, he’d ruin me.”

“And what was the nature of the help he required?”

“He wanted me to take the jewels and the money and keep them
for him until he could join me in South America. He said he
couldn’t take them with him, as he might be searched.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And you agreed?”

“I had no choice. He told me to meet him in the rose-garden at
a quarter past six. He gave me the jewels and the money then,
and I took them away with me.”

“And where are they now?”

“I have them. I was going to take them to South America next
week.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Well, Mr. Lowen, I think you have been
very wise to tell the truth. It will save you a great deal of
trouble in the long run.”

He turned to Japp. “Well, my friend, what do you say to that?”

Japp was speechless. At last he found his voice.

“But—but Davenheim! We’ve got him! He’s in London! He says he
doesn’t remember anything!”

“_Exactly_,” said Poirot. “He doesn’t remember anything because
he has nothing to remember. The man you have in London is not
Mr. Davenheim.”

“Not Mr. Davenheim? Then who is he?”

“He is Mr. Billy Kellett,” said Poirot calmly.

“Billy Kellett! But we saw him at Bow Street! He was a
miserable, half-starved creature with a week’s growth of
beard!”

“_Précisément_,” said Poirot. “But a week is a long time, my
friend. A man can grow a very respectable beard in a week—if he
has the right kind of hair. And as for being half-starved—well,
that is easily managed.”

“But the photograph!” cried Japp. “The photograph in the
newspapers!”

“Ah!” said Poirot. “That is where the cleverness of the plan
comes in. Mr. Davenheim was a man of method. He knew that if he
disappeared, his photograph would be in all the papers. So what
did he do? He grew a beard and a moustache, and he had his
photograph taken. Then he shaved off the beard and the
moustache, and lived for several years as—Mr. Billy Kellett!”

“Lived as Billy Kellett?”

“Certainly. For several months every year he would disappear
from his home, ostensibly on business, and live the life of a
criminal in London. He chose a man who was roughly his own
height and build, and who had no friends or relations. Then,
when the time came for his disappearance, he simply resumed
his character of Billy Kellett. He knew that the police would
never suspect a common criminal of being a wealthy banker.
And to make doubly sure, he arranged for his own arrest on a
minor charge, so that he would be safely in prison while the
search for Mr. Davenheim was at its height.”

“But the ring!” I cried. “What about the ring?”

“That was a very clever touch,” said Poirot. “He threw the ring
away where he knew it would be found. He wanted the police to
think that Billy Kellett had found it. It was all part of the
plan to establish the identity of Billy Kellett.”

“And the clothes?”

“He left them by the lake to suggest suicide. He knew they
would be found sooner or later.”

“But why did he do it?” asked Japp. “Why didn’t he just go off
to South America with the money?”

“Because he knew he would be followed. He wanted to make a
complete break with his old life. He wanted Mr. Davenheim to
die, so that Billy Kellett could live.”

“And what about Mrs. Davenheim?” I asked. “Did she know?”

“I think not,” said Poirot. “She was, as Japp said, a rather
unintelligent woman. She probably believed her husband’s
stories of business trips.”

“And the brother? David Salmon?”

“Ah!” said Poirot. “That was a little idea of mine. I thought
perhaps he was in it too. But it seems I was wrong. Mr.
Davenheim was a solitary worker.”

He turned to Lowen. “And now, Mr. Lowen, if you will be so good
as to hand over the jewels and the money to Inspector Japp, I
think we may consider this little matter closed.”

Lowen rose. He looked like a broken man. “I’ll get them,” he
said. “They’re at my house.”

He went out, followed by Japp.

Poirot turned to me with a smile. “Well, Hastings, what do you
think of my ‘little grey cells’ now?”

“I think they’re marvelous, Poirot,” I said. “But there’s one
thing I don’t understand. How did you know that the man in
London was Billy Kellett?”

“I did not know it, my friend. I suspected it. You see, there
were several things that did not fit in. To begin with, there
was the question of the hair. Japp said Mr. Davenheim’s hair
was short. But the photograph showed it as being long and wavy.
Now, a man can cut his hair, but he cannot make it grow long in
a few days. Therefore, the photograph must have been taken some
time before the disappearance. But why should a man have his
photograph taken with long hair if he usually wears it short?
Only if he wants to use that photograph as a means of
identification later on.”

“I see.”

“Then there was the matter of the ring. Why should a man like
Davenheim throw away a valuable diamond ring? Only if he wanted
it to be found. And why should he want it to be found? Only to
draw attention to Billy Kellett.”

“And the safe?”

“Ah, the safe! That was the most significant thing of all. You
remember Japp said the gardener had seen Mr. Davenheim at the
safe on Saturday afternoon. Now, why should a man who is
planning to disappear let himself be seen at his safe? Only if
he wants to establish the fact that the safe was intact at that
time.”

“I see. It was all very carefully planned.”

“Very carefully. But Mr. Davenheim made one mistake. He forgot
that Papa Poirot has eyes that see more than a London sparrow!”

He leaned back in his chair and smiled contentedly.

“And the fiver, Poirot?” I asked. “What are you going to do with
it?”

“I think,” said Poirot, “that I shall spend it on a very large
and very expensive box of chocolates. And you, my friend, shall
help me to eat them!”

I laughed. “I think you’ve earned them, Poirot!”

And so ended the mystery of the disappearance of Mr. Davenheim.
It was one of the most remarkable cases in which Poirot was
ever involved, and it remains to this day a testament to the
power of his “little grey cells.”

“I do not think that is likely. What do you say, Hastings? Does
that seem a probable solution of the mystery to you?”

“No,” I said slowly. “I think Lowen is the man we want.”

“The question is, where is Davenheim?” said Japp. “If he’s been
murdered by Lowen, as I believe, where is the body? Why didn’t he
take the ring off? If he threw it away, it looks more like a panic
than anything else.”

“A ring is a difficult thing to dispose of,” I suggested. “He may
have thought it was too dangerous to keep.”

“But not too dangerous to throw over a hedge where anyone might
find it?” Poirot shook his head. “No, no, that is not like a clever
man. And Lowen, by all accounts, is a clever man.”

“_Eh bien!_” Japp got up and took his hat. “Well, I’ll be going.
I’ve a good deal to do yet. I’m off to Chingside to-morrow.”

“One moment,” said Poirot. “You told me, I think, that Mr.
Davenheim’s valet was quite positive that no clothes were missing?”

“Quite positive.”

“And you yourself have seen the contents of the wardrobe?”

“Yes.”

“There were no gaps—nothing to show that anything had been taken?”

“Not that I could see.”

“Is there a large number of boots?”

“Boots? What on earth do you want to know about his boots for?”

“I have a fancy for boots. Did you see many pairs?”

“About twenty, I should say.”

Poirot’s eyes glistened. “And were they all clean? Or were some of
them dirty?”

“They were all as bright as mirrors. Davenheim was a very particular
man. Why, I don’t believe he ever went out without his boots being
polished!”

“And you are quite sure they were all there?”

“I’ve no reason to doubt it. But I’ll make a point of asking the
valet, if it’ll satisfy you.”

“Do, my good Japp, do. It would be most kind of you.”

Japp laughed and went out.

“What on earth,” I began, “can his boots have to do with the case?”

Poirot looked at me with an air of mild reproach. “_Mon ami_,” he
said, “do you not realize that it is the small things which are
of the most importance? A man may forget many things, but he will
not forget his boots!”

I felt that he was right, but I could not see how it helped us
in the least.

The next few days passed without any further news. Japp did not
put in an appearance, and Poirot seemed to have forgotten all
about the case. He spent most of his time in building complicated
card-houses, which he demolished as soon as they were completed.
I began to think that his “little grey cells” were not working
to much purpose this time.

On Thursday morning, however, Japp reappeared. He looked tired
and discouraged.

“Well,” he said, as he sat down, “I’ve been all over the place,
and I haven’t found a trace of Davenheim. He’s vanished as
completely as if the earth had swallowed him up. As for the boots,
the valet says there were twenty-three pairs, and they’re all there
now.”

“Twenty-three!” said Poirot. “A most inconvenient number! I should
have expected twenty-four. Are you sure there wasn’t a pair
missing?”

“The valet says not.”

“H’m!” Poirot looked disappointed. “And the lake? Have you dragged
it?”

“Yes, and found nothing but an old kettle and some tin cans.”

“And the boathouse?”

“Nothing there, either.”

“H’m!” Poirot seemed more and more depressed. “It’s very strange—very
strange indeed.”

“Well, I’ve done my best,” said Japp. “I don’t see what more I
can do. Unless you’ve got any suggestions to make?”

Poirot shook his head. “No,” he said. “I have no suggestions. But
I should like to see Mrs. Davenheim.”

“Mrs. Davenheim? What for?”

“I have a little theory—it may be nothing—but I should like to
talk to her.”

“Well, there’s no reason why you shouldn’t, if you want to. I’ll
give you a note to her, if you like.”

“Thank you, my friend. That will be very kind of you.”

So it was arranged that Poirot and I should go down to Chingside
that afternoon. We arrived there about three o’clock, and were
shown into the drawing-room. A few minutes later Mrs. Davenheim
came in. She was a small, fair-haired woman, with a rather anxious
expression. She looked as if she had been crying.

“It is very good of you to come, Monsieur Poirot,” she said. “I
have heard so much of you. I hope you will be able to help me.
It is all so terrible—so mysterious!”

“I will do my best, madame,” said Poirot. “But first, I must ask
you a few questions. Your husband, I believe, was a man of very
regular habits?”

“Oh, yes, most regular. He always did the same things at the same
time every day.”

“And he was not a man who was easily upset?”

“No, not as a rule. Of course, he has been rather worried lately
about business matters.”

“Ah! Business matters! Can you tell me what they were?”

“I’m afraid I don’t know much about them. My husband never
discussed business with me. But I know he was very anxious about
some South American investments.”

“South American! Ah, yes! And Mr. Lowen—was he concerned in these
investments?”

“I believe so. My husband seemed to have a very poor opinion of
Mr. Lowen’s business methods.”

“I see. Now, madame, I want you to think very carefully. Did your
husband ever mention to you that he was afraid of anyone—that he
had any enemies?”

Mrs. Davenheim shook her head. “No, never. He always seemed to
be on good terms with everyone.”

“And you cannot think of any reason why he should want to
disappear?”

“None whatever. He had everything he could possibly want.”

“Exactly. Now, about the night he disappeared. You say he left
the house about half-past five?”

“Yes, about then.”

“And he said he was going to post some letters?”

“Yes.”

“Did he have the letters with him?”

“I don’t know. I suppose so.”

“And did he say where he was going to post them?”

“No, he just said he was going down to the village.”

“I see. And he was expecting Mr. Lowen?”

“Yes, at six o’clock.”

“And when Mr. Lowen arrived, your husband had not returned?”

“No.”

“And Mr. Lowen waited in the study for nearly an hour?”

“Yes.”

“And during that time, did you see or hear anything unusual?”

“No, nothing at all.”

“And you didn’t see Mr. Lowen leave the house?”

“No, the maid let him out.”

“I see. Well, thank you, madame. I think that is all I want to
know for the present.”

As we were leaving the house, Poirot turned to me. “Well, Hastings,
what do you think of Mrs. Davenheim?”

“She seems a very pleasant woman,” I said. “But I don’t think she
knows much about her husband’s affairs.”

“No,” said Poirot. “She is, as Japp said, a nonentity. But she
is an observant nonentity.”

“What do you mean?”

“She noticed that her husband was worried about his South American
investments. That is more than many wives would have noticed.”

“I suppose so. But what does it lead to?”

“It leads to many things, my friend. But for the moment, let us go
to the station. I wish to make a few inquiries there.”

At the station, however, we could learn nothing new. No one had
seen Mr. Davenheim on the Saturday afternoon, and no one had
seen any stranger who might have been Mr. Lowen.

“It is as I thought,” said Poirot, as we were travelling back to
town. “The mystery of Mr. Davenheim is a very simple one—if one
only knows where to look for the key.”

“And do you know where to look for it?” I asked.

“I think so, Hastings. I think so.”

But more than that he would not say.

The next day passed without any further developments. Japp did
not appear, and Poirot spent his time, as usual, in building
card-houses. I was beginning to get very impatient.

“Look here, Poirot,” I said at last. “You’ve only got two days
left. If you don’t find Mr. Davenheim by Sunday, you’ll lose your
bet.”

“I know, Hastings, I know. But do not be in such a hurry. The
little grey cells are working—they are working very hard.”

“But you haven’t done anything!” I protested. “You’ve just sat
here building card-houses!”

“That is where you are wrong, my friend. I have done a great deal.
I have thought. And I have also made one or two little inquiries.”

“Inquiries? Where?”

“Never mind where, Hastings. You shall know all in good time.”

On Saturday morning, Japp arrived, looking more cheerful than he
had for some days.

“Well,” he said, as he sat down, “I’ve got some news for you.
We’ve found the man who pawned the ring!”

“Billy Kellett?” I asked.

“No, not Billy Kellett. Another man—a man called Miller.”

“Miller?” I exclaimed. “The inspector?”

Japp laughed. “No, not the inspector! Another Miller—a small
tradesman in the village. It seems he found the ring in the road,
just where Kellett said he’d seen it thrown.”

“Then Kellett was telling the truth after all!” I said.

“It looks like it. And if he was telling the truth about the ring,
he was probably telling the truth about the man who threw it.”

“Lowen!” I cried.

“Exactly. It looks very black for Lowen now. We’ve got him in
custody, and I think we’ll be able to make a case against him.”

“And Mr. Davenheim?” I asked. “Have you found any trace of him?”

“Not yet. But if Lowen is the murderer, he must have disposed of
the body somewhere. We’re still searching.”

“_Eh bien!_” said Poirot, who had been listening to all this with
the greatest interest. “It is all very satisfactory—very
satisfactory indeed. But I think, my friend, that you are still
looking in the wrong place.”

“The wrong place? What do you mean?”

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that you will never find the body of Mr.
Davenheim—because there is no body to find!”

“No body? Do you mean he’s still alive?”

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that Mr. Davenheim has never been
murdered. He has simply—disappeared!”

“But how? Where?”

“That, my friend, is what I am going to show you.”

Poirot rose and went to the desk. He took out a small piece of
paper and handed it to Japp.

“What’s this?” asked Japp, looking at it.

“It is the address,” said Poirot, “of the man you are looking for.”

Japp looked at the paper, and his face went blank. “But this—this
is the address of a common lodging-house in the East End!”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And if you go there, and ask for a man
called Billy Kellett, I think you will find what you are looking
for.”

“Billy Kellett? But we’ve already seen him! He’s in prison!”

“Is he?” said Poirot. “Are you sure?”

Japp looked at him for a moment in silence. Then he snatched up
