his hat and rushed out of the room.

“Poirot!” I cried. “What does it all mean? Who is Billy Kellett?”

Poirot smiled. “Billy Kellett, my friend, is a very clever man.
He is a man of many parts. He is, in fact—Mr. Davenheim!”

“Mr. Davenheim? But he’s a gentleman—a wealthy banker! How could
he be a common thief like Billy Kellett?”

“It is very simple, Hastings. Mr. Davenheim was in financial
difficulties. He had been speculating heavily in South American
shares, and he knew that a crash was coming. He decided to
disappear—to start a new life with the money and jewels he had
taken from his safe. But he knew that it would be difficult for
a man of his appearance to disappear. So he hit upon a very
ingenious plan.

“He created the character of Billy Kellett. For months before his
disappearance, he spent his weekends in the East End, living as
Billy Kellett. He even went so far as to get himself arrested and
imprisoned for a short time, so that the police would have a
record of Billy Kellett’s fingerprints and appearance.

“Then, on the Saturday of his disappearance, he went down to
Chingside as usual. He staged the burglary of his own safe,
throwing the blame on Lowen, whom he knew to be a rival. Then
he went out, changed into his Billy Kellett clothes, which he had
hidden in the boathouse, and walked to the village.

“On the way, he threw his ring over the hedge, knowing that it
would be found and would serve as a clue against Lowen. Then he
went to London, got himself arrested as Billy Kellett, and was
safely hidden in prison while the police were searching for him
all over the country!”

“But the boots!” I cried. “What about the boots?”

“Ah, the boots!” Poirot smiled. “That was the one thing he
forgot. He had twenty-four pairs of boots, Hastings. But when
Japp counted them, there were only twenty-three. The twenty-fourth
pair was the one he was wearing when he disappeared—the pair of
thick, heavy boots that belonged to Billy Kellett!”

I looked at Poirot in amazement. Once again, his “little grey
cells” had triumphed.

“But what will happen now?” I asked.

“Now, my friend, Japp will go to the prison and confront ‘Billy
Kellett’ with the truth. And I think that Mr. Davenheim will find
that his ‘disappearance’ has not been quite as successful as he
hoped!”

A week later, Poirot received a cheque for five pounds from Japp.
It was accompanied by a note which said: “You win, Monsieur
Poirot. But how on earth did you know about the boots?”

Poirot smiled as he showed it to me. “It is as I said, Hastings.
The senses mislead. One must seek the truth within—not without.”

“Very improbable, _mon ami_. He had no means of disposing of the
body. It would have been found by now. Secondly, the open way in
which he pawned the ring makes it unlikely that he did murder to
get it. Thirdly, your sneak-thief is rarely a murderer. Fourthly,
as he has been in prison since Saturday, it would be too much of
a coincidence that he is able to give so accurate a description of
Lowen.”

“Japp, my friend, have you the photograph of Lowen? Yes? Good.
And also one of Billy Kellett?”

Japp produced two photographs from his pocket. Poirot looked at
them.

“_Eh bien!_” he said, after a minute or two. “Tell me, Japp, how
far is it from the gate of The Cedars to the place where Kellett
was sitting?”

“About half a mile.”

“And what time did Lowen leave?”

“Six twenty-five.”

“Then he could have reached the spot where Kellett was sitting
at about half-past six?”

“Exactly.”

“But the train he caught was at 6.50?”

“Yes.”

“Then he had plenty of time.”

“Loads.”

“He had the ring in his pocket? Why?”

“He must have taken it from the safe.”

“Then he must have known the combination?”

“Not necessarily. If the safe was left open—”

“True.”

“And why throw it away? He could have kept it, and sold it later
on.”

“The sight of it may have made him nervous. He may have thought
it might be found on him if he was searched.”

“Is that likely? The police would have no reason to search him
unless he was arrested, and then he would have had time to get
rid of it.”

“It’s a point, Poirot, it’s a point. But you’ll admit the case
against him is pretty black?”

“It is black—very black. It is so black that I do not believe it.”

Japp laughed. “What do you believe, then?”

“I believe that there is a link missing. When we find that link,
the case will be clear. Tell me, how long did it take Davenheim
to dress?”

“About ten minutes, his valet says.”

“And how long to shave?”

“He did not shave. He wore a beard and moustache.”

“Aha!” Poirot’s eyes twinkled. “Tell me, Japp, did he ever have
his hair cut?”

Japp stared. “I suppose so. Why?”

“Frequently? Or only occasionally?”

“His valet says about once a fortnight. He was very particular
about it.”

“Good. Now, I will ask you another question. Did the Davenheims
sleep in the same room?”

Japp looked more surprised than ever. “No. Separate rooms, but
with a door between them. Why?”

“It is a point. It is a point. Now, Japp, I will give you a piece
of advice. Do not arrest Lowen yet. Wait a little. You will find
it pay in the end.”

“I’m afraid I can’t do that. Miller’s keen on an arrest, and the
public is beginning to get restive.”

“Very well. But you have been warned. Now, there is one thing more.
I should like to have a few words with Mrs. Davenheim.”

“I’ll see if I can arrange it. But I don’t think she’ll be able
to tell you anything you don’t know already.”

“Perhaps not. But one never knows. One never knows.”

Japp took his departure. When he had gone, Poirot turned to me.

“What do you think of it, Hastings?”

“I think the case against Lowen is very strong,” I said. “He was
the last person seen with Davenheim; he was seen near the study
window; and he was seen to throw away the ring.”

“Yes, it is very strong—too strong. That is what I do not like.
It is too easy.”

“Then you think Lowen is innocent?”

“I do not say that. I say the case against him is too complete.
It is as if someone had been at great pains to make it so.”

“But who?”

“That is what we have to find out. There is someone who knows the
truth. Someone who is very clever—very clever indeed.”

“And the link?”

“Ah, the link! I think I know what it is. But I must be sure. I
must be quite sure.”

He fell into a brown study, from which he did not emerge until
bedtime.

“Quite true. It’s Lowen’s story against his. The girl’s evidence
has been a great point in our favour. We’ve also found a small
scrap of paper in the study with the word ‘Buenos Ayres’ on it.
That may lead to something.”

Poirot looked thoughtfully at the Inspector. “Let me see. You’re
going to Chingside tomorrow?”

“Yes.”

“Then I’ll ask you to do me a little favour.”

“With pleasure.”

“Ask Mrs. Davenheim if she remembers whether her husband was a
good-looking man when she first married him. And also, whether he
was in the habit of using a stick.”

“A stick!” Japp stared. “Why, everyone saw him carrying a stick
that afternoon!”

“_Précisément_! But I want to know if he was in the _habit_ of
using one. And don’t forget the first question.”

Japp shrugged his shoulders. “Very well. If you really want to
know.”

“I do.”

“It’s a funny case altogether,” went on the Inspector. “Of course,
the safe-robbery and the disappearance were simultaneous. But
whether the safe was robbed by Lowen or by Davenheim himself is
the question. If it was Davenheim, what’s he done with the money?
And where is he himself? If it was Lowen, he’s a much cleverer
rogue than we gave him credit for. He’s managed to get rid of the
valuables, anyhow.”

“How did he get into the safe?” I asked. “It hadn’t been blown
open, I suppose?”

“No. It was opened by the key. We found it on the floor.”

“The key?”

“Yes. Davenheim must have left it in the lock.”

“Incredible!” I cried.

Poirot smiled. “A man of method, remember!”

“Well,” said Japp, “I must be off. I’ll let you know the result
of my inquiries to-morrow.”

I could see that Poirot was deep in thought after the Inspector’s
departure. He sat with his eyes closed, and I did not like to
disturb him. At last he sighed and opened them.

“Hastings,” he said, “what do you think of it all?”

“It seems to me,” I said, “that there are two possibilities.
Either Davenheim has been murdered by Lowen for the sake of the
money in the safe, and his body disposed of in some way we don’t
yet know of, or else he has staged a disappearance for some reason
of his own, and has probably taken the money with him.”

“And the clothes in the lake?”

“A blind, of course.”

“And the ring?”

“Ah, that’s the difficulty. If he’s still alive, why should he
throw away a valuable ring? It’s not as though it would be easily
recognized. A diamond solitaire is common enough.”

“You are right, Hastings. That ring is the crux of the whole
matter. Why did he throw it away?”

“Because he’s dead,” I suggested.

“But if he’s dead, who threw it away?”

“Lowen, of course.”

“Then why should _he_ throw it away? Why not keep it, or pawn it
himself?”

“He might have been afraid of its being found on him.”

“He had only to throw it into the lake with the clothes.”

“That’s true,” I admitted. “It’s a muddle.”

“On the contrary,” said Poirot, “it’s a very simple and instructive
case.”

I looked at him in surprise. “You’ve solved it, then?”

“Not yet. There are still one or two points to be cleared up. But
the main facts are clear enough.”

“And who is the murderer?”

“My dear Hastings, I have already told you that I do not believe
there has been a murder.”

“Then Davenheim is still alive?”

“I am practically certain of it.”

“And where is he?”

“Ah, that is what I have to find out!”

He relapsed into silence. I watched him for a few minutes, and
then, as he showed no sign of speaking, I took up a book.

Presently Poirot spoke again.

“Hastings, did you notice that Japp said the safe-key was found on
the floor?”

“Yes. It’s a very curious point.”

“It is more than curious. It is significant.”

“In what way?”

“Because it shows that the safe was opened by some one who was in
a great hurry—so great a hurry that he did not even stop to take
the key out of the lock.”

“That might have been Lowen.”

“It might. But would he have been in such a hurry? He had plenty
of time. He was alone in the study for nearly an hour.”

“Then you think it was Davenheim?”

“I am sure of it. And that brings us to another point. Why was he
in such a hurry?”

“Because he wanted to get away before Lowen arrived, I suppose.”

“But he had already seen Lowen. He must have seen him from the
window of the study. No, there must be some other reason.”

“Perhaps he heard some one coming?”

“Possibly. But who? Not his wife, because she was in her boudoir.
Not the servants, because they were in the kitchen. No, it must
have been some one else.”

“Who could it have been?”

“That is what I am going to find out.”

He rose and went to the desk. “I am going to write a little note
to Japp,” he said. “I want him to find out one or two more things
for me.”

He wrote for a few minutes, then blotted the letter and put it in
an envelope.

“There!” he said. “That’s done. And now, Hastings, I think we will
have a little music. Will you play me some Mozart?”

I complied, and for the rest of the evening we did not mention the
Davenheim case again.

The next morning Poirot was in a very cheerful mood. He hummed a
little tune to himself as he ate his breakfast, and seemed
thoroughly pleased with life.

“The sun is shining, the birds are singing,” he remarked. “It is
a beautiful world, is it not, Hastings? And to-day, if I am not
mistaken, we shall have the solution of our little mystery.”

“You really think so?”

“I am sure of it. Japp will be here presently, and then we shall
see.”

He was right. About eleven o’clock the Inspector arrived. He looked
a little crestfallen.

“Well,” he said, as he sat down, “I’ve got the answers to your
questions, Monsieur Poirot. But I don’t see that they help much.”

“Let us hear them, at any rate.”

“Well, first of all, as to whether Mr. Davenheim was a good-looking
man when he was young. Mrs. Davenheim says he was considered very
handsome. She showed me a photograph of him taken about twenty
years ago. He certainly was a fine-looking fellow then—though he’s
changed a good deal since.”

“And the stick?”

“He’s used a stick for the last year or two. He had a fall from
his horse, it seems, and it left him with a slight limp.”

Poirot’s eyes sparkled. “A limp! That is very interesting—very
interesting indeed!”

“I don’t see why,” said Japp. “Lots of people have limps.”

“True. But it is a detail, and as I have told you, details are
sometimes vital. Now, is there any other news?”

“Yes. We’ve found out something about those South American shares.
It seems they’re practically worthless. Davenheim must have lost
a lot of money over them lately.”

“Aha! And what about Lowen?”

“He’s still under arrest. But we haven’t been able to find any of
the stolen property in his possession. He’s as cool as a cucumber,
and denies everything.”

“And the lake?”

“We’ve dragged it from end to end, but there’s no sign of a body.
Only the clothes, as I told you.”

“And the boathouse?”

“Nothing there either. We’ve searched it thoroughly.”

Poirot sat in silence for a few minutes, his brow furrowed in
thought. Then he looked up.

“Japp,” he said, “I want you to take me to Chingside.”

“With pleasure. But I thought you weren't going to move from your
chair?”

“I have changed my mind. There are one or two things I want to see
for myself.”

“Very well. We’ll go down this afternoon.”

The journey to Chingside took about an hour. On our arrival we
were met by Inspector Miller, who looked at Poirot with a good
deal of curiosity.

“This is Monsieur Poirot,” said Japp. “He’s interested in the case.”

“Glad to meet you, monsieur,” said Miller. “I’ve heard of you,
of course. But I’m afraid you won’t find much here. We’ve been
over the ground pretty thoroughly.”

“I do not doubt it,” said Poirot politely. “But I should like,
if I may, to see the study.”

“Certainly. This way.”

He led us into a large, comfortably furnished room. On one side
was a big desk, and behind it a heavy velvet curtain. Miller drew
this aside, revealing a small safe built into the wall.

“This is where the money was kept,” he said. “The door was standing
open when the robbery was discovered.”

Poirot examined the safe and the surrounding wall with great care.
Then he turned to the window. It was a long French window, opening,
as Japp had said, on to a beautiful rose-garden. Beyond the garden
we could see the lake, shimmering in the sunlight.

Poirot stepped out on to the terrace and looked around him.

“A very charming spot,” he remarked. “And that, I presume, is the
boathouse?”

He pointed to a small wooden building on the edge of the lake.

“Yes,” said Miller. “But as I told Inspector Japp, there’s nothing
there.”

“All the same, I should like to see it.”

We walked down through the rose-garden to the lake. The boathouse
was a simple structure, containing two punts and a few oars. Poirot
looked around him with a dissatisfied air.

“Is there no other building near the lake?” he asked.

“Only the gardener’s cottage, about a quarter of a mile away.”

“And there are no other boats?”

“None.”

Poirot turned back towards the house. As we passed through the
rose-garden, he stopped and looked at a large stone vase that stood
on the terrace.

“A very fine piece of work,” he remarked. “Is it old?”

“I believe so,” said Miller. “Mr. Davenheim bought it at a sale
some years ago.”

Poirot leaned over and looked into the vase. It was empty, except
for a little rain-water at the bottom.

“H’m!” he muttered. “Very interesting.”

He continued his walk to the house. As we entered the hall, we
met a middle-aged woman with a kind, rather anxious face.

“This is Mrs. Davenheim,” said Japp.

Poirot bowed. “I am honored to meet you, madame. I am very sorry
for the trouble you are in.”

“It is very kind of you, monsieur,” she said. “But I am beginning
to lose hope. It is four days now, and we have heard nothing.”

“Do not despair, madame,” said Poirot. “I have great hopes that
we shall find your husband before long.”

“You really think so?”

“I am almost sure of it. But I must ask you one or two questions.
On the Saturday afternoon, when your husband went out, did you
notice anything unusual in his manner?”

“Nothing at all. He seemed just as usual.”

“And he said he was going to the village to post some letters?”

“Yes.”

“Did he have any letters in his hand?”

“I didn't notice. But he usually took the letters himself if it
was after the postman had been.”

“I see. And you are sure he didn't take any luggage with him?”

“Quite sure. He only had his walking-stick.”

“Thank you, madame. That is all I wanted to know.”

We took our leave of Mrs. Davenheim and walked back to the station.
During the journey Poirot was very silent. He sat with his eyes
closed, and I could see that he was thinking deeply.

When we got back to our rooms, he threw himself into his armchair
and sighed.

“Well, Hastings,” he said, “what do you think of it now?”

“I’m as much in the dark as ever,” I admitted. “I can’t see any
clue at all.”

“And yet it is all so simple! So very simple!”

“You mean you’ve solved it?”

“I have. I know exactly what happened on Saturday afternoon.”

“Then tell me, for heaven’s sake!”

“Not yet, Hastings. There is still one thing I must do. I must
have a little talk with Billy Kellett.”

“Billy Kellett! But he’s in prison!”

“I know. But Japp can arrange for me to see him. I want you to go
to the police station and ask him to fix it up for tomorrow
morning.”

I did as he requested, and the next morning we went to the police
station. Japp was waiting for us.

“I’ve got Kellett here,” he said. “But I don’t see what you expect
to get out of him. He’s told us all he knows.”

“We shall see,” said Poirot.

We were shown into a small room where Billy Kellett was sitting.
He was a miserable-looking object, with a face that showed only
too clearly the effects of a life of crime and dissipation.

Poirot looked at him for a few minutes in silence. Then he spoke.

“Billy Kellett,” he said, “I want you to tell me the truth.”

“I’ve told it, guv’nor,” said the man surlily. “I told the
Inspector everything.”

“Not everything, I think. For instance, you didn't tell him that
you knew Mr. Davenheim.”

Kellett started. “Me? Know the banker toff? Not me!”

“Are you sure? Think again, Billy. You were in prison last autumn,
were you not?”

“Yes, I was. What of it?”

“And Mr. Davenheim was in Buenos Ayres at the same time, was he
not?”

Kellett looked confused. “I don’t know what you’re talking about,”
he muttered.

“I think you do. Now, Billy, I’m going to tell you what I think
happened. You didn't find that ring in a ditch. It was given to
you by Mr. Davenheim himself.”

Kellett stared at him in amazement. “Giv’n to me? Why should he
give me a diamond ring?”

“That is what I am going to find out. But first, I want you to
admit that I am right.”

Kellett hesitated for a moment, then he broke down. “All right,”
he said. “You’re too clever for me. He did give it to me. But I
don’t know why. He just came up to me in the lane and shoved it
into my hand, and told me to get out of the place as fast as I
could.”

“I thought so,” said Poirot. “And now, Japp, I think we can go.”

As we walked back to the station, Japp was full of questions.

“What on earth does it mean, Poirot? Why should Davenheim give
his ring to a man like Kellett?”

“It’s quite simple, my friend. He wanted to make sure that the
ring would be found in Kellett’s possession.”

“But why?”

“Because he wanted to create a false trail. He wanted everyone to
think that he had been robbed and murdered by Kellett.”

“But then where is he himself?”

“He is in a very safe place, Japp. A place where no one would
think of looking for him.”

“And where is that?”

“In prison!”

Japp stared at him. “In prison? What do you mean?”

“I mean that Mr. Davenheim and Billy Kellett are one and the same
person!”

We both gasped in astonishment.

“But it’s impossible!” I cried. “Davenheim is a well-known man.
He’s got a wife and a partner and dozens of friends. They’d all
recognize him!”

“Would they? Think, Hastings. What did we hear about Mr.
Davenheim? He wore his hair long, he had a full moustache and a
pointed beard, and bushy eyebrows. All those things are easily
altered. A clean shave, a haircut, and a little work on the
eyebrows—and the transformation is complete!”

“But his wife?”

“She hadn't seen him for three months last autumn. That was when
the transformation took place. He went to Buenos Ayres, as he said,
but he didn't stay there. He came back to London, and lived the
life of a criminal under the name of Billy Kellett. He even managed
to get himself arrested and sent to prison for three months. That
was his master-stroke. It provided him with an alibi for his
disappearance, and it also gave him a chance to practice his new
character.”

“But the limp?”

“He had a fall from his horse a year ago. It gave him a slight
limp. He realized that it would be a very good way of identifying
himself as Billy Kellett. When he was in prison last autumn, he
made sure that everyone noticed his limp.”

“And the robbery?”

“He committed it himself, of course. He wanted to have plenty of
money for his new life. He chose a time when Lowen was coming to
see him, so that the suspicion would fall on him. He opened the
safe, took the money and the jewels, and then went out through the
window. He threw his clothes into the lake to make it look like
suicide, and then he changed into his Billy Kellett clothes, which
he had hidden in the boathouse. Then he walked to the village,
postponing the letters as he went, and finally he met himself—or
rather, he met the person he wanted everyone to think had murdered
him. He gave the ring to a passing tramp—who was, of course,
himself—and then he went to London and got himself arrested for
drunkenness and assault. He knew that as Billy Kellett he would
be safe in prison for a few weeks, by which time the search for
Davenheim would have died down.”

“It’s incredible!” said Japp. “But I believe you’re right. It fits
in with everything.”

“Of course it does,” said Poirot. “It was a very clever plan, but
it had one fatal flaw.”

“What was that?”

“He forgot that I, Hercule Poirot, have the little grey cells!”

We all laughed, and Japp promised to go to the prison at once and
confront ‘Billy Kellett’ with the truth.

As for me, I couldn't help feeling a certain admiration for the
unfortunate banker. He had certainly carried out his plan with
great skill and daring. But, as Poirot said, he had forgotten one
thing. He had forgotten the little grey cells of Hercule Poirot.

“You think Lowen did it, then?” Japp asked. “It’s Miller’s theory,
you know. He’s going on the line that Lowen met Davenheim in the
garden, murdered him, and then disposed of the body in some
ingenious way—the boathouse, perhaps. Then he broke into the safe,
stole the valuables, and, as he was leaving, threw the ring over
the hedge, where it was found by Kellett.”

Poirot shook his head again. “No, no, that is too complicated. And
why throw the ring away? Why not keep it? It is small, easily
hidden.”

“Perhaps he was afraid it would be recognized,” I suggested.

“Then why not throw it into the lake?” Poirot countered. “No, there
is something here that does not fit. Tell me, Japp, did you find
any other clothes in the lake?”

“Only the suit he was wearing. Coat, waistcoat, trousers, and a
light overcoat.”

“No boots? No hat?”

“No.”

“And the lake has been thoroughly dragged?”

“Every inch of it.”

Poirot leaned back and closed his eyes. “It is very interesting,”
he murmured. “Very interesting indeed. And the safe—was it a
difficult one to open?”

“Miller says it was a very neat job. Not a professional’s, but
done by someone who knew what they were doing.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And Mrs. Davenheim? How does she take all
this?”

“Distraught, poor woman. Quite distraught. She can’t believe her
husband is dead, yet the evidence of the clothes in the lake seems
conclusive to her.”

Poirot opened his eyes. “The clothes in the lake. Yes. That is
very important. And the ring. Do not forget the ring.”

“Well, that’s Miller’s view. He’s of the opinion that Lowen
murdered the banker and took his ring, but for some reason or other
got the wind up and threw it away. Then Kellett came along and
found it. The fact that Miller saw him for a minute or two on
Sunday and then again to-day, and that he’s always ready to tell
his yarn, is in his favour. Also, the girl says she saw Lowen go
straight from the study window towards the village, and that’s the
road Kellett was on. I think things are beginning to look black
for Lowen.”

Poirot sat for a few moments in silence. Then he looked up at
Japp. “Tell me, my friend, what do you think of Mrs. Davenheim?”

“_Oh, her!_ She’s a poor creature. She’s completely collapsed
under the blow. It’s a very sad case.”

“Would you say that she was a woman of intelligence?”

“Lord, no! She’s as stupid as they make ’em. She was a widow with
a small fortune when Davenheim married her, I believe.”

“_Tiens!_ How did she ever come to be a widow? Did she murder her
first husband?”

Japp laughed. “Good Lord, no! He died in his bed of some common
complaint. No, no, Poirot, don’t you start building up any theories
about Mrs. Davenheim. She hasn’t got the brains of a rabbit!”

Poirot sighed. “It is a pity! It would have been so interesting!”

“And the lake?” I suggested. “What about the clothes?”

“_Ah, oui_,” said Poirot. “The clothes! That is a very curious
point, is it not?”

“I should think so!” cried Japp. “Fancy a man stripping to the
skin before he goes and drowns himself!”

“It is certainly unusual,” admitted Poirot. “But then, we must
always allow for the fact that a man may be a little eccentric.”

“A little eccentric!” Japp laughed. “I should think so! Well, I
must be off. Miller’s expecting me at the Yard.”

As soon as he had gone, I turned to Poirot. “Now then, what do you
really think about it all?”

Poirot smiled. “I think, Hastings, that there are several very
curious points. To begin with, why should a man take the trouble
to strip himself before committing suicide? Secondly, why should
Lowen, if he did murder Davenheim, take the ring and then throw
it away? If he wanted to get rid of it, the lake would have been
a much safer place. Thirdly, why should Davenheim have gone out
to post his letters himself, when he had a houseful of servants
to do it for him? And, fourthly, why did he choose that particular
moment to go? Just when he was expecting a visitor on business!”

“All very interesting questions,” I agreed. “But they don’t seem
to lead anywhere.”

“On the contrary, they lead to the truth. But we have not yet
sufficient data. We must wait. In the meantime, I shall think.”

He composed himself in his chair, and I knew that for the next
hour or two he would be oblivious of my presence.

“But he’s been shown Lowen’s photograph!” Japp looked triumphant.

“I might have known as much! Still, it would be a risky thing for
Lowen to throw away a valuable diamond ring like that. He might
not have been seen, it is true, but he could not _know_ he was not
being followed. He’d much better have kept it in his pocket.”

“But don’t you see, Monsieur Poirot, if he had the ring on him
when he was arrested, it would be a dead cert. against him. By
getting rid of it, he could always say it was a frame-up. In my
opinion he’s a deep one—and a dangerous one. He’s had to do with
South American revolutions, and they’re pretty hot stuff.”

Poirot looked thoughtful. “And what about the clothes—the clothes
you found in the lake?”

“Well, there’s no doubt about _them_. Every one of them is marked
with Davenheim’s name. A suit of light grey tweed, a pair of boots,
a hat, and a light overcoat.”

“And you are quite sure that no others are missing?”

“The valet is positive.”

“_C’est curieux!_” murmured Poirot. “Very strange!”

“Nothing else?”

“Wait! There is one other thing. His safe was found rifled, you
say?”

“Yes.”

“Was the key in it?”

“No. We’ve not been able to find it.”

“And yet it was not blown open?”

“No. It was opened with the key.”

“Then,” said Poirot, “the person who opened it must have been in
possession of the key. Where did Mr. Davenheim keep it?”

“On a chain with his other keys in his pocket.”

“Then,” said Poirot, “it must have been taken from him.”

“Exactly. By Lowen, probably. He might have been watching his
opportunity for weeks.”

“And yet,” said Poirot, “you say the windows were fastened on the
inside?”

“Yes.”

“Then the person who rifled the safe must have been inside the
house?”

“Exactly. It’s a very pretty problem, isn’t it?” Japp rubbed his
hands. “I’m glad you agree it’s a tough nut to crack.”

“I do not agree,” said Poirot. “I find it very simple.”

Japp stared. “Simple? Well, tell me how it was done, then?”

“Not yet, my friend. First, I should like to ask you one or
two questions. Has Mr. Davenheim a hobby?”

“He’s very fond of gardening, I believe.”

“I do not mean that. Does he—for instance—collect things? Old
china, or stamps, or—photographs?”

“No.”

“Then he has no hobby?”

“Not that I know of.”

“_Dommage!_” sighed Poirot. “One more thing. Does he frequently
change his appearance?”

“In what way?”

“Does he—for instance—wear a wig? Or does he—sometimes—shave
off his beard?”

“No.”

“That is also a pity,” said Poirot. “Now, one more question. How
long had he and his wife been married?”

“Ten years.”

“And were they very much attached to each other?”

“I believe so.”

“_C’est une femme de tête_, Mrs. Davenheim?”

“No. As I said before, a very quiet, pleasant woman.”

“_Bien!_” said Poirot. “I think I have all the facts I require.
I will give you my solution in a week’s time—as we agreed.”

Japp laughed. “You’re a wonderful man, Monsieur Poirot! Well,
good-night.”

“Good-night, _mon ami_.”

When Japp had gone, I looked at Poirot. He was sitting with his
eyes closed, and a look of deep concentration on his face.

“Well?” I said.

Poirot opened one eye. “It is very interesting, Hastings—very
interesting indeed. A most ingenious little plot!”

“You have a theory?”

“I have more than a theory. I have a certainty.”

“And Lowen?”

“Lowen is as innocent as a babe unborn.”

“Then who did it?”

“Ah, that is the question!”

“You think it was Billy Kellett?”

“Certainly not. Why should he throw away a diamond ring?”

“Then who was it?”

“I will tell you in a week’s time, Hastings—not before. And now,
if you please, let us dismiss the subject from our minds. I have
a little problem in—shall we say—the arrangement of my wardrobe,
which is of more immediate importance.”

Japp nodded. “I don’t say you’re not right. But all the same, you
won’t get a jury to take much note of a jailbird’s evidence. What
seems odd to me is that Lowen couldn’t find a cleverer way of
disposing of the ring.”

Poirot shrugged his shoulders. “Well, after all, if it were found
in the neighbourhood, it might be argued that Davenheim himself
had dropped it.”

“But why remove it from the body at all?” I cried.

“Why indeed?” said Poirot. “And if he killed him, why not take
the jewellery from the safe as well?”

“That’s another thing!” cried Japp. “If Lowen is the murderer,
how did he know the combination of the safe? Only Mr. and Mrs.
Davenheim, and the junior partner, Salmon, knew it.”

“I’m beginning to wonder whether the robbery was committed at
all!” I suggested. “Suppose Mr. Davenheim has simply made away
with his own money?”

Poirot smiled. “A possibility, Hastings—but a remote one.
Remember, Mrs. Davenheim’s jewels are missing also. Now, even a
wealthy banker would not care to be encumbered with a quantity of
lady’s jewellery when he is making his escape.”

“Wait a bit!” Japp interrupted. “I’ve just had a wire from Miller.
They’ve finished dragging the lake, and they’ve found—nothing!”

“Good!” Poirot said. “Very good! That is what I expected.”

“Eh?” Japp stared at him. “You expected they wouldn’t find
anything?”

“Precisely.”

“Then you think he’s alive?”

“I have no doubt of it.”

“Then where is he?”

Poirot shook his head. “That is the question. But I will tell you
one thing, Japp: if you want to find Mr. Davenheim, you should
look for him in a place where he would be least likely to be
found.”

“A very wise remark, I’m sure!” Japp laughed. “But it doesn’t
help us much. Well, I must be off. I’ll let you know if anything
fresh turns up.”

When he had gone, Poirot sat for some time in silence. Then he
turned to me.

“Hastings, would you mind handing me that book on the table—the
one with the green cover?”

I did so. It was a volume of the _Banker’s Almanac_. Poirot
turned the pages rapidly.

“Ah! Here we are. Davenheim and Salmon. Established 1842. Capital
three millions. Directors: Gerald Davenheim, Victor Salmon.
H’m! Very interesting.”

He closed the book and sat for a long time with his eyes shut. I
did not like to disturb him. At last he spoke.

“Hastings, do you remember that Japp said Mrs. Davenheim was ‘a
pleasant, rather unintelligent woman’?”

“Yes,” I replied. “Why?”

“I was thinking,” said Poirot, “that it might be interesting to
make her acquaintance.”

“You mean you want to go down to Chingside?”

“By no means. I have already told Japp that I shall not leave this
chair. But there is no reason why Mrs. Davenheim should not come
to see _me_.”

“But will she?”

“I think so—if the matter is put to her in the right way. A wife’s
anxiety for her husband’s safety, you know—and the reputation of
Hercule Poirot!”

He smiled. “Write a note for me, Hastings. Invite her to tea
to-morrow afternoon. Say that I have a clue to her husband’s
whereabouts, but that I must see her personally before I can act
upon it.”

I did as he requested, and the following afternoon Mrs. Davenheim
arrived. She was a large, motherly-looking woman, with a somewhat
bewildered expression.

“It is so kind of you to see me, Monsieur Poirot,” she began.
“This is a terrible time for me. My poor husband! Where can he
be?”

“That is what we are going to find out, madame,” said Poirot
soothingly. “But first, I must ask you a few questions. Your
husband, I believe, spent some months in Buenos Ayres last
autumn?”

“Yes, he did. He had a great deal of business there.”

“And since his return, have you noticed any change in him? Has he
seemed worried or anxious?”

Mrs. Davenheim hesitated. “Well, perhaps a little. But he always
had so much on his mind. I didn’t think anything of it.”

“I see. Now, madame, I want you to tell me about the evening he
disappeared. You saw him just before he went out?”

“Yes. He came into my room to say he was going to post some
letters.”

“And did he seem just as usual then?”

“Yes, quite. He was just his ordinary self.”

“He didn’t seem excited or nervous in any way?”

“No, not at all.”

“I see. Now, madame, I want to ask you a rather personal
question. Your husband, I believe, was very fond of jewellery?”

Mrs. Davenheim’s face lighted up. “Oh, yes! He was always buying
me beautiful things. He said it was a good investment.”

“And you kept all these jewels in the safe in his study?”

“Yes. He didn’t like me to keep them in my own room. He said they
were safer there.”

“I see. And you knew the combination of the safe?”

“Yes. My husband told it to me, in case of an emergency.”

“And did anyone else know it?”

“Only Mr. Salmon, my husband’s partner.”

“I see. Now, madame, I want you to think very carefully. On the
day your husband disappeared, did you see anyone else about the
house—anyone you didn’t know?”

Mrs. Davenheim shook her head. “No, no one.”

“Not even in the garden?”

“No. I was in my own room most of the afternoon.”

“I see. Well, madame, I think that is all I need to ask you for
the present. I will let you know as soon as I have any news.”

When Mrs. Davenheim had gone, Poirot sat for some time in silence.
Then he turned to me with a smile.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of her?”

“She seems a very pleasant woman,” I said. “But I don’t see that
she has helped us much.”

“On the contrary,” said Poirot, “she has helped us a great deal.
She has confirmed my suspicions.”

“Your suspicions? What suspicions?”

“That, my friend, I will tell you later. For the moment, I have
some thinking to do.”

And for the rest of the evening, Poirot remained buried in
thought.

The next morning, Japp arrived with fresh news.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot, we’ve found the jewels!”

“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes lighted up. “And where were they?”

“In a small handbag, hidden in a hole in the bank of the lake.
It looks as though Lowen must have hidden them there, intending
to come back for them later.”

“Or,” said Poirot softly, “as though someone _wanted_ it to look
as though Lowen had hidden them there.”

Japp stared at him. “What do you mean?”

“I mean, my friend, that the case against Lowen is becoming
almost too clear. It is, as I said before, ‘clear as daylight’—and
therefore to be mistrusted.”

“But who else could have done it?”

“That is what we have to find out. Tell me, Japp, have you had any
news of Billy Kellett?”

“Only that he’s still in prison. He’ll be coming up for trial in
a day or two.”

“I see. And have you any more information about Mr. Davenheim’s
visit to Buenos Ayres?”

“Not much. He seems to have been there on business connected with
some South American mines. He stayed at the Hotel de la Paix in
Buenos Ayres.”

“I see. Well, Japp, I think I have all the facts I need. Now, if
you will excuse me, I must do some more thinking.”

And once again, Poirot relapsed into silence.

The week was nearly up when Japp arrived for his final visit.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot, the week’s nearly over. Have you found
Mr. Davenheim?”

“I have,” said Poirot quietly.

“What!” Japp and I both stared at him in amazement.

“You’ve found him? Where is he?”

“He is,” said Poirot, “in a place where, as I told you, he was
least likely to be found. He is in prison.”

“In prison!” Japp gasped. “But that’s impossible! We’ve checked
all the prisons. He’s not in any of them.”

“He is in prison,” Poirot repeated, “under the name of Billy
Kellett.”

“Billy Kellett!” I cried. “But Billy Kellett is a well-known
criminal. He’s been in prison before.”

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “And that is why no one would ever
dream of looking for Mr. Davenheim there.”

“But how—how could he do it?” Japp stammered.

“It was very simple,” said Poirot. “Mr. Davenheim knew that his
affairs were in a desperate state. He knew that the firm of
Davenheim and Salmon was on the verge of bankruptcy. He decided
to disappear—but he wanted to do it in such a way that no one
would ever find him. So he created the character of Billy Kellett.
Last autumn, when he was supposed to be in Buenos Ayres, he was
actually in London, living as Billy Kellett and getting himself
arrested for a small theft. In that way, he established an
identity for Billy Kellett that was known to the police. Then,
on the Saturday he disappeared, he simply went to a quiet spot,
changed his clothes, shaved off his beard and moustache, and
became Billy Kellett. He then pawned his own ring—to make sure
he would be arrested—and was safely tucked away in prison before
the hue and cry even began.”

“But the robbery!” Japp cried. “What about the robbery?”

“There was no robbery,” said Poirot. “Mr. Davenheim simply robbed
himself. He took the jewels and the money, hid the jewels where
they would be found and would point the finger at Lowen, and
no doubt he has the money safely hidden away somewhere else,
ready for when he comes out of prison.”

“It’s incredible!” I said. “But how did you know, Poirot?”

“It was the hair,” said Poirot. “In the photograph, Mr. Davenheim
had very long, wavy hair. Now, a man who is going to be away for
some months on business, as he was supposed to be in Buenos Ayres,
would naturally have his hair cut. The fact that his hair was so
long when he disappeared suggested that he had not been to a
barber for some time. Then there was the ring. Why should a
murderer remove a ring from his victim’s finger and then pawn it
in such a way that it was bound to be traced? It only made sense
if the man who pawned it _wanted_ to be caught. And finally,
there was the fact that Billy Kellett was able to give such an
accurate description of Lowen. He could only have done that if
he had actually seen him—and as Mr. Davenheim, he had.”

Japp shook his head in admiration. “Well, Monsieur Poirot, you’ve
won your bet. I’ll go and get the necessary warrants at once.”

And so the mystery of the disappearance of Mr. Davenheim was
solved—not by the discovery of a body, but by the application
of the little grey cells of Hercule Poirot.

“Ah!” said Poirot. “That’s just what I should have expected! Why
did he remove the clothes? Why the ring? Why, indeed, do anything
at all? That’s where the brain comes in—to make things more
difficult for the police by creating an apparent mystery.”

Japp shook his head again. “No, I’m afraid I don’t follow you.
It’s too deep for me.”

“You are right, my friend,” said Poirot. “You are following the
wrong track.”

Japp looked at him. “What track should I be following then?”

“One that leads from the beginning to the end, without a single
deviation,” answered Poirot.

“Well, at any rate,” said Japp, “we’ve got Lowen. He’s safe enough.”

“Yes, he’s safe enough,” repeated Poirot, “and his story is a
perfectly true one. He _did_ step out into the rose-garden for a
moment or two.”

“How can you possibly tell that?” asked Japp.

“Because if he had not done so he would have had no motive for
saying he had!” Poirot looked at him with a mischievous smile.

“_Mon ami_,” he said, “I think you have forgotten one very
important fact.”

“What’s that?”

“The lake!”

Japp stared. “What has the lake to do with it? We’ve dragged it,
and found nothing.”

“_Précisément_!” said Poirot. “That is just what I should have
expected.”

Japp looked more bewildered than ever. “I don’t know what you’re
driving at,” he said. “But I’ll let you know if anything fresh
turns up.”

“One moment,” said Poirot, as Japp rose to leave. “There is one
point on which I should like to be informed. What is the length
of Mr. Davenheim’s hair?”

Japp stared. “I’ve told you already—rather long and wavy.”

“_Non, non_—I mean at the present moment. Does he wear it long now?”

“How should I know? He’s disappeared, hasn’t he?”

“Ah, of course. I forgot. Well, would you mind finding out from
his valet whether he has had it cut lately?”

“I’ll do so if you like, but I don’t see that it can have much
bearing on the case.”

“Everything has a bearing,” said Poirot sententiously. “One should
overlook nothing.”

Japp laughed. “All right. I’ll let you know.”

He was as good as his word. Two days later he called again.

“I’ve seen the valet,” he said. “Davenheim had his hair cut on the
Friday—the day before he disappeared.”

“_A la bonne heure_!” cried Poirot. “Now we are getting on.”

“I’m glad you think so,” said Japp. “For my part, I don’t see that
it helps much. By the way, Miller’s been down to Chingside again.
He’s found a small boathouse on the lake, as you suggested, and
in it he’s found a couple of sets of old clothes belonging to
Davenheim.”

“Aha!” said Poirot. “And what does he make of that?”

“He thinks it’s another clue,” said Japp. “But I’m beginning to
think the whole thing’s a plant. What do you say?”

“I say that you are getting warm,” said Poirot. “The clothes were
put there to be found.”

“But why?”

“To make it appear that Davenheim had changed his clothes before
leaving,” said Poirot. “But why should he do that?”

“To avoid being recognized, of course!”

“But he had already been seen leaving the house in his usual
attire.”

“Exactly. That is where the cleverness comes in. He wanted it to
be thought that he had changed his clothes later on.”

“But why?”

“To make it more difficult for the police!”

Japp looked at him in silence for a moment or two. Then he said:

“I believe you’re right. But if he’s still alive, where is he?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what we have to find out.”

He sat for some time in silence after Japp had gone. Then he turned
to me.

“Hastings,” he said, “I have a little commission for you. I want
you to go down to Chingside and see if you can find out anything
about a man called Billy Kellett.”

“Billy Kellett?” I said in surprise. “But Japp’s already told us
all about him.”

“Not quite all,” said Poirot. “I want you to find out what he was
doing in the village on Saturday afternoon.”

“But he was in a ditch, according to his own account.”

“Precisely. I want to know if anyone saw him there.”

I set off for Chingside the following morning. It was a pleasant
little village, and I had no difficulty in finding the spot where
Kellett said he had been resting. It was a lonely stretch of road,
with no houses in the immediate vicinity.

I spent the best part of the morning wandering about, but could
find no one who had seen Kellett on the Saturday afternoon. I was
just about to give up in despair when I happened to meet a small
boy who was bird-nesting in the hedge.

“Did you see a man sitting in the ditch here on Saturday?” I asked
him.

The boy shook his head. “No, sir. I wasn't here on Saturday. I was
over at the races.”

“Did you see anyone else on the road?”

“I saw a gent with a big black moustache,” said the boy. “He was
walking towards the station.”

“What time was that?”

“About half-past six, I should think.”

“Was he alone?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Did you see him throw anything away?”

“No, sir.”

I thanked the boy and returned to London. Poirot listened to my
report with great interest.

“Aha!” he said. “So the boy saw the 'gent with the big black
moustache,' but he did not see Billy Kellett! That is very
interesting.”

“But Kellett says he was half concealed by a heap of stones,” I
reminded him.

“True, true. But all the same, it is interesting.”

He sat in silence for a long time, his eyes closed. Then he
suddenly opened them and looked at me.

“Hastings,” he said, “I have it! I have solved the mystery of the
disappearance of Mr. Davenheim!”

“You have?” I cried. “Who is the culprit?”

“There is no culprit,” said Poirot. “At least, not in the sense
you mean.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean that Mr. Davenheim has not been murdered. He has
disappeared of his own free will.”

“But why? And where is he?”

“He is in a place where no one would ever think of looking for
him,” said Poirot. “He is in prison!”

“In prison!” I gasped. “But how? For what?”

“For assaulting a policeman,” said Poirot. “Mr. Davenheim and Billy
Kellett are one and the same person!”

I stared at him in amazement. “But—but the description! Kellett
is a common sneak-thief, and Davenheim is a wealthy banker!”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “That is why no one would ever suspect
them of being the same person. But think for a moment. Davenheim
spent all last autumn in Buenos Ayres. What was he doing there?
He was serving a short sentence in prison! He had been arrested
for some minor offence, and had taken the opportunity to disappear
for a while. When he returned to England, he brought with him the
knowledge of how to lead a double life.”

“But the appearance?” I protested. “Davenheim has a beard and a
moustache, and his hair is long and wavy. Kellett is clean-shaven,
with short hair.”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “That is why he had his hair cut on the
Friday! He shaved off his beard and moustache, and with a little
make-up and a change of clothes, he became Billy Kellett. He then
went to Entfield races, where he knew he would be likely to get
into trouble. He pawned his own ring to provide a motive for his
arrest, and then assaulted a policeman to ensure that he would be
sent to prison.”

“But why?” I asked. “Why should he want to go to prison?”

“Because he knew that the firm of Davenheim and Salmon was on the
verge of bankruptcy,” said Poirot. “He had been embezzling the
firm’s money for years, and he knew that it was only a matter of
time before he was found out. By disappearing and going to prison
under an assumed name, he hoped to escape the consequences of his
crimes. He would be safe in prison for a few months, and by the
time he came out, the search for him would have died down, and he
would be able to start a new life with the money and jewels he had
stolen from his own safe!”

“It’s incredible!” I said.

“But true,” said Poirot. “The clue of the haircut was the key to
the whole mystery. Once I knew that he had had his hair cut on the
Friday, I knew that he must have had some reason for doing so.
And when I heard about Billy Kellett, and the way in which he had
pawned the ring, I knew that he and Davenheim must be the same
person.”

“But what about Lowen?” I asked. “What was he doing in the
rose-garden?”

“He was there for exactly the reason he said,” said Poirot. “He
had stepped out for a moment to look at a rose. It was a mere
coincidence, but it served Davenheim’s purpose perfectly by
throwing suspicion on to Lowen.”

“And the clothes in the boathouse?”

“They were put there by Davenheim himself, before he left,” said
Poirot. “He wanted the police to think that he had changed his
clothes and escaped by water.”

“It’s a most ingenious plot,” I said.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “But it was not ingenious enough to baffle
the little grey cells of Hercule Poirot!”

He smiled complacently, and reached for his cup of chocolate.

“And now, Hastings, I think we have earned our tea.”

“Exactly, my friend,” said Poirot. “Why remove it from the body?”
He turned to Japp. “Now, tell me, was anything else found in the
lake?”

“No, only the clothes. In fact, Miller has even gone to the expense
of having a search made for the body, which shows he’s beginning
to be a bit uneasy about it.”

“I do not see that,” murmured Poirot. “Wait! Tell me one thing.
Is it a deep lake? Or a shallow one?”

“Well, it’s not particularly deep. It’s an artificial piece of
water, you know.”

“Exactly. And the bottom?”

“What do you mean?”

“Is it gravel, or mud?”

“Oh, mud! A good deal of mud.”

“_C’est ça!_” said Poirot. “And the clothes? Were they in a bundle,
or just lying about?”

“In a bundle, tied together with a piece of string, and weighted
with a large stone.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “I see very well.”

“And you think?”

“I think,” said Poirot, “that it is a very interesting case. Now,
is there anything else you can tell me?”

“Not a thing.”

“Then,” said Poirot, “I will ask you a question. Or rather, several
questions. Has Mr. Davenheim a brother?”

“No.”

“A twin-brother?”

“No.”

“Had he ever any other partner besides Salmon?”

“No. Salmon died five years ago.”

“Has he any very intimate friend?”

“Not that I’ve heard of.”

“Does he—this is a very important point—does he and his wife
occupy the same bedroom?”

Japp stared. “Really, Poirot, I don’t see what that’s got to do
with it. But as a matter of fact, they don’t. They have separate
rooms, which communicate.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And one last question: How often does Mr.
Davenheim go to the barber?”

“Once a week, I believe. On Saturdays.”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And on this particular Saturday—did he
go to the barber?”

“No, he didn’t. He said he was too busy, and would go on Monday
instead.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And now, Japp, if you will excuse me, I
think I will go to bed. I feel I can do no more tonight.”

“Well,” said Japp, “I must be off, too. Good-night, Monsieur Poirot.
I’ll let you know if anything fresh turns up.”

As soon as he had gone, Poirot turned to me. “Well, Hastings, what
do you think of it?”

“It seems to me,” I said, “that the case against Lowen is very
strong.”

“And yet,” said Poirot, “there are several points that don’t quite
fit. For instance, why should Lowen take the ring and then throw
it away? If he killed Davenheim, he would surely have kept the
ring. And then there is the question of the clothes. Why should
he undress the body and throw the clothes into the lake?”

“Perhaps,” I suggested, “he wanted to make it look like suicide.”

“But in that case, why tie them in a bundle and weight them with
a stone? No, there is something very strange about those clothes.”

He sat for a long time in silence, his eyes closed, his forehead
furrowed. At last he rose.

“Well, Hastings, I think I see a little light. But there is still
much that is obscure. We must wait and see what to-morrow brings.”

But to-morrow brought no fresh news, and the day after was the
same. Japp looked in once or twice, but he had nothing more to
tell us. The lake had been thoroughly dragged, but no body had
been found. Lowen was still under arrest, but the police were
beginning to feel that their case against him was none too strong.
As for Billy Kellett, he was still in prison, serving his sentence
for assaulting the policeman.

It was on the Friday morning that Poirot suddenly jumped up from
his chair.

“Hastings!” he cried. “I have it! I have it!”

“What have you got?” I asked, startled.

“The solution! The solution to the mystery of Mr. Davenheim!
Quick, Hastings, get your hat! We must go to Chingside at once!”

“But Poirot,” I protested, “you said you would solve the case
without moving from your chair!”

“So I have, my friend! So I have! But now I must go and see if
my theory is correct. Come, let us not waste a moment!”

Half an hour later we were in the train, on our way to Chingside.
As we walked from the station to The Cedars, Poirot was in a state
of great excitement.

“You see, Hastings,” he said, “it was the clothes that gave me
the clue. The clothes in the lake, tied in a bundle and weighted
with a stone. Why should anyone do that? Only for one reason—to
make sure they would not be found. But why should anyone want to
hide Mr. Davenheim’s clothes? Only if those clothes would prove
that Mr. Davenheim was still alive!”

“But I don’t see—” I began.

“Wait, Hastings, wait! You will see everything in a moment. Here
is the house.”

He rang the bell, and asked to see Mrs. Davenheim. We were shown
into the drawing-room, and a few minutes later Mrs. Davenheim
appeared. She looked pale and anxious.

“Monsieur Poirot!” she cried. “Have you any news of my husband?”

“I think so, madame,” said Poirot gently. “But first, I must ask
you a few questions. Tell me, when did you last see your husband?”

“On Saturday afternoon, just before he went out to post those
letters.”

“And did you notice anything unusual about him? His manner, his
appearance?”

“No, nothing. He seemed just as usual.”

“And his beard? Was it the same as usual?”

“His beard? Why, yes, I suppose so. I didn’t notice anything.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And now, madame, will you take us to your
husband’s bedroom?”

Mrs. Davenheim looked surprised, but she led the way upstairs.
Poirot went straight to the wardrobe and began to examine the
clothes.

“H’m!” he muttered. “Just as I thought. Hastings, look at this!”

He held up a dark grey suit.

“This is the suit Mr. Davenheim was wearing on Saturday,” he said.

“But Poirot,” I cried, “Japp said the clothes he was wearing were
found in the lake!”

“Exactly, Hastings! Exactly! And yet here they are in the
wardrobe!”

He turned to Mrs. Davenheim.

“Madame,” he said, “I must ask you to be very brave. I believe
your husband is in this house at this very moment.”

Mrs. Davenheim gave a cry of astonishment. “In this house? But
where? We have searched everywhere!”

“Not everywhere, madame,” said Poirot. “There is one place where
you have not looked. Hastings, come with me!”

He led the way to a small room at the end of the corridor. It was
the room occupied by Mr. Davenheim’s valet. Poirot knocked on the
door, but there was no answer. He turned the handle and walked in.

The room was empty, but on the bed lay a wig and a false beard.

“You see, Hastings?” said Poirot. “Mr. Davenheim’s ‘disappearance’
was a very clever piece of acting. He wanted to disappear, but he
didn’t want to leave his comfortable home and his wealth. So he
invented ‘Mr. Lowen’—a man with whom he had a quarrel, and who
would be the perfect suspect if anything should happen to him.
Then, on Saturday afternoon, he went out of the house, changed his
clothes in the boathouse, and returned to the house as ‘Mr. Lowen.’
He had a false beard and wig, and he had even grown his own beard
and hair long so that he could cut them off and no one would
notice the difference. He entered the house through the study
window, robbed his own safe, and then ‘left’ the house as Mr.
Lowen. But instead of going to the station, he simply went back
to the boathouse, changed back into his own clothes, and—as he
thought—hid the ‘Lowen’ clothes in the lake. Then he returned to
the house and hid in his valet’s room, pretending to be the valet
himself!”

“But the valet?” I asked. “Where is he?”

“There is no valet, Hastings! Mr. Davenheim has been playing both
parts for years! He is a man of method, as I said. He knew that
sooner or later his financial affairs would come to a crisis, and
he prepared this ‘disappearance’ as a way out. He would ‘vanish,’
and then, when the trouble had blown over, he would reappear as
someone else, with all the money and jewels he had ‘stolen’ from
himself!”

“But what about Billy Kellett?” I asked. “And the ring?”

“Ah, that was Mr. Davenheim’s one mistake! He wanted to make the
case against ‘Lowen’ even stronger, so he threw his own ring over
the hedge, hoping it would be found and associated with Lowen.
He didn’t bargain for Billy Kellett being in the ditch! And he
didn’t bargain for the fact that a man who has just had his beard
shaved off always has a very pale skin where the beard has been.
That was why he didn’t go to the barber on Saturday—he had already
shaved himself!”

Poirot turned to Mrs. Davenheim, who was staring at him in
speechless amazement.

“I am sorry, madame,” he said, “but I’m afraid your husband is
not the man you thought him. He is at this moment hiding in the
servants’ quarters, but I have no doubt Inspector Japp will soon
be able to find him.”

And so it was. Mr. Davenheim was discovered hiding in a small
room in the basement, and was promptly arrested. He had indeed
been planning his “disappearance” for years, and had even built
a secret room where he could hide. But he had not counted on the
“little grey cells” of Hercule Poirot!

“You see, Hastings,” said Poirot as we sat in the train on our
way back to London, “it is as I said. One must seek the truth
within—not without. The senses mislead, but the brain—ah, the
brain never lies!”

“And the fiver?” I asked with a smile. “Do you think Japp will
pay up?”

“But certainly, my friend! A bargain is a bargain. And besides,”
he added with a twinkle in his eye, “it will just pay for a very
excellent dinner for the two of us!”

“Because a ring is the easiest thing in the world to identify.
And as for the clothes—well, it’s been suggested that Lowen
followed his victim into the rose-garden, and murdered him there;
stripped him of his clothes, and then threw them into the lake.”

“Where’s the body, then?”

“Drowned? I told you Miller’s going to drag the lake to-morrow.”

“And what about the safe?” I asked.

“Well, Lowen might have got the keys from Davenheim’s body and
then gone back and rifled it. The maid, you remember, saw him
actually coming from the study.”

Poirot’s eyes twinkled. “It is all very ingenious,” he murmured.
“And yet, to my mind, there is one thing that does not quite fit.”

“What’s that?”

“The safe! The safe was _rifled_—broken into, was it not?”

“Yes, by an expert, too. Miller thinks it was done on the
Saturday.”

“By Lowen?”

“Yes.”

“Then why did he not use the keys which he must have taken from
M. Davenheim’s body?”

Japp stared. “I never thought of that. Still, he might have been
afraid of being seen with them.”

“Is it more dangerous to be seen with a bunch of keys than with
a jemmy?” asked Poirot mildly.

“Well, anyway, we’ve got Lowen, and I don’t think he’ll get out
of it this time. If the body’s in the lake, his goose is cooked.”

“And if it is not?”

“Then we must look elsewhere. But it’s there all right, you’ll see.”

He took his departure. Poirot remained for a long time in thought.
Finally he rose and began to pace the room.

“Hastings,” he said at last, “have you a stamp-collector’s
magnifying-glass?”

“Yes, I believe I have.”

“Will you be so good as to lend it to me for a moment?”

I fetched the glass. Poirot took it, and began to examine a small
object which he had taken from his pocket.

“What have you there?” I asked.

“A fragment of a cigar-ash,” said Poirot. “I found it this morning
on the carpet in the study at The Cedars.”

“But Japp said Miller wouldn’t overlook a cigar-ash!”

“Neither did he. He found it also.”

“Then why did he not mention it?”

“Because, _mon cher_, it was the ash of a ‘_Petit_’—a very cheap
cigar. And Mr. Davenheim only smoked the most expensive Havanas.”

“Then it must have been Lowen’s!”

“Lowen does not smoke.”

“Then who could it have been?”

“That is what I am asking myself. It is a small point, but not
without interest.”

The next day brought the news that the lake had been dragged, and
that no trace of a body had been found. Japp was visibly
disconcerted. He came round to see us in the evening, and was
unusually silent.

“Well, what’s the next move?” I asked.

“Miller’s going to have the boathouse pulled down. He’s convinced
the body’s hidden there.”

“And what does Monsieur Poirot say?”

Poirot, who was busy building a house of cards, did not look up.
“I say that you will find nothing in the boathouse. You should
look in the village.”

“In the village? But we’ve already made most exhaustive inquiries
there.”

“I do not mean in the houses. I mean—well, for instance, in the
local lock-up.”

“The lock-up? But what on earth—”

“_Attendez, mon ami_. Has it not occurred to you that the most
successful way for a man to disappear is to go to prison?”

“To prison? But Davenheim hasn’t been arrested!”

“Not as Davenheim, certainly. But what if he were arrested as—say,
Billy Kellett?”

Japp stared. “Billy Kellett? But we’ve got Billy Kellett in
custody!”

“Exactly. And has it not occurred to you that Billy Kellett and
Mr. Davenheim might be one and the same person?”

“But Kellett is a well-known thief!”

“Is he? Have you any record of him before last autumn?”

“Well, no, I don’t know that we have. But the two men are
absolutely different in appearance! Davenheim has a beard and
long hair, and—wait a minute! Kellett’s clean-shaven, and his hair
is quite short.”

“Exactly. A very simple disguise! A pair of scissors and a razor,
and the thing is done. Mr. Davenheim goes for a stroll, enters
the boathouse, transforms himself into Billy Kellett, throws his
clothes into the lake, and his ring over the hedge, and then
proceeds to get himself arrested for a small theft. In prison he
is safe. No one will look for a millionaire there!”

“But why—why should he do such a thing?”

“Because, _mon ami_, the firm of Davenheim and Salmon is on the
verge of bankruptcy! By disappearing, and at the same time
arranging that suspicion should fall on his rival, Lowen,
Davenheim hoped to escape from his creditors and start a new life
elsewhere with the contents of the safe, which, of course, he had
already removed and hidden.”

“But how did he get the safe open?”

“He did not need to break into it. He had the keys. The ‘rifling’
was a mere blind. And the cigar-ash—the ‘Petit’—was left there
by him to suggest the presence of a third person.”

“It’s incredible!” gasped Japp. “But if you’re right, how are we
to prove it?”

“By the fingerprints, _mon ami_! Compare the fingerprints of Billy
Kellett with those of Mr. Davenheim, and you will find that they
are identical.”

Japp rushed from the room. A few days later we heard that Poirot
was right. ‘Billy Kellett’ was indeed the missing banker. The
great Davenheim mystery was solved.

“You see, Hastings,” said Poirot, “it was all a question of the
little grey cells! To the eyes of Inspector Miller, the case was
one of murder and robbery. To the eyes of Hercule Poirot, it was
a case of a man who wished to disappear. And once you have the
right point of departure, the rest is easy!”

“That is a very good question, Hastings,” said Poirot. “And one
that I shall have to answer before the week is out.”

“Well,” said Japp, “I must be getting along. I suppose you’re not
quite ready to tell me where to lay my hand on Mr. Davenheim?”

“Wait a bit,” said Poirot. “There are one or two points on which
I should like to be quite clear. First, the safe—how was it opened?”

“With a key.”

“Then Mr. Davenheim must have left his keys behind him?”

“Well, we haven’t found them on him, so it’s more likely he left
them behind in his study. That would be quite a natural thing for
a man to do who was just going for a stroll.”

“You say that it was opened with a key. Was there any sign of
force being used?”

“None. It was opened as easily as any key would open it.”

“And the safe? It was an ordinary safe?”

“Yes, quite. An ordinary iron safe. Any locksmith would have told
you that.”

“Is it an old-fashioned safe?”

“No, on the contrary, it’s one of the latest and most modern
patterns.”

“I see. Now, another thing. Is there any possibility of its being
someone else’s key?”

“Not a chance. We tried all the keys in the house, and not one of
them would fit.”

“One last question. Has Mr. Davenheim a hobby?”

Japp laughed. “Yes, he’s a great collector of curios. In fact,
he’s got quite a museum of them at The Cedars.”

“I see. Well, Japp, I’m much obliged to you. Good-night.”

When Japp had gone, Poirot sat for a long time in silence. Then he
turned to me.

“Hastings,” he said, “I want you to do me a favour. I want you to
go down to Chingside to-morrow. There are one or two things I want
to know.”

“With pleasure, Poirot. What are they?”

“I want you to find out how many times a day the postman calls at
The Cedars, and at what hours. Also, I want you to find out if there
is a small lake or pond in the grounds, and if so, how deep it is.”

“Is that all?”

“Yes, that is all. It’s very simple, isn’t it?”

“It sounds simple enough. But I don’t see what it has to do with
the disappearance of Mr. Davenheim.”

“Perhaps not, but then, you see, you are not a consulting
specialist!”

“There might be a reason for that,” said Japp. “Do you know that
just beyond the lake, a little gate leads out on to the hill, and
not three minutes’ walk brings you to—what do you think?—a _lime
kiln_.”

“Good heavens!” I cried. “You mean that the lime which destroyed
the body would be powerless to affect the metal of the ring?”

“Exactly.”

“It seems to me,” I said, “that that explains everything. What a
horrible crime!”

“Wait a bit, my friend,” said Poirot. “I do not think you have
explained why he should have pawned the ring in his own name.
Lowen, I mean.”

“Oh, Lowen didn’t pawn the ring! That was Kellett. Lowen threw it
over the hedge, according to Kellett, and Kellett picked it up.”

“Oh, I see. Then the mystery of the ring is—at last—solved!”

“Not at all!” Japp laughed. “The ring’s being pawned at all is
what’s so strange. For it was Davenheim’s ring, not Lowen’s.”

“_Tiens!_” said Poirot. “I begin to see. Lowen threw away the ring.
Kellett found it. And then, as you say, he went and pawned it.”

“Exactly,” said Japp. “And now what do you say to our little
problem?”

“I say that it is even more interesting than it appeared. By the
way, did Mr. Davenheim wear his hair long?”

“Yes.”

“And a moustache and beard?”

“Yes.”

“And his clothes? They were found in the lake?”

“Yes. A complete suit of clothes.”

“Including the boots?”

“Yes.”

“And they were not—damaged in any way?”

“No.”

“And there was nothing in the pockets?”

“Only a little loose change.”

“Was there anything else?”

“Wait a bit. I’m forgetting. In the pocket of the coat was a small
flat bottle. It was quite empty, but it had a label on it: ‘The
Grange, Chingside. To be taken three times a day after meals.’”

“Aha!” said Poirot. “That is most interesting. A medicine bottle.”

“Wait. There’s something more. In the other pocket was a small
clasp-knife, very sharp.”

“Aha!” said Poirot again. “A clasp-knife. And was there anything
else?”

“Nothing.”

“One thing more,” said Poirot. “Were there any fingerprints on the
safe?”

“None. It had been carefully wiped.”

“And what about the gardener who saw the figure in the rose-garden?
Could he see the face?”

“No. He was too far off. But he’s sure it was a man.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And now, my friend, I have a little
commission for you. I want you to find out for me if Mr. Lowen
has ever been in prison.”

“In prison? What on earth for?”

“I do not know. But I should like to know. Also, I should like to
know if he has any special hobbies.”

“Hobbies? What do you mean?”

“Does he collect anything? Or does he—play any games?”

“I’ll find out for you,” said Japp, looking rather mystified. “But
what has that to do with the case?”

“Perhaps nothing—perhaps everything. We shall see.”

“And that’s all you want?”

“For the moment, yes.”

“Well, I’ll be off now. I’ve a lot to do.”

“Wait one minute,” said Poirot. “There is one more thing. I want
to know if Mr. Davenheim’s hair and beard were—shall we say—luxuriant?”

“Luxuriant? I don’t know what you mean. They were quite ordinary,
I believe.”

“I see. Well, good-night, my friend. And don’t forget about the
prison.”

“I won’t,” said Japp. “Good-night.”

When he had gone, Poirot sat for a long time in silence. At last
he looked up at me.

“What do you think of it, Hastings?”

“I think it’s a very difficult case,” I said. “There seem to be
so many possibilities.”

“On the contrary,” said Poirot. “It is very simple. There is only
one possible explanation.”

“And what is that?”

“I will tell you—presently. In the meantime, let us have a little
music. Will you put on the ‘Jewel Song’ from _Faust_?”

I complied, and for the rest of the evening Poirot refused to
discuss the case.

The next day passed without any news from Japp. But on the following
morning he arrived, looking very pleased with himself.

“I’ve got the information you wanted,” he said. “Lowen has never
been in prison. As for his hobbies, he is a very fine amateur
conjurer. He’s quite famous for his card tricks.”

“Aha!” said Poirot. “A conjurer. That is very interesting. And
the other thing?”

“The other thing?”

“Mr. Davenheim’s hair and beard. Were they luxuriant?”

“Oh, I see! Yes, they were. His barber says he had a very fine
head of hair, and a very thick beard.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And now, my friend, I will tell you where
to find Mr. Davenheim.”

“You will?” cried Japp.

“But certainly. He is in prison.”

“In prison? But we’ve already searched the prisons.”

“Not all of them,” said Poirot. “You have not searched the prison
where Billy Kellett is.”

“Billy Kellett? But he’s in for three months for assaulting a
policeman.”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And that is where you will find Mr.
Davenheim.”

“But Billy Kellett is—Billy Kellett!”

“Is he?” said Poirot. “Are you sure?”

“Of course I’m sure! We’ve got his fingerprints.”

“And have you got Mr. Davenheim’s fingerprints?”

“No, but—”

“Then how do you know that Billy Kellett is not Mr. Davenheim?”

“But they’re not in the least alike! Davenheim has a beard and
long hair. Kellett is clean-shaven and has his hair cropped.”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And that is why I asked you about the
clasp-knife. Mr. Davenheim used it to cut off his hair and beard.”

“But the clothes? The clothes in the lake?”

“He put them there himself. He wanted it to be thought that he
had been murdered.”

“But why? Why should a rich man like Davenheim want to go to
prison as a common thief?”

“Because he wasn’t a rich man,” said Poirot. “He was on the verge
of bankruptcy. He had been using the firm’s money for his own
speculations, and he knew that the crash was coming. He decided
to disappear, and he hit on this very ingenious plan. He knew
that if he just disappeared, the police would be looking for him
all over the world. But if he was in prison, no one would ever
think of looking for him there.”

“But the robbery? The safe?”

“He robbed it himself. He wanted to make it look like a real
burglary, so that the police would suspect someone else. And he
chose Lowen as his victim, because he knew that Lowen had a
grudge against him.”

“But the ring? Why did he throw the ring away?”

“He didn't throw it away. He pawned it. He wanted to make sure
that he would be arrested and sent to prison. He knew that if he
was caught pawning a stolen ring, he would be sure to get a
sentence.”

“But the description? The description Kellett gave of Lowen?”

“He gave it himself, of course! He wanted to throw suspicion on
Lowen.”

“But how did he know what Lowen looked like?”

“He had seen him, of course. They were business rivals.”

“Well,” said Japp, “it’s the most extraordinary story I’ve ever
heard. But I believe you’re right, Monsieur Poirot. I’ll go and
look into it at once.”

And he did. And, as usual, Poirot was right. Billy Kellett was
indeed Mr. Davenheim. He had been living a double life for years,
and when the crash came, he had decided to disappear in this very
original way.

“You see, Hastings,” said Poirot, as we sat over our tea a few
days later, “it was all very simple. The only thing that was
really puzzling was why a man should want to go to prison. But
when you realize that prison is the one place where no one would
ever think of looking for a missing man, the whole thing becomes
clear.”

“But how did you know about the hair and beard?”

“Because they were the only things that couldn’t be changed. A
man can change his clothes, he can change his name, he can even
change his face to some extent. But he cannot change the fact
that he has a lot of hair and a thick beard—unless he cuts them
off. And that is what Mr. Davenheim did.”

“And the medicine bottle?”

“That was a little touch of detail to make the story more
convincing. It was a bottle of hair-restorer!”

I laughed. Poirot’s grey cells had triumphed once more.

“And Lowen?” asked Poirot.

“We’ve got him safely. Miller’s working for all he’s worth. I
think the five-pound note is mine, eh, Monsieur Poirot?”

“Not yet, my friend. Not yet.”

“Well, I’m not worrying. I see my way clear enough. Anything
further I can do for you?”

“Why, yes, there are one or two points on which I should like
further information.”

“Go ahead!”

“Is it known for how long Mr. Davenheim has been accustomed to
wear his hair long?”

“For some years, I believe.”

“And his beard and moustache?”

“Oh, for years! Since he was quite a young man.”

“Then it is not a recent whim?”

“No.”

“And Mrs. Davenheim? You said she was ‘unintelligent.’ Can you
not be more explicit?”

“Well, she’s a large, fat, comfortable sort of woman. Does not
take much interest in anything but her food and her garden. Not
at all the type to be a help to her husband.”

“And yet he seems to have been very fond of her.”

“Oh, yes. They were a most devoted couple.”

“One thing more. Is it true that Mr. and Mrs. Davenheim have always
slept in separate rooms?”

“Since he came back from South America, yes. It seems he suffered
from sleeplessness and moved into a dressing-room.”

“I see. Now, when did he return from South America?”

“Last November.”

“Thank you, Japp. That is all I wish to know.”

Japp rose and took his hat. “Well, good-night, Monsieur Poirot. I
must be off. See you later.”

He went out, and for some time Poirot sat in silence, his eyes
fixed on the ceiling. I could see that his ‘little grey cells’
were hard at work.

“What do you think of it all, Hastings?” he asked at last.

“It seems a very clear case against Lowen,” I replied. “The
motive—the opportunity—the evidence of the maid—the finding of the
ring—the lime kiln—the clothes in the lake—it all seems to hang
together.”

“You think so?”

“Don’t you?”

“There are one or two points that do not seem to fit. For instance,
if Lowen murdered Davenheim, why did he throw the ring away? Why
not keep it, or pawn it? It was a very valuable ring.”

“He may have been afraid to have it in his possession.”

“Then why not bury it?”

“Perhaps he was interrupted.”

“And then there are the clothes in the lake. Why were they there?”

“To suggest suicide, of course.”

“But they were the _identical_ clothes he was wearing. If he were
drowned, he would have been wearing them. If he were murdered, his
murderer would surely have disposed of them in some other way.”

“Unless he wanted it to look like suicide.”

“But then he would have left the body in the lake! No, Hastings,
there is something very curious about those clothes. And there is
another thing. Why did Davenheim wear his hair long?”

“Some men do,” I said. “It’s a fad of theirs.”

“And his beard and moustache? Why did he wear them?”

“Because he liked them, I suppose.”

“And why did he and his wife sleep in separate rooms?”

“I told you—because he suffered from sleeplessness.”

“_Mon ami_, you are too simple! There is a reason for all these
things—a very good reason. And when we find that reason, we shall
find the solution of the mystery.”

He rose and went to the window. “A week! It is a long time. Too
long. I shall have the answer before then.”

And he did. It was on the following Thursday that Japp again
put in an appearance.

“Well,” he said, as he sat down, “I think the case is pretty well
complete. We’ve found a man who saw Lowen coming out of the lime
kiln on Saturday evening. That’s the last link in the chain.”

“And the body?” asked Poirot.

“We haven’t found it yet. But we shall—we shall!”

“I think not,” said Poirot quietly.

“What do you mean?”

“I mean that you will never find the body of Mr. Davenheim—because
there is no body to find!”

“No body! Then what has become of him?”

“He is alive and well—and at the present moment he is in—prison!”

“In prison! Mr. Davenheim in prison! What on earth for?”

“For assaulting a policeman,” said Poirot calmly.

We both stared at him in amazement.

“You mean,” I cried, “that Billy Kellett is—Mr. Davenheim?”

“Exactly.”

“But it’s impossible!” said Japp. “Billy Kellett is a well-known
character. He’s been in prison before.”

“Has he?” said Poirot. “I think you will find that he was in
prison last autumn—at the very time that Mr. Davenheim was supposed
to be in South America.”

Japp looked thunderstruck. “By Jove!” he whispered. “I believe
you’re right. But why—why did he do it?”

“It is very simple,” said Poirot. “Mr. Davenheim’s affairs were in
a very bad way. He saw that a crash was inevitable. He decided to
disappear with a large sum of money, and to start a new life under
another name. He chose the name of Billy Kellett, a man who, as
you say, was already known to the police. He spent last autumn in
prison, in order to establish his identity as Kellett. When he
came out, he returned to his own home, but he took care to change
his appearance as much as possible. He grew his hair long, and
wore a beard and moustache—things which he could easily get rid of
when the time came. He also insisted on sleeping in a separate
room, so that his wife should not discover the deception. On
Saturday last, he staged his disappearance. He left the house,
went to a quiet spot, shaved off his beard and moustache, cut his
hair, and changed into a suit of old clothes which he had previously
hidden there. Then he threw his own clothes into the lake, and
strolled into the village as Billy Kellett. He had already arranged
to be arrested for assaulting a policeman, knowing that he would
be safe in prison while the police were searching for him all over
the country. He even managed to throw suspicion on Lowen, whom he
