disliked, by throwing his ring over the hedge in his presence.”

“But the safe?” I asked. “Who robbed the safe?”

“He did, of course. He robbed his own safe before he left the
house, and hid the money and jewels where he could easily find
them when he came out of prison.”

“It’s incredible!” said Japp. “But I believe you’ve hit the truth.
I’ll go and look into it at once.”

He hurried away, and Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“You see, Hastings? The little grey cells! They never fail.”

“But how did you guess?” I asked.

“It was the long hair and the beard that first gave me the clue,”
said Poirot. “They were so very convenient for a man who wanted
to change his appearance. And then there was the fact that he and
his wife slept in separate rooms. That was very significant. And
when Japp told me about Billy Kellett and the ring—well, the whole
thing became clear. It was a very clever plan, but he forgot one
thing.”

“What was that?”

“He forgot,” said Poirot, “the intelligence of Hercule Poirot!”

“It is not yet proved,” said Poirot thoughtfully. “By the way,
one or two points I should like to ask you. Was Mr. Davenheim’s
moustache particularly long?”

“Yes, rather. He was a very hirsute man altogether.”

“And his hair?”

“Wavy, and he wore it quite long for these days.”

“And his beard?”

“Pointed.”

“He had a full beard, then?”

“Yes, a full beard.”

“And his eyebrows?”

“Bushy.”

“Ah!” Poirot smiled. “One other thing. What was his relation with
his wife?”

“They’d been married some twenty years, but were quite devoted
to each other.”

“And you say she is a very unintelligent woman?”

“Distinctly.”

“_C’est dommage!_” sighed Poirot. “It is a great pity. Does she
ever see Lowen?”

“She did when he was at the house, and she saw him at the police-court
yesterday. But she could give no evidence of any value.”

“Quite so. Now, one more question. When did Mr. Davenheim last
see his doctor?”

“Some six months ago, I believe. He was suffering from a slight
chill.”

“I see. Now, Japp, if I might trouble you with a small commission?
Will you find out for me if any member of the household is in the
habit of using a very strong scented soap—something in the nature
of ‘Eau de Cologne’ or ‘English Lavender’?”

“I can tell you that now. Mrs. Davenheim always uses a very strong
violet perfume. In fact, her boudoir is quite overpowering.”

“Violet—_c’est bon_!” Poirot murmured. “Thank you, Japp.”

“Well, Monsieur Poirot, do you feel any nearer solving the mystery?”

“I am almost there.”

“Then you know where Mr. Davenheim is?”

“I have a very good idea.”

“Is he dead or alive?”

“I’m afraid he’s very much alive.”

“What!” Japp stared. “Then where is he?”

“I cannot tell you—yet. But I will tell you this. When I have
finished my little investigation, you shall have your fiver.”

“Well, good luck to you!” laughed Japp as he took his leave. “And
don’t forget that Miller is a hard nut to crack.”

“Yes, I agree. Of course, Miller’s out there now, trying to find
what he can—but I should imagine that what with the weather and
the passage of time there won’t be much to be found. But there is
some news for Monsieur Poirot. We’ve found a most suspicious
character, who’s been seen hanging round the neighbourhood for the
last few days. He was seen again last night, and we’re trying to
trace him now.”

“What’s he like?” I asked.

“A tall, thin man, with very bright eyes and a large hat.”

“That doesn’t sound very much like Lowen,” I said.

“No, it doesn’t. But it’s a suspicious character, anyway.”

“_Très bien_,” said Poirot. “Now let me ask you a few more questions.
Mr. Davenheim’s hair, you say, was long and wavy?”

“Yes.”

“And his beard was pointed?”

“Yes.”

“And he was in the habit of using a stick?”

“Yes, he was.”

“And what about the safe? I understand it was of the most modern
type. Was it badly damaged?”

“No, not particularly. It had been opened with a key.”

“A key? But you said it had been ‘rifled’!”

“Well, it was. But it must have been opened first. It’s an
extraordinary thing, because the only key was on Mr. Davenheim’s
bunch.”

“Then you think the murderer must have taken it from him before
disposing of the body?”

“Exactly.”

“And what about the window? Was it broken?”

“No. It was open. But it wasn’t _forced_.”

“I see. Now, tell me about Mrs. Davenheim. Was she very much
upset?”

“She seemed a bit dazed, naturally. But she was quite helpful and
ready to answer any questions.”

“Does she suspect anyone?”

“She doesn’t seem to. She’s a very quiet, middle-aged woman, I
should say, with no very strong feelings of any kind.”

“And what about the junior partner? What is his name?”

“Salmon. He’s been very helpful, too. He seems a very capable young
man.”

“And you say he was at the office on Saturday?”

“Yes, until about four o’clock.”

“And he hasn’t been seen since?”

“Oh, yes, he has. He was at his own house on Saturday evening, and
he’s been at the office ever since.”

“I see. Well, Japp, I’m very much obliged to you. You’ve given me
a lot to think about.”

“Don’t mention it. And I’ll let you know if anything else turns
up.”

When Japp had gone, I turned to Poirot.

“Well, what do you think of it?”

“I think it is a very interesting little problem, Hastings. A very
interesting little problem indeed.”

“Do you think Lowen did it?”

“Ah, that is the question. There are several possibilities. For
instance, why should Lowen have gone to the study at all?”

“To see Davenheim, I suppose.”

“But Davenheim wasn’t there.”

“He might have thought he was.”

“But the maid saw him coming _away_ from the study.”

“Yes, but that was later.”

“True. But why should he have gone there twice?”

“I don’t know. Perhaps he went to see if Davenheim had come back.”

“Perhaps. But if he had already murdered him and disposed of the
body in the lime kiln, why should he go back to the study at all?”

“To get the jewels, of course!”

“But he wouldn’t have known where the key was.”

“He might have found it on the body.”

“But why should he have gone to the study to look for the safe?
He might not even have known there was a safe there.”

“He might have heard about it from Davenheim.”

“Possibly. But it seems a very risky thing to do.”

“Murderers do take risks sometimes.”

“True. But Lowen doesn’t strike me as a man who would take
unnecessary risks. He seems a very cautious and calculating
individual.”

“Then who do you think did it?”

“I haven’t made up my mind yet. There are several people who might
have done it.”

“Mrs. Davenheim?”

“It is possible. She might have had a motive. Perhaps she was
jealous of her husband.”

“But Japp said she was a very quiet, middle-aged woman, with no
very strong feelings of any kind.”

“That is what Japp says. But Japp is not always right. And even
the quietest women can be capable of great things when they are
roused.”

“And what about the junior partner?”

“Mr. Salmon? He seems a very unlikely person. He was at the office
until four o’clock, and he was at his own house on Saturday evening.
He doesn’t seem to have had any motive, either.”

“Then who is left?”

“There is Billy Kellett.”

“But you said yourself that he was a very improbable murderer.”

“So I did. But he might have been an accomplice.”

“An accomplice of whom?”

“That is what we have to find out. And then there is the mysterious
stranger with the bright eyes and the large hat.”

“Do you think he might be the murderer?”

“He might be. Or he might be something else entirely.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean that he might be a witness. Someone who saw something that
we don’t know about yet.”

“Well, it’s all very mysterious.”

“It is indeed, Hastings. But I think we shall find the answer
before long. In the meantime, I shall continue to use my little
grey cells.”

And with that I had to be content.

“_Eh bien!_” remarked Poirot. “You should be very well satisfied
with the progress of the case, Japp. It is most interesting. By
the way, may I ask a question?”

“Certainly.”

“Was there anything else found in the pocket of the clothes?”

“Only some small change—a few shillings and a sixpence. No papers.”

“And when Mr. Davenheim went to post his letters, did he leave
any behind?”

“There were three on his desk. He had apparently forgotten them.
One was to a firm of stockbrokers, another to a firm of solicitors,
the third was to a man at Buenos Ayres—some friend, I believe. All
business letters.”

“I see. Now, about the household. Can you tell me something of
the servants?”

“Well, there’s a cook, a housemaid and a parlour-maid. They’ve
all been there for some years. Then there’s the valet—a Swiss, I
believe—who’s been with Mr. Davenheim about a year. Very quiet,
civil fellow.”

“And the gardeners?”

“One of them has been there ten years, the other two for about
three. Then there’s a boy, who’s been with them for some months.”

“Any of them particularly fond of flowers?”

“I really couldn’t say. The head gardener is a bit of a character.
He’s always trying some new experiment with his roses.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And now, if it’s not too much trouble,
could you let me have a list of all the people who have been to
The Cedars during the last six months—tradesmen, visitors,
everyone? It will be quite a long list, I suppose, but I should
be much obliged.”

Japp stared at him. “What on earth—? Well, I’ll see what I can do.”

“One other thing. Could you tell me if Mr. Davenheim’s hair and
beard were naturally wavy, or whether he used tongs?”

Japp burst into a roar of laughter. “Well, you are a one, Monsieur
Poirot! What on earth can that have to do with it?”

“A great deal, my friend—a great deal. Will you find out for me?”

“I’ll ask the valet. He ought to know!” Japp chuckled. “Well, I
must be off. See you again soon.”

“Wait a moment,” said Poirot. “There is one more thing. Did Mr.
Davenheim have any special hobby or interest?”

“He was a great collector of curios. His study is full of them.
In fact, it’s more like a museum than a study.”

“I see. Thank you. Good-night.”

When Japp had gone, Poirot sat for some time in silence. Then he
turned to me. “Hastings, do you think it is possible for a man to
be in two places at once?”

“I should say it was quite impossible,” I replied.

“And yet—if Mr. Davenheim was at Chingside, how could he also be
in London?”

“But he wasn’t in London!”

“Was he not? Then how did he pawn the ring?”

“But it was Billy Kellett who pawned the ring!”

“Ah, yes—Billy Kellett. A very interesting character, that.”

“You don’t think he’s telling the truth, then?”

“On the contrary, I am convinced of it.”

“Then Lowen must have thrown the ring over the hedge!”

“But why? That is what I cannot see. Why? If he had murdered
Davenheim and disposed of the body in the lime kiln, why should he
take the ring and then throw it away? It is not logical.”

“Perhaps he was afraid it would be found on him.”

“Then why take it at all? No, Hastings, there is something here
that I do not understand. There is a link missing.”

He sat in silence for some time, his brows knitted in thought. At
last he looked up. “I have it! The lake—the boathouse—the lime
kiln—the ring—the wavy hair—the curios! It all fits in! But there
is one thing—one thing that I must know.”

“What is that?” I asked.

“The length of Mr. Davenheim’s stay in Buenos Ayres. I must find
out exactly how long he was there.”

“Japp said he spent all last autumn there.”

“Yes, but I must be more exact. I must know the date of his
departure and the date of his return.”

“I can easily find that out for you,” I said. “I’ll go to the
offices of the steamship company to-morrow.”

“Thank you, Hastings. That will be a great help.”

By common consent we both turned and looked at Poirot. He seemed
lost in reflection, his brow knitted, as though with some supreme
mental effort. I felt that at last his keen intellect was asserting
itself. What would his first words be? We were not long left in
doubt. With a sigh, the tension of his attitude relaxed, and
turning to Japp, he asked:

“Have you any idea, my friend, whether Mr. and Mrs. Davenheim
occupied the same bedroom?”

The Inspector’s jaw dropped. I was not much better. We stared at
him in blank amazement. Japp’s expression was comical in its
bewilderment.

“Oh, well, as it happens, I have,” he said after a long pause.
“Mrs. Davenheim has her own suite of rooms. Her bedroom is next
her husband’s, and communicates with it.”

“And has he a valet?”

“Yes, a man called George.”

“And how long has he been with him?”

“Six years.”

“Good! He will do. Now, another question: Did Mr. Davenheim use
to go to his office every day?”

“No, not every day. Two or three times a week was his rule.”

“And on the days when he stayed at home, did he go into his study
much?”

“Most of the time.”

“Then he would not have much to say to his wife?”

“Nothing much beyond what he would say at meal-times.”

Poirot’s eyes twinkled. “Then her description of him—and she must
know him better than any one—should be absolutely reliable. Has
she any photographs of him?”

“No, unfortunately. He has a great dislike to being photographed.
He says it’s one of his little fads.”

“H’m! That is a pity. Does she happen to have any hairbrushes or—well,
shaving-brushes of his?”

Japp stared again. “Shaving-brushes! No, I’m afraid I didn’t think
to ask her. Why?”

“It occurred to me that there might be something in it,” Poirot
returned smoothly. “Then there is the matter of his hair. You say
it was thick and wavy?”

“Yes.”

“And his moustache and beard?”

“Wavy also.”

“Ah! Then it would be possible to tell if he had recently had it
trimmed, would it not?”

“I suppose so. But what has that to do with it?”

“Oh, nothing—nothing. A mere whim of mine. By the way, how was
the safe opened?”

“With a key. It was found in the lock. The thief had apparently
not even taken the trouble to remove it.”

“Then it must have been an inside job!” I cried.

“Not necessarily,” Japp said. “The safe was not a very strong one.
Any clever burglar could have opened it with a skeleton key.”

“Yes, but the key was _in_ the lock,” I persisted.

“Well, that’s just it. Why should the thief leave it there? It’s
most unusual.”

“Very,” agreed Poirot. “It is one of the most interesting features
of the case.”

“Well,” said Japp, rising, “I must be going. I’ve a lot to do to-morrow.”

“One moment,” said Poirot. “There is just one more thing I should
like to know. Does Mrs. Davenheim wear her hair long or short?”

Japp fairly gasped. “Short? Why, she’s a middle-aged woman! She
wears it in a big knot at the back of her head.”

“Ah!” Poirot looked thoughtful. “Then she would not have a pair
of—well, say, hair-clippers?”

“Hair-clippers! No, I don’t suppose she would. What on earth are
you driving at?”

“Nothing—nothing. I was just wondering. Good-night, Japp. Let me
know if anything fresh turns up.”

“I will. Good-night.”

The question was so unexpected that for a moment Japp could only
stare at him. Then he laughed.

“Bless my soul, monsieur, I don’t know. I can find out if you like.”

“I should be very much obliged,” said Poirot. “As I remarked
before, to some people details are insignificant; to me, they are
all-important. Then I should also like to know if Mr. Davenheim
is a man of his word—I mean, did he usually do what he said he
would?”

“Why, I believe his reputation for integrity was very high in the
City.”

“No, no, I do not mean that. I mean in his private life. If he
said he would post a letter, did he post it?”

“Oh, I see! Well, I’ll find that out too.”

“Is that all?” asked Japp.

“For the present, yes. Except that I should like to know if he
shared his wife’s room, and if he were a man of his word.”

“A most important question!” said Japp, with a laugh. “I’ll get
the answer to it for you.”

I did not see Japp again until the following morning. He looked
radiant.

“Everything is going as I expected,” he cried. “We’re making out
a very strong case against Lowen. His finger-prints have been found
on the safe, and it seems that his financial position was far
worse than anyone had imagined. He was on the verge of bankruptcy.
Moreover, the valet at The Cedars tells me that his master was
a man of the most punctilious habits. If he said he would post
a letter, it was as good as done.”

“And the other point?”

“Oh, that’s all right too. They’ve occupied separate rooms for
the last year or so.”

“_A la bonne heure!_” cried Poirot. “The case is solved.”

“Solved?” I cried. “You mean you know where Mr. Davenheim is?”

“I do.”

“And where is he?”

“In the one place where no one has thought of looking for him.”

“Where is that?”

“In gaol!”

“In gaol!” I gasped. “Why, he’s not been arrested yet.”

“Not as Mr. Davenheim,” said Poirot. “He’s there as Billy Kellett.”

“Billy Kellett!” I cried. “But Billy Kellett’s a well-known
character.”

“He has a well-known record, which is not quite the same thing,”
said Poirot. “Now, listen. Mr. Davenheim, a man of large and wavy
hair, a full moustache and a pointed beard, bushy eyebrows and
dark eyes, disappears. A few hours later, a man called Billy
Kellett is arrested for being drunk and disorderly, and having
in his possession a ring which is identified as having belonged
to Mr. Davenheim. Now, let us suppose that Mr. Davenheim, for
reasons of his own, wished to disappear. What more natural than
that he should assume a character already known to the police,
and one, moreover, whose physical characteristics were as different
as possible from his own?”

“But his hair and beard?” I asked.

“He had three months in which to grow them, while he was in Buenos
Ayres last autumn. Remember, Billy Kellett was in prison then.
Davenheim could study his methods and appearance at his leisure.
The dark eyes and bushy eyebrows were his own; the rest was easy.”

“But the ring?”

“That was the cleverest part of all. By pawning the ring as Billy
Kellett, he established his identity beyond any doubt. Who would
ever dream that Billy Kellett and the great financier were one
and the same person?”

“It seems incredible!” I said.

“But it is true. And it explains why the clothes were found by
the lake. He changed into the rags of Billy Kellett, and then
walked to the station and took the train to London, where he
proceeded to get drunk and be arrested as he had planned.”

“But what was his motive?”

“That, I think, we shall find in the state of his financial
affairs. A large sum of money has disappeared from the safe.
If he is supposed to have been murdered, no one will look for
it—or for him. He will have a nice little nest-egg waiting for
him when he comes out of prison. Now, Hastings, if you will be
so good as to ring up Japp, I think we may as well win that fiver.”

I did as he requested, and Japp’s voice came over the wire, full
of excitement.

“Is that you, Hastings? Tell Poirot he’s won his bet. We’ve just
discovered that Mr. Davenheim and Billy Kellett are the same
person. Miller’s just back from the prison, where he’s been with
Mrs. Davenheim. She recognized him at once!”

I turned to Poirot. “You were right,” I said. “It was Davenheim
himself.”

Poirot smiled, and began to polish the teapot once more.

“The little grey cells, Hastings!” he murmured. “The little grey
cells!”

Japp stared. “Why, I don’t know. I’ll find out, if you’re
interested. But what’s that got to do with the murder?”

“Wait a moment, my friend. I must think. You say that there were
at least two hundred pounds in notes in the safe when it was opened
on Monday? Now, what about those notes? Have you the numbers?”

“Yes, we’ve got them. But so far none of them have turned up.”

“One thing more. Is there anything unusual about the garden?”

“Beyond the lake and the lime-kiln—nothing.”

“How about the house?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing at all?”

“No—except that it’s got a rather good library, and several
valuable pictures.”

“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes were sparkling now. “I’m glad to hear it. And
the staff?”

“Cook, two housemaids, and a kitchen-maid. All been there some
time. Then there’s the valet, who’s been with Mr. Davenheim about
five years.”

“And the gardener?”

“He’s lived in the cottage at the end of the garden for years.”

“Good. Now, I have another question to ask you. Does Mr. Davenheim
wear his hair long or short?”

Japp looked at me and winked. “About medium, I should say. Why?”

“Because,” said Poirot, “if he wore it short, it would have been
extremely difficult for him to have appeared in the village with
a beard and moustache, unless, of course, they were false.”

“His wife says they were his own.”

“Then,” said Poirot, “it seems he must have had some way of making
his hair grow very quickly.”

“What on earth do you mean, Monsieur Poirot?”

“Think, my friend, think. He disappears on Saturday. On Sunday
morning his clothes are found. But no one has seen him. Then on
Monday the safe is found to have been rifled. Does it not strike
you as being a little—just a little—peculiar?”

“Well, of course, the whole thing’s peculiar,” said Japp. “But I
don’t see what you’re driving at.”

“And I,” said Poirot, “see only too clearly. I see it all, even to
the last little detail. My friend, the solution of the mystery
is—as I said—within.” He tapped his forehead. “Now, if you will
excuse me, I will go to my room and think.”

We watched him go in silence. Japp shook his head.

“He’s a queer fish, isn’t he?” he said. “I can’t make him out at
all.”

“Neither can I,” I said. “But he’s a wonderful man.”

“He is that,” agreed Japp. “Well, I must be getting along. Good-night,
Captain Hastings.”

“Good-night, Japp.”

I went back into the room. I felt restless and uneasy. Poirot’s
words had disturbed me. What did he mean by saying that he saw it
all? Was it possible that he really had solved the mystery? I
knew, of course, that he was a genius, but this seemed almost
beyond even his powers. I sat down and tried to think the matter
out for myself. But it was no use. My brain was in a whirl. I gave
it up at last and went to bed.

I was awakened the next morning by Poirot’s voice. He was standing
by my bedside, looking more like an egg than ever.

“_Bon jour, mon ami_,” he said. “I have a little surprise for you.
I am going for a walk.”

“A walk?” I said. “Where to?”

“To the village of Chingside.”

“But I thought you were going to solve the case without moving from
your chair?”

“Ah, but this is different. I am going to the village—not to the
house. I wish to make a little inquiry at the post office.”

“At the post office?”

“Exactly. And if you would like to accompany me, I shall be
charmed.”

I jumped out of bed and was soon ready. We caught the 10.15 from
Victoria and arrived at Chingside just before eleven. Poirot led
the way straight to the post office. It was a small, old-fashioned
shop, where everything from stamps to string was sold.

Poirot went up to the counter and addressed the postmistress.

“Good-morning, madame,” he said. “I wonder if you could help me.
I am looking for a friend of mine, a Mr.—er—Davenheim.”

The postmistress shook her head. “I’m afraid I can’t help you, sir.
Mr. Davenheim has disappeared.”

“Yes, I know. But I thought he might have been here on Saturday.”

“On Saturday? No, sir. I didn’t see him.”

“Are you sure? He didn’t come in to post a letter, for instance?”

“No, sir. I’m quite sure. He wasn’t here at all on Saturday.”

“Thank you,” said Poirot. “I’m much obliged to you. Good-morning.”

He turned and walked out of the shop. I followed him, feeling
more bewildered than ever.

“But what does it mean, Poirot?” I asked. “He said he was going to
the village to post some letters.”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “He said so. But he did not do so.”

“Then where did he go?”

“Ah, that is the question. But I think I can answer it. He went—to
the boathouse.”

“To the boathouse?”

“Certainly. And from the boathouse he went—where do you think?”

“I have no idea.”

“He went to London.”

“To London? But how?”

“By train, _mon ami_. By the 6.15 from Chingside.”

“But they said at the station that he had not been seen.”

“Because they did not recognize him. He was no longer Mr.
Davenheim.”

“Then who was he?”

“He was—Billy Kellett!”

I stared at Poirot in amazement. “Billy Kellett? But Billy Kellett
is in prison!”

“Exactly. He is in prison. And that is why he is so safe.”

“I don’t understand.”

“It is quite simple, _mon ami_. Mr. Davenheim and Billy Kellett
are one and the same person.”

“But the description?”

“Ah, the description! Long hair, full moustache, pointed beard,
bushy eyebrows. All false, my friend—all false! He had been
preparing for this for months. He had even been to prison as Billy
Kellett last autumn, when his wife thought he was in Buenos Ayres.
It was a stroke of genius. He knew that the police would never
look for him in prison.”

“But the safe? The robbery?”

“He robbed himself, _mon ami_. He needed the money to start a new
life. He had been planning it for a long time. The appointment
with Lowen was a mere blind—a way of throwing suspicion on someone
else.”

“And the clothes in the lake?”

“He put them there himself. He changed into his Billy Kellett
clothes in the boathouse, and then threw his own clothes into the
lake.”

“But the ring?”

“He pawned it himself—as Billy Kellett. He wanted to make sure
that the police would find the ring and so be led to Billy Kellett.”

“It’s incredible!” I said. “But how did you find out?”

“I suspected it from the first,” said Poirot. “The description of
Davenheim was so very—what shall I say?—so very easy to assume.
Then there was the matter of his hair. If he had really been
Davenheim, his hair would have been much longer after three days.
But Billy Kellett’s hair was short. And then there was the post
office. He said he was going to post some letters, but he never
went there. That was the final clue.”

“And what are you going to do now?”

“I am going to tell Japp. He will be very surprised, I think.”

And Japp was surprised. But when Poirot had explained it all to
him, he had to admit that it was the only possible solution. Mr.
Davenheim—or Billy Kellett, as he now was—was soon identified and
the money and jewels were recovered. And Poirot won his bet.

“But I must admit,” said Japp, “that I should never have thought of
it myself. You’re a wonderful man, Monsieur Poirot.”

Poirot smiled. “It is the little grey cells, my friend—the little
grey cells!”

Japp looked surprised, then laughed. “What on earth—oh, I see.
No, they don’t. Not for some time, I believe. Mrs. Davenheim’s
room is on the first floor, while her husband’s is on the ground
floor. He’s a bit of an invalid, it appears, and finds the stairs
trying.”

“And what about the maid?”

“She doesn’t sleep on the ground floor. No one but Mr. Davenheim
does.”

“And you say he was expecting a visitor?”

“Yes, Lowen.”

“Does his wife know anything more about this visitor?”

“No, she only knows that her husband told her to expect him.”

“Did he ever speak of him before?”

“Never. And she says that she had never heard of him. He’s quite
a small man, you know.”

“I see. Now, there is one more question I should like to ask. Is
Mr. Davenheim’s hair still long?”

“Why, yes, I suppose so. Why?”

“And his beard? Is that also the same?”

“What an extraordinary question!” Japp laughed again. “I should
imagine so.”

“Wait a minute. I have one more question. Does he, or did he,
possess a large number of boots?”

Japp stared. “Boots? Well, I don’t know. I should imagine a man
in his position would have a good many. But I haven’t counted them.”

“Well, I wish you would.”

“My dear Poirot, what on earth—?”

“Will you do me this small service? I should also be interested
to know if any of them have been recently cleaned.”

“I’ll find out if you really want to know,” said Japp, with a shrug
of his shoulders. “But it seems to me we’re wandering a long way
from the point.”

“On the contrary,” said Poirot. “I think we are getting very near
it.”

“You mean you’ve got a theory?”

“I have a little idea—that is all.”

“Well, I’ll let you know about the boots to-morrow. Is there
anything else?”

“Yes. I should like to know if Mr. Davenheim was in the habit of
using a particular kind of hair-wash.”

“Hair-wash! My dear Poirot!”

“Please—just to humor me.”

“All right. Anything else?”

“No, that is all.”

Japp rose. “Well, I must be off. I’ll let you know as soon as I
get the information you want.”

When Japp had gone, I turned to Poirot. “What’s the idea?” I asked.
“Why all these questions about hair-wash and boots?”

“Because they are of the utmost importance, my friend.”

“In what way?”

“That I cannot tell you—yet.”

I knew from experience that it was useless to try and get anything
out of Poirot when he was in this mood. He would only tell me when
he was ready. So I had to wait with what patience I could command.

Next morning, Japp telephoned. “I’ve got the information you wanted,
Poirot. Mr. Davenheim has quite a large collection of boots—thirty-four
pairs, to be exact. And three of them have been cleaned quite
recently. As for the hair-wash, he uses a very strong-smelling
tonic—something called ‘Harlene,’ I believe.”

“Thank you, my friend. That is very interesting.”

“Is it? I’m glad to hear it. Is there anything else you want to
know?”

“No, thank you. I think that is all.”

“Well, I’ll let you know if anything else turns up.”

“Please do. And, by the way, Japp—”

“Yes?”

“I should be very glad if you could find out if there are any
unusual visitors at the house.”

“Visitors? What do you mean?”

“Oh, anyone who doesn’t usually go there. A beggar, for instance,
or a pedlar.”

“I’ll find out. But I don’t see—”

“Never mind. Just find out if you can.”

“All right. I’ll let you know.”

I waited for Poirot to speak, but he remained silent, lost in
thought. After a few minutes, he got up and began to pace the room.

“Thirty-four pairs of boots!” he murmured. “And three of them
cleaned recently. And the hair-wash. Yes, it is all very
interesting.”

“But what does it mean?” I cried.

“It means, my friend, that we are very near the truth.”

“You mean you know who did it?”

“I have a very good idea.”

“And who is it?”

“Wait, my friend. Wait. All in good time.”

I had to be content with that. But I could see that Poirot was
very pleased with himself. He spent the rest of the day in a state
of suppressed excitement, and I knew that he was on the verge of
a discovery.

The next day, Japp called again. “I’ve found out about those
visitors, Poirot. It seems that a beggar did call at the house
on Saturday afternoon—just about the time Mr. Davenheim
disappeared.”

“A beggar? What kind of a beggar?”

“An old man, apparently. Very ragged and dirty. He asked for money,
and Mrs. Davenheim gave him a shilling. He went away after that.”

“And did anyone else see him?”

“One of the gardeners saw him leaving the grounds. He says the
man seemed to be in a great hurry.”

“I see. And has he been seen since?”

“No. He seems to have vanished completely.”

“Like Mr. Davenheim?”

“Exactly.”

“This is very interesting, Japp. Very interesting indeed.”

“You think he had something to do with it?”

“I am almost sure of it.”

“But how? What could an old beggar have to do with the disappearance
of a wealthy banker?”

“That remains to be seen. But I have a feeling that we shall find
out very soon.”

“I hope so. This case is getting on my nerves.”

“Patience, my friend. Patience. We shall know the truth before
the week is out.”

Japp went away, looking more puzzled than ever. I must confess
that I was equally mystified. What could a beggar have to do with
the case? And what about the boots and the hair-wash? It all
seemed like a hopeless jumble to me.

But Poirot seemed to know what he was doing. He spent the next
two days in a state of quiet contemplation, only occasionally
breaking his silence to ask me some seemingly irrelevant question.

On Friday morning, Japp arrived with fresh news. “We’ve found the
beggar, Poirot! Or rather, we’ve found someone who matches the
description.”

“Where?”

“In a common lodging-house in the East End. He was arrested for
drunkenness and disorderly conduct. His name is Billy Kellett.”

“Billy Kellett!” I cried. “The man who pawned the ring!”

“The same,” said Japp. “It seems he’s been hanging around the
neighbourhood of Chingside for some time.”

“And what does he say for himself?”

“He denies everything, of course. Says he’s never been near The
Cedars. Но we’ve got several witnesses who can identify him.”

“This is very important, Japp. Very important indeed.”

“You think he’s the murderer, then?”

“I think he is the key to the whole mystery.”

“But how?”

“Wait, my friend. Wait. I have one more thing to do before I can
tell you the whole story.”

“And what is that?”

“I must visit The Cedars.”

“But I thought you said you could solve the case without leaving
your chair?”

“I said I could, granted the facts were placed before me. But
there are one or two things I must see for myself.”

“Well, if you must, you must. I’ll go with you.”

“And I,” I added.

“Very well. We will go this afternoon.”

We arrived at Chingside about three o’clock. The Cedars was a large,
imposing house, surrounded by extensive grounds. We were met at the
door by Mrs. Davenheim, who seemed very distressed.

“Oh, Monsieur Poirot,” she cried. “I am so glad you have come.
This is all so terrible. Have you any news of my husband?”

“Not yet, madame. But I hope to have some very soon.”

“Oh, I hope so. I can’t bear this suspense any longer.”

“I understand, madame. Now, if you will allow me, I should like
to see your husband’s study.”

“Of course. This way.”

She led us into a large, well-furnished room. At one end was a
large safe, which had been broken into. At the other end was a
long French window, opening on to the rose-garden.

Poirot spent some time examining the room. He looked at the safe,
the window, and the various objects on the desk. Then he turned
to Mrs. Davenheim.

“Madame, I should like to ask you a few questions.”

“Of course, Monsieur Poirot.”

“Your husband—did he have any enemies?”

“Not that I know of. He was a very kind and generous man.”

“And what about Mr. Lowen?”

“I don’t know much about him. My husband only mentioned him once
or twice.”

“I see. And did your husband have any unusual habits?”

“Well, he was very fond of his garden. He spent a lot of time
there.”

“And did he ever mention a beggar?”

“A beggar? No, I don’t think so. Why do you ask?”

“Because a beggar was seen near the house on the day your husband
disappeared.”

“Oh, yes. I remember now. I gave him a shilling. But surely he
couldn’t have had anything to do with it?”

“We shall see, madame. Now, if you will excuse me, I should like
to see the rose-garden.”

“Of course. This way.”

She led us out through the French window. The rose-garden was
beautifully laid out, with many different varieties of roses. In
the center was a small pond, with a fountain.

Poirot walked slowly round the garden, looking at everything
with great care. Then he stopped and looked towards the lake.

“And that is the lake?” he asked.

“Yes,” said Mrs. Davenheim. “It is very deep in places.”

“I see. And where is the boathouse?”

“Over there, behind those trees.”

“Thank you, madame. I think that is all I need to see for the
moment.”

We returned to the house, and Poirot took his leave of Mrs.
Davenheim. As we were walking down the drive, Japp turned to him.

“Well, Poirot? What do you think?”

“I think, my friend, that we are very near the end.”

“You mean you know who the murderer is?”

“I am almost sure of it.”

“And who is it?”

“Wait, my friend. Wait. I have one more thing to do.”

“And what is that?”

“I must visit the local police station.”

“What for?”

“To see Billy Kellett.”

“But I’ve already seen him. He’s just a common tramp.”

“Perhaps. But I should like to see him for myself.”

“Very well. If you insist.”

We drove to the police station, where Japp introduced us to the
inspector in charge. We were then taken to the cell where Billy
Kellett was being held.

The man was a sorry sight. He was dirty, ragged, and smelled
strongly of stale beer. He looked up as we entered, his eyes full
of fear.

“I didn’t do it!” he cried. “I tell you, I didn’t do it!”

“Calm yourself, my friend,” said Poirot. “I only want to ask you
a few questions.”

“I’ve told the other gentleman everything I know. I found the
ring in a ditch. I didn’t steal it.”

“I know, I know. But tell me, where did you find it, exactly?”

“In a ditch near the village. A man threw it over the hedge.”

“And what did this man look like?”

“He was a tall, dark gent, with a big moustache. A real city toff.”

“I see. And was he alone?”

“Yes, he was alone.”

“And what did he do after he threw the ring over the hedge?”

“He went on towards the station.”

“I see. Now, tell me, have you ever seen this man before?”

“No, never.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes, I’m sure.”

“I see. Thank you, my friend. That is all I wanted to know.”

We left the cell and returned to the inspector’s office.

“Well, Poirot?” said Japp. “What do you think now?”

“I think, my friend, that we have all the pieces of the puzzle.”

“And can you put them together?”

“I think so. But first, I must ask you to do one more thing for
me.”

“And what is that?”

“I want you to bring everyone concerned in this case to my rooms
tomorrow morning at eleven o’clock.”

“Everyone? Who do you mean?”

“Mrs. Davenheim, Mr. Lowen, and Billy Kellett.”

“Billy Kellett? But he’s in jail!”

“I’m sure you can arrange for him to be brought there under
guard.”

“Well, I suppose I can. Но why do you want them all there?”

“Because, my friend, I am going to tell you the truth about the
disappearance of Mr. Davenheim.”

“You mean you’ve solved it?”

“I have.”

“And who is the murderer?”

“Wait, my friend. Wait. All will be revealed tomorrow morning.”

I spent a sleepless night, wondering what Poirot’s solution
would be. Was it Lowen? Or Billy Kellett? Or someone else
altogether? It all seemed so confusing.

Next morning, at eleven o’clock, everyone was assembled in Poirot’s
rooms. Mrs. Davenheim looked pale and anxious. Lowen looked
defiant. Billy Kellett looked terrified, standing between two
sturdy policemen. Japp was there too, looking eager and expectant.

Poirot stood in the middle of the room, looking very calm and
composed. He looked at each of us in turn, and then began to
speak.

“Mesdames et messieurs,” he began. “I have asked you all here
today because I have solved the mystery of the disappearance of
Mr. Davenheim.”

There was a sudden hush in the room. Everyone’s eyes were fixed
on Poirot.

“As you know,” he continued, “Mr. Davenheim disappeared from his
home last Saturday afternoon. At the same time, a large sum of
money and some valuable jewellery were stolen from his safe.”

“The police,” he went on, “at first suspected Mr. Lowen. He was
seen near the house at the time of the disappearance, and he was
known to have an appointment with Mr. Davenheim. Furthermore,
a ring belonging to Mr. Davenheim was found to have been pawned
by a man called Billy Kellett, who claimed to have seen Mr. Lowen
throw it over a hedge.”

“However,” Poirot said, “there were several things that did not
fit in with this theory. In the first place, Mr. Lowen is not the
kind of man to commit a clumsy murder and then throw the evidence
away in a place where it could easily be found. In the second
place, Billy Kellett’s description of the man he saw was a little
too accurate for someone who had only seen him for a few moments.”

“I began to wonder,” Poirot continued, “if there was another
explanation. And then I started to think about the boots.”

“The boots?” cried Japp. “What have they got to do with it?”

“Everything, my friend. Everything. You see, Mr. Davenheim had
thirty-four pairs of boots. And three of them had been cleaned
recently. Why would a man who was about to disappear—or be
murdered—bother to have three pairs of boots cleaned?”

“The answer,” Poirot said, “is that he didn’t. Someone else did.
Someone who was pretending to be Mr. Davenheim.”

“Pretending to be Mr. Davenheim?” cried Mrs. Davenheim. “But who?”

“The person who was in the house all the time,” said Poirot. “The
person who had access to Mr. Davenheim’s clothes, his hair-wash,
and his safe.”

“You mean—?” began Japp.

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that Mr. Davenheim did not disappear.
He was murdered. And his murderer is in this room.”

Everyone looked around the room in alarm.

“But who?” cried Mrs. Davenheim. “Who could have done such a
terrible thing?”

“The person who did it,” said Poirot, “is the person who had the
most to gain. The person who knew all about Mr. Davenheim’s
affairs, and who could easily step into his shoes.”

“He had been planning this for a long time,” Poirot went on. “He
had even gone so far as to create a second identity for himself.
He had spent several months in London, living as a common tramp,
so that he would be familiar with the life of a beggar.”

“And then,” Poirot said, “on Saturday afternoon, he put his plan
into action. He murdered Mr. Davenheim, disposed of the body in
the lime kiln, and then assumed his second identity. He left the
house as a beggar, and then, later that evening, he appeared as
Billy Kellett to pawn the ring.”

“But why the ring?” I asked.

“To cast suspicion on Mr. Lowen,” said Poirot. “He knew that Mr.
Lowen was coming to the house, and he wanted to make sure that
the police would suspect him.”

“But who is this man?” cried Japp.

“The man,” said Poirot, “is none other than—”

He paused for a moment, and then pointed his finger.

“Mr. Davenheim himself!”

There was a gasp of astonishment from everyone in the room.

“Mr. Davenheim!” I cried. “But you said he was murdered!”

“I said he was murdered in a figurative sense,” said Poirot. “He
wanted to disappear, to start a new life with the money and
jewels he had stolen from his own safe. And what better way to
do that than to ‘murder’ himself and then appear as someone else?”

“But how did you know?” asked Japp.

“The boots, my friend. The boots. A man who lives as a beggar
does not need thirty-four pairs of boots. But he does need to have
his boots cleaned regularly. And the hair-wash—he used it to
disguise his appearance.”

“And the beggar who was seen near the house—that was Mr. Davenheim
himself, in his second identity.”

“It was a very clever plan,” Poirot concluded. “But he made one
mistake. He forgot that Papa Poirot has the little grey cells.”

Mr. Davenheim—or Billy Kellett, as he was now known—collapsed
into a chair, his face pale and drawn. He knew that the game was
up.

Japp stepped forward and placed his hand on his shoulder. “I
arrest you, Mr. Davenheim, for the theft of your own property and
for the attempted framing of an innocent man.”

As they led him away, Mrs. Davenheim burst into tears. Poirot
went over to her and took her hand.

“Do not cry, madame,” he said gently. “It is better to know the
truth, even if it is a painful one.”

And so the mystery of the disappearance of Mr. Davenheim was
solved. And once again, Hercule Poirot had proved that the brain
is mightier than the sword.

The week was not yet up, and Japp had to pay Poirot his five
pounds. As for me, I could only marvel at the genius of my friend.

“Poirot,” I said, as we were sitting alone in our rooms that
evening. “How did you really know?”

Poirot smiled. “It was simple, my friend. Simple. When you have
eliminated the impossible, whatever remains, however improbable,
must be the truth.”

“And in this case, the truth was that Mr. Davenheim was his own
murderer.”

“A very pretty problem,” he murmured. “A very pretty problem
indeed.”

I nodded. It was indeed a very pretty problem. And Hercule Poirot
had solved it in his own inimitable way.

The end.

Japp stared. “Why, I don’t know. I should hardly think so. But I
don’t see what that’s got to do with it.”

“Does Mrs. Davenheim use a particularly strong scent?”

“Well, really, Monsieur Poirot, I can’t say I noticed it. I should
say she didn’t. She’s a very quiet, middle-aged lady, you know.”

“Does she wear any particular colour?”

“No. I didn’t notice any.”

“I’m afraid I’ve not much to report on that head.”

“Then it’s not much help?” I said.

“On the contrary,” replied Poirot. “It is most helpful.”

He turned back to Japp. “Now, Japp, I’m going to ask you to do
something for me.”

“Anything you like, Monsieur Poirot.”

“I want you to find out for me how long Mr. Davenheim was in
the habit of wearing his hair and beard.”

“You mean whether he’d ever had it short?”

“No. I mean whether he had ever had it long.”

Japp looked at him for a moment in silence. Then he laughed. “I
see. You think he had it long once and had it cut before he
disappeared, so that he could pass unnoticed?”

Poirot nodded. “Exactly. That is the point. I should also like to
know if he had been in the habit of shaving his upper lip.”

“But he had a moustache!”

“I know. But I want to know if he had had one _always_.”

“I’ll do my best to find out for you.”

“One thing more. Is it a fact that for some time before his
disappearance Mr. Davenheim had been in the habit of having his
meals sent up to his study?”

“Why, yes. Mrs. Davenheim told me so herself. She said her husband
had been much worried over business lately, and had preferred to
remain alone.”

“That is all I want to know. I’m much obliged to you.”

“Well, good-night, Monsieur Poirot. I’ll let you know if anything
fresh turns up.”

“Good-night, Japp.”

When the door had closed on the Inspector, I looked at Poirot. He
was smiling to himself in a way that was both irritating and
perplexing.

“Well?” I asked. “What do you think of it all?”

“I think,” said Poirot, “that it is a very interesting little
problem. A very interesting little problem indeed.”

“You’ve got a theory?”

“I have several. But there is one that seems to me to fit the facts
better than any of the others.”

“And that is?”

“_Wait and see, mon ami, wait and see_.”

And with that I had to be content.

For the next few days I saw very little of Poirot. He seemed to
be always out, and once or twice I found him in close conversation
with a very disreputable-looking individual. On Thursday morning
Japp walked in with a more cheerful air than he had worn of late.

“I’ve got some news for you, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “We’ve
found the body!”

“In the lake?”

“No. In the lime-kiln. Or rather what’s left of it. There was a
heap of charred bones and some metal buttons.”

“And the ring?”

“No. No sign of the ring.”

“That’s what I expected,” said Poirot. “Now, Japp, I want you to
tell me one thing. Have you seen Mrs. Davenheim since the body was
found?”

“Yes. I went down to Chingside this morning to tell her.”

“How did she take it?”

“She seemed very much upset, of course. But she’s a very quiet
woman, and she didn’t make much fuss.”

“Did she identify the buttons?”

“Yes. She said they were off an old coat her husband used to wear
when he was gardening.”

“I see. Now, Japp, I want you to do one more thing for me. I want
you to take me down to Chingside.”

“With pleasure. When will you go?”

“This afternoon, if that’s convenient for you.”

“Perfectly. I’ll call for you at half-past two.”

“Thank you. I shall be ready.”

At half-past two Japp duly appeared, and we all three set off for
Chingside. On the way Japp told us that the inquest was to be held
on Saturday, and that Lowen was to be charged with the murder.

“It’s a clear case,” he said. “There’s the motive—money—and there’s
the opportunity. And there’s the evidence of the maid and the man
who saw him near the lime-kiln.”

“What man was that?” I asked.

“A man called Billy Kellett. He’s the one who pawned the ring, you
know. He says he saw Lowen near the lime-kiln about seven o’clock
on Saturday evening.”

“But I thought you said he was a jailbird?”

“So he is. But that doesn’t mean he’s lying. And his story is
borne out by the maid.”

“I see,” I said. “It certainly does look like a clear case.”

Poirot said nothing. He sat in his corner of the car, his eyes
half-closed, and a look of deep thought on his face.

When we arrived at The Cedars, we were shown into the drawing-room,
where Mrs. Davenheim was sitting. She was a small, fair woman, with
a gentle, rather faded face. She looked very pale and tired, and
there were dark circles under her eyes.

“It is very kind of you to come, Monsieur Poirot,” she said, as she
shook hands. “Inspector Japp has told me how kind you have been.”

“Not at all, madame,” said Poirot. “I only wish I could have been
of more service to you.”

He sat down and began to talk to her in his easy, pleasant way.
I could see that she was much impressed by him. After a few
minutes he asked her if he might see the study where her husband
had been last seen.

“Certainly,” she said. “I will show you the way myself.”

She led the way across the hall and opened a door at the far end.
The study was a large, comfortable room, with a big desk in the
middle and a safe in one corner. There was a large window opening
on to the rose-garden.

Poirot walked over to the window and looked out.

“A very beautiful garden, madame,” he said. “And a very beautiful
view.”

He turned back to the room and began to wander about, looking at
the books and pictures. Suddenly he stopped in front of the safe.

“A very fine safe, madame,” he said. “And a very strong one, I
should imagine.”

“Yes,” she said. “My husband always said it was one of the best.”

“And it was from this safe that the jewels and money were stolen?”

“Yes.”

“And the window was found fastened on the inside?”

“Yes.”

“And there were no signs of any one having entered the room?”

“None at all.”

Poirot nodded. “I see. A very interesting problem. A very
interesting problem indeed.”

He walked over to the desk and began to examine it.

“Did your husband always keep his papers in this desk, madame?”

“Yes, most of them.”

“And did he always keep the key himself?”

“Yes.”

“I see.”

Poirot turned away from the desk and began to look at the books
again. Suddenly he stopped and took a volume from the shelf.

“A very interesting book, madame,” he said. “A very interesting
book indeed.”

It was a copy of _The Life of Napoleon_, by Lord Rosebery.

“Yes,” she said. “My husband was very fond of it.”

Poirot replaced the book on the shelf and turned to Japp.

“I think that is all I want to see here, Japp,” he said. “Perhaps
madame will be so kind as to show us the rose-garden?”

“Certainly,” she said. “If you will come this way.”

She led the way out through the window and into the garden. It was
a beautiful afternoon, and the garden was looking its best. We
wandered about for some time, Poirot admiring the roses and asking
Mrs. Davenheim many questions about them.

At last we came to the lake. It was a large, still piece of water,
with a boathouse at one end.

“A very beautiful lake, madame,” said Poirot. “And a very peaceful
one.”

He walked over to the boathouse and looked in.

“A very nice boathouse, madame,” he said. “And very well kept.”

He turned back to Mrs. Davenheim.

“I think that is all I want to see, madame,” he said. “I am much
obliged to you for your kindness.”

“Not at all,” she said. “I am only too glad to have been of any
help.”

We walked back to the house, and after a few more words with Mrs.
Davenheim, we took our leave.

On the way back to London, Japp was very silent. I could see that
he was disappointed with the result of our visit.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he said at last. “What do you think of
it all?”

“I think,” said Poirot, “that it is a very interesting case. A
very interesting case indeed.”

“But you haven’t found anything new?”

“On the contrary, I have found a great deal that is new.”

“What is it?”

“I will tell you on Saturday, Japp. On Saturday, after the
inquest.”

And with that we had to be content.

On Saturday morning we all three went down to Chingside for the
inquest. The room was crowded, and there was a great deal of
excitement. Lowen was there, looking very pale and anxious. Billy
Kellett was also there, looking more disreputable than ever.

The evidence was much the same as Japp had told us. The maid
testified to having seen Lowen near the study window, and Billy
Kellett testified to having seen him near the lime-kiln. The
charred bones and the metal buttons were produced, and Mrs.
Davenheim identified the buttons as being off her husband’s
gardening coat.

When the evidence was all in, the coroner turned to the jury.

“Gentlemen,” he said. “You have heard the evidence. It is for you
to decide whether Mr. Davenheim was murdered, and if so, by whom.”

The jury retired, and after a short time they returned with their
verdict.

“We find,” said the foreman, “that Mr. Davenheim was murdered by
James Lowen.”

There was a murmur of excitement in the room. Lowen turned even
paler than before, and I saw his hands tremble.

As we were leaving the room, Poirot touched Japp on the arm.

“One moment, Japp,” he said. “I have something to say to you.”

“What is it?”

“I want you to come with me to The Cedars. I have something to
show you.”

“What is it?”

“I will show you when we get there.”

We all three drove to The Cedars, and Poirot led the way into the
study. He walked over to the desk and opened it with a key he
took from his pocket.

“How did you get that key?” asked Japp in surprise.

“I had it made,” said Poirot. “From a wax impression I took when
we were here on Thursday.”

He began to search through the papers in the desk. At last he
found what he was looking for. It was a small, leather-bound
notebook.

“What is it?” asked Japp.

“It is Mr. Davenheim’s private diary,” said Poirot. “And it
contains some very interesting information.”

He began to read from the diary.

“‘September 10th. Arrived in Buenos Ayres. Met a man called
Miller. A very clever fellow. He has a plan for a big financial
deal. If it comes off, we shall both be rich men.’

“‘October 15th. The deal is going well. Miller is a genius. We
shall be millionaires.’

“‘November 20th. The deal has failed. Miller has disappeared with
all the money. I am ruined.’

“‘December 10th. Back in London. I must find Miller. He is the
only man who can save me.’

“‘January 5th. I have found Miller. He is living in a small
village called Chingside. He is calling himself Billy Kellett.’”

Japp gasped. “Billy Kellett! You mean that Billy Kellett is
Miller?”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And he is the man who murdered Mr.
Davenheim.”

“But how did he do it?”

“It was very simple. He knew that Mr. Davenheim was in financial
difficulties, and he saw a way to get rid of him and at the same
time to get hold of his money and jewels. He knew that Mr.
Davenheim was expecting a visitor on Saturday evening, and he saw
his chance. He met Mr. Davenheim in the lane, murdered him, and
disposed of the body in the lime-kiln. Then he went to the house,
entered the study through the window, and robbed the safe. He
knew that Lowen was expected, and he saw a way to throw the blame
on him. He took the ring and pawned it, and then he gave the
description of Lowen to the police.”

“But how did you find all this out?” asked Japp.

“It was the little grey cells, my friend,” said Poirot. “The
little grey cells.”

He turned to me with a smile.

“You see, Hastings, it is as I said. The senses mislead. One must
seek the truth within—not without.”

And with that he walked out of the room, leaving Japp and me
staring after him in amazement.

The question seemed so ludicrously inappropriate that for a moment
we both stared in silence. Then Japp burst into a laugh. “Good
Lord, Monsieur Poirot, I thought you were coming out with something
startling. As to your question, I’m sure I don’t know.”

“You could find out?” asked Poirot with curious persistence.

“Oh, certainly—if you _really_ want to know.”

“_Merci, mon ami_. I should be obliged if you would make a point
of it.”

“Well, I must be going. I’ve plenty of work on my hands. I’ll keep
you posted as to any new developments.”

“Wait!” called Poirot as Japp was half-way through the doorway.
“One little point. Was it known that Mr. Davenheim was expected in
the village?”

“Everyone knew of his custom of posting his own letters,” said
Japp. “But as to whether they knew he was going that particular
evening, I can’t say.”

“Quite so. One more thing. How did he wear his hair?”

“Wait a minute. I have his photograph here.” Japp fumbled in his
pocketbook. “There you are. See for yourself.”

Poirot looked at the photo.

“He wears it long—very long for these days. And his beard?”

“Very full—almost hides the lower part of his face.”

“And his moustache?”

“Luxuriant, as you see.”

“_Merci, mon ami_. You have been most kind.”

When Japp had gone, I looked at Poirot. He was sitting with his
head on one side, a look of almost infantile satisfaction on his
face.

“Well?” I asked. “Is it all clear?”

“Not yet, Hastings. But the fog is beginning to lift.”

“And do you really believe that Lowen is the murderer?”

“I have not said so.”

“But he’s under arrest!”

“So he is. But I have not heard that he is being tried for his
life.”

“He will be.”

“We shall see.”

“But the ring! Billy Kellett’s story! The clothes in the lake!
What can it all mean?”

“It means,” said Poirot, “that it is a very clever case—a very
clever case indeed. But there is one thing that I do not quite
understand.”

“What is that?”

“Why the gardeners were not dismissed when Mr. Davenheim went away
on his travels.”

“Really, Poirot!” I cried. “What on earth has that got to do with
it?”

“Everything, my friend. Everything.”

I shook my head. Poirot’s methods were sometimes beyond me.

“One more thing,” he said, as I was leaving the room. “Is there
any mention in the papers of Mr. Davenheim’s having had a
collection of—say, old silver?”

“Not that I’ve seen.”

“Ah!” Poirot sounded disappointed. “I thought perhaps—but no
matter.”

I left him still sitting in his chair, with that same look of
placid satisfaction on his face.

“Well, and what do you think of our friend Miller now? He’s a
smart one, eh? The dragging of that lake, for instance. And the
way he’s kept his eye on Lowen. He’s been in the village ever since
the Saturday. He’s seen the house and the grounds, and he knows
the people. If he hasn’t found out anything more, it’s because
there’s nothing more to find.”

“It’s very easy to be mistaken, Japp,” said Poirot. “The eye may
see, but it is the brain that must interpret.”

Japp rose. “Well, I must be going. I’ll let you know as soon as we
get any news.”

Poirot sat motionless for some time. Then he rose, walked to the
table, and began slowly and methodically to build a house of cards.
I watched him with some impatience. It seemed to me a childish
occupation at such a time. When he had completed the first storey,
he turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it all?”

“I think the lime kiln is the answer to the whole mystery,” I
replied. “I should say that Lowen and the banker had a quarrel.
Possibly Lowen had some hold over him. At any rate, he killed him,
probably in the rose-garden, and then disposed of the body in the
kiln. He must have taken the ring from the dead man’s finger and
the clothes from his body, and then, fearing they might be
identified, he probably threw the clothes into the lake, and the
ring where it was subsequently found.”

“And the safe?”

“Well, Lowen had been shown into the study. He probably found the
key in the dead man’s pocket, and helped himself to the contents.”

Poirot shook his head. “It’s a possible theory, Hastings, but it
doesn’t quite fit all the facts. For instance, why should Lowen
have bothered to take the clothes off the body? Why not have burnt
them in the kiln with the body itself?”

“Because he might have been afraid of the smell of burning cloth,”
I suggested.

“No, I don’t think that will do. There must be some other
explanation.”

“And what is it, then?”

“I am not sure yet. I must think. One little point, Hastings.
Suppose the ring was _never_ on the dead man’s finger at all?
Suppose it was in the safe?”

“In the safe? But what on earth—”

“Wait, wait! I have an idea. It is only a tiny one as yet, but it
may grow.”

I said no more, for I knew from experience that when Poirot was
in one of his ‘thinking’ moods, it was best to leave him alone.
The next three days passed without any further news from Japp.
On the Thursday morning, however, he again made his appearance.
He looked, I thought, a trifle discouraged.

“Well,” he said, in answer to our inquiries. “Miller’s been down
to Chingside again. He’s had that lake dragged from end to end,
but not a sign of a body. And as for the lime kiln—well, it seems
there’s been no fire in it for over a month. So that’s that!”

“And Lowen?”

“We’ve had to let him go. There wasn’t enough evidence to hold
him.”

Poirot smiled. “So the smart Inspector Miller is at a standstill,
is he? It’s a pity. And yet, the solution of the mystery is so
simple.”

Japp stared at him. “Simple? You mean to say you’ve solved it?”

“I think so. There are just one or two points I should like to
clear up. For instance, did you find out about the bedrooms?”

“Oh, yes. They occupied separate rooms.”

“Ah! And did Mrs. Davenheim seem much upset by her husband’s
disappearance?”

“Naturally. She was very distressed.”

“And the junior partner—Mr. Salmon—what is his opinion of the
matter?”

“He’s distracted. The firm’s in a very bad way. It seems that
Davenheim had been speculating heavily lately, and with the loss
of the money and securities from the safe, they’re on the verge of
bankruptcy.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And now, Japp, if you will be so good as to
take me down to Chingside this afternoon, I think I can promise
to show you where Mr. Davenheim is to be found.”

Japp’s eyes nearly started out of his head. “You mean it? You’ve
really got a clue?”

“More than a clue, my friend. I have the solution. But it must be
done in my own way. You will come with us, Hastings?”

“Of course,” I cried.

“Then we will start at two o’clock.”

Japp stared again. “But what can that have to do with it?”

Poirot smiled, and shook his head with mock mystery. “I have my
own little ways. You have your clues—your footprints, your
cigar-ash, your crumbs—I have mine.”

He rose, and crossed to the door. “By the way,” he said, “did I
not see a box of chocolates on the hall table? They are for me,
I think? No?”

Japp laughed. “You think of nothing but those _bonbons_ of yours,
monsieur.”

“It is my only weakness!” said Poirot, with a comic gesture of
despair. “Even the greatest of us have our little faults.”

“A fiver to a toothpick, Hastings,” said Japp, as the door closed
behind Poirot. “He’s losing his grip. You saw him just now—thinking
of chocolates at a time like this! A box of chocolates!”

“Still,” I said, with a shake of the head, “I have never known
him fail yet.”

“Well, there’s always a first time. He’s getting old, that’s what
it is. It’s a pity, too.”

Japp shook his head again. “Well, I must be getting along. I’ll
let you know if any new developments turn up.”

And with a nod of farewell, he left the room.

Poirot re-entered it a few minutes later, his face beaming.

“They are delicious!” he exclaimed. “One must allow that for the
English. They have the secret of the _fondant_.”

“What has happened to your little grey cells, Poirot?” I asked
rather reproachfully. “Japp thinks you’re losing your grip.”

“Does he?” Poirot smiled. “Well, let him think so. It will do him
no harm. And now, my friend, let us go for a little walk.”

I stared. “A walk?”

“But certainly. The evening is fine, the air is fresh. It will
do us both good.”

“But the case?”

“Ah, the case! We will talk of that as we walk. There is one little
point that puzzles me—only one. When I have solved that, all will
be clear.”

“And what is that?”

“The safe.”

“The safe?”

“Precisely. Why was the safe broken into?”

“To get the contents, I suppose.”

“But if Mr. Davenheim were going to disappear—if he were going to
make away with himself, as it were—why should he break into his
own safe? He would have the key, would he not?”

“But if Lowen broke into it?”

“Ah! that is different. But then, why should Lowen break into it?
He was in the study for an hour. He had plenty of time to find the
key. Mr. Davenheim would surely have it on him.”

“He might have it on his watch-chain.”

“Exactly. And if Lowen murdered him, he would have no difficulty
in getting it. No, there is something about that safe that I do
not understand. It is—what shall I say?—an anomaly.”

“It’s a very common one in a burglary,” I remarked.

“But this was not a common burglary. Everything points to that.
No, there is something—something—that I have not yet grasped.
But it will come—it will come!”

He tapped his forehead. “The little grey cells, Hastings! They
never fail me. They are working—working even now.”

We walked on in silence for some time. Then Poirot suddenly stopped.

“I have it!” he cried. “I have it!”

“What?”

“The reason why the safe was broken into! It is so simple—so very
simple! How is it that I did not see it before?”

“Well, what is it?” I asked, with some excitement.

“That, my friend, I shall not tell you—yet. You would only laugh
at me. But it is the key to the whole mystery.”

I was used to Poirot’s little ways, so I did not press him. We
returned home, and spent a quiet evening.

The next few days passed without any further news from Japp. Poirot
seemed quite content to wait. He spent most of his time reading,
or playing patience. Once or twice he went out for a short walk,
but he always returned in time for his beloved chocolate.

On Friday morning, Japp walked in. He looked tired and harassed.

“Well,” he said, “I’ve got some news for you. But it’s not the
kind of news you’ll like.”

“Indeed?” said Poirot. “And what is it?”

“We’ve found the body.”

“The body? Where?”

“In the lake. It was recovered late last night.”

“And it is the body of Mr. Davenheim?”

“No doubt about that. It’s been in the water for some days, of
course, but the identification is quite certain. Mrs. Davenheim
has seen it, and she’s positive.”

“I see. And the cause of death?”

“A blow on the back of the head. He must have been struck down
from behind, and then thrown into the lake.”

“And Lowen?”

“We’ve got him. There’s no doubt now. The maid’s evidence, the
ring, and now the body—it’s a clear case.”

“I see,” said Poirot again. He seemed quite unmoved by the news.
“And the safe?”

“Oh, the safe! We’ve found the tools that were used. They were
hidden in the shrubbery. Lowen must have brought them with him.”

“I see,” said Poirot for the third time. “Well, Japp, I suppose
you’ve won your bet.”

“It looks like it,” said Japp with a grin. “But I won’t be hard
on you. We’ll call it off, if you like.”

“No, no,” said Poirot. “A bet is a bet. I will pay you your five
pounds. But first, there is one little thing I should like to ask
you.”

“And what is that?”

“Did you find out about the bedrooms?”

Japp stared. “Oh, that! Yes, I did. As a matter of fact, they did
not occupy the same room. Mr. Davenheim had his own suite of rooms
on the ground floor.”

“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes lit up. “I thought as much. And was there a
communicating door between his bedroom and the study?”

“Yes, there was. But what on earth has that to do with it?”

“Everything, my friend, everything! And now, if you will excuse
me, I have a little business to attend to. But if you will come
here this evening at eight o’clock, I think I shall be able to
hand you over the true culprit.”

Japp stared at him in amazement. “The true culprit? But we’ve got
him! Lowen is the man!”

“Is he?” Poirot smiled. “We shall see, my friend, we shall see.
At eight o’clock, then?”

“All right,” said Japp, though he still looked puzzled. “I’ll be
here.”

When he had gone, Poirot turned to me. “And now, Hastings, I must
ask you to do something for me.”

“What is it?”

“I want you to go down to Chingside this afternoon. I want you to
find out one thing—and one thing only.”

“And what is that?”

“I want you to find out if anyone saw Mr. Davenheim on the Saturday
afternoon—_after_ he had left the house at half-past five.”

“But Japp said that nobody had seen him.”

“Japp says many things. But I want you to find out for yourself.
Go to the village, talk to the people, see if you can find anyone
who saw him.”

“All right,” I said, though I did not see the point of it. “I’ll
go.”

I spent the afternoon at Chingside, but my mission was quite
fruitless. No one had seen Mr. Davenheim after he left his house.
I returned to London feeling rather depressed.

Poirot was waiting for me. “Well?” he asked.

“Nothing,” I said. “No one saw him.”

“Excellent!” said Poirot. “That is just what I expected.”

I stared at him. “Then why did you send me?”

“Because, my friend, it was necessary to be sure. And now, I think,
all is ready.”

At eight o’clock punctually, Japp arrived. He was accompanied by
another man, whom I recognized as Inspector Miller.

“Well,” said Japp, “here we are. Now then, Monsieur Poirot, where’s
your culprit?”

Poirot smiled. “One moment, my friends. First, let us have a little
refreshment.”

He rang the bell, and our landlady appeared with a tray of coffee.
When she had gone, Poirot turned to Japp.

“And now,” he said, “let us talk. You are quite sure that Lowen is
the man?”

“Of course I am,” said Japp. “The evidence is overwhelming.”

“And you, Inspector Miller?”

“I agree with Japp,” said Miller. “It’s a clear case.”

“I see. And yet, there are one or one or two things that puzzle
me. For instance, the safe. Why was it broken into?”

“To get the money and the jewels, of course,” said Japp.

“But Lowen was a guest in the house. He was in the study for an
hour. He had plenty of time to find the key. Why should he use
force?”

“Perhaps he couldn’t find the key,” said Miller.

“But Mr. Davenheim would have it on him. If Lowen murdered him,
he would have no difficulty in getting it.”

“He might have been in a hurry,” said Japp.

“Perhaps. But then, why should he hide the tools in the shrubbery?
Why not take them with him?”

“He might have been afraid of being caught with them,” said Miller.

“Perhaps. But there is another thing. The ring. Why should he give
it to a man like Kellett? Why not throw it into the lake, or the
lime-kiln?”

“He might have been afraid of being seen,” said Japp.

“Perhaps. But there is one more thing. The body. Why was it found
in the lake? If Lowen had killed him, and wanted to dispose of the
body, why not use the lime-kiln? It was only three minutes’ walk
away. The lake was much further.”

“Perhaps he didn’t know about the lime-kiln,” said Miller.

“Perhaps. But it seems a lot of ‘perhapses,’ does it not?”

Poirot smiled. “Now, let me tell you my theory.”

“Your theory?” said Japp. “But we don’t want theories. We want
facts.”

“And I will give them to you. But first, let us consider the
character of Mr. Davenheim. He was a man of method, a man of
intelligence. He was also a man who was fond of his wife—in his
own way. He gave her many expensive presents—jewels, for instance.”

“We know all that,” said Japp.

“But did you know that he was also a man who was very much afraid?”

“Afraid? Of what?”

“Of ruin. Financial ruin. The firm of Davenheim and Salmon was
not as prosperous as it seemed. Mr. Davenheim had been speculating
heavily, and he had lost. He knew that, sooner or later, the crash
must come. And he decided to prepare for it.”

“How?” asked Japp.

“By disappearing. But not in the ordinary way. He wanted to
disappear, and yet to remain—how shall I say?—in touch with his
money. So he devised a very clever plan.”

“What was it?”

“He decided to create a second personality. For several months,
he spent a great deal of his time in London. He took a small room
in a poor quarter of the town, and he lived there as—shall we say?—
Billy Kellett.”

“Billy Kellett!” I cried. “But Kellett is a real person!”

“Is he?” Poirot smiled. “We shall see. Mr. Davenheim—as Kellett—
became known to the police. He even did a short term of
imprisonment. That was a very clever move. It gave him a perfect
alibi. No one would ever suspect a well-known banker of being a
common thief.”

“But the appearance?” said Japp. “Davenheim had a beard and a
moustache. Kellett was clean-shaven.”

“Exactly. That is where the cleverness came in. Mr. Davenheim
grew a beard and a moustache for the purpose of his business life.
But when he was Kellett, he shaved them off. It is much easier to
shave off a beard than to grow one!”

“But Mrs. Davenheim?” I said. “She would have known.”

“That is why I asked about the bedrooms. Mr. Davenheim had his
own suite of rooms. He could come and go as he pleased. He could
change his appearance at his leisure. And his wife, being—as Japp
said—a rather unintelligent woman, would never suspect anything.”

“But the Saturday?” said Japp. “What happened then?”

“On Saturday, the crash was imminent. Mr. Davenheim knew that he
must act. He had already prepared his ‘Kellett’ personality. He
had even arranged for a ‘burglary’ at his own house. He broke into
the safe himself, and took the money and the jewels. Then he left
the house, and walked down the drive. But he did not go to the
village. He went to the boathouse. There he changed his clothes—
the clothes he was wearing were found in the lake, you remember—
and shaved off his beard and moustache. Then he walked to the
station, and took the train to London.”

“But what about Lowen?” asked Japp.

“Lowen was a very convenient scapegoat. Mr. Davenheim had an
appointment with him. He knew that Lowen would be in the study.
He even arranged for the maid to see him in the rose-garden. It
was all very carefully planned.”

“But the body!” I cried. “What about the body in the lake?”

“Ah, the body!” Poirot’s eyes twinkled. “That was the most clever
part of all. You see, there _was_ no body.”

“No body?” said Japp. “But we found it! Mrs. Davenheim identified
it!”

“Did she?” Poirot smiled. “Mrs. Davenheim is, as we have said, a
rather unintelligent woman. And she was also—how shall I say?—
very much in need of the insurance money.”

“The insurance money!” I cried.

“Precisely. Mr. Davenheim had insured his life for a very large
sum. If he were dead, his wife would be well provided for. And if
he were—shall we say?—not really dead, they could both enjoy the
money together, in some other country.”

“But whose body was it, then?” asked Japp.

“It was the body of a man who had been drowned in the river some
days before. Mr. Davenheim—as Kellett—had heard about it. He
arranged for it to be brought to the lake, and placed there. It
was a very simple matter.”

“But the blow on the head?” said Miller.

“That was also easily managed. A blow with a heavy stone, after
death, would produce the same effect.”

“It’s incredible!” said Japp. “I can’t believe it!”

“And yet, it is the only explanation that fits all the facts.
The safe, the ring, the clothes, the body—they all fall into
place.”

“But where is Davenheim now?” asked Miller.

“He is—where he has been for the last few days. In prison. As
Billy Kellett.”

“In prison!” I cried.

“Precisely. He wanted a safe place to hide until the search for
him had died down. What could be safer than a prison? He arranged
to be arrested for pawning the ring—the ring he had ‘found’ in
the ditch. It was a master-stroke!”

“But how did you find out?” asked Japp.

“It was the chocolates,” said Poirot, with a smile.

“The chocolates?”

“Yes. You remember I said I had seen a box of chocolates on the
hall table? Well, I had not. I only said that to see your reaction.
You laughed at me. You thought I was losing my grip. But it told
me what I wanted to know.”

“And what was that?”

“It told me that you were not looking for the truth. You were only
looking for what you expected to find. And that is a very dangerous
thing for a detective to do.”

He turned to Japp. “And now, my friend, if you will go to Bow
Street, and look at Billy Kellett—really look at him—I think you
will find that he is Mr. Davenheim. And you will also find that
he has a very interesting story to tell.”

Japp and Miller left the room in silence. Poirot turned to me with
a smile.

“And now, Hastings, let us have another cup of coffee. I think we
have earned it.”

I looked at him in admiration. “Poirot,” I said, “you are a
genius!”

“I know,” said Poirot simply. “It is a great responsibility.”

Japp took up his hat and prepared to leave. “I’m afraid I’ve a
lot to do yet. Good-night, Monsieur Poirot.”

“_Bonne nuit, mon ami_.”

I let Japp out, and returned. Poirot had not moved. He was leaning
back in his chair, his eyes closed. He looked so small and
insignificant that I felt a momentary pang of pity for him. Then,
as I watched, he began to speak in a low, musical voice.

“Let us re-examine the situation, Hastings. First, we have a man
who vanishes into thin air. He is seen at half-past five; his
clothes are found in a lake; his ring is pawned. Then we have a
visitor who is also seen by a maid going to the rose-garden. His
name is Lowen, and he is a speculator in quite a small way.”

“Yes,” I said, as he paused. “And it seems to me that the case
against him is a very strong one. He had a motive, he was there
at the time, and he was seen by two different people.”

Poirot opened his eyes. “A little too strong, perhaps?” he murmured.

“Too strong? What do you mean?”

“The ring, for instance. Why did Lowen take it from the finger of
a dead man? And then why should he throw it over a hedge, as if
he were trying to get rid of it? It would have been far safer to
keep it in his pocket.”

“Perhaps he was afraid it might be found on him,” I suggested.

“But he had just murdered a man!” Poirot retorted. “The ring was
comparatively a small matter. And why throw it into a ditch? Why
not have buried it?”

“I suppose he was in a hurry,” I said.

“Perhaps—perhaps. And then the clothes. Why were they in the
lake?”

“To make people think he had committed suicide, of course.”

“But they were the _only_ clothes missing from the house. If a
man commits suicide, he does not usually take off all his clothes
first.”

“He might have wanted to make sure they wouldn’t be found.”

“Then why not have burnt them? It would have been much more
effectual.”

“I don’t know,” I said. “But they _were_ in the lake.”

“Precisely. They were in the lake. And that is why I find the whole
thing so very—what shall I say?—so very _theatrical_.”

“Theatrical?” I repeated. “What do you mean?”

“Everything is so—so well arranged. It is like a play. The ring,
the clothes, the witness—it is all a little too perfect.”

I shook my head. “I don’t see it,” I said. “It seems to me a very
strong case.”

“We shall see,” said Poirot. “We shall see.”

He fell into a silence which lasted for some time. Then he spoke
again.

“There is one thing which puzzles me, Hastings. Why did Mr.
Davenheim want to see Mr. Lowen?”

“Japp said it was about some South American shares.”

“Yes—yes. But why did he ask him to come to his house? Why not
have seen him at his office in the City?”

“Perhaps he wanted to keep it a secret,” I suggested.

“Perhaps. But if so, why tell his wife and the servants that he
was expecting him? No, there is something behind all this—something
which we do not yet understand.”

“And what about the safe?” I asked. “Who broke into that?”

“Ah, the safe! That is another interesting point. It was broken
into on Saturday night, or early on Sunday morning. And yet it
was not discovered until Monday. Why was that?”

“I suppose because no one had occasion to go to it,” I said.

“Perhaps. But it is curious, is it not? And then there is the
question of the jewels. Why were they all in the safe? Mrs.
Davenheim, I think Japp said, was very fond of them. Would she
not have some of them in her own room?”
