“Japp said they were all kept in the safe.”

“Yes—yes. It is all very strange. Very strange indeed.”

He fell into another silence, which lasted until I suggested that
it was time for bed.

“Yes,” he said, rising. “It is time for bed. But before you go,
Hastings, I want you to do something for me.”

“What is it?” I asked.

“I want you to go down to Chingside to-morrow, and find out one
or two things for me.”

“Certainly,” I said. “What do you want to know?”

“First, I want to know if Mr. and Mrs. Davenheim occupied the same
bedroom. Second, I want to know if Mr. Davenheim had any special
hobbies or interests. And third, I want to know if there is anything
unusual about the household—anything at all, no matter how small
it may seem.”

“I’ll do my best,” I said. “But I don’t see how any of those things
can help you to find Mr. Davenheim.”

“Perhaps not,” said Poirot. “But then, you see, I am not looking
for Mr. Davenheim.”

“Not looking for him? Then what are you looking for?”

“I am looking for the truth, Hastings. And the truth is often
hidden in very unlikely places.”

“Anything else?” Japp asked sarcastically. “Any other small points
of interest?”

Poirot reflected. “Yes, there is one. Has Mrs. Davenheim been
long-sighted for some time? Has she, for instance, been in the
habit of using a lorgnette?”

Japp laughed again. “Wait, I’ll ask my friend Miller that also.
He’s sure to know!”

“I’m really surprised at you, Poirot,” I said, as the door closed
behind our visitor. “What on earth can such details have to do
with the case?”

“They might have a great deal,” replied my friend, but would not
say more.

Japp stared at him a few minutes longer, but Poirot seemed to have
forgotten us both. The detective shook his head sadly at me, and
murmuring, “Poor old fellow! War’s been too much for him!” gently
withdrew from the room.

I looked at my friend. He was now engaged in building a house of cards with a pack that lay on the table. “Poirot,” I said, “you are surely not serious? What can the sleeping arrangements of the Davenheims have to do with the case?” “Everything, my friend,” Poirot replied, without looking up as he placed a five of diamonds delicately upon a six of clubs. “It is a question of the habits, the little daily routines. If a man is to disappear, he must either leave his habits behind or take them with him. To know which he has done, one must first know what those habits were. Japp, he sees the footprints, the open safe, the pawned ring. He sees the ‘how.’ But I, Hastings, I look for the ‘why’ and the ‘who.’ And for that, I must understand the man himself. A man who shares a room with his wife cannot easily hide a secret—unless, of course, the wife is also a part of the secret.”

I felt a pang of pity for my friend. It seemed that, for once, his “little grey cells” were failing him. His obsession with the Davenheims’ sleeping arrangements appeared to be the height of absurdity when a man’s life and a fortune in jewels were at stake. I ventured to point out that the evidence against Lowen was becoming overwhelming, especially with the discovery of the clothes near the lime kiln. Poirot only smiled and shook his head. “My dear Hastings, you are like the good Japp—you see the things that are meant to be seen. But have you considered the significance of those clothes? A man who is murdered does not usually provide his own evidence so obligingly. There is a psychological element here that is being overlooked. To disappear is one thing; to leave a trail of breadcrumbs like the children in the fairy tale is quite another.”

I looked at Poirot with some concern. His obsession with the Davenheims’ bedroom seemed to me a sign of failing powers. “Really, Poirot,” I expostulated, “what can that possibly matter? The man is gone, his clothes are found, his ring is pawned by a known thief, and a lime kiln is conveniently adjacent to the property. The case against Lowen seems overwhelming.” Poirot sighed, a sound of infinite patience. “You see the facts, Hastings, but you do not see their significance. You see the clothes in the lake—but do you ask yourself *why* they are there? You see the ring—but do you ask why it was thrown into a ditch? To understand the crime, one must understand the criminal. And to understand the criminal, one must first understand the victim. There are three things, Hastings, that are very strange in this case: the timing of the visitor, the nature of the jewels, and the length of the master’s hair.”

“Poirot,” I said, as the door closed behind Japp, “what on earth
has the bedroom to do with it? Surely the lime kiln and the
pawned ring are the vital points?” Poirot shook his head
reprovingly. “My friend, you are like the good Miller. You see the
obvious, and you are dazzled by it. To me, the most important
fact is that Mr. Davenheim had been in South America last autumn.
Also, I should like to know if he was a man of regular habits.
Does he, for instance, go to the same barber every week to have
his hair cut?”

I turned to Poirot, who was now meticulously rearranging the spilled matches in a tin box on the mantelpiece. “Really, Poirot,” I said, “I cannot see what the sleeping arrangements of the Davenheims have to do with the disappearance. It seems to me a most irrelevant and—if I may say so—slightly impertinent question.”

“On the contrary, Hastings,” replied Poirot, his eyes twinkling, “it is of the first importance. It is a matter of the habits, the little daily routines which reveal the truth. But let us leave that for a moment. Does it not strike you as remarkable that the only things found were the clothes Mr. Davenheim was wearing? A man does not usually divest himself of his attire before being murdered and disposed of in a lime kiln. It lacks the—how do you say?—the logic.”

As Poirot still seemed sunk in a daydream, I took a sheet of paper,
and amused myself by scribbling notes upon it. My friend’s voice
aroused me. He had come out of his reverie, and was looking brisk
and alert.

“_Que faites-vous là, mon ami?_”

“I was jotting down what occurred to me as the main points of
interest in this affair.”

“You become methodical—at last!” said Poirot approvingly.

I concealed my pleasure. “Shall I read them to you?”

“By all means.”

I cleared my throat.

“‘One: All the evidence points to Lowen having been the man who
forced the safe.

“‘Two: He had a grudge against Davenheim.

“‘Three: He lied in his first statement that he had never left the
study.

“‘Four: If you accept Billy Kellett’s story as true, Lowen is
unmistakably implicated.’”

I paused. “Well?” I asked, for I felt that I had put my finger on
all the vital facts.

Poirot looked at me pityingly, shaking his head very gently. “_Mon
pauvre ami!_ But it is that you have not the gift! The important
detail, you appreciate him never! Also, your reasoning is false.”

“How?”

“Let me take your four points.

“‘One: All the evidence points to Lowen having been the man who
forced the safe.’ _Eh bien_, no! It does not. All the evidence
points to the safe having been forced _while Lowen was in the
study_. But that is not the same thing. On the contrary, if Lowen
had forced the safe, he would never have remained in the room
afterwards. That would have been the height of folly. For the same
reason, he would not have been seen in the garden. He would have
flown at once.”

“Unless,” I suggested, “he had some other motive for remaining.”

“Such as?”

“Wait!” I cried. “I have it! He wanted to meet Davenheim. He did
meet him, and killed him—either in the garden or elsewhere. Then
he returned to the study, and opened the safe. That would explain
everything.”

“Except,” said Poirot, “the fact that the safe was not opened with
the key, but _forced_. If Lowen had killed Davenheim, he would
have had the key in his pocket.”

“True,” I admitted. “I had forgotten that.”

“‘Two: He had a grudge against Davenheim.’ Granted. But why should
he choose that particular moment for his revenge? One does not
usually combine a grudge with a burglary.

“‘Three: He lied in his first statement that he had never left the
study.’ Now there, _mon ami_, you are on the right track. He _did_
lie. Why? Why should a man like Lowen, who is no fool, make such
a transparently false statement? There is only one possible
reason—to conceal something even more damaging to himself.

“‘Four: If you accept Billy Kellett’s story as true, Lowen is
unmistakably implicated.’ I do not accept Billy Kellett’s story.
The man is a common thief. Why should he tell the truth? Besides,
the whole thing is too thin. Why should Lowen throw away a valuable
diamond ring? Even if he were afraid of its being found on him, he
could have hidden it in a hundred better places than a ditch.”

“Then,” I said, “you think Lowen is innocent?”

“I did not say so. I only said that your four points were
unconvincing.”

“What do you consider the important points, then?”

Poirot leant back in his chair, and half closed his eyes.

“First: The fact that Mr. and Mrs. Davenheim occupied separate
rooms.

“Second: The length of Mr. Davenheim’s hair.

“Third: The fact that he was for some months in Buenos Ayres last
autumn.”

“I don’t see how those things can possibly be relevant,” I said.

“I did not expect you to,” replied Poirot. “But they are the only
things that interest me.”

I felt slightly huffed. “Is there anything else?” I asked.

“Yes. There is the question of the _clothes_.”

“The clothes found in the lake?”

“No. The clothes Mr. Davenheim was wearing when he left the house.”

“But they _are_ the clothes found in the lake!”

“Are they? That is just what I should like to be sure of.”

I stared at him. Was it possible that Poirot’s mind was really
beginning to fail? The clothes had been identified by the valet.
What more did he want?

“And there is one other thing,” added Poirot. “I should like to
know whether any of the gardeners are particularly fond of their
master.”

“Really, Poirot!” I exclaimed. “What on earth has that to do with
it?”

“A great deal, _mon ami_—a great deal.”

He refused to say any more, and for the next few days he remained
strangely silent and preoccupied. He spent a good deal of time
pacing up and down the room, his hands behind his back, his brow
furrowed in thought. Once or twice I caught him looking at the
photograph of Mr. Davenheim with a very curious expression.

On Friday morning Japp walked in. He looked tired and discouraged.

“Well,” he said, sitting down heavily, “I’m afraid the fiver’s
yours, Monsieur Poirot. We’re no nearer the truth than we were a
week ago.”

“You have found nothing fresh?”

“Nothing. We’ve dragged the lake from end to end, but there’s no
sign of a body. We’ve searched the lime-kiln, too, but with the
same result. As for Lowen, we’ve had to let him go. There wasn’t
enough evidence to justify his detention.”

“And the ring?”

“Billy Kellett’s still in ‘the jug.’ He’s to be brought up to-morrow
on the charge of being in possession of stolen property. But I
don’t suppose we shall get anything more out of him.”

“_Tiens!_” said Poirot. “That is interesting.”

“What is?”

“That Billy Kellett is still in prison. It simplifies matters
considerably.”

“I don’t see how.”

“No? But it is very simple. By the way, Japp, did you find out
about the bedrooms?”

“Yes. They did occupy separate rooms. Also, I’ve found out that
none of the gardeners are particularly attached to Mr. Davenheim.
In fact, they seem to have disliked him quite a lot. He was a hard
master, it seems.”

“Aha!” said Poirot. “That is most satisfactory.”

“I’m glad you think so,” grunted Japp. “It doesn’t seem to lead anywhere.”

“On the contrary, it leads straight to the truth.”

We both stared at him.

“You mean,” I cried, “that you have solved the mystery?”

“I have.”

“And where is Mr. Davenheim?”

“At the present moment,” said Poirot, “he is in—let me see—yes,
he is in gaol.”

“In gaol!”

“Precisely.”

“But for what?”

“For—if I mistake not—stealing a gold watch from an old gentleman!”

“Billy Kellett!” I gasped.

“Exactly. Billy Kellett _is_ Mr. Davenheim.”

“But the description—the beard—the long hair!”

“All disappeared, _mon ami_, when he became Billy Kellett. A very
clever disguise, I admit. It had been carefully prepared. For
months he had been leading a double life. Last autumn, when he was
supposed to be in Buenos Ayres, he was really in London, creating
the character of Billy Kellett. He had a small room in a poor
neighbourhood, where he lived for weeks at a time, becoming
thoroughly familiar with the part he was to play. He chose his
moment well. The firm of Davenheim and Salmon was on the verge of
bankruptcy. He decided to disappear, taking with him all the
available cash and jewels. He staged his disappearance with great
ingenuity. He knew that Lowen was coming to see him. He also knew
that Lowen was a man whom it would be easy to implicate. He went
out, as though to post his letters. In the rose-garden, he changed
his clothes—he had already hidden a suit of rags there—and threw
his own clothes into the lake. He had previously shaved off his
beard and moustache, and cut his hair short. The transformation
was complete. He then made his way to the village, and so to
London, where he disposed of the ring in such a way as to throw
suspicion on Lowen. But he had not counted on being arrested for
theft! That was a stroke of ill-fortune which he had not foreseen.
However, it served his purpose in one way—it provided him with an
unassailable alibi.”

“But the safe?” I asked. “Who robbed the safe?”

“Mr. Davenheim himself, of course—before he left the house. He
forced it to make it appear like a burglary.”

“And Mrs. Davenheim? Did she not recognize him?”

“She had not seen him for years—except across a dinner-table.
Remember, they occupied separate rooms. And he had changed his
appearance so completely that even his own wife might well be
deceived. Besides, he took care that she should not see him closely
after his ‘return.’ It was a bold plan, and it nearly succeeded.”

“But how did you guess, Poirot?” I asked. “What was it that first
aroused your suspicion?”

“The separate bedrooms, _mon ami_. That suggested to me that the
relations between husband and wife were—shall we say, formal?
Then the long hair and the beard—they are so easy to remove! And
the visit to Buenos Ayres—it provided him with the necessary time
to create his second personality. Once I had the clue, the rest
was easy.”

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” said Japp, “you’ve won your fiver. I’ll
see that the matter is investigated at once.”

“And you, Hastings,” said Poirot, turning to me with a smile, “you
see that the little grey cells, they have their uses, after all?”

“One: Lowen could not possibly have known where the safe was,
unless some one—his wife, for instance—had told him.

“Two: That is just the reason why he should _not_ have been likely
to rob him. He’d be the first person suspected.

“Three: He was a man of the world, and must have seen that he’d
been spotted by the maid. He’d therefore have known that his best
plan was to make light of the matter.

“Four: I think we have already decided that Billy Kellett’s story
is at once too good to be true, and also too circumstantial to be
the work of an imagination. Therefore it _is_ true.”

I stared at him. “What do you mean, Poirot?”

“Think, my friend. Use your little grey cells.”

“Then you think Lowen _is_ the man?”

“_Au contraire_,” said Poirot, “I think it is very unlikely that
Lowen is the man.”

I sighed. “You’re beyond me! Any more clues?”

“There is one very interesting one,” he replied.

“What is that?”

“The lake.”

“But they’ve dragged it!”

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, “I do not mean that the body is in the
lake. What I meant was—did they find anything else?”

“They found Mr. Davenheim’s clothes—and a couple of punts.”

“_Précisément_. But they found nothing else? No—boots, for
example?”

“Boots?” I stared at him. “Why should they find boots?”

“I have my reasons,” said Poirot, but he refused to say what they
were. I have never seen him so obstinate. He would say no more.

“One: It is true that Lowen was in the study, and that the safe was
broken into. But it is very possible that it was done _not_ by
him.

“Two: That he had a grudge against Davenheim is a reason for him
not to have gone to see him at all.

“Three: His lie was a stupid one, I grant you, but it might have
been the result of fear.

“Four: It is Kellett’s story that is the _clef_ to the whole
business. You did not notice one or two very interesting points
in his description of Lowen?”

“‘Dark-complexioned gent, with a big moustache, one of them city
toffs,’ were his words, I think,” I answered.

“Exactly! Did it not strike you as being a very remarkable
coincidence that Billy Kellett should be able to give so accurate
a description of Lowen?”

“I don’t quite follow you.”

“You will, _mon ami_, you will—one of these days. Now, let us have
tea.”

I felt it was useless to pursue the subject further. Still, I could
not but feel that my list was a very good one.

The next few days were uneventful. Each afternoon Japp dropped in
for a few minutes, but he had nothing of importance to communicate.
The lake had been dragged, with no result. Miller was still
prosecuting his inquiries at Chingside, but without any fresh
discovery. Lowen had been released, for lack of evidence, but was
under constant surveillance.

As for Poirot, he seemed to have lost all interest in the case.
The only things that seemed to interest him were the various
reports of the daily papers. One morning, however, I found him
poring over a map of the neighbourhood of Chingside.

“Tell me, Hastings,” he said, as I entered, “have you any idea of
the distance from The Cedars to the lime-kiln?”

“About a mile, I should think.”

“And from the lime-kiln to the station?”

“A little more, perhaps.”

“So it would be quite possible for a man to walk from the house
to the lime-kiln, and then on to the station, in—say—half an hour?”

“Quite. But what of it?”

“Wait, _mon ami_, wait.”

That afternoon Japp arrived, looking very crestfallen.

“I’m afraid the fiver is yours, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “The
week is up to-day, and we’re no nearer the truth than when we
started. But I’ve some news for you. Miller’s found the missing
jewellery.”

“Where?”

“In a small wood on the other side of the lake. They were hidden
in a hollow tree.”

“Any clue to the thief?”

“Not a sign of one. Miller’s very disappointed. He says it looks
as if the thief had taken fright and hidden them there, intending
to come back for them later.”

“Or as if they had been placed there to be found!” murmured Poirot.

“What do you mean?”

“_Rien, mon ami_, _rien_.”

“There’s one other thing,” said Japp. “I’ve found out what you
wanted to know. Mr. and Mrs. Davenheim occupied the same bedroom.”

“Ah!” said Poirot. “That is most interesting. Most interesting
indeed!”

He remained for some time in deep thought. Then he looked up. “Tell
me, Japp, have you ever known a case of a man—not a criminal—who
voluntarily disappeared?”

“Dozens of them. Men who wanted to start a new life—men who were
unhappy at home—men who were in debt.”

“And they are usually found?”

“If they are well-known men, yes—eventually.”

“But if they were _not_ well-known?”

“Then it’s a different matter.”

Poirot nodded. “Exactly. If a man is not known, he may disappear
for ever.”

“But Davenheim _was_ well-known.”

“_Précisément_. That is the difficulty.”

Suddenly he turned to me. “Hastings, be so good as to fetch me the
_Daily Megaphone_ for last Saturday week.”

I did so. Poirot turned to the column headed “The Missing Banker.”

“Listen to this,” he said. “‘Mr. Davenheim’s appearance is very
striking. He has long, wavy hair, a thick moustache, and a pointed
beard. His eyebrows are unusually bushy.’ Does that suggest
anything to you, Hastings?”

“Nothing,” I said, “except that he would be an easy man to
recognize.”

“Exactly. Now, Japp, I have a request to make. I want you to take
me to see Billy Kellett.”

“Billy Kellett? But he’s in prison!”

“I know that. But it can be arranged?”

“Oh, I think so. But what on earth do you want to see him for?”

“I have a fancy to ask him a few questions.”

“Well, if you must, you must. I’ll see what can be done.”

Two days later, we were all three at the prison where Billy Kellett
was serving his sentence. The man was brought into the room where
we were waiting. He was a miserable-looking object, with a
depraved, cunning face.

Poirot looked at him for a few minutes in silence. Then he spoke.

“_Eh bien_, Billy Kellett, you are in trouble again, it seems.”

The man grunted. “Always my luck, it is.”

“You found a ring, I believe?”

“That’s right. Picked it up in the road.”

“And you saw a man throw it there?”

“I did.”

“What was he like?”

“I’ve told the police once. A dark-complexioned gent, with a big
moustache.”

“Was he like this?” Poirot produced a photograph. It was the one
of Lowen which had appeared in the papers.

“That’s ’im, right enough.”

“You are sure?”

“Certain.”

“You would swear to him in a court of law?”

“I would.”

“And you have never seen him before?”

“Never.”

“Are you quite sure of that?”

“Positive.”

“Think again, Billy Kellett. Last autumn, for instance. Where were
you then?”

“In the ‘jug,’ most of the time.”

“Ah! And where was that?”

“In Maidstone.”

“I see. And you did not see this gentleman there?”

“Not likely! They don’t send ‘city toffs’ to Maidstone.”

“Perhaps not. But they might send them to other places. Now, Billy
Kellett, I want you to tell me the truth. Have you ever seen this
man before?”

He held out another photograph. It was the one of Mr. Davenheim.

The man looked at it, and then at Poirot. A look of cunning came
into his eyes.

“Maybe I have, and maybe I haven’t,” he said.

“It would be to your advantage to tell me the truth,” said Poirot
quietly.

The man hesitated. “Well, then, I _have_ seen him. But not as he
is there.”

“How then?”

“Without the beard and moustache—and with his hair cut short.”

“Ah!” said Poirot. “And where did you see him?”

“In the same place as I was myself—last autumn.”

“In Maidstone prison?”

“That’s it.”

“Under what name?”

“Well, I don’t know as I ought to say——”

“It will be to your advantage, I tell you.”

“Well, then—Billy Kellett!”

“What?” cried Japp. “You mean he was using _your_ name?”

“That’s it. He’d got into some trouble—I don’t know what—and he
was serving three months under my name. We was in the same gang.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Thank you, Billy Kellett. That is all I
wanted to know.”

As we came away from the prison, Japp was full of excitement.

“What a find!” he cried. “But I don’t see how it helps us to find
Davenheim.”

“Do you not?” said Poirot. “To me it is very clear. But we must
have one more piece of evidence. Japp, I want you to find out for
me whether Mr. Davenheim has a large sum of money in any bank
abroad—in Buenos Ayres, for instance.”

“I can do that for you,” said Japp.

Three days later he came to see us.

“You were right, Monsieur Poirot. Davenheim has a very large
account in a bank in Buenos Ayres. It seems he’s been paying in
large sums for the last year.”

“_Précisément_,” said Poirot. “And now, my friend, I can tell you
where to find Mr. Davenheim.”

“Where?” cried Japp and I in one breath.

“In the place where he has been for the last week—in prison!”

“In prison?”

“Yes. He is Billy Kellett.”

“But Billy Kellett is a well-known thief!”

“Exactly. Mr. Davenheim, for reasons of his own, decided to
disappear. He knew that a well-known man cannot disappear easily.
So he decided to become a man who was _not_ well-known—a man, in
fact, who was already in the habit of disappearing from time to
time. He chose Billy Kellett. Last autumn, when he was supposed
to be in Buenos Ayres, he was really in Maidstone prison, serving
a sentence for a small theft, in the name of Billy Kellett. He
wanted to see if he could successfully impersonate the man. He
found he could.

“When the time came for his final disappearance, he staged the
burglary of his own safe, and then walked out of the house,
changed his clothes in the boathouse, and became Billy Kellett.
He had already arranged to be arrested for a small offence, so
as to have a safe hiding-place for the first few weeks of his
disappearance. He knew that nobody would look for Mr. Davenheim
in a police-cell! As for the ring, he threw it away where it would
be found, and then gave a description of Lowen as the man who
had thrown it, so as to throw suspicion on his enemy. It was a
very clever plan, but he made one mistake.”

“What was 그건?” I asked.

“He forgot that Billy Kellett would be recognized by someone who
had known him in prison! When I saw the photograph of Mr.
Davenheim, I was struck by the fact that his features were very
similar to those of Billy Kellett—if one imagined him without the
beard and moustache. And when I found that Billy Kellett had
been in prison at the same time that Mr. Davenheim was supposed
to be in Buenos Ayres, I was sure. The rest was easy.”

“But the clothes?” asked Japp. “Why did he leave them in the lake?”

“Because he wanted it to be thought that he had been murdered.
He knew that if his clothes were found, people would look for a
body. And as long as they were looking for a body, they would
not be looking for a living man!”

“Well,” said Japp, “you’ve won your fiver, Monsieur Poirot. And
I must say, it’s the cleverest thing I’ve ever heard of!”

“It was a simple matter,” said Poirot modestly. “A little
application of the grey cells, that is all!”

“First, as to the safebreaking. You say all the evidence points
to Lowen. On the contrary, to me it points _away_ from Lowen. A
man like Lowen would not have the necessary skill to force a safe
in such a way that there would be no clues left behind. It was
clearly the work of a professional.

“Second, as to his grudge. If he had a grudge, why should he not
have waited and taken his revenge in some other way—on the Stock
Exchange, for instance?

“Third, as to the lie about his not having left the study. He may
well have forgotten it. Even an innocent man might be confused
into such a statement.

“Fourth, the description given by Billy Kellett. This, I admit,
is the most serious point against him. But even so, it is not
conclusive.”

I could see Poirot was in one of his most aggravating moods.

“Have it your own way, then!” I said. “But what do you consider
the points of importance?”

“The lake, the boathouse, and—most important of all—the fact that
the clothes found were the identical ones Mr. Davenheim was wearing
when he left the house.”

“But,” I said, “surely that is only natural? He had no others with
him.”

“Exactly. He had no others with him. That is the point!”

I stared. “I really don’t see what you mean.”

“Don’t you? Then you should think it over—in the quietness of your
chamber.”

I did think it over—but it led me nowhere. On Wednesday evening
Japp called again. He was in a somewhat subdued mood.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, “I’ve found out about those
rooms for you. They did not occupy the same bedroom.”

“_Ah!_” said Poirot, and his eyes gleamed. “Then that is the last
link in the chain.”

“Do you mean to say you’ve solved it?” I cried.

“Not quite. There is still one point that remains a little
obscure.”

“Only one?” Japp laughed. “Well, I must say you’re a marvel,
Monsieur Poirot! What is this point?”

“I have been wondering,” said Poirot, “if there is any chance of
recovering the money. If I were Mr. Davenheim, I should have
taken—let me see—at least five thousand pounds in notes.”

“Well, as it happens, you’re quite right. Five thousand pounds in
notes was missing.”

“Only five thousand? Then I fear the rest is lost.”

“Lost?”

“Yes. But what about the jewellery? Was it all there?”

“The safe was quite empty.”

“_Ah!_” said Poirot. “Then there is still hope. Now, Japp, I want
you to do me a small favour. Will you take me down to Chingside
to-morrow?”

“Certainly, if you wish it. But I can’t see what good it’s going
to do.”

“Perhaps none. But I should like to have a look at the house and
grounds.”

“Well, I’ll call for you at ten o’clock to-morrow morning.”

I went with them. The Cedars was a large, modern house, standing
in its own grounds. We were shown into the study, where Miller was
busy with some papers. He looked up as we entered.

“Any news, Miller?” asked Japp.

“Nothing fresh. We’ve had the lake dragged, but without result.
We’re going to have another try to-morrow.”

“I don’t think you’ll find anything there,” said Poirot quietly.

Miller looked at him. “Indeed, monsieur? And why not?”

“Because it is not there,” said Poirot.

The detective shrugged his shoulders. “Well, we’ve got to make
sure. We can’t leave any stone unturned.”

“_Précisément_,” said Poirot. “But you are looking in the wrong
place.”

“And where would you suggest looking?”

“In the boathouse,” said Poirot.

Miller laughed. “We’ve been through the boathouse with a
fine-tooth-comb. There’s nothing there.”

“I think you’ll find I’m right,” said Poirot.

We went out into the grounds. As we approached the lake, we saw a
small, dark-complexioned man coming towards us.

“That’s Lowen,” whispered Japp.

He passed us with a slight nod, and Poirot looked after him with
interest.

“A clever face,” he remarked. “Very clever.”

We reached the boathouse, and Poirot went inside. He looked round
him for a few minutes, then walked over to a large cupboard in the
corner. He tried the door, but it was locked.

“What’s in here?” he asked.

“Oh, only some old fishing-tackle and things of that sort,” said
Miller.

“Have you the key?”

“No. I expect the gardener has it.”

“I should like to see inside,” said Poirot.

Miller looked at Japp, who nodded.

“Oh, very well,” he said. “I’ll get the gardener to open it.”

He went off, and returned in a few minutes with the gardener and
the key. The cupboard was opened, but there was nothing in it
except some old nets and a few fishing-rods.

Poirot looked disappointed.

“Is that all?” he asked.

“That’s all,” said Miller.

Poirot turned away. “Then I have been mistaken,” he said. “I
apologize.”

We walked back to the house. As we were leaving, Poirot turned to
Japp.

“There is just one more thing I should like to see,” he said. “Mr.
Davenheim’s bedroom.”

“Oh, certainly, if you wish it.”

We went upstairs. The bedroom was a large, airy room, comfortably
furnished. Poirot looked round him with interest. He walked over
to the dressing-table, and picked up a hair-brush. He examined it
attentively for a few minutes, then put it down again.

“Well,” he said, “I think that is all.”

We drove back to town in silence. Poirot seemed lost in thought,
and I did not like to disturb him. As we reached our rooms, Japp
said:

“Well, Monsieur Poirot, have you solved the mystery?”

“I think so,” said Poirot. “But I should like another twenty-four
hours to make sure.”

“Very well. I’ll call round on Friday evening.”

When Japp had gone, I turned to Poirot.

“Look here, Poirot,” I said, “I’m completely in the dark. What on
earth did you expect to find in that cupboard?”

“Nothing,” said Poirot.

“Then why did you ask to have it opened?”

“Because I wanted to see if it _was_ locked.”

“And what did you find in the bedroom?”

“I found—nothing,” said Poirot.

“Then why did you go there?”

“Because I wanted to see if there _was_ nothing there.”

I gave it up. Poirot was in one of his most exasperating moods.

On Friday evening Japp arrived punctually at nine o’clock.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, “time’s up! Have you found Mr.
Davenheim?”

“I have,” said Poirot.

“Where is he?”

“He is in gaol,” said Poirot.

“In gaol? What for?”

“For assaulting a policeman,” said Poirot.

“You mean—Billy Kellett?” I cried.

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “Billy Kellett is Mr. Davenheim.”

We both stared at him in amazement.

“But it’s impossible!” I cried. “The description—the long hair,
the beard, the bushy eyebrows——”

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, “have you never heard of a wig? Or of
a false beard? Or of the effects of a little burnt cork?”

“But why—why should he do such a thing?”

“To escape the consequences of his financial ruin,” said Poirot.
“He knew that his firm was on the verge of bankruptcy. He knew
that his only chance of safety lay in a complete disappearance.
But he also knew that a common disappearance is easily found out.
So he planned a more elaborate one. He created the character of
Billy Kellett—a man with a criminal record, who would be known to
the police. For months he has been leading a double life, spending
part of his time as Mr. Davenheim and part as Billy Kellett. He
arranged the burglary himself, taking care to leave no clues that
would implicate anyone but a professional thief. He then ‘vanished,’
leaving behind him the clothes he had been wearing as Mr. Davenheim,
to give the impression that he had been murdered and his body
disposed of in the lime-kiln. He then assumed the character of
Billy Kellett, pawned the ring which he had ‘found,’ and got
himself arrested for assaulting a policeman. In prison, he was
safe—no one would ever dream of looking for Mr. Davenheim there.”

“But the description?” I persisted. “Lowen saw a man who answered
to the description of Billy Kellett.”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “That was part of the plan. He knew that
Lowen was coming to see him that evening. He also knew that Lowen
would be shown into the study to wait for him. So he went out by
the front door, as if to post some letters, and then came back
round the side of the house to the rose-garden. He knew the maid
would be fastening the windows, and he took care to let her see
him—not as Mr. Davenheim, but as the man who was to be Billy
Kellett. He then went into the study by the French window, broke
open the safe, and took out the money and jewels. He then went
out again, leaving the window open, and made his way to the road,
where he ‘found’ the ring and threw it over the hedge, as if to
implicate Lowen. He then went to town, pawned the ring, and got
himself arrested.”

“But how did you know?” asked Japp.

“By the exercise of the little grey cells, my friend! There were
several points that struck me as significant. First, the fact that
only the clothes he was wearing were missing. That suggested that
he had not gone far. Second, the fact that he and his wife did
not occupy the same bedroom. That made it possible for him to lead
his double life without her suspecting anything. Third, the
hair-brush. When I examined it, I found—nothing! No hair at all!
Now, a man with long, wavy hair and a full moustache and beard
cannot brush his hair without leaving some trace of it behind.
The fact that there was no hair on the brush suggested that the
hair, the moustache, and the beard were all false!”

“And the money?” asked Japp. “You said there was five thousand
pounds missing.”

“That was the money he took with him as Billy Kellett,” said Poirot.
“He knew he would need it when he came out of prison. The rest of
the money and the jewels he had already sent to South America,
where he intended to join them as soon as he was free.”

“Well,” said Japp, “I must say you’ve beaten us again, Monsieur
Poirot! I’ll go and see about having Billy Kellett—or Mr.
Davenheim—identified at once.”

As Japp left the room, Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“You see, Hastings? The little grey cells! They never fail!”

“Point one: Does all the evidence point to Lowen? On the contrary,
I should say that it all pointed away from him. It is too clear.
If he had committed the robbery, he would not have left so many
clues. No, my friend, that is the work of a man who wished to
incriminate Lowen.

“Point two: If Lowen had a grudge against Davenheim, it is possible
he would wish to get his revenge in a more subtle way.

“Point three: If he had committed the robbery, he would have had
his story ready, and would have stuck to it.

“Point four: It is true that Billy Kellett’s story, if true,
implicates Lowen. But suppose for a moment it is _not_ true?”

“But Poirot!” I cried. “How could he have described Lowen so
accurately?”

“Exactly! That is the point. How _could_ he? How could a man in
a ditch, at dusk, describe a passer-by with such minute detail?
No, my friend, that description was supplied to him!”

“But by whom?”

“By the person who gave him the ring, of course!”

“Then you think Lowen gave it to him?”

“Not for a moment! Lowen is not a fool! Why should he give away
the most damning piece of evidence against himself?”

“Then who did?”

“Ah, that is the question! And there is another small point that
strikes me. Why did Davenheim, a man of method, leave his house
to post letters? There was a pillar-box at his gate. Why did he
not use it? No, my friend, the fact that he went to the village
is significant.”

“And the lake?” I asked.

“Ah, the lake! That is very interesting—very interesting indeed!”

I looked at him, but his face told me nothing. He was once more
sunk in a reverie. I felt that I was on the track of a great
discovery, but for the life of me I could not see where it was
leading.

“One: Mr. Lowen could not possibly know that he would have the
chance to open the safe. He came for a business interview. He could
not know beforehand that Mr. Davenheim would be absent posting a
letter, and that he would consequently be alone in the study!”

“He might have seized his opportunity,” I suggested.

“And the tools? City gentlemen do not carry round housebreaker’s
tools on the off chance! And one could not cut into that safe with
a penknife, _bien entendu_!”

“Well, what about Number Two?”

“Number Two: If he had a grudge against the man, it would surely
be simpler to ruin him financially? One does not usually commit
murder for a grudge! Also, the safe had been broken into, and the
jewels were missing. That does not look like the action of a
business rival.”

“Number Three?”

“The study window! He says he walked through it to look at a rose.
One could hardly find a more flimsy excuse. And yet—and yet—he
must have been doing _something_!”

“And Number Four?”

“My dear Hastings, do you suppose that even a criminal of the
vilest type would be such a fool as to throw away a valuable diamond
ring into a ditch, in full view of a man who might be watching
him?”

“He did not see the man.”

“Then why throw it away at all?”

“You are right,” I said, somewhat Crestfallen. “What, then, do you
think is the truth?”

“I have three questions to ask you, Hastings.”

“Go on!”

“_Primo_: Does a man who is about to post letters usually do so
without his hat?

“_Secondo_: What was the nature of the large financial transaction
Davenheim and Salmon were engaged in?

“_Tertio_: Do Mr. and Mrs. Davenheim occupy the same bedroom?”

I laughed. “The last seems to me to be quite beside the point!”

“On the contrary,” said Poirot, “it is the most important of all!”

I could only stare at him in amazement.

For several days we saw nothing of Japp. Then on the Thursday
evening he turned up again. He looked a trifle depressed.

“Well,” he said, “I’ve found out about the bedrooms. They _didn’t_
occupy the same one. Mrs. Davenheim’s room is at the back of the
house, and her husband’s at the front.”

“_Merci, mon ami_. That is very satisfactory.”

“And I’ve something else to tell you. We’ve found the jewels. They
were in the lake.”

“In the lake?” I cried.

“Yes, in a small tin box. But the bank-notes and the bonds are
still missing.”

“That is very interesting,” said Poirot. “By the way, have you
searched the boathouse?”

“Of course! We’ve searched every inch of the grounds. But what on
earth should we find in the boathouse?”

“Nothing, I suppose,” said Poirot. “I merely asked. Tell me, has
the lake been thoroughly dragged?”

“Every inch of it.”

“And you found—the jewels?”

“Yes.”

“And nothing else?”

“Not a thing.”

“That is very curious,” said Poirot. “Very curious indeed!”

Japp looked at him. “What’s on your mind?”

“I was wondering,” said Poirot, “if there might not be a second
box.”

“A second box? What for?”

“For the bank-notes and the bonds, of course.”

“But they were in the same box!”

“Ah! You found them, then?”

“No, I tell you! We found the jewels in the box—nothing else.”

“Then why do you say they were in the same box?”

“Because the box was only half full. There was plenty of room for
the notes and the bonds.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “I see.”

He fell into a brown study. Japp and I watched him in silence.
Presently he looked up.

“Tell me,” he said, “what was the large financial transaction the
firm was engaged in?”

“A big South American loan. It seems it’s been a bit of a frost.
The firm is in rather a shaky condition, I believe. In fact, if
Davenheim doesn’t turn up soon, I shouldn’t be surprised if they
went bankrupt.”

“_A la bonne heure!_” cried Poirot. “The light begins to break!”

“You’ve got a clue?” asked Japp eagerly.

“I have a certainty. Tell me, has any one been to see Billy Kellett
in prison?”

“His wife went to see him yesterday.”

“Ah! And what is she like?”

“A big, masculine-looking woman. Why?”

“Nothing—nothing. Just a passing thought. Now, I have a little
experiment I want you to carry out for me.”

“What is it?”

“I want you to go down to Chingside to-morrow, and take a good
stout crowbar with you.”

“A crowbar! What for?”

“To break into the boathouse.”

“But I tell you we’ve searched it!”

“Search it again. And this time, look _under_ the floor.”

“The floor? But it’s a concrete floor!”

“Exactly. That is why you will need a crowbar.”

Japp stared at him. “You think the body’s there?”

“I am certain of it!”

“But we should have noticed if the concrete had been disturbed!”

“Not if it had been done some time ago. Mr. Davenheim spent all
last autumn in Buenos Ayres, did he not? Well, it was then that the
work was done!”

“But what on earth—?”

“Do as I tell you, my friend. To-morrow evening I shall expect you
here—with the news of your discovery.”

Japp shook his head. “It sounds like a wild-goose chase to me. But
I’ll do it, to please you.”

He was as good as his word. On Friday evening he duly appeared. He
looked even more depressed than before.

“Well?” asked Poirot. “You have been to Chingside?”

“I have.”

“And you broke up the floor of the boathouse?”

“I did.”

“And you found—?”

“A lot of damp earth!”

“Nothing else?”

“Not a thing.”

Poirot’s face fell. “It is impossible!” he murmured. “Impossible!”

“I’m afraid your grey cells have failed you this time, Monsieur
Poirot,” said Japp, not without a certain smug satisfaction. “The
mystery of Mr. Davenheim remains a mystery still.”

“No,” said Poirot suddenly. “It is not a mystery. It is a very
simple case—so simple that I have been a fool not to see it
sooner!”

“You know where he is?”

“I do.”

“Dead or alive?”

“Neither!”

“Neither? What do you mean?”

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that Mr. Davenheim has never existed!”

“Never existed? But I’ve seen him!” cried Japp.

“And I’ve seen his photograph!” I added.

“You have seen a man who called himself Mr. Davenheim. But the real
Mr. Davenheim—the man who was the senior partner of Davenheim and
Salmon—he is a very different person!”

“I don’t understand,” said Japp.

“Listen, then. What was the first thing that struck me in this
case? The extraordinary resemblance between the description of the
missing man and the description of Billy Kellett. Both had dark
hair and a big moustache. Both were of about the same height and
build. Then there was the matter of the ring. Billy Kellett pawns
a ring which is identified as Mr. Davenheim’s. He says a man threw
it into a ditch. But why should any man do such a thing? It was
preposterous! But suppose Billy Kellett _was_ the man? Suppose he
had the ring because he was Mr. Davenheim?”

“But Billy Kellett is a well-known criminal!” cried Japp. “He was
in prison all last autumn!”

“Exactly!” said Poirot. “And where was Mr. Davenheim? In Buenos
Ayres! At least, so he told his wife. But did he go to Buenos
Ayres? No! He went to prison—under the name of Billy Kellett!”

“But why?” I asked, bewildered.

“Because he knew that the firm was on the verge of bankruptcy. He
wanted to disappear—to start a new life with the money he had
stolen from the safe. But how was he to do it? If he just ran away,
he would be hunted by the police. He needed a safe hiding-place.
And what better hiding-place could there be than a prison? So he
invented the character of Billy Kellett—a man who was ‘known to
the police.’ He spent the autumn in prison, establishing the
identity. Then he came back to Chingside as Mr. Davenheim. On
Saturday afternoon, he staged his ‘disappearance.’ He went out to
post his letters—without his hat, you remember, because he wasn’t
going any further than the gate. There he met his ‘wife’—the big,
masculine-looking woman Japp saw in the prison—who was really an
accomplice. He changed his clothes, shaved off his beard and
moustache, and became Billy Kellett once more. Then he went to
London, pawned his own ring to make sure he would be arrested, and
went back to his comfortable cell in Bow Street!”

“But the jewels?” I asked. “And the safe?”

“He robbed his own safe, of course—before he went out to post the
letters. He threw the jewels into the lake, knowing they would be
found and would help to point the finger of suspicion at Lowen.
The bank-notes and the bonds he gave to his accomplice—the woman
who visited him in prison.”

“It’s incredible!” said Japp. “But if it’s true, who is the man
we’ve got in prison now?”

“He is the real Billy Kellett,” said Poirot. “Or rather, he is the
man who has been playing the part of Billy Kellett for the last
five days. Mr. Davenheim, of course, is no longer in prison. He
was released on Monday morning, after paying his fine for being
drunk and disorderly!”

“Then where is he now?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I want you to find out. But I think,
if you look for a man who has just arrived in a certain South
American port—without a beard or a moustache, but with a very
large sum of money in his possession—you will not be far from the
truth!”

Japp rose to his feet. “By Jove, Monsieur Poirot, I believe you’re
right! I’ll get on to it at once!”

He hurried from the room. Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“You see, Hastings? The little grey cells—they do not fail! And
now, let us have some more of your ‘English poison.’ I find I am
very thirsty!”

I poured him a cup of tea. “But Poirot,” I said, “there’s one thing
I don’t understand. Why did you think the body was in the
boathouse?”

Poirot chuckled. “I didn’t, my friend! I merely wanted to get Japp
out of the way for a few hours while I made some inquiries of my
own! It is always well to have a little—how do you say?—diversion!”

I shook my head. “You are a most extraordinary man, Poirot!”

“No,” said Poirot, sipping his tea with relish. “I am only Hercule
Poirot!”

“Number Two: If he had a grudge against Davenheim, why visit him
by appointment in his own house? He would be certain to be
suspected.”

“Point Three?”

“Number Three: He might have been a-tired—a-weary of his
confinement, and strolled out for a breath of air. He lied because
he was afraid—and small wonder!

“Number Four: If you believe the evidence of Billy Kellett, you
must believe all he says. He says that the man he saw throw away
the ring was coming _towards_ the station, _from_ the village.
Now, the maid says she saw Lowen at 6.15. The 6.28 train to town
was the one he caught. It would have been impossible for him to
have gone to the village and back in the time.”

“But,” I cried, “the ring was thrown away. If Lowen didn’t do it,
who did?”

“Ah, that is the question! And there is one other—did Mr. and Mrs.
Davenheim occupy the same bedroom?”

“I don’t see how that can affect the matter,” I said.

“No? But I should like to know—all the same.”

He was silent for a few minutes. Then he said suddenly:

“Hastings, have you a grain of salt?”

“Salt?” I said, staring. “In the kitchen, I suppose.”

“_Alors_, bring me a little. Also a glass of water.”

I complied with his request. He poured a small quantity of the
salt into the water, and then watched it with the most intense
interest as it dissolved.

“The little things!” he murmured. “The little things! They are
everything!”

I could only shake my head. Truly, my poor friend’s mind was
becoming unhinged!

At our next meeting with Japp, the Inspector looked at Poirot
with a look in which pity and amusement were blended.

“I’ve got the information you wanted,” he said. “Mr. and Mrs.
Davenheim have not occupied the same bedroom for the last six
months. He’s been suffering from insomnia, and has been very
restless, often getting up in the middle of the night and going
for long walks. Does that help you at all?”

“It is of the first importance!” said Poirot, with such emphasis
that I stared at him.

“I’ve something else for you,” went on Japp. “Miller’s been at
the lake again. He’s had it dragged. No body—but he’s found
something else. A small safe-key. There’s no doubt it’s the one
belonging to the safe in the study. So that rather looks as though
it was Davenheim himself who—but there, it’s all very confusing.
Lowen’s been released, by the way. There’s no evidence against
him.”

Poirot nodded. “I expected that.”

“And Billy Kellett?” I asked.

“Oh, he’s in for three months for the assault on the police. So
he’s out of the way for a bit. The police are absolutely at a
loss—don’t know what to do next.”

“But they must do something!” I cried. “The man’s vanished into
space. It’s the most extraordinary case I’ve ever heard of!”

“You think so?” said Poirot. “I find it—on the contrary—most
simple.”

“Simple!” Japp and I spoke in one breath.

“Very simple. There are only one or two points that are not quite
clear, but I expect to have those settled by to-morrow.”

“I say, Poirot, you’re not joking, are you?” Japp’s tone was
suspicious.

“I never joke on a matter of business,” said Poirot. “Wait until
to-morrow, and you shall have the solution of your mystery.”

“Well,” said Japp, “I’ll be here at this time to-morrow evening.
If you’ve got the solution then, I’ll take off my hat to you.
Good-night!”

“Good-night, _mon ami_.”

When he had gone, Poirot turned to me.

“Hastings, I have a little commission for you. I want you to go
down to Chingside to-morrow. I will give you a list of the things
I want you to do.”

The list was a fairly long one. I was to call at The Cedars and
interview the gardener who had seen the figure in the rose-garden.
I was to see the maid who had seen Lowen. I was to find out all I
could about the habits of Mr. Davenheim. And finally, I was to
visit the local police station and see if I could get a glimpse of
Billy Kellett.

I started early the next morning. It was a beautiful day, and I
thoroughly enjoyed my trip. I did all that Poirot had asked me,
and was back in town by five o’clock. Poirot was waiting for me.

“Well?” he asked. “You have been successful?”

“I think so. I’ve got all the information you wanted.”

“_C’est bien!_ Now, tell me all about it.”

I gave him a full account of my day’s work. He listened
attentively, nodding his head from time to time. When I had
finished, he sat for a few minutes in silence.

“Yes,” he said at last. “It is as I thought. The case is now quite
clear. There is only one more thing I must do.”

He rose and went to the telephone. After a few minutes’
conversation, he returned.

“It is arranged. Japp will be here at eight o’clock. And now,
Hastings, let us have dinner. We have earned it.”

At eight o’clock punctually Japp arrived. He looked as though he
had had a hard day, but he was as cheerful as ever.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, “I’m here. Have you got the
criminal for me?”

“I have,” said Poirot quietly.

“Who is it?”

“If you will have the kindness to wait a few minutes, you shall
see for yourself. I have asked a certain person to call here this
evening.”

“Who?”

“The person who can tell us the truth about the disappearance of
Mr. Davenheim.”

Even as he spoke, there was a ring at the bell. A few minutes
later, the door opened, and a lady was shown into the room. It was
Mrs. Davenheim. She was a tall, fair woman, with a rather pleasant,
unintelligent face. She looked at us with a certain amount of
apprehension.

“You wished to see me, monsieur?” she said, addressing Poirot.

“If you please, madame. Will you not sit down?”

Poirot placed a chair for her.

“Madame,” he said, “I have asked you to come here because I think
you can help us in our search for your husband.”

“I?” she said, with a start. “But I have told the police everything
I know. I can tell you nothing more.”

“Are you sure of that, madame?” asked Poirot. “Think again. Is
there nothing you have omitted—nothing that seemed to you too
trivial to mention?”

“Nothing, monsieur. I am sure of it.”

“Then,” said Poirot, “I must ask you a few questions. For instance,
on the Saturday afternoon of your husband’s disappearance, you say
he post some letters. Did he mention to whom they were addressed?”

“No, monsieur.”

“Did you see him post them?”

“No, monsieur. I was in my boudoir.”

“I see. Now, madame, I have another question to ask you. It may
seem to you a strange one, but I have my reasons. Has your husband
any—physical peculiarity?”

“Physical peculiarity?” she repeated. “I don’t understand.”

“I mean, is there anything about his appearance that would make
him easily recognizable? Any scar—any birthmark?”

“No, monsieur. None that I know of.”

“I see. And his hair—it was naturally curly, was it not?”

“Yes, monsieur.”

“And he wore it rather long?”

“Yes.”

“Thank you, madame. That is all I wanted to know. I will not detain
you any longer.”

Mrs. Davenheim rose. “I hope you will find him, monsieur,” she said
plaintively. “It is very distressing—all this publicity.”

“We will do our best, madame,” said Poirot, escorting her to the
door.

When he returned, Japp was looking at him with a puzzled
expression.

“I don’t see what you’ve gained by that,” he said. “We knew all
that before.”

“Did we?” said Poirot. “I think not. But let us proceed. There is
another person I am expecting. Ah, here he is!”

Again the bell rang, and a few minutes later a man was shown into
the room. It was the junior partner of the firm of Davenheim and
Salmon. He looked anxious and harassed.

“You have news of Mr. Davenheim?” he asked eagerly.

“I think I can say that I have,” replied Poirot. “But first, I
want you to tell me something. What was the exact nature of the
business that Mr. Davenheim was engaged upon in South America last
autumn?”

“It was a matter of some importance,” said the other. “We were
contemplating opening a branch in Buenos Ayres, and Mr. Davenheim
went out there to make the necessary arrangements.”

“I see. And while he was there, did he have any—illness?”

“Illness? Not that I know of. He seemed very well when he
returned.”

“Thank you. That is all I wanted to know.”

The junior partner looked disappointed. “But you said you had
news!” he cried.

“So I have. But I must ask you to be patient for a little longer.
If you will call at Scotland Yard to-morrow morning, Inspector
Japp will be able to give you all the information you require.”

When the man had gone, Japp turned to Poirot.

“Look here, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, “I’ve been very patient,
but I’m beginning to think you’re having a joke at my expense.
What’s the meaning of all this? You ask a lot of questions that
don’t seem to have anything to do with the case, and then you tell
people to come to Scotland Yard to-morrow! What’s the idea?”

“The idea, my friend, is very simple. I have been testing my
theories. And I am happy to say that they have all been proved
correct.”

“Then you know where Mr. Davenheim is?”

“I do.”

“Where is he?”

“He is,” said Poirot, “in a place where the police would never
think of looking for him.”

“Where’s that?”

“In prison!”

“In prison!” we both cried.

“Exactly.”

“But what’s he in prison for?”

“For assaulting a policeman,” said Poirot calmly.

“You mean—Billy Kellett?” I cried.

“Precisely.”

“But Billy Kellett is a well-known thief!” said Japp.

“He is also,” said Poirot, “Mr. Davenheim.”

“Nonsense!” said Japp. “Billy Kellett is a small man with a
smooth face. Mr. Davenheim is a big man with a beard and long
hair.”

“Nature,” said Poirot, “is a great magician. But she cannot
change a man’s height. As for the beard and the hair—they are
easily disposed of. A razor and a pair of scissors will do the
work in ten minutes.”

“But the description!” I cried. “The maid—the gardener—they all
saw a man like Lowen!”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “They saw what they expected to see. Mr.
Davenheim had carefully prepared the way. He had even gone to
the length of having an appointment with Lowen, so that there
should be a convenient person to suspect. He left the house,
changed his clothes in the boathouse, shaved off his beard and
moustache, cut his hair, and then walked to the village. On the
way, he met himself—or rather, he met the person he had
intended to be—coming from the station. He threw away his ring,
knowing it would be found, and then went to London, where he
deliberately got himself arrested. In prison, he was safe. No one
would ever think of looking for the missing banker in a common
jail.”

“But why?” I asked. “Why should he do such a thing?”

“Because,” said Poirot, “the firm of Davenheim and Salmon is on
the verge of bankruptcy. Mr. Davenheim has been preparing for
this for a long time. He has been systematically robbing the
firm, and the money is safely hidden away. By ‘disappearing’ in
this way, he hoped to escape the consequences of his crimes. He
knew that if he were arrested as Billy Kellett, he would only
get a short sentence, and when he came out, he would be free to
enjoy his ill-gotten gains.”

“It’s incredible!” said Japp. “But if it’s true—how did you find
out?”

“It was the little things,” said Poirot. “The salt in the water—to
see how long it took to dissolve. The fact that Mr. and Mrs.
Davenheim did not occupy the same bedroom—which gave him the
opportunity to change his appearance without her knowledge. The
long hair and the beard—which were so easily changed. And
finally, the description of Billy Kellett. It was too accurate.
No one but Mr. Davenheim himself could have described Lowen so
well.”

“Well,” said Japp, “I must say you’ve beaten us this time,
Monsieur Poirot. I’ll go and see about it at once.”

“And the fiver?” said Poirot, with a smile.

Japp laughed. “You shall have it to-morrow. Good-night!”

When he had gone, Poirot turned to me.

“You see, Hastings? The little grey cells! They are everything!”

I could only agree. Truly, my friend was a remarkable man.

“_Bon!_ Number Two. You say Lowen had a grudge against Davenheim.
Now, I should have thought that would be a very good reason for
_not_ murdering him—if you wished to avoid suspicion. Then Number
Three. You say he lied when he said he had never left the study.
I agree. But why did he lie? Because he had something to conceal.
Was it a murder, or something else?”

“What else could it be?” I asked.

“The maid’s evidence!” Poirot said with an air of triumph. “She
saw him coming _towards_ the house through the rose-garden. Why
not _from_ the house?”

“I don’t see that it makes much difference.”

“Ah, but there is a great deal of difference! One other point.
You do not mention the most important fact of all—that the clothes
of the missing man were found in the lake. Also, why did he not
take his walking-stick? It was a very handsome one, and he usually
carried it. Then there is the question of the bedroom.”

“I don’t see that that can have anything to do with it.”

“On the contrary, it is the most vital point of all. Wait until
Japp brings me the answer to my question.”

I gave it up. Poirot’s mind was too subtle for me. It seemed to
me that he was merely being perversely difficult.

Two days later, Japp looked in again.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, “I’ve got your answer. Mr. and
Mrs. Davenheim occupied separate bedrooms.”

“_A la bonne heure!_” cried Poirot. “The case is solved!”

We both stared at him.

“You mean you know where Mr. Davenheim is?” I asked.

“Perfectly. He is at this moment—in gaol!”

“In gaol!” I cried. “But how? What for?”

“For a very simple reason. He is the man you call Billy Kellett!”

“Billy Kellett!” Japp and I both spoke at once. “But Billy Kellett
is in gaol for three months—since last Saturday!”

“Precisely.”

“But Billy Kellett is a well-known thief!”

“Not at all. He is—or rather he _was_—Mr. Davenheim.”

“But Davenheim had a big moustache and a beard and long hair!”

“Had he? How do you know? From his photograph, and because his
household had seen him with them for years. But did you see him
on Saturday?”

“Well, of course, no one’s seen him since—except Billy Kellett,
who’s the man himself.”

“Exactly. Now, listen. Davenheim had been in South America last
autumn. Suppose that, while there, he found that he would be
obliged to ‘disappear’ in the near future. He might be able to
return to England as some one else. He had already begun to make
his plans. He would need to be away from home for a time. So he
shaved his beard and moustache, and cut his hair short, and then—_he
went to gaol as Billy Kellett!_”

“But why go to gaol?”

“To have an unbreakable alibi! As Billy Kellett, he was in a
police-cell on Saturday night, and in gaol from Monday onwards.
He couldn’t have committed the burglary at Chingside—it was done
while he was in the hands of the police!”

“But why did he want to disappear?”

“Because he’d been embezzling the bank’s funds for years, and
things were coming to a head. He’d got everything ready—the bearer
bonds and the notes were all in his pocket when he ‘disappeared.’
He only needed to hide them safely, and then, after he’d served
his time as Billy Kellett, he’d be free to go off with his loot.”

“But the clothes in the lake?”

“He put them there himself. He probably went out by the study
window, went down to the lake, changed into the Billy Kellett
clothes which he had hidden there, and threw his own into the
water. Then he went off to pawn his own ring—to make sure he’d be
arrested!”

“And Lowen?”

“He probably saw Lowen from the rose-garden, and that gave him the
idea of throwing the blame on him. He threw the ring over the
hedge where he knew it would be found—and then told the story as
having been done by ‘a man like Lowen.’”

“And the safe?”

“He’d probably robbed it himself before he left. The tools were
already there. He knew the combination, so he didn’t need much in
the way of tools.”

“But the maid?”

“She didn’t see Lowen—she saw Davenheim! That’s why she said he
was coming _towards_ the house. He was just coming back from the
lake after changing his clothes.”

“But why the question about the bedroom?”

“Because, _mon ami_, if he and his wife had shared a room, she
would have known that he’d shaved his beard and moustache! As it
was, he could do it in his own room, and she’d never know until
he ‘disappeared.’”

Japp drew a long breath. “Well, I’m damned! Monsieur Poirot, you’ve
won your fiver. I’ll go and see Miller at once. I think we’ll find
Mr. Billy Kellett is Mr. Davenheim all right!”

Poirot smiled. “It was a pretty little problem. But, as I told
you, Japp, it is the little grey cells—the little grey cells that
count!”

He turned to me. “You see, Hastings, the importance of the bedroom?
It was the one thing that made the whole thing possible!”

I nodded. Poirot’s ‘sitting-in-his-chair’ method had certainly
triumphed this time.

“Two: If he had a grudge against the banker, would he choose his
house as the place for his revenge? It is too clumsy.”

“And Three?”

“Three: He was afraid. He saw he was in a hole, and he made a
clumsy attempt to get out of it by lying. That is only human
nature.”

“And Four?”

“Four: If Billy Kellett’s story is true, it is the most important
point of all. But is it true? We must ask ourselves that.”

“Japp’s view,” I said, “is that it is not.”

“It is not my view,” said Poirot with a faint smile.

I looked at him. “What is your view, then?”

“I do not know—yet.”

“You are very mysterious.”

“It is my way,” Poirot answered. “One must not allow one’s
theories to be upset by facts.”

He went on, half to himself: “The lime kiln—that is very neat.
The clothes in the lake—the ring in the ditch—the safe—the bank
failure—the South American shares—there are many things which
require to be coordinated.”

“Wait a minute,” I cried. “The bank failure? Is there a bank
failure?”

“Did you not see it in the morning paper?” Poirot asked. “The
bank of Davenheim and Salmon has suspended payment. It’s a very
bad business. Thousands of poor people will lose their savings.”

“But this is a new factor!” I cried.

“It is the _old_ factor—the vital factor!” Poirot cried with
sudden energy. “The key to the whole mystery!”

I felt more than ever at sea. What had the bank failure to do with
Mr. Davenheim’s disappearance?

“Is it your opinion that he has absconded, then?” I asked.

“If he has, he’s a very clever man,” said Poirot. “As Japp says,
he could hardly fail to be recognized. And he could not possibly
hope to escape with his wife’s jewels and the money from the safe.
The ports are watched.”

“Then you think he’s dead?”

“I do not,” Poirot said. “I think he’s very much alive. But where—and
who? That is the question.”

He fell into a silence once more.

The next morning Japp appeared again. He looked crestfallen and
depressed.

“Well,” he said, “the lake’s been dragged—and there’s no body.
And Miller’s been to the lime kiln—and there’s no trace of any
human remains there. So we’re as far off as ever.”

“Any news from the bank?” Poirot asked.

“It’s a bad business. The books are in a terrible state. It seems
that for years Davenheim has been living on the firm’s capital.
If he hadn’t disappeared, he’d have been in the dock for fraud
by now.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Anything else?”

“Only your silly question about the bedrooms,” said Japp with a
grin. “The Davenheims had separate rooms. They have had for years.
Does that help you?”

“It does,” Poirot said. “It helps me very much.”

Japp looked at him. “Well, I must be going. I suppose you haven’t
any idea where Davenheim is?”

“I have a very good idea,” Poirot said.

Japp jumped. “What! Where?”

“I am not quite sure—yet,” Poirot said. “But I will tell you this.
Mr. Davenheim is not far off.”

“In the house?” Japp cried.

“No, not in the house. But not far away.”

Japp stared at him for a moment, and then went out. I saw that he
did not believe a word Poirot had said.

As for me, I was as much in the dark as ever. I knew Poirot’s
methods, but this time they seemed more than usually eccentric.

The days of the week slipped by. Friday came. On Saturday morning
Japp arrived. He looked more cheerful.

“Well,” he said, “time’s up to-day. Have you got your man?”

“I have,” Poirot said.

Japp’s jaw dropped. “You have? Where is he?”

“He is in a very safe place,” Poirot said. “In fact, he is in
gaol.”

“In gaol? But we’ve only got Lowen and Billy Kellett. Which of
them is it?”

“It is Billy Kellett,” Poirot said.

Japp burst into a roar of laughter. “Billy Kellett! The pickpocket!
You’re joking, Monsieur Poirot.”

“I was never more serious in my life,” Poirot said. “Billy Kellett
_is_ Mr. Davenheim.”

We both stared at him in speechless amazement.

“Let me explain,” Poirot said. “It is really very simple. Mr.
Davenheim knew that the bank was on the verge of ruin. He knew
that his only hope was to disappear with as much money and as
many jewels as he could lay his hands on. But he also knew that,
in these days of easy communication, it is almost impossible for
a well-known man to disappear. He hit on a very clever plan.

“Last autumn he went to Buenos Ayres. But he did not stay there.
He came back to London, and in the character of Billy Kellett,
committed a small robbery, and was sentenced to three months’
imprisonment. During that time he studied his part. He grew his
hair and his beard, and he learned the ways and the speech of a
professional thief.

“When he came out of prison, he went back to his own life as Mr.
Davenheim. He let his hair and beard grow in the same way, so
that he looked the same in both characters.

“On the Saturday of his disappearance, he went out to post his
letters. He had already hidden a suit of old clothes in the
boathouse. He went there, changed his clothes, and threw his
gentleman’s suit into the lake. He had already sent his ring and
some of the jewels to a safe place in London.

“He then walked to the village, and from there to Entfield. He
was careful to be seen by the gardener in his character of Mr.
Davenheim, and later, in his character of Billy Kellett, he was
careful to be seen by the same gardener.

“He then went to London, pawned his own ring—a thing no real thief
would have done—and then deliberately got himself arrested for
drunk and disorderly conduct. He knew that as Billy Kellett, a
small-time thief, he would be perfectly safe in gaol, while the
police were searching for Mr. Davenheim all over the country.

“The robbery of the safe was a simple matter. He had robbed it
himself before he left the house, and had left the window open
to make it look like an outside job. He knew that Lowen was
coming, and he timed his disappearance so that Lowen would be the
natural suspect.”

“But the ring?” Japp asked. “Why did he pawn it?”

“To establish his identity as Billy Kellett,” Poirot said. “And
also to provide a clue that would lead the police to Lowen. He
knew that his description of the man he saw throwing the ring
away would fit Lowen perfectly.”

“It’s incredible!” Japp said. “But it’s possible. By Jove, I
believe you’re right!”

“Of course I am right,” Poirot said. “The separate bedrooms
clinched the matter. If he and his wife had shared a room, she
would have noticed that he was growing his hair and beard to a
particular pattern. As it was, he could do as he liked.”

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” Japp said, “you’ve won your fiver. I’ll
go and see Miller at once. If Billy Kellett is really Davenheim,
he’s in for a longer sentence than he bargained for!”

“_Précisément_,” Poirot said. “The way of the transgressor, it is
hard.”

He turned to me with a smile. “Well, Hastings, what do you think
of my little grey cells now?”

I could only shake my head in admiration. Poirot had done it again.

“Two: That is just what you should notice! A man does not commit
a murder because of a business rivalry. He might ruin his enemy,
but he does not kill him.

“Three: You say he lied in his first statement? Why? For the simple
reason that he had no doubt some reason of his own for wishing
his presence in the rose-garden to remain a secret.”

“And what about Billy Kellett’s story?” I persisted.

“One: It is either true or it is not. If it is true, it is because
he _did_ see Lowen. If it is not true, it is because some one paid
him to say so. But why should Lowen, a clever man, go about the
country in that ostentatious way, throwing away a valuable ring?
_C’est idiot!_ No, my friend, you have not the flair!”

“Well, let’s see what you make of it,” I said.

Poirot took a sheet of paper. “I will make you a list of the points
which I consider of interest.

“_Un: Pourquoi_ did Mr. Davenheim spend all last autumn in Buenos
Ayres?”

“To do business, I suppose.”

“_Bien. Deux:_ What did he do with his money?”

“_Eh?_”

“He was a very rich man. Yet he had no expensive tastes. He did
not go in for racing, or yachting, or any of the usual ways of
spending money. His only hobby was his wife’s jewels.

“_Trois:_ Why did he and his wife occupy separate bedrooms?”

“So you found that out?”

“Japp told me this morning.

“_Quatre:_ How did he manage to break into his own safe?”

“His _own_ safe?” I cried.

“_Mais oui. Mais oui. C’est évident!_”

“But why should he rob himself?”

“That is the question. _Cinq:_ Why did he wear his hair so long?”

I burst out laughing. “You are joking, Poirot!”

“I never joke,” said Poirot. “I am very serious. _Six:_ Was the
safe opened with a key or by force?”

“Miller says it was forced.”

“_Sept:_ Why did Billy Kellett happen to be in that particular
ditch at that particular time?”

“I don’t know,” I said. “It seems to me you’re only making it more
confused than ever.”

“On the contrary,” said Poirot. “To me it is as clear as—what do
you say—_le jour_!”

I sighed. “I give it up!”

“And yet it is so simple! Now I go to bed. To-morrow, no doubt,
we shall have further news from Japp.”

But it was not until Thursday that Japp again made his appearance.
He looked somewhat discouraged.

“Well,” he said, “we’ve dragged the lake, but not a sign of a
body. Nor in the lime-kiln either. We’ve been through the house
from top to bottom, but there’s no trace of the missing man.
We’ve been through Lowen’s house, too, but with no better result.”

“And the bank?” asked Poirot.

“Davenheim and Salmon have suspended payment. There’s a regular
panic in the City. It seems that the assets are practically
non-existent. Davenheim must have been juggling with the funds
for years.”

“Ah!” said Poirot. “_C’est ça!_ That is what I expected. The bank
was on the verge of failure. He knew it. He decided to disappear.”

“Yes, but _where_?” asked Japp. “And _how_?”

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, “it is very simple. He has merely to go
to a place where he will not be recognized.”

“But where would that be? Every one knows him.”

“Do they?” asked Poirot. “Do they really? Do they know anything
of him but his hair, his beard, and his bushy eyebrows?”

“Well, what more do you want?”

“Nothing,” said Poirot. “I want nothing more.”

Japp stared at him. “You mean that he—but it’s impossible!”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Wait and see.”

It was on the following Monday that Poirot finally sent for Japp.
The week was up.

“Well,” said Japp, as he entered the room, “have you found him?”

“I have,” said Poirot.

“Where is he?”

“He is,” said Poirot, “at this moment in the custody of the police.”

“In their custody? But we haven’t got him!”

“Oh, yes, you have! You have had him for the last nine days!”

“What?”

“The man who called himself Billy Kellett—_is_ Mr. Davenheim!”

Japp’s jaw dropped. I was equally taken aback.

“But—but—it’s impossible!” I cried. “The two men are totally
different! Billy Kellett is a common thief—a jailbird!”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “That was the cleverness of it. Mr.
Davenheim knew that his bank was going to fail. He knew that if
he disappeared in the ordinary way, he would be hunted for
everywhere. So he decided to disappear in a way that no one would
ever dream of. He decided to become—a criminal!”

“But how did he do it?” asked Japp.

“It was very simple. Last autumn, when he was supposed to be in
Buenos Ayres, he was really in London, leading a double life. He
took a small room in a poor neighbourhood, and there he practiced
the role of Billy Kellett. He let his hair and beard grow, and
learned the slang and the ways of the criminal classes. He even
managed to get himself arrested and imprisoned for a short time,
so as to establish his identity as a criminal. Then, when the time
came for him to disappear, he had his plan all ready.

“On that Saturday afternoon, he went to the post office as he had
said. But once out of sight of the house, he went to a small hut
he had prepared in the woods. There he shaved off his beard and
moustache, and cut his hair. He changed into the old clothes of
Billy Kellett, which he had hidden there. Then he walked to the
road, and waited for Lowen to pass. He knew that Lowen was coming
to see him, and he had timed his disappearance accordingly. When
Lowen appeared, he threw the ring over the hedge, and then went
on to the station. He knew that he would be arrested for pawning
the ring, and that was exactly what he wanted. As Billy Kellett,
he was safe in prison, while the police were looking for Mr.
Davenheim all over the country!”

“But the safe?” I asked. “How did he rob his own safe?”

“He did that before he left the house,” said Poirot. “He had
already moved the money and the jewels to a safe place. He merely
made it look as though it had been forced, to throw suspicion on
Lowen. He knew that Lowen would be in the study alone for some
time, and that he would be the natural person to suspect.”

“And the clothes in the lake?” asked Japp.

“He threw them there himself, before he changed into his Billy
Kellett clothes. He wanted to make it look as though he had been
murdered, or had committed suicide.”

“But the ring?” I said. “Why did he throw it away like that?”

“To make sure that he would be arrested as Billy Kellett,” said
Poirot. “He knew that if he pawned it, it would be traced back to
him. And by giving a description of Lowen, he made it even more
certain that he would be identified as the man who had found the
ring.”

Japp shook his head in admiration. “Well, Monsieur Poirot, you’ve
won your bet. I must say, it’s the cleverest thing I’ve ever heard of.”

“It was a very pretty little problem,” said Poirot, smiling. “But,
as I told you, it was all a matter of the little grey cells!”

He turned to me. “You see, Hastings, how important it is to
observe the small details? The long hair, the separate bedrooms—all
these things were significant. Mr. Davenheim needed time to grow
his beard again, you see! That is why he wanted to be in prison
for a few months.”

“Well,” said Japp, “I’d better get along to Bow Street and see
about getting Mr. Davenheim—or Billy Kellett—identified. It’ll
be a bit of a surprise for him, I expect!”

And with a wave of his hand, he was gone.

Poirot leaned back in his chair and closed his eyes. “A very
satisfactory case, Hastings. Very satisfactory indeed.”

I looked at him, and then at my list of points. I had to admit
that, once again, the little grey cells had been too much for me.

“But tell me one thing, Poirot,” I said. “How did you know it
was him? What was the one thing that made you sure?”

Poirot opened one eye and looked at me with a twinkle.

“_Mon ami_,” he said, “it was the ring. Why should a man like
Billy Kellett, who is a professional thief, be so clumsy as to
pawn a ring that could be so easily traced? It was only when I
realized that he _wanted_ to be caught that the whole thing
became clear.”

He closed his eye again. “And now, if you do not mind, I will
resume my meditations. There is a very interesting problem in
the evening paper about a missing lap-dog...”

I left him to his meditations. After all, when one has just
solved one of the most baffling mysteries of the day, one is
entitled to a little relaxation!

“You say Lowen had a grudge against Mr. Davenheim. What you mean
is that he had once or twice got the better of him. And presumably
those transactions were entered into with the view of benefiting
himself. In any case you do not as a rule bear a grudge against a
man you have got the better of—it is more likely to be the other
way about. Whatever grudge there might have been would have been
on Mr. Davenheim’s side.”

“Well, you can’t deny that he lied about never having left the
study?”

“No. But he may have been frightened. Remember, the missing man’s
clothes had just been discovered in the lake. Of course, as usual,
he would have done better to speak the truth.”

“And the fourth point?”

“I grant you that. If Kellett’s story is true, Lowen is undeniably
implicated. That is what makes the affair so very interesting.”

“Then I did appreciate _one_ vital fact?”

“Perhaps—but you have entirely overlooked the two most important
points, the ones which undoubtedly hold the clue to the whole
matter.”

“And pray, what are they?”

“One, the passion which has grown upon Mr. Davenheim in the last
