few years for buying jewellery. Two, his trip to Buenos Ayres last
autumn.”

“Poirot, you are joking!”

“I am most serious. Ah, sacred thunder, but I hope Japp will not
forget my little commission.”

But the detective, entering into the spirit of the joke, had
remembered it so well that a telegram was handed to Poirot about
eleven o’clock the next day. At his request I opened it and read
it out:

“‘Husband and wife have occupied separate rooms since last winter.’”

“Aha!” cried Poirot. “And now we are in mid June! All is solved!”

I stared at him.

“You have no moneys in the bank of Davenheim and Salmon, _mon
ami_?”

“No,” I said, wondering. “Why?”

“Because I should advise you to withdraw it—before it is too
late.”

“Why, what do you expect?”

“The crash, my friend! The great crash of the house of Davenheim and Salmon. It is coming, and that quickly. Within twenty-four hours, the news will be in all the papers. The firm is insolvent. For years, I suspect, Davenheim has been playing a losing game. The trip to Buenos Ayres—was it not to hide the traces of his speculations? The buying of the jewels—was it not a convenient way of turning his remaining capital into a form easily carried and easily realized? And now, he has vanished. But where? That is the question that Inspector Japp and the clever Miller are asking. They look for him in the lake, in the lime-kiln—they look for his body. But I, Hercule Poirot, I look for the man!”

“I expect a crash, Hastings. A very big crash. The firm of
Davenheim and Salmon is on the verge of bankruptcy. That is why
our friend Mr. Davenheim has vanished. He has prepared for it for
a long time. The jewels—they were not for his wife, they were for
himself, a portable form of capital. The trip to Buenos Ayres—it
was to arrange for a new life under another name. But he is a man
of method, as I said. He does not wish to be a hunted fugitive for
the rest of his days. He has found a much more ingenious way of
‘disappearing’ than by merely taking a boat to South America.”

“I expect the crash, my friend. The great house of Davenheim and Salmon will totter to its fall. It is inevitable. For some time, Mr. Davenheim has been preparing for this—ever since his return from Buenos Ayres, in fact. He has been converting all his available assets into a form that can be easily handled—notes and jewels. The ‘robbery’ was no burglary from the outside, Hastings. It was an internal affair. We have only to wait for the official confirmation.”

“The crash,” said Poirot. “The great house of Davenheim and Salmon will suspend payment within forty-eight hours. It is a mathematical certainty. When a man of Davenheim’s intelligence begins to convert his assets into portable form—jewels and bearer bonds—it is because he knows the end is near. He was preparing for a very different kind of disappearance than the one you imagined, Hastings. The separate bedrooms were the final link in my chain of reasoning. They provided the privacy necessary for a man to—shall we say—alter his appearance at will, without the constant supervision of a wife.”

The crash came two days later. The great banking house of Davenheim and Salmon suspended payment, and the news sent a wave of panic through the City. It was then that Japp reappeared, looking considerably more harassed than when we had last seen him. He dropped into a chair and wiped his forehead with a large handkerchief. “You were right, Monsieur Poirot,” he admitted heavily. “The bank’s gone to glory, and it looks as though Davenheim’s been systematically looting it for years. But the man himself—where is he? We’ve searched every corner of the country, and Miller is still haunting that lake, but not a sign of him! And as for Lowen, we’ve had to let him go for lack of evidence. The case is at a standstill.”

“I expect a big smash in a few days—perhaps sooner. Which reminds
me, we will return the compliment of a _dépêche_ to Japp. A pencil,
I pray you, and a form. _Voilà!_ ‘Advise you to withdraw any money
deposited with firm in question.’ That will intrigue him, the good
Japp! His eyes will open wide—wide! He will not comprehend in the
slightest—until to-morrow, or the next day!”

The next morning, the papers were full of the sensational news of the failure of the great banking house of Davenheim and Salmon. It was a crash such as had not been known for years. Japp arrived shortly after breakfast, looking ten years older. He sank into a chair and stared at Poirot with something like awe. “You were right, Monsieur Poirot,” he groaned. “The whole thing’s a regular muddle. But I don’t see how it helps us to find the man. If he’s bolted with the money, he’s done it right enough, for we’re no nearer finding him than we were three days ago.”

My friend’s prediction proved only too true. Two days later the
headlines of the morning papers were black with the news of the
spectacular failure of the great banking house of Davenheim and
Salmon. The liabilities were enormous, and it was freely
rumoured that the senior partner had decamped with a vast amount
of securities and cash. Japp arrived late that afternoon,
looking haggard and frustrated. He flung himself into a chair
and stared at Poirot with a mixture of respect and irritation.
“You were right, monsieur,” he groaned. “The whole thing’s a
regular smash-up. But it doesn't help us find the man. If
anything, it makes it worse. He’s probably halfway to South
America by now, though how he got out of the country beats me.
And as for Lowen, we’ve had to let him go for lack of evidence,
despite the ring business.”

It was on the following Thursday that the news of the great
financial crash broke. The papers were full of it. Davenheim
and Salmon had suspended payment! The liabilities were
enormous. Consternation reigned in the City. I was still
staring at the headlines when Japp was announced. He looked
hag-ridden and exhausted. “You were right, Monsieur Poirot,”
he said, flinging himself into a chair. “The whole thing’s a
colossal fraud. It’s been going on for years. Davenheim must
have known for months that the end was coming. But what I want
to know is—where’s the money? And where’s Davenheim? He’s the
only one who can tell us. Lowen’s still in custody, but he
swears he knows nothing about the bank’s affairs.”

The events of the next forty-eight hours proved the unerring accuracy of Poirot’s forecast. On Thursday morning the Great City Bank of Davenheim and Salmon suspended payment. The news created a tremendous sensation, and the papers were full of little else but the “Davenheim Smash.” It appeared that the liabilities were enormous, and that for some time the firm had been in a very shaky condition. Japp himself brought us the news on Saturday morning, exactly a week after the disappearance. He looked weary and discouraged, but his eyes lit up as he saw Poirot.

The crash came even sooner than Poirot had predicted. On the following afternoon, the evening papers were full of the sensational news that the great banking firm of Davenheim and Salmon had suspended payment. A run on the bank followed, and it was soon clear that the liabilities were enormous. The disappearance of the senior partner was now seen in a new and more sinister light. Japp fairly burst into our rooms shortly after five o’clock. He looked haggard and worried, and I noticed that he did not even stop to remove his hat. “You were right, Monsieur Poirot,” he cried. “The whole thing’s a blooming swindle! Davenheim’s been cooking the accounts for years. He’s cleared out with every penny he could lay his hands on. But where is he? That’s what I want to know. Where is he?”

I remained sceptical, but the morrow forced me to render tribute
to my friend’s remarkable powers. In every paper was a huge headline
telling of the sensational failure of the Davenheim bank. The
disappearance of the famous financier took on a totally different
aspect in the light of the revelation of the financial affairs of
the bank.

Japp, when he appeared that evening, looked quite a different man.
The jovial, mocking tone of a few days before had vanished, and
he seemed to have aged ten years. His face was drawn and anxious.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, “your fiver’s as good as won.
Miller’s heart-broken, poor chap. It seems that if he’d had his
eyes open, he’d have suspected the state of things months ago.
Davenheim’s been playing a double game for years—using the bank’s
money for his own private speculations, and losing it. He was at
the end of his tether, and saw no way of escape except
disappearing.”

“And you have not found him?”

“No. We’ve found a car he’d hidden in a wood, but that doesn’t
help us much.”

“And Lowen?”

“He’s been released. There’s no evidence against him. His story’s
simple enough. He’d had a hint from a friend that things were
going wrong with the bank, and he’d gone down to see Davenheim to
get some money back he’d invested in those South American shares.
He admits he’d been in the rose-garden, but says he was only
looking for Davenheim.”

“And the ring? What about that?”

“Oh, we’ve found out about that, too. Kellett’s story was true.
Lowen _did_ throw the ring over the hedge. He’d found it in the
rose-garden, and thought it was Davenheim’s. He says he was
frightened and threw it away. Of course, that’s all bunkum. He’d
have given it to the police if he’d been honest.”

“I do not agree with you,” said Poirot. “He would probably have
been accused of having stolen it! But let us come to the point.
I have won my bet?”

“You have! But I’m hanged if I know how you did it!”

“_Mon cher Japp_, it was so very simple. Do you not see?”

“I’m blessed if I do!”

“Let us start with the first point. Mr. Davenheim’s trip to Buenos
Ayres last autumn. Why did he go?”

“On business, I suppose.”

“_Non, non, non!_ To go to prison!”

“To prison!” I cried.

“_Mais oui!_ For some small crime—lifting a watch, perhaps? He
knew the crash was coming, and he wanted to prepare his ‘disappearance.’
He wanted to be able to vanish at a moment’s notice. So he went
to Buenos Ayres, and while there he committed a small crime, and
was sent to prison for three months. That is why he was away so
long. He wanted to see if he could pass unrecognized—and he
succeeded! He came back, grew his hair and beard, and waited for
the crash. When it came, he simply walked out of his house,
changed his clothes in the boathouse, and—became Billy Kellett!”

“Billy Kellett!” I gasped. “But he was in prison!”

“Exactly! That was the beauty of his plan! He knew that if he
were in prison, the police would never look for him there! He
simply committed a small crime, and got himself sent to prison
under an assumed name. He knew that his wife would not recognize
him, as they had occupied separate rooms for some time, and he’d
carefully prepared her for the change in his appearance. It was
really a very clever plan!”

“But how did you know?” asked Japp.

“_Mon ami_, it was the only possible solution. When I heard that
he’d been away in Buenos Ayres for so long, and that he’d
afterwards grown a beard and moustache, I suspected something of
the kind. Then, when I heard about the ring, I was sure of it.
No one but Davenheim would have had that ring! And why should
Kellett have it, unless he _was_ Davenheim? The rest was simple.
I knew that the bank was about to fail, and that Davenheim would
want to disappear. And where better than in prison? It was the
one place where he would be safe from the police!”

“Well, I’m blowed!” said Japp. “You’re a marvel, Monsieur Poirot!”

“_Au contraire_,” said Poirot, “I am only a man of method. And now,
if you will excuse me, I think I will have a little more of that
excellent chocolate!”

“Poirot!” I cried. “You were right!”

Poirot smiled. “But certainly. I saw that the bank was in a very
precarious condition—and I was sure that Mr. Davenheim knew it.
Therefore he prepares for a ‘disappearance’—what you would call
a ‘bolt.’ But as he is a man of method, he does it with a certain
amount of care. He is away from home for several months in the
autumn. Where does he go? To Buenos Ayres? No! He goes into hiding
in some quiet spot in England. He lets his hair and beard grow.
He probably lives as a simple man of the people. No one knows him.
No one suspects. He becomes, as it were, another person. Then,
when the time is ripe, he returns. He resumes his old life, but
he prepares his way for his disappearance. He makes a large haul
of ready money and jewels. He has his new personality all ready
to step into.”

“And Lowen?”

“Was his tool—his ‘cat’s-paw.’ He has him to the house on purpose
to throw suspicion on him. He leaves his clothes by the lake, to
suggest suicide—or murder. He throws his ring over the hedge to
be found by some passer-by, and to be another link in the chain
against Lowen.”

“But Lowen saw him!”

“No, Lowen saw a man who looked like him. He saw a man with a big
moustache and a pointed beard. But it was not Mr. Davenheim.”

“Then who was it?”

“It was the man into whom Mr. Davenheim was about to be
transformed!”

“But where is he now?”

“That is what we have to find out. But I think I can tell you.
Think of the description of the man who pawned the ring. ‘Dark-
complexioned gent, with a big moustache.’ Does that not suggest
someone to you?”

“Billy Kellett!” I cried.

“Exactly. Billy Kellett and Mr. Davenheim are one and the same
person!”

“But Billy Kellett is in prison!”

“Precisely. That is the ‘quiet spot’ in which Mr. Davenheim is
hiding! He has been in prison since Saturday. What safer place
could he find? He knew he would be run in for the assault on the
policeman. He had it all arranged. He knew his description would
be circulated, but who would look for a well-known financier in
a common jailbird?”

“It’s incredible!” I said.

“It is simple—like all great ideas. He has been planning it for
months. He goes to Buenos Ayres—really to some little village in
the country where he lives as Billy Kellett. He gets himself known
to the police. He does a short term of imprisonment. Then he comes
back, and resumes his life as Mr. Davenheim. When the crash is
imminent, he prepares his disappearance. He makes an appointment
with Lowen. He goes out to ‘post his letters.’ He changes his
clothes in the boathouse—where he has previously hidden his Billy
Kellett outfit. He goes to the village, pawns his ring, gets drunk,
and is arrested. He is safe! No one would ever dream of looking
for him in prison!”

“But his wife—would she not have recognized him?”

“That is why I asked if they occupied the same bedroom. They have
not done so since last winter—the time when he was supposed to be
in Buenos Ayres. He has been careful to avoid her as much as
possible. And remember, he has been growing a beard and moustache,
and his hair is long and wavy. A very different appearance from
the clean-shaven Mr. Davenheim of a few years ago.”

“It’s amazing!” I said. “And you solved it all without leaving
your chair!”

“The little grey cells, my friend—the little grey cells! They
never fail one if one uses them with method and precision.”

“But what about Lowen? Why should he have been so ready to fall
into the trap?”

“Because he also had his little games. He was probably trying to
get some information about the bank’s affairs. He was glad of the
chance to be alone in the study. He may even have tried to open
the safe himself—though he would not have succeeded without the
proper tools. And his lying about leaving the study was just the
natural reaction of a man who has something to hide.”

“And the clothes in the lake?”

“A mere ‘blind’—to suggest suicide. But Mr. Davenheim was too
clever for that. He wanted to make sure that the suspicion fell
on Lowen. That is why he was seen by the gardener and the maid.
He wanted it to be known that some one had been in the rose-garden.
It was all very carefully planned.”

“Well,” I said, “you’ve won your bet with Japp. I wonder what he’ll
say when he hears the truth?”

“He will say that I am a very clever man,” said Poirot, with a
twinkle in his eye. “And for once, he will be right!”

The door opened, and Japp himself entered. He looked a little
downcast.

“Well,” he said, “you’ve won, Monsieur Poirot. The Davenheim bank
has gone smash, and Mr. Davenheim is nowhere to be found. Miller’s
fairly at his wits’ end.”

“Be comforted, my friend,” said Poirot. “I can tell you where to
find him.”

Japp stared. “You don’t mean it?”

“But certainly. He is at this moment in—let me see—I think it is
called Bow Street Police Station.”

“What!”

“He is there under the name of Billy Kellett. If you go there and
confront him with his wife, I think you will find that I am right.”

Japp stayed to hear no more. He dashed out of the room, and a few
minutes later we heard his car start.

Poirot turned to me with a smile. “And now, Hastings, let us have
some more of that excellent chocolate. It is a little cold, but no
matter. To the success of the little grey cells!”

I poured out the chocolate, and we toasted the health of M. Hercule
Poirot. It was not the first time, and I felt sure it would not be
the last, that I should have occasion to marvel at the
extraordinary powers of my friend’s mind.

The end.

The same evening Japp burst into our rooms. His face was a picture.
“I’ve come to give in,” he said. “How did you know it?”

“_Eh bien!_” Poirot smiled. “It was obvious! If a man like
Davenheim, a great financier, goes out for a walk and does not
return, what is the most likely reason? That he does not _want_
to return! That he has good reasons for remaining elsewhere. Now,
if he had merely been robbed and murdered, his body would have
been found. If he had intended to ‘disappear’ and start a new life
as another man, he would have prepared for it beforehand. His
growing passion for buying jewels, which are easily portable, and
can be turned into money anywhere in the world, was a significant
fact. The separate bedrooms of himself and his wife, and his long
absence in South America, all point to the same thing—that he had
for some time been leading a double life. But, even then, he would
be recognized. No, he must become some one whom nobody would dream
of connecting with the great banker. And what was the best way
to do that? To go to prison!”

Japp’s jaw dropped. “To prison?” egli si esclamò.

“_Précisément!_ To do that he must commit some small crime. And
what did he do? He became Billy Kellett!”

“Billy Kellett?” I cried. “But—the description!”

“Ah! think of the photograph I studied so carefully! A man who
could, at will, hide his features behind a heavy beard and
moustache, and a long, wavy head of hair. Shave them all off, and
what have you? Billy Kellett, with his short-cropped hair and
clean-shaven face. He knew his bank was on the verge of ruin. He
knew he would be ruined—perhaps arrested—himself. He had already
placed his wife’s jewels and a large sum in notes and bonds in a
safe place. All he wanted was a safe hiding-place for himself
until the first storm should have blown over. And where could he
be more securely hidden than in one of His Majesty’s prisons? He
chose a time when his ‘double’ was at the races, went there,
disposed of his clothes, and assumed those of the ‘human derelict’
in the ditch. Then he pawned his own ring—being careful to be seen
by as many people as possible—and got himself arrested.”

“But Lowen?” I asked. “Why did he try to implicate him?”

“Because he knew that Lowen was coming to see him that evening,
and it was a simple matter to throw the ring over the hedge as
he passed. He knew that the maid would see Lowen coming through
the garden. It was a very clever piece of work. He even managed
to ‘rob’ his own safe, so that there should be no money left for
his creditors! A very clever man—but he forgot the little grey
cells of Hercule Poirot!”

“Well,” said Japp, “I must be off. I’ve a lot to do to-night. But
you’ve won your fiver, Monsieur Poirot!”

“And you, Hastings,” said Poirot, turning to me with a smile, “you
see now that it is not necessary to leave one’s armchair in order
to solve a mystery? One has only to use—the little grey cells!”

“You must admit,” I said as I read the news, “that this does
unquestionably make it more than likely that Davenheim has made
off with the booty. But then, how does that square with Lowen?
You don’t surely believe they were in league together?”

“I do not.”

“Then Lowen must be innocent?”

“If he is, it is the most extraordinary piece of luck that ever
befel a man—his presence in the study, his visit to the
rose-garden—even the fact that he was at the races and on the road
at the same time as Billy Kellett. It is a long chain of
coincidences, Hastings!”

“What can you suggest, then?”

“Wait, and you will see. For once, the good Japp has a clear road
ahead. He will follow it. _Mais oui_, it is a race between the
police and Monsieur Poirot—the consulting specialist.”

The telephone-bell rang. Poirot went to it. After a few minutes’
conversation he came back to me, his face alight with excitement.

“That was Japp. A further development! Billy Kellett has made a
fresh statement. He’s had a talk with the prison chaplain—a very
worthy man, no doubt—and his conscience is pricking him. He now
confesses that he did not find the ring. It was given to him by
a man on the road to Chingside on Saturday afternoon.”

“Lowen!” I cried.

“Wait. Kellett says he had never seen the man before, but he can
give a minute description of him. And that description, Hastings,
does not tallly with Lowen. It is a description of Mr. Davenheim
himself!”

“But Davenheim was at ‘The Cedars’ at that time!”

“Exactly. That is the point. Now, what do you make of it?”

“I don’t know what to make of it,” I said, “unless Kellett is
simply a first-class liar.”

“I do not think so. It is a new and interesting development. And
there is more. Japp has been to ‘The Cedars’ again. He has
interviewed the gardeners and the servants. He’s found out one
thing—Mr. Davenheim’s hair and beard were not his own. He wore a
wig and a false beard!”

“Then,” I cried, “the man who gave the ring to Kellett was
Davenheim—shorn of his wig and beard!”

“_Bravo_, Hastings! You are truly making strides! Now, can you
explain why a man should wish to go about in a wig and a false
beard, which he could dispense with at any moment?”

“I suppose because he was afraid of being recognized.”

“But he would be much more likely to be recognized in a wig and
false beard than without them. No, there is some other reason.”

“Well, what is it?”

“You will know soon. Japp is coming round this evening. He says
he has ‘got his man.’ I wonder who it is?”

I wondered, too. Lowen—Billy Kellett—Mrs. Davenheim—or even Mr.
Davenheim himself! Which of them would Japp have decided was the
guilty person?

When the Inspector arrived he looked extremely pleased with
himself.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, “I’ve come to claim my fiver.
The case is as good as over.”

“You have arrested some one?”

“Yes. Billy Kellett. We’ve got enough evidence to hang him. The
finding of the clothes—the ring—his own confession that he met
Davenheim. It’s a clear case.”

“And what about Lowen?”

“Oh, we’ve let him go. There was no real evidence against him.
As for his being in the rose-garden, he probably _was_ looking at
a rose. At any rate, we can’t prove he wasn’t. No, Kellett’s our
man. He’s a bad lot, and the world will be well rid of him.”

“So you have ‘laid your hand’ on the murderer of Mr. Davenheim?”
said Poirot. “But have you found Mr. Davenheim?”

“We shall find him—in the lime-kiln,” said Japp grimly.

Poirot turned to me. “Hastings, be so kind as to give me that five-pound note I put in the small vase on the mantelpiece.”

I did so. Poirot handed it to Japp.

“I have lost my bet, it seems,” he said. “But I should like to
ask one or more questions. Where did Billy Kellett spend the last
autumn?”

“In gaol,” said Japp promptly. “I told you he did three months
for pocket-picking.”

“And where was the gaol?”

“In London. Maidstone, to be precise.”

“Thank you. And one more thing. You are quite sure that Billy
Kellett is Billy Kellett?”

“Of course he is. We’ve got his finger-prints and his photograph
in our records. There’s no doubt about his identity.”

“Then,” said Poirot, “I have no more to say. The case is indeed
closed.”

I could see that Japp was more than a little puzzled by Poirot’s
manner, but he was too pleased with his own success to dwell on
it. With a few more words of triumph he took his leave.

“Poirot,” I said, as the door closed behind him, “do you really
believe that Billy Kellett is the murderer?”

Poirot did not answer for a moment. He was looking out of the
window. At last he turned.

“Hastings,” he said, “do you remember that I said there were three
classes of disappearances? Well, this is a fourth. It is a
disappearance which is also a reappearance.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean, my friend, that Mr. Davenheim has not only disappeared,
he has also reappeared. And in a most unexpected character!”

“You mean that he is still alive?”

“I am certain of it.”

“Then where is he?”

“He is in a place where no one would ever dream of looking for
him. A place where he is perfectly safe—and where he is provided
with board and lodging at the expense of the country!”

“Poirot!” I cried. “You don’t mean——”

“I mean that Mr. Davenheim _is_ Billy Kellett!”

I sank into a chair, gasping. “But the finger-prints—the photograph!”

“Precisely. Billy Kellett has a police record. Mr. Davenheim
has—none. Therefore, if Mr. Davenheim can successfully personate
Billy Kellett, he is safe. He chose his ‘double’ with care—a man
of his own height and build, who was in prison at the time he
himself was in Buenos Ayres. He must have spent hours in study
and imitation. Then, when the crash was imminent, he prepared his
_mise en scène_. He ‘disappeared’ from ‘The Cedars,’ assumed the
character of Billy Kellett, and committed a small theft which he
knew would lead to a short term of imprisonment. In prison he is
safe from his creditors—and from the police! It was a stroke of
genius!”

“But the ring—the clothes?”

“All part of the plan to throw dust in the eyes of the police. He
wanted them to believe he had been murdered—and he wanted them
to suspect Lowen. But he overreached himself. It was the ring that
first made me suspicious. It was so unlike a man of Lowen’s
intelligence to dispose of it in such a way. And then, the wig and
beard! Why should a man who was planning to disappear wear a wig
and beard—unless he wanted to be able to ‘disappear’ by merely
taking them off? The rest was simple. The separate bedrooms showed
that he had something to conceal—the fact that he was spending his
nights in transforming himself into Billy Kellett! And his trip
to Buenos Ayres gave him the opportunity to study his subject.”

“It’s incredible!” I said.

“It is the triumph of the little grey cells!” said Poirot
complacently. “And now, Hastings, if you will ring the bell, we
will have some more chocolate. I feel that I have earned it.”

Japp arrived to find us both absorbed in the morning’s news.

“_Eh bien!_” cried Poirot, as the detective entered the room. “So
the bank is in a bad way?”

“I should think it is! But what on earth put you on to it, Monsieur
Poirot?”

“A very simple thing. The purchase of all that jewellery for Mrs.
Davenheim. It is the old, old story! When a man’s affairs are
going to the dogs, what does he do? He realizes as much of his
available capital as he can, and invests it in something that can
easily be turned into cash at any moment—jewels, for instance.
These he gives to his wife. Then, if the crash comes, and he
himself is not made a bankrupt, his wife’s property is at his
disposal. But in this case Mr. Davenheim evidently saw that things
were too far gone for that. He must disappear.”

“Yes, but where to?”

“Ah, that is the point! Let us go back. Last autumn he spent in
Buenos Ayres. Why?”

“He had business interests there, I suppose.”

“_C’est possible_—but it is more than possible that he was
providing for the future. He may have been making a little ‘cache’
there, for his old age. But to go to South America, one must have
a passport. To have a passport, one must have a name. It is not
easy to obtain a passport in a false name. It is much easier to
go in one’s own name. Therefore Mr. Davenheim must have gone as
Davenheim. But if he is Davenheim in Buenos Ayres, he cannot be
Davenheim in London. So for some months before he goes, he must
have a double. He must be two people. He must lead a double life.
Do you follow me?”

“Up to a certain point,” I said, “but I don’t see how he could
manage it.”

“It is not so difficult as you think. Suppose that for some time
past Mr. Davenheim has been in the habit of absenting himself from
home for say, a week at a time. He has only to say he is going to
Paris or some such place. He has a small flat in some quiet part
of London. There he lives as—shall we say, Mr. Billy Kellett? He
has his hair cut short, shaves off his moustache and beard, and
wears a different kind of clothes. After a few days he resumes
his character as Mr. Davenheim. When the time comes for him to go
to Buenos Ayres, he goes as Mr. Davenheim. When he returns, he
becomes Mr. Billy Kellett again for a while, and then Mr.
Davenheim. You see?”

“And what about his wife?” I asked.

“That is where my question about the bedrooms comes in. If they
had been in the habit of occupying the same room, she must have
discovered his secret. But if they had separate rooms, it would be
comparatively easy. He has only to say he has a headache and wishes
to be undisturbed. Or he can even go away for a few days, as I
suggested.”

“But the burglary?” said Japp. “Who broke into the safe?”

“Mr. Davenheim himself, of course! Who else would have the
necessary knowledge and opportunity? He had the key, didn’t he?
He probably did it on the Saturday afternoon, before he left the
house. He would then have plenty of time to dispose of the
jewellery and bonds, and to make his way to London as Billy
Kellett.”

“But Billy Kellett is in prison!” I cried.

“Exactly! That is the cleverest part of the whole thing! He knew
the police would be looking for Mr. Davenheim. He didn’t want to
be found. What better place of concealment than a prison? He had
already been in prison as Billy Kellett, so the police would not
be likely to suspect that he was anyone else. He had only to
commit some small crime, and he would be safe for a few months—by
which time the interest in the Davenheim case would have died
down, and he could quietly slip away to South America.”

“But the ring?” asked Japp. “How do you explain the ring?”

“That was a stroke of genius! He knew that if he were arrested
as Billy Kellett, the police would search him. If they found the
ring on him, they would at once identify him as the man who had
robbed Mr. Davenheim—or rather, as having been in possession of
stolen property. So he had to get rid of it. But he didn’t want to
throw it away—it was too valuable. So he ‘pawned’ it! He knew that
the police would find it, and that it would be another link in the
chain against Lowen. For of course he had already planned to throw
the suspicion on Lowen. He had probably been seen by the gardener
going towards the rose-garden—he would see to that! And he knew
the maid would see Lowen. It was all beautifully planned.”

“But why did he throw the ring over the hedge?” I asked.

“He didn’t! That was just a story he made up to account for his
having the ring. He probably had it in his pocket all the time,
and just ‘produced’ it when he was being questioned by the police.
He’s a clever actor, you see!”

“Well,” said Japp, “it’s a most extraordinary story. I must say I
don’t quite see how we’re going to prove it.”

“It will be easy enough,” Poirot replied. “You have only to
compare Billy Kellett’s fingerprints with Mr. Davenheim’s. I think
you will find they are the same. And then there is the matter of
his hair and beard. They will grow again, you know!”

Japp laughed. “Well, Monsieur Poirot, I must hand it to you! You’ve
won your bet. I’ll send you that fiver to-morrow.”

“And I,” said Poirot, “will spend it on a new pair of patent
leather shoes. These are beginning to show signs of wear!”

And he looked down with satisfaction at his tiny, exquisitely
shod feet.

Before we were half-way through breakfast, the door flew open and
Japp rushed in. In his left hand was a paper; in his right was
Poirot’s telegram, which he banged down on the table in front of
my friend.

“How did you know, Monsieur Poirot? How the blazes could you know?”

Poirot looked up. “But it was so simple! Why did Davenheim buy
jewellery? Because he was a man of method—even in his
misfortunes. He knew that the crash was coming. If he had sold
his securities, he would have been at once suspected. But jewellery
is another matter—a safe and portable form of wealth. It was his
reserve fund, which he had been steadily building up for some
time.”

“But the burglary?”

“There was no burglary! It was a very clever piece of work on
Davenheim’s part. He wanted to make it appear that his assets—or
at least part of them—had been stolen, and so to make things look
better for himself. Then, the night he disappeared, he went into
his study, opened his own safe, took out the jewellery, and
rifled the notes and bonds—which, of course, he would have in
readiness. Then he stepped out of the window—the maid saw him,
remember—leaving the window unfastened behind him, so that it
should appear that the burglar had entered that way. He then
hurried to the lime kiln, and disposed of his clothes. And then,
presto!—he vanished!”

“But where did he go to? Where is he now?” Japp’s face was a study.

“Ah! That is where your little friend, the grey cells, comes in.
You have looked for him everywhere, Japp—except in the right
place!”

“And where is that?”

“In prison!”

Japp gasped. “In prison? What for?”

“For the theft of a ring! You see, he had to provide himself with
an alias, and also with a safe hiding-place where he would be
unlikely to be recognized. Now, as I told you, he had spent all
the autumn in Buenos Ayres. He had no doubt made a study of the
character of Billy Kellett, who was there at the same time. He
knew Kellett’s history, and he also knew that he was about his
own size and build. He shaved his beard and moustache, had his
hair cut short, and then, on the Saturday, he went to Entfield
and there met Lowen. He knew Lowen would be coming to see him
that evening. He managed to follow Lowen along the road, and
threw the ring over the hedge—the ring which, of course, he had
taken from his own finger—making sure that Kellett saw him do
it. He then went on to the station, and took the train to London.
In London he pawned the ring, as I have told you, and then,
having previously ‘borrowed’ some of Kellett’s clothes, he got
himself arrested as Billy Kellett, for a small theft, and was
safely lodged in gaol—the last place in the world where any one
would think of looking for the great financier, Mr. Davenheim!”

“But why did he want to go to prison?”

“For two reasons. Firstly, because it was the best possible
hiding-place. Secondly, because it gave him a perfect alibi for
the time when the crash of the bank would come. He would be in
prison, and therefore could not possibly be responsible for
anything that might have happened!”

“But how did you know, Monsieur Poirot?” Japp repeated.

“Ah! That was where the little grey cells came in! There were two
things which struck me as being very significant. First, the
fact that Mr. and Mrs. Davenheim had occupied separate rooms for
the last six months. That suggested to me that Mr. Davenheim
was already leading a double life. Secondly, his trip to Buenos
Ayres. I knew that Billy Kellett had been there at the same time.
The rest was easy!”

“Well, you’ve won your fiver, Monsieur Poirot!” said Japp, as he
prepared to depart. “And I must say, you’ve earned it!”

“_Merci, mon ami_. And you will remember to tell Miller that the
London sparrow is not such a bad little bird after all?”

Japp laughed as he went out of the door.

“_Eh bien_, Hastings,” said Poirot, turning to me. “What do you
think of my little theory?”

“It’s wonderful, Poirot! Simply wonderful!”

“And now,” said Poirot, “we will have another cup of chocolate.
It is very good for the grey cells!”

Poirot smiled at him. “A man of method, _mon ami_. You say that
Davenheim’s disappearance was totally unexpected. But no! Not to
a man of method. He had known for months that his bank was on the
verge of a crash, and that the only thing which could save it was
a large sum of money. He has accordingly, with great forethought,
prepared for his disappearance.”

“Prepared?”

“But certainly! He has been buying jewels for years—portable
property, you understand. He has been out of England for months
together, and no one has questioned his absence. He has even gone
so far as to have a separate bedroom from his wife—so that he could
come and go at any hour of the night without her being any the
wiser.”

“But how could he possibly have disappeared so completely?” Japp
demanded.

“By being another person! By the simple device of leading a double
life for a year or two—and then, when the crash came, of simply
ceasing to be one of those two persons!”

“But how?” Japp asked, his eyes growing wider and wider.

Poirot turned to me. “Hastings, my friend, have you the paper
containing the description of the missing man?”

I found the sheet and handed it to him.

“Read it out, I pray you.”

“‘Long, wavy hair; full moustache and pointed beard; bushy
eyebrows; dark eyes; hair and beard turning grey; aged about fifty;
height five foot ten; well built.’”

“And now,” said Poirot, “will you read the description of the man
who was arrested for pawning the ring—Billy Kellett?”

I found the paragraph in the evening paper of two days ago.

“‘Billy Kellett, an old offender, well known to the police, was
arrested last Saturday for pawning a valuable diamond ring. Kellett
is about five foot ten in height, with dark eyes and hair, and
is clean-shaven. He is about fifty years of age.’”

Japp gave a long whistle. “You mean Billy Kellett is Davenheim?”

“But certainly! It is the most natural thing in the world! He
had been preparing the part for months. He had a room in some
back-street of London, where he went from time to time as Billy
Kellett. He had even been in prison as Billy Kellett, as a further
precaution. On Saturday, when he left the house to post his
letters, he simply went to his hiding-place, shaved off his beard
and moustache, and cropped his hair, and—_voilà!_ He was Billy
Kellett! Then he pawned the ring to make sure of being arrested.
He knew that in prison he would be perfectly safe until the hue
and cry was over!”

“But how about Lowen?” I cried. “And the ring Kellett says he saw
him throw over the hedge?”

“Lowen was a very necessary part of the plot. He was the scapegoat!
Davenheim, in his character of Kellett, must have some one to lay
the blame on. He knew Lowen was coming to the house that evening.
He probably saw him from the road, and deliberately threw the ring
over the hedge so that Kellett—the _real_ Kellett, if there were
one—could find it. But there was no real Kellett! It was Davenheim
himself! He wanted to make sure that the police would suspect
Lowen—and he knew that his own description of Lowen would be
sufficient to link him with the crime.”

“But the clothes in the lake?” Japp asked. “And the safe?”

“Davenheim himself robbed his own safe! He wanted the contents for
his new life. He then put his clothes in the lake to make it appear
that he had been murdered. He had, of course, a second suit of
clothes ready for Billy Kellett. He probably threw the suit into
the lake from the boathouse—hence my interest in it!”

“And the ring?” I asked. “Why did he pawn it?”

“To get himself arrested, of course! He knew that as Billy Kellett
he would be safe in a police-cell, with a perfectly good alibi for
the time the bank failed! It was a stroke of genius!”

Japp shook his head. “Well, you’ve beaten us again, Monsieur
Poirot. I’ll go and have a word with Billy Kellett—or Mr. Davenheim,
as I suppose I should call him now!”

As the door closed behind him, Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“_Eh bien_, Hastings! You see that the little grey cells have not
failed me after all! It was a pretty little problem—and one which
required only a little thought and—method!”

I could only agree. Once again, Poirot had proved that the mind
is indeed superior to the senses.

“_Ah, mon ami_,” said Poirot, with a smile. “I knew that the smash
must come soon. If it had not been imminent, Mr. Davenheim would
not have disappeared. The two go together.”

“But the burglary?”

“That also fits in. Mr. Davenheim must have known that his house
of cards was falling. He would want to provide for his own future.
A man like Davenheim would never allow himself to be a pauper. He
rifled his own safe, and disposed of the contents—partly in cash,
partly in jewellery. When the crash came, he could then begin life
under a new name—and with his wife’s jewels!”

“Then you think he’s _not_ dead?”

“Dead? Certainly not! Why should he be? He has merely disappeared.
Which brings us back to our original point. He is a man of method.
He has planned his disappearance for months, even for years.”

“And what of Lowen?”

“A very convenient scapegoat! Mr. Davenheim has always had his
eye on him. It was a master-stroke to make it appear that Lowen
had robbed and possibly murdered him. Hence the appointment, and
hence the cleverness of throwing the ring over the hedge where a
man of Kellett’s type was likely to find it. Lowen’s story would
never be believed against the word of a man like Kellett.”

“But the clothes in the lake?” I cried.

“Aha, that brings us to the core of the mystery! How to make a
man disappear, so that he cannot be found even if his description
is in every newspaper in the land? There is only one way—for him
to be already in a place where no one would dream of looking for
him.”

“And that is?”

“_En prison_,” said Poirot. “In a common jail!”

“In prison?”

“Listen, my friends! Last autumn Mr. Davenheim goes to Buenos
Ayres. He is away for several months. Does he really go to Buenos
Ayres? I think not. I think he goes to some small town, and there,
under the name of Billy Kellett, he commits a small robbery and
is sentenced to three months’ imprisonment. He wants to see if the
disguise he has prepared is a good one, and if he can successfully
pass as a man of Kellett’s type. He finds that he can. He comes
back to England, and resumes his own personality. But he prepares
for the future. He lets his hair and beard grow. He makes his wife
occupy a separate bedroom, so that he can slip out at night and
resume his Billy Kellett character when he chooses. Then, when the
time is ripe, he stages the disappearance. He walks out of his
house, changes his clothes in the boathouse, and sinks them in the
lake. Then, as Billy Kellett, he ‘finds’ the ring he has himself
thrown over the hedge, pawns it, gets ‘gloriously drunk,’ and is
promptly arrested. He is safe in a police cell while the whole of
England is looking for Mr. Davenheim!”

“But the man who threw the ring?” Japp cried. “Kellett saw him!”

“No, _mon ami_, he _said_ he saw him. It was necessary to implicate
Lowen. Who would believe the word of a man like Kellett? But it
would be different if Kellett’s story was ‘confirmed’ by the maid’s
evidence that she saw Lowen in the rose-garden. It was all part of
the plan.”

“Good Lord!” said Japp. “And the safe?”

“He robbed it himself, before he left the house. He had the tools
hidden in the boathouse. It was a simple matter.”

“And where is he now?” I asked.

“In a police cell, as I said,” replied Poirot. “Under the name of
Billy Kellett. If you go to the police station where he is
detained, you will find that he is Mr. Davenheim—without his
beard and with his hair cropped!”

“I’ll go at once!” cried Japp, and rushed from the room.

Poirot turned to me with a smile. “You see, Hastings, the value
of the little grey cells? One must seek the truth within—not
without!”

I could only marvel at his extraordinary genius. Once again,
Hercule Poirot had proved that he was indeed the greatest detective
in the world.

Poirot smiled. “But did I not tell you, my friend, that the human
brain—the little grey cells—must solve the problem? You would not
believe me. You said to yourself: ‘Poor old Poirot—he is getting
old! He is what you call “doddering”!’ But no, I was not doddering!
I was thinking—and with the results you see.”

Japp wiped his forehead. “You were right enough—though what put
you on to it I can’t imagine. It’s a pretty black business for
Davenheim. He’s been a systematic robber of the public for years.
No wonder he’s disappeared! But where? That’s what we want to
know.”

Poirot did not answer. He was busy in the consumption of a very
large and very sweet-looking _brioche_, and appeared absorbed in
his occupation.

“Where did he go?” Japp repeated. “The week is nearly up, and we’re
not a step nearer finding him.”

Poirot finished his _brioche_, and wiped his mouth with his napkin.

“Let us review the case,” he began. “Mr. Davenheim walked out of
his house on Saturday afternoon, and vanished. No one saw him pass
through the village, or at the station. In his study his safe was
rifled of a large sum in notes and bonds, and of a quantity of
valuable jewellery. Then we have the discovery of his clothes in
the lake, and of his ring in the hands of a common thief who says
he saw a man answering to Lowen’s description throw it away.
Lowen, too, is seen coming from the direction of the study-window
at an hour which would give him time to have rifled the safe.”

“Exactly,” said Japp.

“_Bien_,” said Poirot. “And now let us look at it from another
point of view. Mr. Davenheim has been preparing for this smash for
some time. He has been steadily converting his assets into cash.
This cash he has been stowing away—where? Not in his bank,
certainly! No, he has been investing it in jewellery—jewellery
which can be easily concealed and as easily turned into money
anywhere in the world. Next we have his trip to Buenos Ayres. He
spends all last autumn there. Why? We do not know. But when he
returns, what do we find? A change in the habits of the household.
He and his wife no longer occupy the same room. He has a reason
for this, but it is not the reason he gives his wife. What is it?”

“You tell us!” said Japp.

“I will. He wants to be able to be absent from his room for part
of the night—perhaps for the whole of it—without her knowledge.
He is busy. He is very busy—at what? At his transformation!”

“His transformation?” I cried.

“But certainly. Think of his appearance as shown in the photograph
in the _Daily Megaphone_. The long hair, the full moustache and
pointed beard, the bushy eyebrows. How easy to alter! A little
clipping, a little shaving—and he is another man!”

“But why should he want to alter his appearance?” I asked.

“To become someone else, of course. Someone who would not be
suspected.”

“But who?”

“Is there no one in the case who has been in prison, and whose
description would be known to the police?”

“Billy Kellett!” I cried.

“_Précisément_,” said Poirot. “Billy Kellett! Billy Kellett, who
had done three months last autumn—in London? No, in Buenos Ayres!
He had planned it all. He was to disappear as Davenheim, and
reappear as Kellett. He would have a perfect alibi—he would be
in prison! The clothes in the lake, the ring—all were intended to
throw suspicion on Lowen. The burglary—Davenheim committed it
himself, of course! He wanted the money and the jewels for his
future life. The maid who saw Lowen? Davenheim had seen to that,
too. He had probably dressed up as Lowen—it would be easy enough
with a false moustache—and walked past the window just at the
right moment.”

“But the ring?” asked Japp. “Why should he throw that away?”

“Because he could not wear it as Billy Kellett, and it would have
been dangerous to keep it. So he ‘threw it away’ where it would be
found—and where it would help to incriminate Lowen.”

“And where is he now?” I asked.

“In gaol,” said Poirot calmly. “In gaol as Billy Kellett. You have
only to go to Bow Street and you will find him there. He was
arrested on Saturday night, you remember, for being drunk and
assaulting the police.”

Japp stared at him for a moment, and then dashed out of the room.
He returned an hour later, looking a different man.

“You’ve won your fiver, Monsieur Poirot!” he cried. “It’s he, right
enough! He’d shaved off his beard and moustache, and had his hair
cropped, but the fingerprints settled it. He’s Davenheim all
right!”

“It was the eyebrows that first put me on the track,” said Poirot
complacently. “You can’t change your eyebrows—not easily. And his
were very marked. Then the trip to Buenos Ayres—it was so
unnecessary. Why should a man like Davenheim go there himself?
Unless he had some very special reason. And what could that reason
be but to establish an identity for himself as Billy Kellett?”

“And the clothes in the lake?” I asked.

“A master touch, that! It made everyone think of murder—and of
Lowen. Everything was planned to point to Lowen. If it hadn’t been
for my ‘little grey cells,’ Lowen would probably have been hanged!”

“It’s a wonderful case,” said Japp admiringly. “I don’t know how
you do it, Monsieur Poirot.”

“I do it,” said Poirot, “by sitting in my chair and thinking. It
is the only way.”

He turned to me with a smile. “You see, Hastings, the ‘London
sparrow’ was not so clever as he thought himself! He saw the
crumbs—but he did not see the trap!”

We all laughed, and Japp rose to go.

“Well, I must be off,” he said. “I’ve got a lot to do. But I’ll
see you get your fiver, Monsieur Poirot.”

“_Merci, mon ami_,” said Poirot. “It will go towards the purchase
of a new pair of patent leather shoes. My present ones are
beginning to show signs of wear!”

And with a wave of his hand, the little man returned to his
beloved task of building a card house.

Poirot smiled. “I did not know. I guessed—but with the help of my
little grey cells!”

“Well, you’ve hit the bull’s-eye this time. The bank’s smashed to
atoms. Not a penny in the pound. Davenheim must have known for
the last two years. He’s been cooking the accounts for some time.”

“Exactly. And it was for that reason he went to Buenos Ayres—to
see how he could best arrange to salt away some of his ill-gotten
gains.”

“But the burglary, and his disappearance?”

“All a plant, _mon ami_. As he saw the smash was inevitable, he
prepared his little scheme. He meant to disappear and start life
again in another country under another name. But he meant to
disappear with a well-filled purse. The safe was broken into by
himself, and the contents are at this moment probably safely
hidden.”

“And the clothes?”

“Also a plant. He had to make it appear that he was dead—or at
any rate that he had been made away with. He left the house, went
to the boathouse, changed his clothes for those of a tramp, and
departed. He probably threw his own clothes into the lake to make
believe he was drowned.”

“But Billy Kellett’s story? How do you account for that? And
Lowen?”

“That is the most interesting part of the whole affair. Billy
Kellett’s story is true—and yet it is false!”

“How?”

“Because the man who threw the ring was not Lowen.”

“Then who was it?”

“Mr. Davenheim himself!”

“But Billy Kellett’s description of Lowen—it was identical!”

“_Précisément_! That is what I find so interesting! It was a clever
plot. Mr. Davenheim had long had his eye on Lowen as a scapegoat.
He knew he was coming to see him that evening. He went to the gate
at the time Lowen was expected, and then, as he had previously
arranged, he threw the ring over the hedge. Then he went on to
the village and caught a train.”

“But what about the description?” Japp persisted.

“It was not a description of Lowen. It was a description of Mr.
Davenheim as he appeared at that moment—minus his beard and
moustache, and with his hair cropped short!”

“You mean—?”

“I mean that for some months—since his wife and he had occupied
separate rooms, in fact—Mr. Davenheim had been leading a double
life. For some time past he had been known to the police as—who
do you think?”

“Not—?”

“Yes! Billy Kellett!”

Japp’s jaw dropped. “But Billy Kellett was in prison!”

“Exactly! That was the cleverest part of the whole thing! Mr.
Davenheim, in the character of Billy Kellett, committed a small
theft, was arrested, and sentenced to three months’ imprisonment.
In this way he had a perfect alibi for the time of the bank’s
smash and his own disappearance. No one would dream of looking
for the great financier in a common jail! He had only to wait
until his sentence was up, and then he could go off to South
America with his gains.”

“But the description?” I asked. “Billy Kellett didn’t look like
Davenheim.”

“Of course not! He had shaved off his beard and moustache, and
his hair was cropped. Any man can look like another if he tries.
Davenheim had carefully studied Lowen’s appearance, and when he
threw the ring he made himself up to look as much like him as
possible. The dark complexion was easy—a little stain did that.
The rest was just a matter of a few minutes’ work.”

“But how did you know about the separate rooms?” asked Japp.

“Because if he were leading a double life he must have some place
where he could change his appearance without being seen. His own
bedroom was the obvious place, but that would only be possible
if his wife did not share it with him. Then his frequent absences
from home, and his trip to Buenos Ayres, all fitted in.”

“It’s a most extraordinary story,” said Japp. “But I believe you’re
right, Monsieur Poirot. I’ll go and have another look at our
friend Billy Kellett.”

“Do,” said Poirot. “And don’t forget that he’s probably got a
large sum of money hidden away somewhere—possibly in that lime
kiln you were so interested in!”

Japp hurried away. Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“_Eh bien_, Hastings, what do you think of my little grey cells
now?”

“I think they’re wonderful, Poirot. But there’s one thing I don’t
understand. Why did he throw the ring over the hedge?”

“To draw attention to the fact that Lowen was in the neighbourhood.
He wanted to make sure that the police would suspect him. It was
a little bit of over-elaboration that nearly ruined him—as so
often happens with the criminal mind!”

“And the clothes in the lake?”

“Another piece of over-elaboration. He wanted to make doubly sure!
But he forgot one thing—that even a great financier cannot be in
two places at once!”

Poirot leaned back in his chair and closed his eyes. “And now,
Hastings, I think I will have a little nap. All this thinking is
very exhausting!”

I left him to his reflections. Truly, as he had said, the little
grey cells were not to be despised. In one week he had solved a
mystery that had baffled the whole of Scotland Yard—and that
without even leaving his armchair! It was a triumph of the
intellect—the pure, cold logic of the mind over the clumsy,
groping methods of the police. As I went out of the room, I could
not help feeling a certain pride in my friend. He might be
eccentric, he might be vain, but there was no doubt about it—he
was a genius!

The end.

Poirot smiled placidly at him. “Ah, _mon ami_, after your wire, it
was a certainty! From the commencement, see you, it struck me that
the safe burglary was somewhat remarkable. Jewels, ready money,
bearer bonds—all so conveniently arranged for—whom? Well, the good
Monsieur Davenheim was of those who ‘look after Number One’ as your
saying goes! It seemed almost certain that it was arranged
for—himself! Then his passion of late years for buying jewellery!
How simple! The funds he embezzled, he converted into jewels, very
likely replacing them in turn with paste duplicates, and so he put
away in a safe place, under another name, a considerable fortune
to be enjoyed all in good time when every one has been thrown off
the track. His arrangements completed, he makes an appointment with
Mr. Lowen (who has been imprudent enough in the past to cross the
great man once or twice), drills a hole in the safe, leaves orders
that the guest is to be shown into the study, and walks out of the
house—where?” Poirot stopped, and stretched out his hand for
another boiled egg. He frowned. “It is really insupportable,” he
murmured, “that every hen lays an egg of a different size! What
symmetry can there be on the breakfast table? At least they should
sort them in dozens at the shop!”

“Never mind the eggs,” said Japp impatiently. “Let ’em lay ’em
square if they like. Tell us where our customer went to when he
left The Cedars—that is, if you know!”

“_Eh bien_, he went to his hiding-place. Ah, this Monsieur
Davenheim, there may be some malformation in his grey cells, but
they are of the first quality!”

“Do you know where he is hiding?”

“Certainly! It is most ingenious.”

“For the Lord’s sake, tell us, then!”

“_Mais oui_,” said Poirot. “Where is the one place where no one
would ever think of looking for a missing millionaire? In a
common gaol! You told me yourself, Japp, that Billy Kellett was
known to the police—that he had served a short sentence last
autumn. And where was Mr. Davenheim last autumn? In Buenos Ayres!
At least, so he told his wife and his partner. In reality, he
was serving that sentence in an English prison, carefully
rehearsing the character of Billy Kellett, the human derelict!”

“He is in a place where he is perfectly safe from all your
inquiries—where he is well-fed and has his lodging provided for
him free of charge—and where, I may add, it would never occur to
the police to look for a missing man. In short, my friend,
Mr. Davenheim is at this moment in a police cell, having
secured for himself the most perfect of alibis by the simple
expedient of getting himself arrested!”

“Wait a moment,” said Poirot, checking his friend’s impetuosity. “Let us use our little grey cells. Where would a man be most safe from police interference? Surely, in a place where the police themselves have put him! You told me, Japp, that Billy Kellett was already known to the police—that he had done three months last autumn. And where was Mr. Davenheim last autumn? In Buenos Ayres, you said? No, my friend, he was in gaol, under the name of Billy Kellett, practicing for the part he was to play later!”

Poirot smiled. “But you have told me yourself, Japp! Or rather, you have seen him and did not recognize him. Consider the description of Billy Kellett. A man known to the police—yes, for he took care to be ‘known’ last autumn when he spent three months in gaol. It was then, during his ‘trip to Buenos Ayres,’ that Mr. Davenheim created the character of Billy Kellett, the petty thief. He practiced the role, established the record, and then returned to his life as a financier, waiting for the inevitable crash of his bank. When the time came, he simply stepped into his second identity.”

“_Mais oui_, my friend. Consider the man you have in your cells at
this very moment—Billy Kellett. You told me yourself that he
had been ‘in’ last autumn for three months. That was while
Mr. Davenheim was supposed to be in Buenos Ayres! It was then
that he created the character of Billy Kellett. He lived a
double life, dividing his time between the financier and the
wastrel. He grew his hair and beard as Davenheim, so that when
the time came for the bank to fail, he had only to shave them
off and—_voilà_!—he was Billy Kellett once more, a man already
known to the police, and the last person any one would suspect
of being the missing millionaire!”

Poirot gently collected every fragment of shell from his plate,
placed them in the egg-cup, and reversed the empty egg-shell on
top of them. This little operation concluded, he smiled on the neat
effect, and then beamed affectionately on us both.

“Come, my friends, you are men of intelligence. Ask yourselves the
question which I asked myself. ‘If I were this man, where should
_I_ hide?’ Hastings, what do you say?”

“Well,” I said, “I suppose I should make for a seaport, or a small
country cottage in some out-of-the-way spot.”

“And you, Japp?”

“Oh, I should put on a disguise and go to a big hotel.”

“Ah!” cried Poirot. “A big hotel! To hide in a big hotel, one must
first have a name and a past—it is a difficult matter. To go to
a seaport, one must be able to escape the lynx-eyes of the police.
A country cottage? It is a mark for all the gossips of the village!”

“Well, then, where _did_ he go?”

“_Mon ami_, he went to—prison!”

Japp jumped from his chair. “_Prison!_”

“Precisely. He committed a small crime—say, an assault on a
policeman—for which he was certain to get a short term of
imprisonment. And he committed it on the Saturday evening, at
London, where his identity was not known, and where he would be
sent to a London prison. And that is why I asked you to find out
whether he and his wife occupied the same bedroom! If they did,
his task would have been an almost impossible one. As it was, he
had only to slip out of the house, take the train to London, and
be run in that very evening.”

“But,” I cried, “how could he hope to escape recognition?”

“Recognition? Why, my friend, look at his photograph! It is a mass
of hair—luxuriant hair, a thick beard and moustache, and bushy
eyebrows! Take all those away, and what have you left? A totally
different man! A man with a clean-shaven face and short-cropped
hair. No one would dream of connecting the two!”

“But how did he get rid of them?”

“He did not! He never had them! His hair, his beard, his moustache,
his eyebrows—they were all _false_! He had worn them for years!
Ever since his trip to Buenos Ayres—when he doubtless stayed a
month or two longer than was necessary, in order to grow his own
hair and beard to the required length! Then he had his photograph
taken, and came home, wearing his false face, as it were. He knew
that the time would come when he would want to disappear, and he
prepared for it accordingly.”

“But why did he leave his clothes in the lake?”

“Because he had to have a different suit of clothes to be arrested
in! He could not be arrested in his own clothes without being
recognized at once. So he went to the boathouse, changed into a
suit of ‘shabby’ clothes he had previously hidden there, put his
own into the lake (to suggest suicide), and then made his way to
London.”

“And the ring?”

“_Eh bien_, he threw it over the hedge—not to get rid of it, but
to implicate Lowen! He knew that Lowen would be in the study, and
that it would be known that he had been there. By throwing the
ring where he did, he hoped to bring the crime home to him.”

“Then,” said Japp, “the man Billy Kellett is—”

“_Is_ Mr. Davenheim!” said Poirot. “I knew it from the description
Kellett gave of the man who threw the ring. It was a description
of—Lowen! Now, how could a man who had never seen Lowen (and
remember they had never met) give such an accurate description of
him? Only by being Davenheim himself!”

“But why did he pawn the ring?” I asked.

“Because he had no money! He had to have money to get drunk on—and
he had to get drunk in order to be arrested! It was a masterpiece,
my friends, a masterpiece!”

“And now,” said Japp, reaching for his hat, “I’m off to Bow Street
to have a look at our friend Billy Kellett. If he’s Davenheim,
I’ll eat my hat!”

“You will find,” said Poirot, “that he has a small scar over his
right eye. It is not in the photograph, but it is a mark that Mr.
Davenheim had.”

“I’ll look for it,” said Japp, and he hurried out of the room.

Poirot turned to me with a smile. “Well, Hastings, what do you
think of my little grey cells now?”

I could only murmur my admiration.

“It was the hair that first put me on the track,” said Poirot
meditatively. “Why should a man who was going to disappear leave
his clothes behind, but not his hair? And then there was the
boathouse—a most convenient place for a change of costume. And
lastly, there was the fact that he was a man of method! A man of
method, Hastings, always provides for every contingency!”

He sighed. “And now, if you have finished your breakfast, we might
go for a little walk. It is a beautiful morning.”

I rose and followed him. As we went down the stairs, I said:

“It’s a pity you can’t claim that fiver from Japp, Poirot. You’ve
solved the case within the week, but you haven’t exactly ‘laid
your hand’ on Mr. Davenheim!”

Poirot stopped and looked at me. “My friend,” he said, “you are
sometimes very dense! Where is Billy Kellett at this moment?”

“In prison.”

“And where is Mr. Davenheim?”

“In prison also—according to you.”

“_Precisément!_ Then if Japp lays his hand on Billy Kellett, is
he not also laying his hand on Mr. Davenheim? The fiver is mine,
Hastings—the fiver is mine!”

He chuckled, and we walked out into the sunshine.

“Well,” I said, “I should go to some out-of-the-way village where
no one would know me, or better still, bury myself in the heart
of London. I should change my appearance, of course.”

“_Mon Dieu!_” Poirot’s eyes were raised to heaven. “Is it possible
to be so lacking in imagination? A well-known man like Mr.
Davenheim—is it likely that he should not be recognized? London—a
village—it is the same thing! To-day, in this country, you cannot
be buried and remain so! No, no, _mon ami_, think again!”

Japp looked as if he would like to suggest something, but was too
frightened.

“Think, think!” Poirot beat his fist on the table. “How would you
get away? Every port watched—the wireless—the newspapers with your
photograph—all the world looking for you? How can you hope to
escape? Why, only by becoming some one who is _already_ in the
keeping of the police! No one looks for a man who is already
found!”

“In the keeping of the police?” Japp stared. “You don’t mean to
say—?”

“But I do! Who is it that is in the hands of the police at this
moment? Billy Kellett! Billy Kellett, who was ‘run in’ on Saturday
evening for being drunk and disorderly, and for having a stolen
ring in his possession! What could be more simple?”

“Billy Kellett? But he’s a well-known crook!”

“Is he? Have you ever seen him? No, Miller saw him. And Miller
did not know Mr. Davenheim. Japp saw him—but he did not know Mr.
Davenheim either, except by his photograph. And what is a
photograph? A matter of a beard, a moustache, and bushy eyebrows!
Shave them off, and what have you? A different man! If you do not
believe me, go to the prison and ask Billy Kellett to—_wash his
face!_”

Japp gave a long, low whistle. “By Jove!” he said. “If you’re
right—!”

“Of course I am right! Why did he and his wife occupy separate
rooms since last winter? To allow him to practice the ‘disappearing
trick’—to grow a beard and moustache, and then to shave them off,
so that no one should see the change. That is why I asked that
question. It was the one thing needed to make my theory certain.
Billy Kellett—last autumn—three months’ imprisonment. Mr.
Davenheim—last autumn—three months in Buenos Ayres. He was
preparing his ‘_alibi_.’ The South American trip was a blind. He
never left the country. He spent those three months in gaol—as
Billy Kellett! He knew that as Billy Kellett he would be safe from
the police! When the time came, he had only to repeat the
performance. He goes out to post his letters—in reality he goes
to a prearranged hiding-place, where he has his ‘Billy Kellett’
clothes and his ‘make-up’ ready. He shaves, changes his clothes,
and leaves the Davenheim ones in the lake to be found. Then he
throws his ring over the hedge to be ‘found’ by himself later,
and goes on to the village. There he acts the ‘drunk and
disorderly,’ is ‘run in’—and is safe! No one will ever look for
Mr. Davenheim in the person of Billy Kellett!”

“But why did he throw the ring away?” I asked.

“_Mon Dieu!_” Poirot’s eyes were again raised to heaven. “To
identify himself, of course! He wanted to be sure that the police
would connect Billy Kellett with the Davenheim case. Otherwise,
they might have just let him go after a day or two, and he would
have had to start all over again! This way, he was ‘found’ at once,
and his safety was assured!”

Japp rose. “I’m off!” he said. “If this is true—!”

“It is true,” said Poirot. “And don’t forget that you owe me a
fiver!”

Japp’s reply was lost as he dashed out of the room.

Poirot turned to me with a smile. “Well, Hastings, what do you
think of my ‘little grey cells’ now?”

“It’s wonderful!” I said. “Absolutely wonderful! But what about
Lowen? Was he in it?”

“Lowen? Not he! He was only the ‘scapegoat’—the person on whom
suspicion was to be thrown. A very clever piece of work, _mon
ami_, very clever indeed!”

I could only agree. It was indeed a most remarkable case, and
Poirot’s solution of it was even more remarkable.

“And now,” said Poirot, “let us have some more coffee. It is
getting cold.”

I poured him out a cup, and we sat in silence for a few minutes.
Suddenly Poirot looked up.

“You know, Hastings,” he said, “there is one thing that still
worries me.”

“What is that?” I asked.

“The size of those eggs,” said Poirot with a sigh. “It is really
most distressing!”

“I’m afraid I’m not as clever as you, Poirot. I haven’t the
slightest idea.”

“And you, Japp?”

“I have no doubt he’s in London, or possibly in Paris, by this
time. But where, I can’t imagine.”

“No,” said Poirot, shaking his head. “You have both failed.
Consider. In every way, this man’s appearance—well-known and
conspicuous—must be against him. He cannot change his face. He
must, therefore, choose a hiding-place where his face is already
known—and where, consequently, no one will look for him. Where,
then, is that?”

“I give it up,” I said.

“I also,” said Japp.

“Think, my friends! Think!”

We both shook our heads.

“There is only one such place,” said Poirot. “_In prison._”

“In prison?” we both cried.

“But certainly! Since last Saturday, Mr. Davenheim has been in
custody. Under what name? Why, the name of the man who pawned the
ring! _Billy Kellett_!”

“Billy Kellett!” Japp’s eyes were starting out of his head. “But
Billy Kellett is a well-known crook!”

“Precisely. That is the stroke of genius! To make use of the
identity of a man who is already known to the police, and who has
recently been in prison. No one would dream of looking for a
missing millionaire in the person of a common thief!”

“But the difference in their appearance?” I cried. “The long hair,
the beard, the moustache?”

“_Eh bien!_ As for the hair, the prison authorities would attend
to that! And for the rest—_un rasoir_, and the thing is done!”

“But how did he manage it?”

“Ah, that is where Buenos Ayres comes in! Last autumn, he did not
go to South America. He went, I suspect, to some quiet retreat,
and there he ‘created’ Billy Kellett! He probably had some
shady transactions with the real Billy Kellett in the past, and
when the man died, or disappeared, he stepped into his shoes. He
would go to the race-meetings, get himself known to the police,
and finally do his ‘three months’ for a small theft. Then, when
his plans were mature, he staged his own ‘disappearance.’ The
clothes he left in the lake were his own. He then assumed his Billy
Kellett personality, and ‘found’ the ring which he himself had
thrown over the hedge! He knew that as Billy Kellett he would be
arrested, and his ‘disappearance’ would remain an unsolved
mystery—while he himself would be safely hidden in a police-cell!”

“It’s incredible!” gasped Japp. “But if it’s true—”

“It is true, my friend. You will find that ‘Billy Kellett’s’
fingerprints are those of the great Mr. Davenheim!”

“I’ll go at once!” cried Japp, and he rushed from the room.

Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“You see, Hastings? The little grey cells! They never fail one!
And now, if you have finished your breakfast, we might perhaps go
for a little stroll. The morning is too beautiful to remain
indoors.”

“I should take the boat for South America,” I said.

“No, no! Too simple, too obvious! He has been there before, and
that is why he would _not_ go there again!”

“Well, what about you, Japp?”

“I should hide in London—the most lonely place in the world.”

“Wait, my friends! Let us return to the facts. A man—an elderly
man, who has lived a luxurious and pampered life—is suddenly to
disappear. He is to leave his wife, his servants, his home, and
all the ease and comfort that he has been used to. For three months
previous to the ‘disappearance’ he has been growing his hair and
his beard. Why? To disguise himself? Not so! For he will be less
likely to be recognized if he is _clean-shaven_!”

“By Jove, that’s true!” I cried.

“But if he wished to remain recognized as some one else?”

“I don’t follow,” said Japp.

“I was about to tell you. This man, then, is to lead a life of
hardship—comparative hardship. He is to be at a moment’s notice
under the thumb of the police—unable to leave the country—his
movements carefully noted. He is to have no money—hardly enough
to buy himself a meal. He is to sleep, perhaps, in a police-cell,
on a hard wooden bed. Is it likely, I ask you, that a man of his
habits would do such a thing—unless he had no choice? And why did
he and his wife occupy separate rooms? Ah, that was the most
telling fact of all! If he were to be away from home all night,
it would be noticed—unless he had an excuse! But if he were to be
away _altogether_—ah, that is a different matter!”

“But he was seen to leave the house at half-past five!” I cried.

“Exactly. And at six o’clock—not ten minutes after Lowen arrived—a
man is seen by one of the gardeners to go round to the side of the
house. He is seen, mind you—not recognized! And he goes toward
the rose-garden. Why? Because the study window opens on to it! He
enters the study, rifled the safe, and—what next? Why, he walks
out again, of course, but not by the window! He goes out by the
_front door_, after having first rung the bell to say he can wait
no longer! For, my friends, the man who was shown into the study
as Lowen—and the man who left it an hour later—was _not_ Lowen
at all! It was Mr. Davenheim himself!”

“Then who was the man who was shown into the study at a quarter past
six?” asked Japp, bewildered.

“There was no such man! Mrs. Davenheim’s evidence on that point is
not to be relied on—she is, as you said, a ‘nonentity,’ and
besides, she had not seen her husband for some hours. The maid?
Ah, but the maid only saw a man ‘coming towards the study.’ She
did not see his face! And Lowen—where was he all this time? Why,
he was at the station, or on his way to it! He had been for a walk,
perhaps, and was returning to catch his train. He never went near
The Cedars that evening!”

“But the ring?” I cried. “Billy Kellett’s story?”

“Ah, that is the most brilliant part of the whole affair! Billy
Kellett’s story is true in every detail. He did see a man throw
a ring over the hedge! He did see a man who he thought was Lowen!
But the man was Mr. Davenheim—disguised as himself! He had only
to put on his own clothes, which he had previously hidden in the
boathouse, and he was Mr. Davenheim once more! Then he walked to
the village, posted his letters, and—vanished! And where did he
vanish to? Why, to the one place where no one would ever dream of
looking for him! To a place where he would be under the eye of
the police—where his every movement would be known—where he would
have no money, and would be forced to lead a life of hardship!
In short, my friends, Mr. Davenheim is at this moment in gaol—as
Billy Kellett!”

“Billy Kellett!” Japp and I cried out together.

“Precisely! Don’t you see? He had been preparing for months. He
had grown his hair and beard to the required length. He had
distributed his clothes in various places. He had even ‘done time’
the previous autumn, in order to be known to the police! As Billy
Kellett, he was a known criminal. He had only to ‘lift’ a watch,
be arrested, and his identity was fixed! When the time came for
his ‘disappearance,’ he had only to ‘reappear’ as Billy Kellett!
The clothes he was wearing as Davenheim he left in the lake—all
but the ring, which he threw over the hedge in the sight of the
real Billy Kellett, whom he had previously ‘squared’ to be in that
particular spot at that particular time! Thus he provided himself
with an alibi, and at the same time implicated his enemy, Lowen!
A masterly plan, my friends—masterly!”

“But Mrs. Davenheim?” I asked. “Did she know?”

“No. But she was a ‘nonentity’—as Japp said. And they had occupied
separate rooms for some time! It was easy to deceive her.”

“And the lime kiln?”

“A ‘plant’—to lead the police to think he had been murdered!”

Japp rose. “Well,” he said, “I must be off. I’ve a lot to do. You’ve
won your fiver, Monsieur Poirot! I’ll send it to you to-night.”

“_Merci, mon ami_,” said Poirot, smiling. “It will go towards the
expenses of my next case. A very pretty little problem—very
pretty indeed!”

He turned to me as the door closed behind the detective.

“You see, Hastings? The little grey cells! One must always rely
on the little grey cells!”

He took up his cup of chocolate, and sipped it with every
appearance of enjoyment.

“A very good lunch!” he murmured. “And a very interesting case!
Now, let us see if we cannot find a more—symmetrical—egg!”

“Well, I should have many ideas,” I answered. “The most obvious
was that he went to Buenos Ayres—but as his photograph and
description have been sent there by cable, that’s impossible.”

Poirot shook his head. “Quite impossible, as you say. My friend
Miller’s lime kiln? No. It is too messy for a gentleman who is
evidently so—methodical. Then why did he take with him no clothes
to change into? No man of his position would think of going out
to travel without even a clean collar. No, the answer is simple.
He must have had a change of clothes—at his destination. Where
was that destination?”

“Not London—not any of the big towns,” I suggested.

“No, no, _mon ami_, that would be too much of a risk. He would be
recognized. He would go somewhere where his presence would cause
no surprise. Some small place where he was known, but where he
would be least expected.”

“But that’s a contradiction in terms!” I cried.

“Not at all. Think. Where is a man best hidden? Why, in a crowd.
Where can he be sure of his features being familiar but his identity
unsuspected? Where but in his own town? But that is too dangerous.
Where then? In a place where he has been before—where his appearance
is known, but under another name.”

“But he has only been away once lately—to South America.”

“Precisely. And what did he do there?”

“He was there for three months.”

“Exactly. And during that time he was—where? He was at the Buenos
Ayres branch of his own bank. He was well known there. But his
beard and his hair—they were different then?”

“How do you know that?”

“Because he has been growing them for the last two years. Ever
since he first planned this little—_coup de théâtre_. He knew that
the time would come when he would need a new identity. And what
better than that of a man who had already been seen and accepted
as someone else?”

“But who?” Japp and I cried together.

“Think, my friends, think! Who is the person who has appeared on
the scene since Saturday—whose description tallies with that of
Mr. Davenheim, allowing for the difference of a beard and a wig?
Who is the man who was in the neighbourhood of Chingside on Saturday
evening—who was seen by Lowen—who even spoke to him?”

A light broke in upon me. “Billy Kellett!” I cried.
