“_Précisément_,” said Poirot. “Billy Kellett! Or, to give him his
real name—Mr. Davenheim!”

“But Kellett is in prison!” Japp exclaimed.

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “Where could he be safer? Who would look
for a missing millionaire in a common lock-up? He had his plan
ready. He would ‘disappear’—leaving evidence to incriminate Lowen.
Then, as Billy Kellett, he would be arrested for some small
offence—the very one he had already ‘done time’ for in the autumn.
His identity as Kellett was already established. He had only to
wait until the affair had blown over, and then, as Billy Kellett,
he would be free to enjoy his ill-gotten gains.”

“But the ring?” I asked. “Why did he throw away the ring?”

“A very clever touch, that. He knew it would be found—and he knew
that, if he were arrested as Kellett, the ring would be found on
him. By throwing it away, and then ‘confessing’ to finding it, he
made his story as Kellett more plausible, and at the same time
linked Lowen even more closely with the crime. He is a man of
method, this Monsieur Davenheim!”

“But what about the clothes in the lake?” Japp asked.

“Ah, that was a little mistake. He had to get rid of his own
clothes, and he thought the lake was the best place. But he forgot
one thing—that clothes will float! It was the one weak link in
an otherwise perfect chain.”

“And the bedroom?” I asked. “Why was that so important?”

“Because, _mon ami_, a man who is growing a beard and a wig must
have some place where he can work in private. If he and his wife
shared a room, she would surely have noticed something. But with
a room of his own, he was safe. He could spend hours, if necessary,
perfecting his ‘Billy Kellett’ disguise.”

“Well,” said Japp, rising, “I must be off. I’ve got a little
business to attend to at Bow Street. I think Billy Kellett will be
surprised to see me!”

He turned to Poirot. “You’ve won your bet, Monsieur Poirot. I’ll
send you that fiver to-day. And I’ll admit it—you’re a marvel!”

As the door closed behind him, Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“You see, Hastings? The little grey cells! They never fail! And
now, if you will be so good as to hand me that silk handkerchief,
I will just give a little polish to this teapot. It is not quite
as bright as it should be.”

“Well,” I said, “I’m rather inclined to think I’d not do a bolt at
all. I’d stay in London—in the heart of things, travel by tubes
and buses; ten to one I’d never be recognized. There’s safety in
a crowd.”

Poirot turned inquiringly to Japp.

“I’m for a quiet little village in the country, myself,” said the
detective. “What do you say, Monsieur Poirot?”

“I? No! I should have preferred something more original—something
to ensure my absolute safety. For I should not have the confidence
of you two. I should always expect some one to find me out. And
I should ask myself, ‘Where is the one place in the world where
a man is absolutely safe from the police?’”

“And the answer?”

“A prison!”

Japp stared at him. “A prison? What do you mean?”

“The little grey cells, they have worked! For three days, I have
puzzled—what can be the reason for the hair, the beard, the bushy
eyebrows? To change one’s appearance? _Mais non_—it is too
dangerous. One is always found out. But if the hair, the beard,
and the eyebrows were all _false_? If they were a disguise which
this man has worn for years—for weeks at a time, possibly? Why?
Because he has a double life! Because he is known to the police
under another name! He is Billy Kellett!”

Japp gasped. “Billy Kellett! The man who pawned the ring!”

“_Précisément_. Let us follow his movements. On Saturday afternoon,
Billy Kellett—a man with no hair, no beard, no bushy eyebrows—is
sitting in a ditch. He sees a ‘city toff’ coming along. The ‘toff’
throws something over the hedge. Billy Kellett—who is also the
‘toff’—finds it. He goes to town, and tries to pawn the ring at
five different places. He makes himself as conspicuous as
possible—and finally he gets run in for assaulting the police!
For the next few days he is in safety! No one will dream of
looking for the great financier, Mr. Davenheim, in a police-court
cell!”

“But how did he get rid of his disguise?” I cried.

“The boathouse!” said Poirot. “He went there, changed his clothes,
and threw them into the lake. Then he emerged as Billy Kellett,
the human derelict. All he had to do was to make sure that his
real self, Mr. Davenheim, was seen to leave the house. He did that
by walking down the drive in full view of any one who might be
looking. Then he slipped back through the rose-garden—it was he
whom the gardener saw—to the boathouse. There he changed, and
as Billy Kellett he walked to the village. The ring he threw over
the hedge, and then ‘discovered’ it. It was a masterly stroke!”

“But why the separate bedrooms?” asked Japp.

“Because he must have some place where he could be alone to assume
his disguise—and to resume his own appearance. If he and his wife
shared a room, he would have no opportunity of doing so. It was
that which gave me the final clue.”

“And the lime-kiln?” I asked.

“A ‘blind’—to make the police think he had been murdered!”

Japp rose. “Well, I must be off! I’ll go and have a look at our
friend Billy Kellett! I expect he’ll be surprised to see me! You’ve
won your fiver, Monsieur Poirot!”

“_Merci, mon ami_,” said Poirot. “By the way, did you notice
the name of the junior partner?”

“Salmon?”

“Exactly. Salmon and Davenheim! I have always a little weakness
for the fish—but the two together—it was too much!”

“I don’t see it!” said Japp.

“_Mon Dieu!_” cried Poirot. “Do you not see that if one partner
is a Salmon, the other must be—a ‘_poisson_’—a fish? And a
Davenheim—is he not a ‘_daven-poisson_’—a ‘_demi-poisson_’—a
half-fish? It is a sign, I tell you!”

Japp went out, shaking his head.

“The little grey cells!” murmured Poirot. “They have not failed
me!”

“I should have thought a quiet country village would be the safest.”

“Neither of you is right,” said Poirot. “He did something much
more daring. He went—to _prison_! And it was the safest place in
England!”

“The devil he did!” Japp cried. “But how? He must have committed
a crime, then.”

“Exactly. And the crime was to hand!”

I felt a sudden illumination. “Billy Kellett!” I cried.

“_Précisément_,” Poirot said. “He had no intention of doing three
months’ hard labour, but he had to have a safe hiding-place until
the hunt was over. In the role of the human derelict, he was
absolutely safe. No one would ever think of looking for the
millionaire financier in the cell of a common thief!”

“But what of his wife?” I asked. “She would have known him.”

“Ah,” said Poirot. “That is where the separate bedrooms came in.
It was not her husband she saw—not the man she knew! He had
carefully prepared for his disappearance by a change of appearance.
He had shaved his beard and moustache, and had his hair cropped
to the roots! He had also, no doubt, practised a different walk
and voice. He was careful, you see, to make his disappearance as
striking as possible, so that no one would dream of looking for
him in his new guise. He even went so far as to throw his own clothes
into the lake, and the ring—ah, the ring! That was the master-stroke!
By throwing it where it was certain to be found, he ensured that
the police would believe him murdered—and who would look for a
dead man in a prison cell?”

“But how could he be Billy Kellett?” Japp asked. “Kellett was
known to the police.”

“Yes, but not, I think, to the _Chingside_ police. He would have
taken care to choose a name that was known, but a man who was
not—at least, not in that particular district. And as for his
appearance—well, a man with a week’s growth of beard, and his hair
cropped, looks very different from a man with a wavy mane and a
pointed beard! The maid who saw Lowen—or rather, the man she _thought_
was Lowen—was the only person who saw him after he had ‘disappeared.’
And it was not Lowen she saw, but her master, in his new character.”

“But Lowen?” I asked. “What of him?”

“_Mon ami_,” Poirot said, “Lowen was the ‘stalking-horse.’ Davenheim
knew that Lowen had a grudge against him, and he used that fact
to throw suspicion on him. He probably even arranged the appointment
for that very purpose. He knew that Lowen would be seen entering
and leaving the house, and that, with the evidence of the rifled
safe, he would be the first person to be suspected.”

“And the ring?” Japp asked.

“The ring,” Poirot said, “was the final touch. By throwing it where
it was certain to be found, and where it would be associated with
Lowen, he made doubly sure that the police would be put on the
wrong scent.”

“But Billy Kellett?” I persisted. “What has become of him?”

“Billy Kellett,” Poirot said, “is at this moment serving his
sentence in—I think you said Bow Street, Japp? He will be very
surprised when you go to fetch him, and tell him that he is really
Mr. Davenheim, the famous financier!”

Japp rose, and reached for his hat. “Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he
said, “you’ve won your fiver. I’ll go and see about it at once.
Miller will have a fit when he hears this!”

“Wait a moment, Japp,” I said. “There’s one thing I don’t
understand. If Davenheim was Billy Kellett, who was the man Kellett
saw—the ‘dark-complexioned gent’ who threw the ring over the hedge?”

Poirot smiled. “There was no such man, Hastings. That was part of
Davenheim’s story—the story he told as Billy Kellett. He wanted to
make sure that the ring was found, and that it was associated with
Lowen. So he invented the ‘dark-complexioned gent’ to account for
its presence.”

“But the maid?” I asked. “She saw Lowen.”

“She saw a man she _thought_ was Lowen,” Poirot corrected me. “In
the gathering dusk, a man with a big moustache—it would be easy to
mistake one for the other, especially if one were already expecting
to see him.”

“It’s amazing!” Japp said. “Simply amazing! I’ll be off now, and
get the handcuffs ready for Mr. Davenheim—alias Billy Kellett!”

And with a nod to us both, he hurried from the room.

Poirot turned to me with a smile. “Well, Hastings,” he said, “what
do you think of my ‘little grey cells’ now?”

“They’re wonderful, Poirot,” I said. “Simply wonderful!”

“_N’est-ce pas?_” he said, as he reached for another piece of
toast. “And now, if you have finished your breakfast, perhaps you
will be so good as to hand me the _Daily Megaphone_. I wish to see
if there is any further news of this most interesting case.”

I handed him the paper, and as he began to read, I couldn't help
thinking that, for all his eccentricities, Hercule Poirot was
indeed the greatest detective in the world.

“Well, I think I’d find some out-of-the-way little place, where
one wouldn’t be likely to be known.”

“_Très bien!_ But let us see! What was the greatest difficulty our
friend Davenheim had to contend with? His personal appearance, of
course! His height, his long wavy hair, his moustache and beard—all
those would be fatal. How could he disguise them? Shave? Yes—but
the hair would remain. No, his beard and moustache were his most
noticeable features. They must go—every hair of them. But, even
then, his face would be known to many, and his height—five feet
ten—is a very common one. He would still be in danger. So he
must find some place where he would be _safe_ from recognition.
Where—where—could a well-known man be safe from being recognized
as himself?”

“He might go to the colonies,” I suggested.

“No, no! Think!”

“The lime kiln?” suggested Japp.

Poirot shuddered. “No, no! Think again! Where is a man most
effectively concealed?”

We both shook our heads.

“In _prison_!”

“In prison?” we both cried.

“_Mais oui!_ What more simple? He commits some small crime—a crime
which will not lead to more than a few months’ imprisonment—and
he is _safe_! No one would dream of looking for the great financier
there!”

“But how?”

“Think of the man Billy Kellett. He is an old hand. He is known
to the police. On Saturday evening he is arrested for being drunk
and assaulting the police. He is given three months’ hard labour.
Is it not so, Japp?”

“Yes, but what has that to do with Davenheim?”

“Everything! Billy Kellett _is_ Davenheim!”

“Davenheim!” Japp’s voice was a crescendo of astonishment. “But
Davenheim’s a man of fifty, with a beard and moustache and long
wavy hair!”

“Exactly! And Billy Kellett is a man of about the same age, but
with his hair cropped short and his face clean-shaven!”

“But the difference in their appearance!”

“Is it so great? Think! You have only seen Davenheim’s photograph.
In that he has a beard and moustache and long hair. Take those
away, and what have you? A man of fifty, of middle height, with
dark eyes and bushy eyebrows. Those were the features Poirot
noted. The rest were—as you say in England—window-dressing!”

“But the ring!” I cried. “The ring he pawned!”

“Precisely! He had to have some way of accounting for that ring.
So he tells a cock-and-bull story about seeing a man throw it over
a hedge. He knew the police would not believe it—they would think
he had stolen it. That was what he wanted! He wanted to be arrested
and sent to prison under a name that was not his own!”

“It’s incredible!” gasped Japp. “And yet—”

“And yet it is true! Why did he and his wife occupy separate rooms?
Because for the last few months he has been gradually shaving
himself—first a little of his beard, then his moustache, then his
hair—until his wife would no longer have recognized him. He was
preparing for his ‘disappearance.’ The clothes found in the lake
were his own—the clothes he had been wearing that day. He changed
them for the rags of Billy Kellett which he had no doubt hidden
in the boathouse some time previously. Then he walked to the
village, got drunk, and was arrested—as he had intended!”

“But Lowen?” I asked. “What about him?”

“Ah, _ce pauvre_ Lowen! He was the ‘scapegoat.’ Davenheim had a
grudge against him, and he saw a way of paying it off. He knew
Lowen was coming that evening; he knew he would be alone in the
study. What more simple than to leave the safe open and the tools
handy? He knew the police would jump to the conclusion that Lowen
was the thief!”

“And the maid?”

“She was a clever girl—she saw what she was meant to see! Davenheim
had no doubt tipped her well to ‘see’ Lowen in the rose-garden!”

Japp rose. “Well, Monsieur Poirot, you’ve won your fiver! I’ll go
straight to Bow Street and have ‘Billy Kellett’ identified. If
you’re right—and I’ve a feeling you are—it’s the cleverest thing
I’ve ever heard of!”

Poirot smiled. “It was a pretty little problem,” he said. “But,
after all, it was only a matter of using the little grey cells!”

“I’m with you there,” said the detective. “He wouldn’t go abroad,
too risky. He’d hide in a back-street of some big town—Birmingham,
Leeds, Liverpool, any of ’em—the bigger the better. He’d change
his name, shave off his beard and moustache, and lead a quiet
life.”

“You are both wrong,” Poirot said. “Neither of you has put himself
in the place of this man. He has been making his plans for months—nay,
years. He has been living a double life. For months he has had his
hiding-place ready. Think! He had been to South America, had he
not?”

“Yes.”

“And when he came back, what happened? He—and his wife—occupied
separate rooms! Why? Because he needed to be able to leave his
house at night—unobserved—and to return as he had come. For months
he has been leading this double life—as two separate and distinct
personalities! He must be some one whose absence from his usual
haunts would not be noticed. And he must have a reason for his
disappearance from Chingside.”

“But where is he?” cried Japp.

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, “I am afraid that you will never find
him. He has vanished!”

“Do you mean he’s dead?”

“Not at all! He has merely—ceased to exist! He has become another
person!”

“But who? Where?” Japp was getting more and more exasperated.

“_Ecoutez, mon ami_. This Billy Kellett, who is in prison? You
told me he was at Entfield races on Saturday. You told me he was
in prison—did three months last autumn? Where was Mr. Davenheim
last autumn? In South America! It was then that the double life
began. When Mr. Davenheim was in South America, Billy Kellett was
in London—or in prison! When Billy Kellett was in prison, Mr.
Davenheim was at Chingside!”

“You mean,” I cried, “that Billy Kellett _is_ Mr. Davenheim?”

“_Précisément!_”

“But the description?” said Japp. “Billy Kellett is a thin,
undersized man, with a clean-shaven face and short, dark hair.
Davenheim is a big, powerful man, with a beard and moustache and
long, wavy hair.”

“Exactly! Shave off the beard and moustache, cut the hair short,
and what have you? A different man! As for being ‘big and powerful,’
Davenheim was only ‘big and powerful’ in his clothes! Those clothes
you found in the lake! He had them padded! When he took them off
and put on the rags of Billy Kellett, he was the thin, undersized
creature he really was!”

“But the ring?” I asked. “How do you explain the ring?”

“That was the most ingenious part of the whole thing! He knew that
Lowen was coming to see him. He knew that Lowen was his enemy. He
wanted to fix the guilt of his disappearance on Lowen! So he
waited until he saw Lowen coming towards the study, then he stepped
out of the window, and as he passed the road, he threw the ring
over the hedge, where he—as Billy Kellett—could ‘find’ it later!
He had it all beautifully planned. He would be arrested as Billy
Kellett for some small offence, and so would be safely ‘hidden’
in prison while the search for Mr. Davenheim was at its height!
When he came out of prison, he would have his fortune in jewels
waiting for him, and could disappear for ever!”

“But how did you know?” Japp asked, his face a study in amazement.

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, “it was the only possible solution.
When I heard that he and his wife occupied separate rooms, I knew
that he must have been leading a double life. And when I heard the
description of Billy Kellett, and the story of the ring, the whole
thing was clear to me. It was the only way in which he could
disappear so completely and yet be so close at hand!”

Japp drew a long breath. “Well, I’m damned!” he said. “I’ll go and
see Miller at once. He’ll have a fit!”

As the door closed behind him, Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“You see, Hastings? The little grey cells! They never fail!”

He picked up a large, fat, juicy-looking pear, and began to peel
it with the same meticulous care he had bestowed on the egg-shells.

“A very pretty little problem,” he murmured. “Very pretty indeed!”

“I think he must have been a bit of a sportsman—and he’s off to
some little country village where the last thing they’d suspect
is—a millionaire from the City!”

Poirot smiled. “_Eh bien_, you have both a certain sense of the
dramatic! But you are not simple enough, neither of you. Is there
no better hiding-place than a crowd—or a village? What of—a
prison? Ah, _mon Dieu!_ A prison—that is the ideal spot for a
disappearance! No one is ever looked for in a prison!”

“A prison?” I gasped. “What do you mean?”

“Mr. Davenheim—as Billy Kellett—has been in prison since Saturday!”

“Billy Kellett!” Japp’s jaw dropped.

“Certainly! Why did I ask you if they occupied separate rooms?
Because it was a physical impossibility for Mrs. Davenheim not
to have known if her husband’s appearance had undergone a
transformation. And why should he have gone last autumn to Buenos
Ayres—where the sun is so much stronger than in England? To
gradually get his face and neck and hands into a state of deep
tannage, which would enable him to dispense with any further
make-up for his skin. Why did he wear his hair so long, and his
moustache and beard so full? Why, so that he could have them all
shaved off, and be completely unrecognizable! Then there were those
busy eyebrows of his. Do you know what happens if you shave off
half your eyebrows?”

“I can’t say I do,” said Japp.

“They grow again very much thicker and darker. It is an old trick.
Then for the finishing touch, he must be able to account for his
presence on the road on Saturday afternoon, and provide a witness
who can testify to his seeing—Lowen! He is lucky enough to find
Kellett’s ring—which he had already dropped over the hedge—and
to be able to tell his little story to the police! A stroke of
genius, that!”

“But Mrs. Davenheim?” I cried. “She must have known!”

“Ah, but did she? Remember that she is described as ‘pleasant,
unintelligent, a nonentity.’ And that she and her husband have
occupied separate rooms since last winter. Her husband, with his
long hair and beard and bushy eyebrows, was a very different
looking person from the clean-shaven, tanned individual who
appeared before the world as Billy Kellett. And if, for a few
months, he chose to live a somewhat secluded life, and see as
little of his wife as possible, it would be easy enough to carry
out the deception. Besides, he had his trip to Buenos Ayres to
account for any change in his appearance.”

“But the ring?” Japp persisted. “How did he get hold of that?”

“He did not ‘get hold’ of it—he had it all the time! He just
dropped it over the hedge—and then, as Billy Kellett, he
‘found’ it! A very simple and effective way of bringing Lowen
into the business.”

“And the clothes?”

“He had them on under his other ones. It would be a matter of
moments to slip them off and hide them in the lake. Then he was
ready to play his part as the human derelict, Billy Kellett!”

“By Jove!” said Japp. “It’s a big thing, if it’s true! I’ll go
and have another look at our friend Billy.”

“Do!” said Poirot. “And just see if he’s got any little trick of
twisting his ring round on his finger. That was a habit of Mr.
Davenheim’s, I believe.”

“I will,” said Japp, and hurried away.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as the door closed behind him, “you’ve
done it again! I must say, I never should have thought of a
prison as a hiding-place.”

“It is the one place where no one ever looks for a missing man,”
said Poirot. “And for a man who wants to disappear, it is ideal.”

He was silent for a moment, and then he added, with a little
smile:

“But I think I shall have to find another bank for my small
savings, Hastings! The bank of Davenheim and Salmon is, I fear, no
longer a safe place for them!”

“I don’t agree. Get clear away at once—that’s the only chance. I
would have had plenty of time to prepare things beforehand. I’d
have a yacht waiting, with steam up, and I’d be off to one of the
most out-of-the-way corners of the world before the hue and cry
began!”

We both looked at Poirot. “What do _you_ say, monsieur?”

For a moment he remained silent. Then a very curious smile flitted
across his face.

“My friends, if _I_ were hiding from the police, do you know
_where_ I should hide? _In a prison!_”

“_What?_”

“You are seeking Monsieur Davenheim in order to put him in prison,
so you never dream of looking to see if he may not be already
there!”

“What do you mean?”

“_Eh bien!_ Billy Kellett, who was arrested on Saturday night
in London, is Mr. Davenheim! It is true that he was formerly a
successful financier, but now he is what you call a human derelict
in a ditch—for a time! He has just the same dark complexion, just
the same dark eyes, just the same wavy hair, and his moustache is
now gone. You will say he had a beard, also. True, and it was a
most excellent one, too, for it was fake! He had to wear it to hide
the fact that he was already known to the police—as Billy Kellett!
The face of a man who is clean-shaven is not the same as the face
of a man with a beard, as any one can tell you! And his clothes?
He had a spare suit of ‘Kellett’s’ clothes concealed in the
boathouse. When he left the house on Saturday, he went to the
boathouse, took off his own clothes, put on the others, and walked
to the station, where he took the train to London as Billy Kellett.
He had no time to lose, and he had to be careful that he was seen
at the station as a different person, so he had to be quick. He
had already thrown his ring over the hedge for himself to ‘find’
later, when he would be the human derelict in the ditch! The ring
was his ‘identification’ for himself when he was arrested! It was
a stroke of genius!”

“Good Lord!” gasped Japp. “You mean that he was actually the man
who pawned his own ring?”

“Exactly! He knew that his own ring was too well known to be
anything but a clue to his whereabouts if he was to be found. But
he did not want to lose it, for it was worth a great deal. So he
‘found’ it, and pawned it, and then got himself arrested for
assaulting a policeman! No one would ever think of looking for
Mr. Davenheim in a prison cell—especially as Billy Kellett!”

“But why did he want to be arrested?” I asked.

“Because it was the safest place in the world for him! No one
would ever look for him there, and he would be provided with food
and shelter until the hue and cry had died down. Then he would
have come out, and gone to his hiding-place with his ‘jewels’ and
his money. It was a most ingenious plan!”

“But how did you know?” Japp asked, his eyes wide with astonishment.

“_Mon ami_, there were several things. First, the clothes in the
lake. Why were they there? If a man is murdered, his clothes are
not usually taken off and thrown into a lake! If he is a suicide,
he does not take off his clothes before he jumps in! So they must
have been put there for a reason. And what could that reason be,
except to make people think he was dead? But if he were dead, why
were the clothes there? It was a contradiction! Then there was
the ring. Why did the man who ‘found’ it pawn it so openly? Unless
he _wanted_ to be caught! And why did he want to be caught?
Because he wanted to be in prison! It was the only explanation!”

“And the trip to Buenos Ayres?” I asked.

“Ah, that was where he ‘disappeared’ for the first time! He went
there as Billy Kellett, and stayed there for several months, so
that he would be known to the police there as a ‘human derelict’!
It was his ‘rehearsal’ for the real thing! And when he came back,
he had to wear a beard to hide the fact that he was Billy Kellett!
That is why he had a beard!”

“And the separate bedrooms?” Japp asked.

“That was so that his wife would not find out that his beard was
a fake! He could not have worn it in bed, you see! So he had to
have a separate room!”

Japp shook his head in admiration. “Monsieur Poirot, you are a
marvel! I’ll go and see about it at once!”

And he hurried out of the room.

Poirot turned to me with a smile. “You see, Hastings, it is the
little grey cells that count! The senses mislead—one must seek the
truth within!”

“You’ve won your bet, Poirot,” I said. “And I must say, it was a
most remarkable piece of work!”

“_Merci, mon ami_. And now, if you will excuse me, I must go and
see if I can find a dozen eggs of the same size for to-morrow’s
breakfast! It is really most important!”

And with a little bow, he left the room.

“The man called Billy Kellett, who pawned the ring and got run in,
_is_ Monsieur Davenheim!”

Japp jumped to his feet. “But, man, he’s not a bit like him! Look
at the description! Look at the photograph!”

Poirot waved his hand at me. “Hastings, be so kind as to read to
Inspector Japp the description I made out to myself of Monsieur
Davenheim.”

I turned to my notebook. “‘Wears his hair rather long and wavy,
full moustache and pointed beard, bushy eyebrows. Eyes dark. Hair
and beard turning grey.’”

Poirot nodded. “Exactly. Now, what does a man do who wants to
disguise himself? He _adds_ things—a wig, a false beard, a pair of
spectacles. But Monsieur Davenheim _took things away_! He shaved
his beard and moustache, he had his hair cropped close. And his
eyebrows—ah, there is the touch of the artist! He did not shave
them—that is always a mistake; it gives a curiously unnatural
appearance to the face. He merely _thinned_ them—a very delicate
operation. He could not, of course, change the colour of his eyes,
but for a man with dark eyes, a very few months in a South American
sun will produce a very pretty ‘dark complexion’!”

“But how did he know he’d be arrested?” I asked.

“He didn’t know! But he wanted to be. He could have just ‘disappeared’
altogether, but that is difficult. He would have to take care
never to be seen, never to be recognized. Now, in a police cell,
he would be ‘Billy Kellett,’ a man with a ‘past,’ a man who would
be easily identified. He takes the ring, he goes to pawn it in
London, he sees Lowen and throws the ring over the hedge to
implicate him. Then he gets ‘gloriously drunk,’ and is ‘run in.’
The police will be looking for Monsieur Davenheim—they will never
dream of looking for him in the person of Billy Kellett, who is
safely under lock and key!”

Japp was already half-way to the door. “By Jove! I believe you’re
right!” he cried. “I’ll be off to Bow Street this minute!”

He dashed out.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, when we were once more alone, “it’s
extraordinary—perfectly extraordinary! But what about the clothes
in the lake?”

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, “if he was going to be ‘Billy Kellett,’
he had to have a suit of Billy Kellett’s clothes. He could not
very well walk into the police station in his own immaculate
garments, could he?”

“And the maid?”

“Ah, that was a stroke of luck for him! He’d probably intended to
implicate Lowen, and the maid’s evidence just clinched the matter.”

“And why did you want to know if he and his wife occupied the same
bedroom?”

“Because, _mon cher Hastings_, if they had, it would have been
impossible for him to spend his nights in the rose-garden, gradually
shaving his beard and moustache, and generally transforming
himself into ‘Billy Kellett’!”

“And now,” said Poirot, looking at his watch, “I think we might
go for a little walk. It is a beautiful morning, and the air will
be most refreshing after our labours!”

I rose and followed him.

“I suppose,” I said, as we walked along, “that Japp will win his
fiver after all?”

Poirot smiled. “I do not think so. You see, I have already given
him the name of the man—and it is not ‘Davenheim’!”

“Then who _is_ it?”

“It is Billy Kellett, of course!”

And Poirot chuckled to himself as we turned into the park.

“Where did Monsieur Davenheim go on Saturday last? Why, he went
to London! What did he do there? He pawned his own ring—he, the
great financier! He was _so_ clumsy about it that he succeeded at
only the fifth attempt! Then he gets gloriously drunk and assaults
a policeman, and is run in for three months! No one will ever
recognize him, for he has no beard or moustache, and his hair is
cropped close. He is Billy Kellett, who did three months last
autumn for lifting an old gentleman’s watch!”

“Good Lord!” I cried. “The man with whom Davenheim spent last
autumn in Buenos Ayres!”

“Precisely. He must have found out that his features were somewhat
similar to those of his victim. He would have known that once he
was in prison no one would ever suspect him. He could rely on his
wife’s not identifying him, for they lived in separate rooms—and
he had probably not even seen her for months. It was a masterpiece
of ingenuity!”

“But how did you find out?” gasped Japp.

“I didn’t. I thought. If the ring were found near the house, it
would be argued that Davenheim had dropped it. But why remove it
from the body at all? To destroy the body! Then why throw it over
a hedge into a ditch? Because you want it to be found—and found
at once! If the ring is found, then the person who found it must
have seen the man who threw it away. He gives a description—not
of Davenheim, but of Lowen! Then I asked myself: ‘Who is this
man who gives such a wonderfully accurate description of Lowen?’
He is a man who has been in prison before. He is Billy Kellett.
_Then_ I began to see. The whole thing was a plant to throw
suspicion on Lowen. But for that to be successful, Billy Kellett
must be _found_. And where would he be most likely to be found?
Why, in a police station! So I asked myself: ‘Is it possible that
Billy Kellett _is_ Davenheim?’ And then everything became clear.
The trip to Buenos Ayres, the growing of the beard and moustache,
the separate rooms—it was all part of a deep-laid plot. Even the
clothes in the lake—the final touch to make it appear a case of
murder!”

“It’s the most extraordinary thing I ever heard of,” said Japp.
“But I must be off. I’ve a lot to do!”

“One moment,” said Poirot, as the detective was at the door. “You
remember our little bet?”

Japp laughed. “I’ve lost it, monsieur. I’ll send you the fiver
this evening. You’ve earned it!”

“_Merci, mon ami_,” said Poirot, with a little bow. “It will pay
for my new—what do you call them?—spats.”

He turned to me with a twinkle in his eye.

“And now, Hastings, what do you think of my little grey cells?”

“I think they’re the most wonderful thing in the world, Poirot!”

He smiled. “_C’est vrai!_ They are—as you say—the most wonderful
thing in the world!”

I could not help but agree. For once again, Poirot had proved that
even without moving from his chair, he could solve the most
perplexing of mysteries.

“I mean this: Monsieur Davenheim goes out for a walk—it is a
half-past five. He has plenty of time to reach the station—but
he does not go there. No, he goes—where?” Poirot smiled. “He goes
to the ditch where Billy Kellett is resting! This Billy Kellett,
he is a very well-known character to the police—did three months
last autumn for lifting an old gentleman’s watch. Now, that is a
very interesting point—the last autumn. Where was Mr. Davenheim
last autumn?”

“In Buenos Ayres!” I cried.

“Exactly! But did he go to Buenos Ayres? No! He went—where? Into
some quiet corner of the country, where he could study the
appearance and the manners of Billy Kellett—the man who was in
prison for three months. It was a very clever idea! He shaves his
beard and his moustache, he cuts his hair short, he puts on old
clothes, and he becomes Billy Kellett! Then he goes to London,
pawns the ring, and gets himself arrested for being drunk and
assaulting a policeman. He is safe for a week or two—until he can
disappear as he pleases, with the money and the jewels!”

“But how did you know?” Japp gasped.

“Ah, _mon ami_, it was the telegram that settled it! Why should
Monsieur Davenheim have a separate bedroom? Because he must
re-grow his beard and his moustache! It was a very necessary
precaution, for he could not go on being Billy Kellett for ever!”

“Simply this. Monsieur Davenheim spent last autumn—where? In
Buenos Ayres! Why? To grow a beard! And also to arrange a certain
business transaction! No, no, _mon ami_! He was not in South
America! He was in—London! And he was—let us say—forming a small
but select acquaintance in the criminal world! He was getting
points from his fellow-associates!”

“But how?”

“I will tell you. Last autumn, a certain old gentleman was robbed
of his watch. A man called Billy Kellett did three months for the
theft. Now, Billy Kellett was Mr. Davenheim himself! You remember
how I asked if he and his wife occupied the same room? At that
time, you see, he was beginning to grow his beard, and he must
have some excuse for his appearance! Then, last Saturday, he
strolls out of the house, walks to the village, and there—what
does he do? He changes his clothes—which he has previously hidden
in the boathouse—and becomes Billy Kellett once more! He then
proceeds to London, where he pawns the ring—his own ring, mark
you!—to provide himself with a little pocket-money, and then he
proceeds to get himself arrested. He is now in—where did you say,
Japp?”

“Bow Street!” gasped the detective.

“_Précisément!_ To-day he will be brought before the magistrate
for his assault on the policeman. And he will be sentenced to
another term of imprisonment! What safer place for a man who is
being hunted by the police of two continents? Even his own wife
would not recognize him!”

“Good heavens!” I cried. “And Lowen?”

“Aha! _Ce pauvre Lowen!_ It was Davenheim himself who threw the
ring over the hedge. He knew Lowen would be in the study, and he
must have a victim for the burglary! He saw the man from the
ditch—himself!—and later he gives the description of the man he
saw! Is it not a masterpiece?”

Japp didn’t wait for more. He was out of the room in a flash.

“Poirot,” I said, “it’s marvelous! But how did you know?”

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, “I told you. It is the little grey
cells! The man who is a man of method—he does not ‘disappear.’
He—transfers himself! And he does it with—precision!”

He smiled at me, and then, with a sigh, began once more to polish
the teapot with his silk handkerchief.

“You tell me Madame Davenheim is not a very intelligent woman.
Nevertheless I think that if you took her to Bow Street and
confronted her with the man Billy Kellett, she would recognize him!
In spite of the fact that he has shaved his beard and moustache
and those bushy eyebrows, and has cropped his hair close. A woman
nearly always knows her husband, though the rest of the world may
be deceived!”

“Billy Kellett? But he’s known to the police!”

“Yes, that is the beauty of it! Last autumn Mr. Davenheim spent
three months in South America—or so it was said. In reality he
lived a double life. As Billy Kellett he was a criminal, known to
the police! When the time came, he had only to commit some small
offence, and disappear into the security of a prison—the last
place in the world where anyone would think of looking for a
missing millionaire! By the way, my friend, that is why he and
his wife have occupied separate rooms since last winter. He had
to practice being Billy Kellett, you see, and to grow his hair
long, and then—at the last moment—to shave it all off!”

Japp jumped up. “Heavens! I believe you’re right! I’ll take Mrs.
Davenheim to Bow Street at once.”

He hurried from the room.

Poirot turned to me. “Well, Hastings?”

“Since when? Not before last autumn, surely? It was then that he
was in prison for three months for lifting a watch! During his
visit to Buenos Ayres, Monsieur Davenheim would have many
opportunities of picking up various little accomplishments of a
disreputable nature. It was his chance to disappear, and for some
time he had been making his preparations. Then he went down to
The Cedars on Saturday, and for the last time. He gave various
directions to his gardeners, and after tea he left the house
leisurely—dressed in his usual clothes. Then he changed them—into
what? Not into a suit he was carrying with him, but into one he
had already hidden in the boathouse! Then he threw his own clothes
into the lake, and with them his ring (carefully keeping a paste
imitation with which to play his part as the human derelict!).
Then he walked to the road and sat down in a ditch to wait for
his victim, Mr. Lowen, who he knew would be arriving at any moment.”

“You mean that Lowen was his victim, not his accomplice?” Japp
inquired.

“Certainly. He had a grudge against Lowen, and he saw his chance.
As soon as Lowen came along, he threw the ring over the hedge. If
Lowen had been an honest man, he would have picked it up and
restored it. But as he had been a bit of a ‘sharp’ in his time,
Monsieur Davenheim—or rather Billy Kellett—correctly judged he’d
do nothing of the kind. Then he went on to London, got drunk,
and was promptly arrested for assaulting a policeman. He was
assured of a safe hiding-place for the next few months, while the
search for him was at its height. No one would think of looking
for the missing financier in a common jail-bird!”

“By Jove!” I cried. “And Mrs. Davenheim? Did she know?”

“_Précisément!_” cried Poirot. “A clever man, _n’est-ce pas_? He
went to South America, not for business, but to acquire the
peculiarities of a well-known criminal, Billy Kellett. He came
back, and when he was ready, he ‘disappeared.’ He had only to
shave his face, and commit some small crime which would ensure
him a short term of imprisonment, and there he was—safe! And while
every one was searching for ‘Davenheim the financier,’ no one
would think of looking for a petty thief in the cells of a police
station! The ring? He simply threw it away for some one to find,
so that the police should be sure to link him up with the crime!
As for Lowen, he was merely the ‘red herring’ he used to draw
across the trail.”

Japp sat for a moment as though petrified. Then he sprang to his
feet.

“By the Lord!” he cried. “I believe you’re right! I’ll go and get
a warrant at once.”

He rushed out of the room, and we heard him clattering down the
stairs.

“A most interesting case,” murmured Poirot, as he reached for the
marmalade. “I think I have won my five-pound note, Hastings?”

“You have, indeed. But how did you know about the separate
bedrooms?”

“Ah, _mon ami_, that was the final clue! If a man is going to play
the part of a common criminal, he must have a ‘base of operations’
where he can make his changes in private. He must be able to
remove his beard and moustache, and the rest of it, without fear
of interruption. And where could he do that so well as in his own
bedroom? If his wife had shared it with him, the game would have
been up at once.”

“And the ring?” I asked. “Why did he throw it away?”

“Because he wanted to be caught, _mon ami_! He wanted to be Billy
Kellett, and he wanted to be Billy Kellett _at that particular
time_! If he had not been caught, he would have had to commit some
other crime. The ring was his ‘passport’ to the safety of a prison
cell!”

“It was a big risk,” I remarked.

“Everything is a risk, _mon ami_! But this man Davenheim, he had
the ‘spirit of the gambler’! He played for high stakes—and he
nearly won. But he forgot one thing—the little grey cells of
Hercule Poirot!”

And Poirot, with a smile of supreme satisfaction, proceeded to
spread marmalade on his toast with his usual mathematical
precision.

“Exactly. To the police. But did any of _you_ know Billy Kellett
before Saturday? No. Then what more simple? Monsieur Davenheim
goes to Buenos Ayres last autumn, where he is not known. He
conceives the idea of ‘making away’ with himself. He goes into the
slums of London, and comes into contact with the criminal classes.
He makes himself known as a ‘fence’—a receiver of stolen goods—and
is lucky enough to get a three months’ sentence. In this way he
establishes a past and a personality for the character of Billy
Kellett. No one will dream of looking for a well-known financier
in a common pickpocket who has just ‘come out’! Then on the fatal
Saturday, he leaves his house, walks to a spot he has already
determined on, changes into the clothes of ‘Billy Kellett’ which
he has hidden there, and throws his own into the lake. Then he
posts his letter—mark that, Japp!—to provide himself with a little
loose change, he pawns his own ring. He has no doubt that he will
be arrested for ‘loitering’ or ‘lifting a watch.’ He _wanted_ to
be in prison for the next month or two, so as to give his
personality time to be forgotten.”

“But the description of Lowen!” I cried. “How did he know _that_?”

“_Eh bien!_ He had just left him in the study! He knew what he
looked like! He could describe him to a hair!”

Japp jumped to his feet. “Lord! I believe you’ve hit it! I’ll go
and get a warrant at once. But what about the money—the
jewels?”

“The jewels? They are no doubt in a safe-deposit—in the name of
Billy Kellett.”

“And you knew all this from—what?”

“From the fact that the husband and wife occupied separate rooms!
Think of it, my friend! This man decides to disappear. He must
practice his part—his voice, his walk, his every gesture. He must
be able to do so without being overheard or observed. He must hide
his changes of appearance—the shaving of his beard and moustache.
How can he do this if his wife is in the same room? It was the
one essential!”

“And the ring?” I asked. “Why did he pawn it?”

“Ah, _mon ami_, even a financier must have a little ready money!
He could not risk having any large sum of his own on him. If he
had been searched and a large amount found, it might have led to
his identity being questioned. But a few shillings from a pawnshop
is natural for a man of Kellett’s class. Also, it was a master
stroke of policy! It linked Lowen with the affair at once.”

Japp hurried away. I looked at Poirot. He was again contemplating
the symmetry of his egg-shells.

“A week’s time, I think you said, Japp? Well, there are still
three days to run. A fiver, I think?”

“I shall never hear the end of this,” I sighed.

“_Du tout_, Hastings! You were most helpful. Your list of ‘vital
points’ was—_unique_!”

He smiled at me, and I felt that, after all, I had not done so
badly. But I determined that in the future I would be more careful
how I challenged the “little grey cells” of Hercule Poirot.

“That is just why he chose the name! He knew his man, and he knew
his business. He must have been a very clever man, this Billy
Kellett. No doubt he was! For Monsieur Davenheim, as Billy Kellett,
had himself arrested and spent the last three months in prison—a
most ingenious _alibi_!”

“But why his wife?”

“Ah, she was in it from the first! She knew it was her only chance.
If her husband were caught, her own future was at stake. So she
helped him, and played her part—very well!”

“I don’t believe it!” cried Japp. “Why, that man Billy Kellett
was in prison at the time that Davenheim was in South America!”

“_Au contraire_,” said Poirot gently. “It was then that he
prepared the way! He was ‘Billy Kellett’ for those few months, and
afterwards, when he returned as ‘Mr. Davenheim’ he took care to
keep his hair and beard as they were when he was ‘Billy Kellett’—it
is a small detail, but it tells! Then, when the time came, he
became ‘Billy Kellett’ once more. It was simple, was it not?”

“But the ring?”

“Ah, that was a stroke of genius! He knew that Lowen would be
suspected. So he took the ring—the one thing that might identify
him as Mr. Davenheim—and as Billy Kellett, he pawned it, and
afterwards told his story about the man he had seen throw it over
the hedge! He knew that Lowen would be identified as that man! It
was a very clever piece of work.”

“Well, I’m—_blest_!” Japp stared at him. “But why should they
have occupied separate rooms?”

“_Mon ami_, that was the final clue! If you are a man with a beard
and moustache, and you have to shave them off, you cannot do it
in a moment! It takes time—and it must be done in secret! If you
occupy the same room as your wife, she must see you do it! If you
occupy separate rooms, you can do it at your leisure, and then,
when the time comes, you can walk out of the house as another
man!”

“Well, it’s a most extraordinary story,” said Japp, with a whistle.
“I’ll go down to Bow Street at once and see if there’s any truth
in it.”

“You will find I am right, _mon ami_,” said Poirot. “And don’t
forget our little bet!”

“Did I not tell you Davenheim was a clever man? He prepared his
alibi long beforehand. He was not in Buenos Ayres last autumn—he
was creating the character of Billy Kellett, ‘doing three months,’
so that the police should have no suspicions when the time came.
He was playing, remember, for a large fortune, as well as liberty.
It was worth while doing the thing thoroughly. Only——”

“Yes?”

“One thing he forgot—his ring! He was so much in the habit of
wearing it on his little finger that he forgot to remove it before
he ‘discovered’ it in the ditch for the benefit of the police!
Also, it was somewhat of a giveaway—to a man like myself. A common
tramp like Billy Kellett would not be very likely to possess a
valuable diamond ring. It was a slip—a very small slip, but enough
to set the little grey cells at work!”

Japp sat back and stared. “But, monsieur, if he’s already in
prison, he won’t be able to enjoy the money he’s embezzled—even
under another name!”

“_Mon cher_, he would have come out of prison in another week’s
time—the very week I have been allowed to solve the problem! And
by then the hue and cry for Mr. Davenheim would have died down.
Nobody would have thought of looking for him in the person of a
discharged prisoner. He would have gone away quietly to enjoy his
ill-gotten gains!”

Japp jumped up. “I’m off to Bow Street! We’ll see if Mrs. Davenheim
will recognize our friend Billy Kellett!”

“Take my tip, Japp,” said Poirot. “Ask her if her husband has a
small mole on his right arm, just above the elbow! If she says
‘Yes,’ then you’re all right!”

He turned to me as Japp went out.

“You see, Hastings, why I asked about the bedrooms? If a man is
about to lead a double life, he must have a room to himself—one
where he can change his appearance at will, without fear of
discovery. That was the first point that struck me.”

“And the second?”

“The South American trip! I knew at once that it was a myth. No
man who has lived in the tropics for months can possibly have the
complexion of a Londoner! And I remembered that Billy Kellett had
only been out of prison a very short time when he was ‘run in’
again on Saturday. It was all very simple—once you had the key!”

I sighed. “You’re a wonderful man, Poirot!”

“_Mais oui!_” he said complacently. “But I think I have earned
that five-pound note, eh, Hastings?”

“He made one mistake! He was not expecting the visit of Mr. Lowen,
nor did he foresee the maid’s story—which gave the police a clue.
And his ring—which he had to get rid of, because he couldn’t very
well have pawned it _afterwards_—nearly proved his ruin. For he
was seen throwing it away, and when the description of Lowen was
given, he had to give it also—to account for his knowledge of
the man! And now, Japp, if you will only do as I suggest, I think
you will have your man!”

Japp jumped to his feet. “You’re right, Monsieur Poirot! You must
be! Only one thing—why did you ask about the husband and wife
having separate rooms?”

Poirot’s eyes twinkled. “Ah, _mon ami_, it was a very simple point.
A man who is going to lead a double life, who is going to be away
for long periods—in prison or elsewhere—must be sure that his
disappearance from his own home will not be noticed too soon or
too easily. If they occupied the same room, his absence at night
might have been discovered much earlier than he intended. It was
the final link in my little chain of reasoning.”

“And the fiver?” I asked.

Poirot turned to Japp. “You will pay it, _n’est-ce pas_?”

Japp laughed. “I will—and with a good will! Miller will never
hear the end of this! And now I’m off to Bow Street. You’ll hear
from me later!”

He hurried out of the room. I looked at Poirot. He was once more
straightening the objects on the breakfast table.

“You’re a wonderful man, Poirot,” I said.

“_Pas de tout, mon ami_. It was a very simple case. But it had
its points—yes, it had its points.”

“And what about Lowen?”

“Ah, Lowen! He was merely a convenient scapegoat. Mr. Davenheim
is, as I said, a very clever man. But not quite clever enough
for Hercule Poirot!”

“He was a little _too_ thorough. He need not have pawned the ring.
But his passion for jewels was his undoing. He could not bring
himself to part with it, and yet he knew it would be found on him
at the police station if he kept it. He thought of a way out. He
would throw it away where it would be found by—himself! He could
not resist the temptation to make it an extra piece of evidence
against Lowen. It was a mistake. If he had only been content with
the clothes in the lake, it might have been more successful.”

Japp rose hurriedly. “I’m off!” he said. “If this is true, I’ll
see it through at once.”

“Wait a moment, my friend,” said Poirot. “There is something else.”

“What’s that?”

“You remember my asking whether Mr. and Mrs. Davenheim occupied
the same bedroom? Well, that was the most important point of all.”

“Why?”

“Think, my friend. If they did, then Billy Kellett must have been
a very good actor indeed to deceive his own wife! But they did not.
They had separate rooms, and for months—since last winter—they
hardly ever spoke to each other. It was easy for him to come and
go as he pleased, and she would never know.”

“I see,” said Japp. “Well, I must be going. I’ll let you know if
your tip’s a winner.”

He hurried out of the room. I turned to Poirot.

“How did you know, Poirot?” I asked. “It seems so simple now you’ve
explained it.”

“It was the beard and the hair, _mon ami_. No man disappears
totally unless he has a very good reason—and a very good disguise.
And when I heard that Billy Kellett was already known to the
police, I saw the whole thing. It was a masterpiece of planning.”

“And the ring?”

“Ah, the ring! That was the one mistake. He should have left the
ring alone. But, as I said, his passion for jewels was too strong.
It is often the little things that trip up the greatest criminals.”

He paused, a look of satisfaction on his face. “And now, Hastings,
if you have finished your breakfast, perhaps you would be so kind
as to hand me the _Times_. I wish to see how the markets are
reacting to the news of the Davenheim failure.”

“I began to have a suspicion when Japp told me how exactly Billy
Kellett had described Lowen. It was so obviously a plant! And then,
his wife’s and his own separate rooms. That was the most important
point—the one that really gave me the clue. It meant that his
wife was in the secret—that she knew he was going to disappear,
and that her grief was all a farce. He’d probably told her some
story to account for it all. And it was a very clever idea,
too—much more original than the usual ‘disappearance’ methods!”

Japp jumped up. “I’ll be off to Bow Street at once—and if you’re
right, Monsieur Poirot——”

“You owe me a fiver!” said Poirot with a chuckle.

And a few hours later Japp telephoned to say that he was right.
Billy Kellett was indeed the missing financier, Mr. Davenheim.
Mrs. Davenheim had identified him immediately. He had been safely
lodged in a cell, and the great Davenheim mystery was at an end.
I felt that Poirot had more than earned his fiver. He had shown
once more that it is the brain, and not the senses, that must be
relied upon to solve a mystery.

“Even the cleverest of us may overreach ourselves. The robbery of
the ring—he did not intend that to be traced to himself. It was
intended for the undoing of Mr. Lowen, whom he hated. It was also,
as Japp said, a clever way of accounting for the ring’s
preservation, as the lime would have had no effect upon it! It was
an unlucky stroke of fate for him that he was seen by the maid
near the window, and that the police, for once, were _too_ smart!
They arrested Billy Kellett within a few hours of the crime, before
he could get back and change into his own character. If they had
not done so, he would no doubt have managed his disappearance with
even greater skill. As it was, he was trapped in his own snare.”

Japp stood staring. “You think that Billy Kellett is Davenheim?”

“I am sure of it! It was the only possible solution. Why else
should he have had separate rooms? So that he could be away for
weeks at a time, ‘creating’ the character of Billy Kellett, without
his wife being any the wiser. He would probably tell her he was
going away on business—to Buenos Ayres, for instance! She is, as
you say, not an intellectual woman. She would believe anything.”

Japp did not wait to hear any more. He was already half-way to
the door. “I’ll get Mrs. Davenheim at once!” he shouted.

“One moment, Japp,” said Poirot. “You’ve forgotten something!”

The detective turned. “What’s that?”

“My fiver!”

Japp grinned, and reached for his pocket-book.

“You’ve won it, monsieur!” he said. “I’ll be seeing you later.”

He dashed out of the room. I remained behind, still a little
dazed.

“So Billy Kellett was Mr. Davenheim all the time!” I said. “What
a truly remarkable man!”

“_Eh bien_, afterwards he had to wear a false beard and wig, had
to _make up as himself_ again, and to sleep with a false beard is
not easy—it invites detection! He cannot risk continuing to share
the chamber of madame his wife. You found out for me that for the
last six months, or ever since his supposed return from Buenos
Ayres, he and Mrs. Davenheim occupied separate rooms. Then I was
sure! Everything fitted in. The gardener who fancied he saw his
master going round to the side of the house was quite right. He
went to the boathouse, donned his ‘tramp’ clothes, which you may
be sure had been safely hidden from the eyes of his valet, dropped
the others in the lake, and proceeded to carry out his plan by
pawning the ring in an obvious manner, and then assaulting a
policeman, getting himself safely into the haven of Bow Street,
where nobody would ever dream of looking for him!”

“It’s impossible,” murmured Japp.

“Ask Madame,” said my friend, smiling.

The next day a registered letter lay beside Poirot’s plate. He
opened it, and a five-pound note fluttered out. My friend’s brow
puckered.

“It is a pity,” he sighed. “I had hoped for five crisp one-pound notes. One note, you see, it has no fellow. It lacks the—how do you say?—the balance. But no matter. After all, Japp has paid for his lesson. And I? I have proved once more that to the ‘little grey cells’ of Hercule Poirot, even the most impenetrable stone walls of a prison are no more than a pane of glass.” He carefully folded the note and placed it in his pocket-book with mathematical precision. “And now, Hastings, if you have finished your breakfast, let us go for a walk. The air is pleasant, and I perceive that your tie is, for once, almost straight.”

“It is the bet of the good Japp,” he murmured. “A fiver, as you English say. It will just pay for that little clock I saw yesterday in Bond Street—a clock of the most exquisite symmetry, Hastings! It will be a pleasure to look upon it. As for the late Mr. Davenheim, he committed the one error of the egoist: he thought himself more intelligent than Hercule Poirot. A grave mistake, _mon ami_, a very grave mistake.” He sighed and picked up his spoon. “And now, let us commence our breakfast. This egg, at least, appears to be of a respectable and symmetrical shape.”

“It is a pity,” sighed Poirot. “The bank-note, it is not new. It
has a fold—see, Hastings—that is not central. It offends the eye.”
He smoothed it out with a fastidious finger. “But no matter. Japp
has just telephoned. It is as I said. Faced with ‘Billy Kellett’ in
the flesh, Mrs. Davenheim’s nerves gave way. She recognized her
husband instantly, despite the absence of the wavy hair and the
pointed beard. Mr. Davenheim’s ingenious plan to hide from the law
within the law’s own keeping has failed him at the last. He was a
man of method, yes, but he forgot that while one may deceive the
Inspector Millers of this world with a clever disguise, one cannot
so easily deceive the little grey cells of Hercule Poirot. And so,
the ‘missing’ banker goes from one cell to another. It is, as you
say, a grand symmetry, is it not?”

“It is the fiver of the Inspector Japp,” he murmured. “But see you,
Hastings, he has folded it with a most deplorable lack of symmetry.
One corner, it is quite crushed! It is a pity. Still, the challenge
is met, the wager is won. The little grey cells, they have not
failed us. To find a man, one does not need to run to and fro; one
has only to sit and think. Mr. Davenheim thought to hide in the one
place where no one would look for a wealthy banker—a prison cell.
A clever man, _mon ami_, but not quite clever enough to deceive
Hercule Poirot!” And with a sigh of satisfaction, he began to
smooth out the crumpled bank-note with his small, manicured hands.

“It is a pity,” sighed Poirot. “I had hoped to buy a new pair of
patent leather shoes with this—but since the bank of Davenheim and
Salmon has failed, I fear the general gloom may be quite
distressing. Still, it will pay for many eggs—provided they are of
a uniform size! You see, Hastings, the mind, it must have order.
Without order, there is no truth. And without the little grey cells,
there is only the confusion of the Inspector Millers of this world,
who look at a man and see only a tramp, whereas I look at a man and
see—the method!” He dusted a speck of fluff from his sleeve and
sighed. “A most interesting case, Hastings. But, alas, it has quite
ruined my appetite for breakfast. That last egg—it was decidedly
lopsided.”

“_Ah, sacré!_ But what shall I do with it? I have much remorse!
_Ce pauvre Japp_! Ah, an idea! We will have a little dinner, we
three! That consoles me. It was really too easy. I am ashamed. I,
who would not rob a child—_mille tonnerres! Mon ami_, what have
you, that you laugh so heartily?”
